O(mn) time and O(mn) space — space optimized to O(min(m,n)) using two rows

answer is dp[m][n] — LCS of full strings

semantic_targets: LCS is based on comparing prefixes
naive recursion has 2^(m+n) calls — dp reduces this to O(mn) via table reuse
Subsequence preserves relative order but not continuity
dp[i][j] encodes optimal solution for prefixes of length i and j
LCS recurrence has optimal substructure: LCS(i,j) = LCS(i-1,j-1)+1 if match, else max(LCS(i-1,j), LCS(i,j-1))
common_mistakes: writes recurrence but fills table in wrong direction
confuses with longest common substring — substring requires contiguity
fills table in wrong direction — top-down not bottom-up or wrong index direction
forgets base case row and column of zeros

logic_context: A binary tree is symmetric (mirror of itself) if the left subtree is a mirror of the right subtree, checked recursively by comparing corresponding nodes: left's left with right's right, and left's right with right's left.

mandatory: recursive mirror comparison
compare corresponding symmetric nodes
concept_groups: base case: both null returns true
advanced_bonus: compare outer pair (left.left vs right.right) and inner pair (left.right vs right.left)
base cases: both null = true, only one null = false, both non-null = check values
iterative solution uses queue with pairs of nodes — O(n) time O(w) space
O(n) time — every node visited once
checks both structure and values — structural symmetry alone is insufficient
not same as checking left subtree equals right subtree (which is not mirroring)

semantic_targets: Symmetry requires both structural and value match
mirror comparison means outer nodes paired with outer, inner with inner
comparison pairs: (left.left, right.right) and (left.right, right.left) — outer with outer, inner with inner
common_mistakes: Comparing only node values without structure
compares subtrees directly not mirrored — misses structural symmetry
only checks values not structure — misidentifies structurally asymmetric trees
wrong base case — does not handle case where one child is null and other is not

logic_context: Spiral matrix traversal processes the matrix layer by layer by maintaining four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and traversing edges in order (left-to-right, top-to-bottom, right-to-left, bottom-to-top), then shrinking boundaries inward.

mandatory: four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right)
traverse edges in spiral order
concept_groups: traverse bottom row right-to-left, decrement bottom
traverse left column bottom-to-top, increment left
advanced_bonus: four boundaries shrink inward after each direction traversal
must check top <= bottom and left <= right before each direction to avoid revisiting
these checks handle single row or single column matrices correctly
O(m*n) time — every element visited exactly once
O(1) space not counting output
direction order: left→right, top→bottom, right→left, bottom→top

semantic_targets: Spiral traversal processes matrix in layers
Shrinking boundaries moves to inner layers
four pointers (top, bottom, left, right) define the current unprocessed layer
loop invariant: after each full spiral iteration, top>bottom or left>right signals completion
common_mistakes: omits boundary check before reverse pass — revisits processed elements
updates boundaries in wrong order or direction
misses single remaining row/column in odd-dimension matrices

logic_context: To reverse words in a sentence while keeping word order, identify word boundaries (spaces), then reverse the characters within each word independently using two-pointer swap, preserving the positions of words in the sentence.

mandatory: identify word boundaries
reverse characters within each word only
concept_groups: detect start and end of each word
advanced_bonus: find word start, find word end (space or string end), then two-pointer reverse within
preserves spaces and word order — only characters within each word are reversed
O(n) time O(1) space — in-place character swaps
handles consecutive spaces correctly by treating each word independently
handles leading/trailing spaces by skipping non-word characters
alternative: reverse entire string then reverse each word — classic trick for reversing word order

semantic_targets: Word order in sentence remains unchanged
Only characters inside each word are reversed
word boundaries delimited by spaces — scan for space or string end
word boundary detection: scan until space or end-of-string, then reverse [word_start, current-1] in-place
common_mistakes: Not handling edge cases like leading/trailing spaces
reverses entire sentence — reverses word order not just characters within words
fails on multiple consecutive spaces — index arithmetic breaks

logic_context: Merge Sort recursively divides the array into two halves until single elements remain, then merges the sorted halves back together in sorted order, following the divide-and-conquer paradigm.

mandatory: recursively divide array into halves
merge sorted subarrays
concept_groups: base case: single element is sorted
advanced_bonus: stable sort — equal elements maintain their relative order
O(n log n) guaranteed — no worst case degradation unlike QuickSort
O(n) auxiliary space required for merging — not in-place
divide step: mid = (left + right) / 2, recurse on both halves
merge step requires O(n) temporary array to merge without overwriting
preferred for linked lists — no random access needed, O(1) merge space
external sort uses merge sort pattern for sorting data on disk

semantic_targets: Merging two sorted arrays produces sorted output
merge step is where sorted order is created — recursion only decomposes, never sorts
divide-and-conquer reduces problem size by half each level
merge sort is stable because equal elements from left subarray are placed before equal elements from right subarray
common_mistakes: Ignoring space cost of merge step
Incorrect merge logic for sorted subarrays
returns wrong pivot position after partition
no auxiliary array — in-place merge is impractical in O(n log n)
incorrect merge logic — does not handle remaining elements from either half
confuses merge sort with quick sort (pivot vs mid point)

logic_context: The equilibrium index is found by maintaining a running prefix sum on the left and calculating the suffix sum on the right, checking equality at each position during a single traversal.

mandatory: calculate total sum first
maintain left sum and right sum
concept_groups: right sum = total - left - current element
advanced_bonus: total_sum computed first, then left_sum accumulated step by step
right_sum = total_sum - left_sum - arr[i] at each position
O(n) time O(1) space — single pass after total sum calculation
handles negative numbers correctly — sums can be negative
multiple equilibrium indices may exist — return first or all based on problem
current element excluded from both sides in the comparison

semantic_targets: Left and right sums must be equal at equilibrium
Current element is excluded from both sums
left_sum grows as we iterate; right_sum derived as total minus left minus current
formula: right_sum = total_sum - left_sum - arr[i] — no need to recompute suffix sum from scratch
common_mistakes: includes current element in one or both sums — incorrect comparison
uses nested loops to recalculate prefix/suffix sums — O(n²)
does not compute total sum first — cannot derive right_sum from left_sum

logic_context: Postfix expression evaluation uses a stack where operands are pushed, and when an operator is encountered, it pops the required operands, performs the operation, and pushes the result back onto the stack.

mandatory: push operands onto stack
pop operands when operator encountered
concept_groups: maintain correct operand order (second pop is left operand)
advanced_bonus: pop second operand first, then first operand — order matters for subtraction/division
for a-b: first pop is b (right operand), second pop is a (left operand)
O(n) time and O(n) space in worst case (all operands before operator)
handles multi-character operands by reading until space delimiter
final result is the only element left on stack
stack has exactly one element at end — if more, expression is malformed

semantic_targets: Stack naturally handles postfix evaluation order
Operators work on most recent operands via LIFO
No parentheses needed in postfix notation
LIFO structure naturally models nested or sequential dependencies
operand order matters: pop second operand FIRST then first operand — stack is LIFO so last pushed is left operand
common_mistakes: Reversing operand order (confusing left and right operands)
uses stack correctly but forgets to check if stack is empty at end
pops operands in wrong order — a-b computed as b-a
applies infix evaluation logic — fails for expressions without proper precedence
does not verify stack has exactly one element at end

logic_context: Finding median from a data stream uses two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half of numbers and a min-heap for the upper half, maintaining balanced sizes so the median is always accessible at the heap roots.

mandatory: max-heap for lower half
min-heap for upper half
concept_groups: balance heap sizes (differ by at most 1)
add to appropriate heap based on value
rebalance by moving root between heaps
advanced_bonus: max-heap for lower half: root is largest of lower half
min-heap for upper half: root is smallest of upper half
invariant: max-heap root <= min-heap root always maintained
if odd count: larger heap's root is median; if even: average of both roots
rebalance by moving root between heaps when size difference exceeds 1
O(log n) per insertion, O(1) median query
adding to wrong heap first then rebalancing is a common clean implementation

semantic_targets: Median is at boundary between two halves
Balanced heaps enable constant-time median access
heap property guarantees O(log n) access to extremum
invariant: max_heap.size() == min_heap.size() OR max_heap.size() == min_heap.size()+1 — maintained after every insert
common_mistakes: Incorrect median calculation for even/odd counts
uses max-heap instead of min-heap for Kth largest
fails to pop when heap exceeds size K
uses only one heap — cannot compute median in O(1)
does not rebalance after insertion — heaps drift unequally
computes wrong median for even count — average of wrong elements

logic_context: Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting uses BFS by maintaining in-degrees for all nodes, starting with zero in-degree nodes in a queue, processing them, and reducing in-degrees of neighbors until all nodes are processed.

mandatory: calculate in-degree for each node
queue for zero in-degree nodes
concept_groups: process node and add to result
add neighbors with zero in-degree to queue
advanced_bonus: in-degree counts how many nodes must come before each node
zero in-degree nodes have no prerequisites — safe to process first
after processing a node, decrement in-degree of all its neighbors
if a neighbor's in-degree reaches zero, add to queue
if processed count < total nodes, a cycle exists — topological sort impossible
O(V + E) time and O(V) space
result order depends on queue implementation — different valid orderings possible

semantic_targets: Zero in-degree nodes have no prerequisites
Works only on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs)
in-degree zero = no unmet dependencies — node is ready to process
cycle detection is free: if processed_count < V after BFS, the remaining nodes form a cycle
common_mistakes: Not detecting cycles when nodes remain unprocessed
applies to undirected graphs — topological sort is only for DAGs
does not check if all nodes were processed — misses cycle detection
incorrect in-degree initialization — counts wrong number of incoming edges

logic_context: The diameter of a binary tree (longest path between any two nodes) is computed by recursively calculating subtree heights and tracking the maximum path that goes through each node as the sum of left and right heights.

mandatory: calculate left and right subtree heights
diameter through node = left height + right height
advanced_bonus: diameter = longest path between any two nodes — may not pass through root
at each node: path through it = left_height + right_height
global maximum must be tracked — not just returned from recursion
function returns height to parent while updating diameter as side effect
O(n) single DFS — computing height and diameter simultaneously
path is in edges: height = max(left, right) + 1; diameter through node = left_h + right_h

semantic_targets: Diameter is the longest path between any two nodes
diameter through a node is sum of heights of both subtrees
function must return height (for parent) while updating global diameter — dual-purpose return value
common_mistakes: Multiple separate traversals for height and diameter
Assuming diameter always passes through root
returns diameter not height — misses paths not through root
computes height and diameter in separate traversals — O(n²) instead of O(n)
confuses diameter with height — different quantities

logic_context: KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) algorithm improves pattern matching by preprocessing the pattern to build an LPS (Longest Proper Prefix which is also Suffix) array, which indicates how far to shift the pattern on mismatch without rechecking already matched characters.

mandatory: build LPS (failure function) array
use LPS to skip redundant comparisons
concept_groups: LPS[i] = length of longest proper prefix-suffix
on mismatch, shift using LPS values
matching phase with no backtracking in text
advanced_bonus: LPS[i] = length of longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix
LPS allows pattern to shift by more than 1 on mismatch — avoiding redundant comparisons
building LPS: two-pointer approach where i tracks current prefix end
on mismatch during LPS build: lps[i] = lps[lps[i-1]-1] fallback
O(n + m) total — O(m) preprocessing + O(n) matching
text pointer never moves backward — each character examined at most once
pattern pointer resets using LPS on mismatch, not to 0 — key efficiency

semantic_targets: Pattern preprocessing enables linear time matching
LPS array captures pattern's internal structure
LPS encodes internal structure of pattern — how much matched prefix is reusable on mismatch
hardest step: in LPS build, fallback is lps[i] = lps[lps[i-1]-1] not 0 — this is the step most candidates get wrong
common_mistakes: Restarting pattern match from beginning on mismatch
Confusing with naive brute force search
resets pattern pointer to 0 on every mismatch — degrades to O(nm) brute force
confuses LPS array construction — incorrect values corrupt the matching phase
explains LPS as 'a lookup table' — cannot describe why shifting is valid

logic_context: Moving zeroes to the end while maintaining the relative order of non-zero elements uses a two-pointer technique: one pointer tracks position for next non-zero element, the other scans the array.

mandatory: two-pointer technique
maintain relative order of non-zero elements
concept_groups: swap or overwrite non-zero elements forward
advanced_bonus: insertPos pointer starts at 0 and advances only when non-zero placed
after scan, fill arr[insertPos..n-1] with zeros
O(n) time O(1) space single pass plus fill
swap variant: swap arr[i] with arr[insertPos] when non-zero — avoids separate fill
fill variant is slightly more cache-friendly than swap on zero-heavy arrays
stable — relative order of non-zero elements preserved

semantic_targets: Non-zero elements move forward maintaining order
Zeroes accumulate at end without explicit movement
insertPos tracks where next non-zero should go — everything before it is already placed
swap variant avoids explicit zeroing: swap arr[i] with arr[insertPos] when non-zero found — zeros naturally accumulate at end
common_mistakes: Using extra space for new array
changes relative order of non-zero elements — stable partition not maintained
uses extra array — O(n) space not O(1)
forgets fill step — zeros at end not guaranteed

logic_context: The Tower of Hanoi problem is solved recursively by: (1) moving N-1 disks from source to auxiliary using destination, (2) moving the largest disk from source to destination, (3) moving N-1 disks from auxiliary to destination using source.

mandatory: recursive decomposition into subproblems
three steps: move N-1, move largest, move N-1 again
concept_groups: base case: single disk moves directly
recursive case uses all three rods
auxiliary rod changes role in recursion
advanced_bonus: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 — minimum moves is 2^n - 1
three steps: move n-1 from src to aux, move disk n from src to dst, move n-1 from aux to dst
base case: move 1 disk directly from src to dst
O(2^n) time — exponential but optimal (cannot do fewer moves)
recursion depth is exactly n — O(n) call stack space
for 64 disks: 2^64 - 1 moves — mathematically interesting

semantic_targets: Problem decomposes into identical smaller subproblems
total moves = 2^n - 1 — provably optimal because the largest disk must move exactly once and each move of it requires 2^(n-1)-1 moves for the other disks
common_mistakes: states recursive formula but forgets base case
assumes recursion is O(n) without justification
swaps auxiliary and destination roles — disks placed on wrong rods
claims O(n) moves — actual minimum is 2^n - 1

logic_context: The minimum coin change problem uses dynamic programming where dp[i] represents the minimum number of coins needed to make amount i, built by trying each coin denomination and taking the minimum.

mandatory: DP array for each amount
dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - coin] + 1) for each coin
concept_groups: optimal substructure: use solution for smaller amount
advanced_bonus: dp[0] = 0 (base), dp[i] = infinity initially for i > 0
for each coin, update dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - coin] + 1) if i >= coin
O(amount * coins) time and O(amount) space

unbounded knapsack variant — each coin usable multiple times

semantic_targets: without DP: exponential branching — each amount tries every coin denomination again
Each amount builds on solutions for smaller amounts
dp[i] = minimum coins to make amount i exactly
initialization: dp[0]=0 (zero coins needed for amount 0); dp[1..amount]=infinity (unreachable until proven otherwise)
common_mistakes: writes recurrence but fills table in wrong direction
uses greedy (largest coin first) — fails for arbitrary denominations
does not initialize dp[i] to infinity — min comparison corrupted
confuses with 0/1 knapsack — coins can be reused here

logic_context: After detecting a cycle using Floyd's algorithm (slow and fast pointers meet), the cycle's starting node is found by moving one pointer to the head and advancing both pointers one step at a time until they meet again.

mandatory: use Floyd's algorithm to detect cycle first
reset one pointer to head after meeting
concept_groups: move both pointers one step at a time
single-step movement from head and meeting point
advanced_bonus: after slow and fast meet inside cycle, move one pointer to head
advance both one step at a time — they meet at cycle start
mathematical proof: distance from head to cycle start equals distance from meeting point to cycle start
O(n) time O(1) space — uses results from detection phase
detection phase finds meeting point; phase 2 finds cycle entry
handles case where cycle starts at head

semantic_targets: Cycle starting node is found deterministically
No extra memory required beyond two pointers
Distance relationship ensures convergence at cycle start
phase 1 (detection) and phase 2 (cycle start) are two distinct steps

mathematical proof: let cycle start at distance k from head, cycle length L — meeting point is (L-k) steps before cycle start, so moving k steps from head and k steps from meeting point both reach cycle start
common_mistakes: Using hash set to store visited nodes
uses hash set for cycle start — O(n) space, misses mathematical insight
does not run phase 2 — only detects cycle existence not its start
resets both pointers to head — loses the meeting point information

logic_context: A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. It is declared using the asterisk (*) operator and provides indirect access to data.

mandatory: stores memory address of another variable
declared using asterisk (*)
advanced_bonus: pointer arithmetic: incrementing by 1 moves by sizeof(type) bytes
void* pointer can hold any address but must be cast before dereferencing
pointer to pointer (**) enables modifying a pointer from a function
NULL pointer should be checked before dereferencing
array name decays to pointer to first element in most expressions

semantic_targets: Pointers refer to memory locations not values
Pointers enable indirect access and modification
pointer stores address not value — dereference with * to access the value
common_mistakes: Confusing pointer with the value it points to
Incorrect declaration syntax (int *p vs int* p)
declares pointer without initializing — undefined behavior on dereference
confuses * in declaration (pointer type) with * in expression (dereference)

logic_context: malloc allocates a block of uninitialized memory, whereas calloc allocates memory and initializes all bytes to zero. calloc also takes two arguments (count and size) while malloc takes one (total size).

mandatory: malloc allocates uninitialized memory
calloc initializes memory to zero
concept_groups: calloc takes count and size arguments
advanced_bonus: calloc(n, size) = malloc(n*size) + memset to zero — slightly slower

realloc can resize previously allocated block
calloc zero-initialization is useful for arrays and structs

Both allocate on heap and require free()
key difference: calloc zero-initializes, malloc does not
common_mistakes: Saying both initialize memory to zero
Ignoring the difference in argument count
uses malloc'd memory without initializing — relies on uninitialized values
does not check return value for NULL — dereferences null on allocation failure

logic_context: A dangling pointer is a pointer that references memory that has already been freed or deallocated, leading to undefined behavior and potential crashes when dereferenced.

mandatory: points to freed/deallocated memory
undefined behavior when accessed
concept_groups: pointer remains but memory is freed
advanced_bonus: occurs after free(), after function returns (stack variable), after realloc()

Should set pointers to NULL after freeing

Thinking OS always protects against access
assumes freed memory is inaccessible — it may be readable until reallocated

logic_context: Big O notation describes the upper bound of an algorithm's time or space complexity in terms of how it grows relative to input size, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.

mandatory: describes growth rate with input size
upper bound of complexity
advanced_bonus: Big O is upper bound (worst case), Big Omega is lower bound (best case), Big Theta is tight bound
constant factors and lower-order terms are dropped — O(2n) = O(n)
O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2^n) < O(n!)

semantic_targets: Big O represents worst-case or upper bound
Compares algorithm scalability not exact runtime

Big O describes how runtime scales with input size, not actual runtime
common_mistakes: Treating Big O as exact runtime measurement
confuses Big O (upper bound) with average case complexity
keeps constant factors — O(3n) and O(n) are the same Big O

logic_context: The static keyword controls variable lifetime and visibility. Static local variables persist across function calls, while static global variables/functions have internal linkage restricted to the file scope.

mandatory: controls lifetime and visibility
static local variables persist across calls
concept_groups: static global limits to file scope
advanced_bonus: static local variable: persists across function calls, initialized once
static global variable: file scope only — internal linkage

static in struct member: not valid in C (only C++)

static local: lifetime = program duration, scope = function
common_mistakes: Assuming static always means global scope
conflates static local (persistence) with static global (file scope)

logic_context: A structure allocates separate memory for each member (size is sum of all members plus padding), whereas a union shares the same memory location among all members (size is the largest member).

mandatory: structure allocates separate memory for all members
union shares same memory among members
concept_groups: structure size = sum of members + padding
all members accessible simultaneously in struct
only one member valid at a time in union
advanced_bonus: struct size = sum of member sizes + padding for alignment
union size = size of largest member
only one union member valid at a time — reading wrong member is undefined behavior
union used for type punning, memory overlays, tagged unions

semantic_targets: Unions overlay members in same memory
Union saves memory when only one member needed at a time

reads a different union member than the one last written — undefined behavior

logic_context: Function pointers are variables that store the address of a function, enabling dynamic function invocation, callbacks, and runtime polymorphism in C.

mandatory: stores address of a function
enables dynamic function invocation
advanced_bonus: declaration: int (*fp)(int, int) — reads as fp is a pointer to function taking two ints returning int
enables callbacks, strategy pattern, and dispatch tables in C

incorrect declaration syntax — parentheses around *fp are mandatory

logic_context: Arrays provide O(1) random access via indexing but O(n) insertion/deletion due to shifting elements. Linked lists provide O(1) insertion/deletion at known positions but O(n) search due to sequential traversal.

mandatory: arrays have O(1) random access
linked lists have O(1) insertion/deletion at known position

semantic_targets: Data structure choice involves performance trade-offs
Arrays excel at access, lists excel at modification
trade-off: random access vs dynamic sizing and O(1) insert at pointer

logic_context: Pass by value creates a copy of the argument, so modifications inside the function don't affect the original. Pass by reference (simulated in C using pointers) passes the address, allowing the function to modify the original data.

mandatory: pass by value creates a copy
pass by reference allows modification of original

claims C has pass-by-reference natively — it does not, only pointer simulation

logic_context: A segmentation fault is a runtime error that occurs when a program attempts to access invalid memory, such as dereferencing null pointers, accessing freed memory, or going out of bounds in arrays.

mandatory: runtime error from invalid memory access
examples: null pointer, out-of-bounds, freed memory

common in C due to no bounds checking — programmer's responsibility

Blaming the OS instead of code logic

logic_context: A hash collision occurs when two different keys produce the same hash value and thus map to the same index in a hash table. This is resolved using techniques like chaining or open addressing.

map to same index/bucket

Resolution techniques maintain hash table functionality
collision inevitable when keys > buckets — resolution strategy determines performance
common_mistakes: Saying collisions mean the hash function failed

logic_context: On a 64-bit system, a pointer variable occupies 8 bytes (64 bits) of memory regardless of the data type it points to, because it stores a memory address.

mandatory: 64-bit system
8 bytes or 64 bits

assumes 4 bytes — common on 32-bit, wrong on 64-bit systems

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct factual knowledge of pointer size

logic_context: A memory leak occurs when dynamically allocated memory (using malloc/calloc) is not released using free() after use, causing that memory to remain occupied and unavailable for reuse.

mandatory: dynamically allocated memory not freed
memory remains occupied unnecessarily
concept_groups: memory no longer accessible but not released
advanced_bonus: Valgrind detects leaks by tracking all allocations and checking freeing at exit
leaks in long-running programs cause gradual memory exhaustion
set pointer to NULL after free — does not prevent leak but prevents double free
RAII pattern (common in C++) avoids leaks by tying lifetime to scope
every malloc/calloc must have a corresponding free on all code paths

semantic_targets: Leaked memory is lost until program terminates
memory leak = allocated memory no longer reachable but not freed
common_mistakes: Confusing memory leak with dangling pointer
Saying OS automatically prevents all leaks
Thinking leaks only matter in short programs
frees in success path but not error path — leak on error exit
assumes OS reclaims memory during run — it does only at process termination

evaluation_rubric.focus: Understanding cause and prevention of leaks

logic_context: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last In First Out (LIFO) principle, where elements are added and removed from the same end called the top.

mandatory: LIFO principle
linear data structure
advanced_bonus: LIFO: last pushed element is first popped
operations: push, pop, peek/top — all O(1)
implemented via array (fixed-size) or linked list (dynamic)
applications: function call stack, undo/redo, expression evaluation, DFS
stack overflow: pushing beyond capacity; underflow: popping empty stack

semantic_targets: Last element added is first removed
Used in function calls, undo operations, parsing
LIFO structure naturally models nested or sequential dependencies
common_mistakes: uses stack correctly but forgets to check if stack is empty at end
only names one application — question asks for two

logic_context: A const variable cannot be modified after initialization (enforced at compile-time), whereas a volatile variable tells the compiler that its value may change unexpectedly from external sources, preventing optimization.

mandatory: const prevents modification after initialization
volatile prevents compiler optimization
advanced_bonus: volatile prevents compiler from caching variable in register — re-reads from memory each time
const prevents modification — compiler enforces at compile time
volatile const is valid: value may change externally but not by this code (e.g., read-only hardware register)
volatile critical in embedded systems for hardware registers and ISR-shared variables
volatile does NOT guarantee atomic access — mutex still needed for multi-threading

semantic_targets: volatile prevents optimization assumptions about value
const = immutable to programmer; volatile = may change outside programmer's control
common_mistakes: claims volatile ensures thread safety — atomicity needs separate mechanisms
confuses volatile (optimization hint) with const (modification restriction)

logic_context: A full binary tree is one where every node has either zero or two children (no nodes with one child). A complete binary tree is filled level by level from left to right, with all levels completely filled except possibly the last.

mandatory: full: every node has 0 or 2 children
complete: filled level by level from left to right
concept_groups: last level may be incomplete in complete tree
advanced_bonus: full (proper/strict): every node has 0 or 2 children
complete: all levels full except last, last level filled left to right
perfect: both full and complete — all leaves at same level
complete binary tree can be efficiently stored in array: children of i at 2i+1 and 2i+2
heaps are implemented as complete binary trees in arrays

semantic_targets: Full and complete binary trees are different concepts
Full tree focuses on child count per node
Complete tree focuses on level-order filling
common_mistakes: Saying full and complete trees are the same
Confusing complete with perfect binary tree
Not understanding the filling order for complete trees
confuses full and complete — they are distinct properties
claims 'all leaves at same level' for complete — only true for perfect trees

logic_context: The free() function releases dynamically allocated memory back to the heap, making it available for reuse. It must be called on memory allocated by malloc, calloc, or realloc.

mandatory: releases dynamically allocated memory
returns memory to heap for reuse
advanced_bonus: free(NULL) is safe and does nothing — by C standard
double free is undefined behavior — corrupts allocator metadata
after free, pointer is dangling — set to NULL immediately
free does not zero memory — content may still be readable briefly
free must be called with the exact pointer returned by malloc/calloc

semantic_targets: Prevents memory leaks by releasing unused memory
Only works on heap-allocated memory, not stack
free releases ownership of the block back to the allocator — memory may be reused
common_mistakes: Saying free() deletes or destroys variables
Attempting to call free() on stack memory
Not understanding it only frees heap allocations
calls free on a pointer to middle of an allocated block — undefined behavior
double frees the same pointer — corrupts heap

logic_context: Breadth First Search (BFS) explores nodes level by level using a queue for FIFO processing, whereas Depth First Search (DFS) explores as deep as possible along each branch using a stack or recursion for LIFO processing.

mandatory: BFS uses queue and explores level by level
DFS uses stack/recursion and explores depth first
concept_groups: BFS finds shortest path in unweighted graphs
DFS useful for cycle detection and topological sort
advanced_bonus: BFS uses queue (FIFO), DFS uses stack or recursion (LIFO)
BFS finds shortest path in unweighted graphs
DFS is better for: topological sort, cycle detection, maze solving, strongly connected components
BFS space: O(w) where w is max width; DFS space: O(h) where h is depth
for deep graphs, DFS risks stack overflow — iterative DFS safer

semantic_targets: BFS and DFS differ in traversal strategy and data structure
BFS explores all neighbors before going deeper — shortest path property
common_mistakes: Saying BFS uses stack or DFS uses queue
Claiming DFS always finds shortest path
Not understanding data structure impact on traversal
claims BFS always uses less space — for wide shallow trees DFS uses less
confuses traversal order — BFS visits level by level, DFS goes deep first

evaluation_rubric.focus: Traversal strategy and data structure usage

logic_context: Preprocessor directives are instructions processed before compilation that handle tasks such as macro expansion (#define), file inclusion (#include), and conditional compilation (#if, #ifdef).

mandatory: processed before compilation
handles macro expansion and file inclusion
advanced_bonus: #define macros are textual substitution — no type checking
#include <> for system headers, #include "" for user headers
#ifdef / #ifndef for conditional compilation and header guards
#pragma is compiler-specific — not portable
macros with arguments can cause issues with operator precedence — use parentheses

semantic_targets: preprocessor runs before compiler — it never executes code, only transforms text
#define, #include, #ifdef are the three core directive categories
common_mistakes: assumes macros are type-safe — they are text substitution, no type checking
omits parentheses in macro arguments — causes operator precedence bugs

logic_context: Searching in a balanced Binary Search Tree has O(log n) time complexity because the tree height is logarithmic, allowing the search to eliminate half the remaining nodes at each step.

mandatory: O(log n) time complexity
balanced tree with logarithmic height
concept_groups: eliminates half the tree at each step
advanced_bonus: balanced BST height = O(log n) — search is O(log n)
unbalanced BST (worst case: sorted insertion) degrades to O(n)
AVL trees and red-black trees maintain balance — guarantee O(log n)
BST search: compare with root, go left if smaller, right if larger
in-order traversal of BST gives sorted output — O(n)

semantic_targets: Balanced BST ensures logarithmic search time
Search complexity depends on tree height
BST property enables elimination of half the tree at each comparison
common_mistakes: Saying time complexity is always O(n)
claims O(log n) without qualifying it is for balanced BST — skewed tree is O(n)
confuses BST search with binary search on array — different structures

logic_context: Internal linkage restricts a symbol (variable or function) to a single source file using the static keyword, while external linkage allows a symbol to be accessed across multiple files using the extern keyword or default behavior.

mandatory: internal linkage limits to single file
external linkage allows cross-file access
advanced_bonus: internal linkage: static keyword restricts symbol to current translation unit
external linkage: default for global variables and functions — accessible via extern
extern declaration says 'defined elsewhere, I'll use it'
prevents name collision across files for file-private helpers
function declared in header and defined in .c file has external linkage

semantic_targets: Linkage controls symbol visibility across files
Internal linkage prevents name conflicts between files
internal linkage = visible only within the file; external = visible across files
common_mistakes: Saying extern allocates memory (it only declares)
confuses static local variable (storage class) with static global (linkage)
uses extern without a matching definition somewhere — linker error

logic_context: An l-value (locator value) refers to an expression that designates an object with an identifiable memory location that can appear on the left side of an assignment. An r-value represents a temporary value or literal without a persistent address that typically appears on the right side.

mandatory: l-value has identifiable memory location
r-value is temporary without persistent address
concept_groups: r-value cannot be on left of assignment
advanced_bonus: l-value: has address, can appear on left of assignment (variable, array element, deref ptr)
r-value: no persistent address, cannot appear on left (literal, temp, arithmetic expression)
arrays are l-values but not assignable (array name is non-modifiable l-value)
function return values are r-values (unless returning reference in C++)
const l-values cannot appear on left of assignment

semantic_targets: Assignment requires l-value on left side
l-value = locator value — has a memory address that persists
common_mistakes: Saying r-values cannot be used in expressions at all
Thinking all constants are not l-values (const variables are)
Confusing with left/right side of assignment only
tries to assign to r-value — compile error
equates l-value with 'left side' — l-values can appear on either side

logic_context: An adjacency matrix uses a 2D array where matrix[i][j] indicates an edge between vertices i and j. An adjacency list stores a list/array of neighbors for each vertex. Matrix uses O(V²) space, list uses O(V+E) space.

mandatory: adjacency matrix uses 2D array
adjacency list stores neighbors for each vertex
concept_groups: matrix: O(V²) space, O(1) edge lookup
list: O(V+E) space, O(degree) edge lookup
advanced_bonus: matrix: O(1) edge check, O(V²) space — good for dense graphs
list: O(degree) edge check, O(V+E) space — good for sparse graphs
matrix: add/remove edge O(1); list: add edge O(1), remove O(degree)
BFS/DFS: matrix O(V²), list O(V+E) — list always at least as fast
choose matrix when V is small and E is close to V²

semantic_targets: Graph representations differ in space and time efficiency
Matrix wastes space for sparse graphs
Choice depends on graph density and operations
common_mistakes: Claiming adjacency matrix is always better
always recommends one over the other without considering density
claims matrix edge check is O(1) while ignoring its O(V²) space cost

logic_context: The enum keyword defines a user-defined type consisting of a set of named integer constants. It is preferred over #define because it provides type safety, scope control, and better debugging support.

mandatory: defines named integer constants
user-defined type
advanced_bonus: enum constants are int by default — values are 0, 1, 2... unless specified
type safety: compiler warns on wrong enum type (better than bare #define integers)
enum values visible in debugger by name — #define values not
can assign specific values: enum { A=1, B=5, C=10 }
enum does not create a new type in C (unlike C++) — just named integers

semantic_targets: Enums improve code maintainability and clarity
common_mistakes: Saying enums store strings or non-integer values
Claiming enums allocate memory like arrays
Not understanding enums are just integers
assumes enum values are unique by default — can assign same value to two names
confuses C enum (int) with C++ enum class (scoped, typed)

logic_context: Amortized analysis evaluates the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations, not average-case. Example: dynamic array resizing where occasional expensive O(n) resize operations are amortized over many O(1) insertions.

mandatory: average cost over sequence of operations
spreads expensive operations across many cheap ones
advanced_bonus: amortized cost = total cost of n operations / n — not worst case of one operation
dynamic array doubling: O(n) resize happens after 1, 2, 4... operations — total extra work = O(n)
per-operation amortized cost = O(1) even though occasional resize is O(n)
accounting method: charge 2 units per push — 1 for current, 1 banked for future resize
distinct from average case — amortized is worst-case sequence, average is random input

semantic_targets: Amortized cost differs from worst-case single operation
Expensive operations are infrequent and spread out
Dynamic arrays achieve O(1) amortized insertion time
Not the same as average-case complexity
common_mistakes: Confusing amortized analysis with average-case analysis
Saying resizing happens on every insertion
Not understanding the spreading of costs
confuses amortized with average case — amortized is a worst-case guarantee
claims each dynamic array push is O(n) — only resize is O(n), amortized is O(1)

logic_context: Type punning refers to accessing or interpreting the same memory location using different data types. In C, this is commonly achieved using unions, which allow multiple members to share the same memory.

mandatory: accessing same memory with different types
reinterpreting data representation
advanced_bonus: union shares memory — writing one member and reading another reinterprets the bits
common use: inspect IEEE 754 float bits as integer
undefined behavior in C++ but explicitly allowed in C99/C11 via union
memcpy is the portable alternative for type punning in both C and C++
useful in serialization, networking, embedded register manipulation

semantic_targets: Unions provide a way to view same data as different types
Can cause undefined behavior if not careful
Useful for low-level programming and bit manipulation
common_mistakes: Ignoring undefined behavior and portability issues
uses pointer cast for type punning — strict aliasing violation in C
assumes type punning is well-defined in C++ — it is UB there, use memcpy

logic_context: Infix to postfix conversion (Shunting Yard algorithm) uses a stack to temporarily hold operators while scanning the infix expression left to right, respecting operator precedence and associativity, and handling parentheses.

mandatory: stack stores operators temporarily
respects operator precedence and associativity
advanced_bonus: Shunting Yard algorithm by Dijkstra
operands go directly to output; operators pushed to stack with precedence handling
higher precedence operator pops and outputs lower ones before pushing itself
left parenthesis pushed, right parenthesis pops until matching left
left associativity: pop equal precedence before pushing; right: push equal precedence
O(n) time and O(n) space

semantic_targets: Stack manages operator ordering during conversion
Higher precedence operators are output first
common_mistakes: incorrect precedence handling — outputs operators in wrong order
does not pop operators from stack at end of expression

logic_context: Stack memory is automatically allocated and deallocated for local variables and function calls with LIFO behavior. Heap memory is manually allocated using malloc/calloc and must be explicitly freed, allowing dynamic memory allocation with flexible lifetime.

mandatory: stack: automatic allocation and deallocation
heap: manual allocation with malloc/free
concept_groups: stack: function calls and local variables
advanced_bonus: stack: LIFO allocation, automatic deallocation at function return, fixed size (~1-8MB)
heap: manual allocation/deallocation, fragmentation possible, very large (limited by RAM)
stack is faster — simple pointer bump; heap slower due to allocator overhead
stack overflow: local variables exceed stack size
VLAs in C use stack — dangerous for large sizes

semantic_targets: Stack is automatic, heap requires manual management
Stack is faster but limited in size
Heap allows dynamic sizing but slower
common_mistakes: Saying stack memory must be manually freed
claims heap is always slower — true in general but allocator varies
returns pointer to local variable — dangling pointer after function returns

logic_context: The diamond problem occurs in multiple inheritance when a class inherits from two classes that both inherit from a common base class, creating ambiguity. C does not suffer from this problem because it does not support class inheritance or object-oriented programming.

mandatory: occurs in multiple inheritance
C does not support class inheritance
advanced_bonus: diamond problem arises in multiple inheritance hierarchies
C has no classes or inheritance — problem cannot exist
C++ solves with virtual inheritance to share a single base instance
C struct composition (not inheritance) avoids this entirely
protocol/interface patterns in C use function pointers in structs

semantic_targets: Diamond problem is an OOP inheritance issue
Creates ambiguity about which base class member to use
C avoids it entirely by not having inheritance
common_mistakes: Confusing C structs with C++ classes
Not understanding it's an OOP-specific problem
claims struct embedding causes diamond problem — it is composition not inheritance

logic_context: Linear data structures store elements in a sequential manner where each element has exactly one predecessor and one successor (except first and last). Non-linear data structures organize elements hierarchically (like trees) or with arbitrary connections (like graphs).

mandatory: linear: sequential arrangement with predecessor/successor
non-linear: hierarchical or graph-like relationships
concept_groups: linear examples: arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues
non-linear: multiple levels or complex connections
advanced_bonus: linear: array, linked list, stack, queue — sequential, one predecessor/successor
non-linear: tree, graph — hierarchical or arbitrary connections
linear traversal visits all elements in one pass; non-linear may require BFS/DFS
memory: linear usually contiguous or linked; non-linear more complex allocation
trees are special graphs — connected, acyclic, directed

semantic_targets: Linear structures follow a sequence or line
Non-linear structures model hierarchical or network relationships
Structure choice depends on data relationships
Traversal strategies differ between linear and non-linear
common_mistakes: classifies trees as linear — trees are non-linear hierarchical structures
equates linear with contiguous memory — linked lists are linear but not contiguous

logic_context: C storage classes (auto, register, static, extern) define the scope, lifetime, and visibility of variables. They control where variables are stored and how long they persist.

mandatory: define scope, lifetime, and visibility
four types: auto, register, static, extern
advanced_bonus: auto: default for local variables, stack-allocated, scope = block
register: hint to store in CPU register, address cannot be taken with &
static: persistent lifetime, scope depends on declaration location
extern: references a definition in another translation unit
modern compilers largely ignore register hint — optimizer does it better

semantic_targets: Different classes serve different programming needs
Default is auto for local variables
common_mistakes: Saying register guarantees CPU register storage (it's just a hint)
confuses scope with lifetime — static has function scope but program lifetime
tries to take address of register variable — compile error

logic_context: The extern keyword declares a variable or function that is defined elsewhere (in another source file). It tells the compiler that the symbol exists but its memory is allocated in another translation unit, enabling cross-file linkage.

mandatory: declares symbol defined elsewhere
enables cross-file access
concept_groups: links to definition in other file
advanced_bonus: extern declares without defining — no storage allocated
extern int x; declares x; int x; or int x = 0; defines it
omitting extern for function declaration is fine — functions are extern by default
static and extern are mutually exclusive for the same symbol
linker resolves extern references by finding the definition across object files

semantic_targets: extern enables sharing variables/functions across files
extern declares but does not define or allocate
Links to actual definition at link time
common_mistakes: Saying extern allocates memory (it only declares)
Using extern incorrectly with local variables
conflates extern declaration with definition — only one definition allowed
uses extern for static globals — static globals have internal linkage only

logic_context: The height of a binary tree is computed recursively as 1 + max(height of left subtree, height of right subtree). Base case: height of null node is -1 or empty tree is 0.

mandatory: recursive computation
1 + max of left and right subtree heights
concept_groups: height is longest path to leaf
advanced_bonus: height of empty tree (NULL) = 0 or -1 depending on convention
height = 1 + max(height(left), height(right))
O(n) time — every node visited exactly once
O(h) space for call stack — O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed
iterative: BFS with level counter — avoids stack overflow risk
single-node tree has height 1 (or 0 if counting edges not nodes)

semantic_targets: Tree height is length of longest path from root to leaf
Empty tree has height 0 or -1 by convention
common_mistakes: Adding heights of both subtrees instead of taking max
Confusing height with number of nodes
returns sum instead of max of left and right heights
wrong base case value — confuses edge-based and node-based height conventions

logic_context: Inline functions (using inline keyword) suggest to the compiler to replace function calls with the actual function body to reduce function call overhead. The compiler may ignore this hint.

mandatory: replaces function call with function body
reduces function call overhead
advanced_bonus: inline is a suggestion to compiler — may be ignored
eliminates function call overhead: no stack frame setup, no return jump
downside: code bloat if large function inlined many times
typically small, frequently-called functions benefit most
inline in header files avoids ODR violations (must be same definition in all TUs)
compiler with -O2/-O3 may inline without inline keyword

semantic_targets: Inline functions optimize performance by avoiding calls
Inlining is a compiler suggestion not command
Best for small, frequently called functions
May increase code size through duplication
common_mistakes: Confusing inline functions with preprocessor macros
assumes inline guarantees function is actually inlined — compiler decides
inlines large complex functions — increases binary size unnecessarily

logic_context: typedef creates a type alias or synonym for an existing data type with type checking at compile time. #define performs simple textual substitution by the preprocessor without any type checking or semantic understanding.

mandatory: typedef creates type alias with type checking
#define does textual substitution without type checking
advanced_bonus: typedef creates a true type alias — participates in type checking
#define is text substitution before compilation — no type awareness
typedef can be forward-declared; #define cannot
typedef for function pointers is significantly cleaner: typedef int (*FuncPtr)(int)
#define can define expressions and constants; typedef only aliases types

semantic_targets: typedef improves type safety and readability
common_mistakes: Saying typedef defines or allocates variables
Claiming #define understands or checks data types
Not understanding preprocessor vs compiler distinction
#define int* INTP: INTP a,b makes only a a pointer — typedef handles this correctly
assumes typedef creates a new type — it creates an alias, not a new type

logic_context: Heapify is the process of converting a binary tree into a valid heap by ensuring the heap property (max-heap or min-heap) is satisfied. This is done by comparing a node with its children and swapping if needed, then recursively applying to affected subtrees (percolate/sift down).

mandatory: enforces heap property on a subtree
percolate down or sift down operation
concept_groups: swap with larger/smaller child if needed
advanced_bonus: sift-down heapify: compare node with children, swap with larger/smaller, recurse down

O(n) build-heap is non-obvious — most nodes are near leaves, sift-down cost is small

semantic_targets: Heapify restores or maintains heap property
Essential for heap construction and maintenance
common_mistakes: Assuming heapify sorts the entire array

logic_context: A self-referential structure is a structure that contains a pointer to another structure of the same type. This enables creation of linked data structures like linked lists and trees.

mandatory: structure contains pointer to same type
enables linked data structures
concept_groups: pointer member points to same struct type
used in linked lists and trees
advanced_bonus: struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; } — pointer not direct embed (would be infinite size)
pointer to same type is possible; direct member of same type is not
enables singly linked list, doubly linked list, binary tree, graph nodes

common_mistakes: Trying to embed the structure directly inside itself
Not understanding why pointer is necessary

confuses pointer to self type with embedding self type

logic_context: Bubble Sort repeatedly compares and swaps adjacent elements if they are in wrong order, causing larger elements to 'bubble up'. Selection Sort repeatedly finds the minimum element from unsorted portion and places it at the beginning.

mandatory: bubble sort: adjacent element swaps
selection sort: finds and places minimum element
advanced_bonus: bubble sort: O(n²) worst/average, O(n) best case (with early termination flag)
selection sort: always O(n²) — no early termination possible

Selection sort performs fewer swaps than bubble sort
Bubble sort can terminate early if sorted
Neither is efficient for large datasets
common_mistakes: Claiming one is always significantly faster
claims selection sort can terminate early — it cannot, always n² comparisons
claims bubble sort is always O(n²) — O(n) best case with termination flag

logic_context: A priority queue is an abstract data type where each element has a priority, and elements are removed based on priority rather than insertion order (not FIFO). Commonly implemented using heaps.

mandatory: elements processed by priority not insertion order
highest/lowest priority element served first
advanced_bonus: implemented typically as a binary heap — O(log n) insert/extract, O(1) peek
applications: Dijkstra's algorithm, Prim's algorithm, Huffman coding, task scheduling
hospital triage systems: highest priority patient treated first

event-driven simulation: events processed by earliest time

semantic_targets: Priority determines processing order not time
Higher priority elements served before lower priority
Essential for scheduling and graph algorithms
common_mistakes: Treating priority queue as a normal FIFO queue
confuses priority queue with sorted array — PQ has O(log n) insert not O(n)
names fewer than three distinct applications

logic_context: Recursion solves problems by having a function call itself with a simpler version of the problem until a base case is reached. Iteration solves problems using loops (for, while) to repeat operations.

mandatory: recursion: function calls itself
iteration: uses loops for repetition
advanced_bonus: every recursive algorithm can be converted to iterative using an explicit stack
recursion: cleaner for naturally recursive problems (trees, divide-and-conquer)
iteration: O(1) space; recursion: O(n) call stack space

semantic_targets: Recursion uses function call stack for state
Recursion more elegant for some problems
Both can solve same problems with different approaches
common_mistakes: Claiming recursion is always slower (tail optimization exists)
claims recursion is always less efficient — TCO can make it equivalent
claims iteration cannot solve tree problems — it can, with explicit stack

logic_context: In C, when an array is passed to a function, the array name decays into a pointer to its first element, losing size information. This means functions receive only the address, not the array structure itself.

mandatory: array decays to pointer to first element
size information is lost

advanced_bonus: sizeof(array) gives total bytes; sizeof(pointer) gives pointer size — after decay, size is lost

exception: sizeof, &array, and _Alignof do not cause decay

Original array size is not preserved in function
Must pass size as separate parameter
common_mistakes: Assuming array size is automatically passed
Confusing array decay with pointer assignment
Using sizeof on array parameter expecting full size
uses sizeof on array parameter — gets pointer size (8), not array size
treats 2D array as int** — different memory layout and pointer type

logic_context: A NULL pointer is a pointer that points to no valid memory location (typically address 0), used to indicate an invalid or uninitialized pointer. A void pointer (void*) is a generic pointer that can hold the address of any data type but must be cast before dereferencing.

mandatory: NULL points to no valid location
void pointer holds address of any type
advanced_bonus: NULL: special pointer value (typically 0) indicating invalid/missing address
void*: generic pointer type — can store any data pointer, no type information

semantic_targets: NULL indicates absence of valid reference
void pointer lacks type information for dereferencing
Different purposes: sentinel vs generic type
common_mistakes: Assuming NULL holds or allocates memory
Confusing NULL value with void* type
dereferences void* directly without casting — compile error
treats NULL and void* as the same — NULL is a value, void* is a type

logic_context: Bit masking uses bitwise operations (AND, OR, XOR, NOT) to selectively set, clear, toggle, or check specific bits in a variable without affecting other bits, commonly used for hardware registers and flags.

mandatory: uses bitwise operations
selectively manipulate specific bits
concept_groups: clear bit with AND and NOT
advanced_bonus: set bit N: reg |= (1 << N)
clear bit N: reg &= ~(1 << N)
toggle bit N: reg ^= (1 << N)
check bit N: (reg >> N) & 1
applications: GPIO pin control, flag registers, packet headers, permission bits
use unsigned types for bit manipulation — behavior of shifts on signed is undefined

semantic_targets: Bit masking enables precise low-level control
Essential for embedded and systems programming
More efficient than multiple boolean variables
common_mistakes: Using arithmetic operators instead of bitwise
shifts signed integers — left shift UB, right shift implementation-defined
uses wrong operation (OR to clear, AND to set) — corrupts other bits

logic_context: A Trie (prefix tree) is a tree-based data structure where each node represents a character, and strings are stored by sharing common prefixes along paths from root to nodes, enabling efficient string operations.

mandatory: tree structure for string storage
shares common prefixes
concept_groups: O(m) search where m is string length
advanced_bonus: O(m) search, insert, delete where m is string length — independent of number of strings
each node: array of 26 children (or hash map for arbitrary alphabet)
isEnd flag marks nodes that are complete words
space: O(ALPHABET_SIZE * m * n) — can be large
applications: autocomplete, spell checking, IP routing (longest prefix match)

logic_context: GDB (GNU Debugger) is a debugging tool that allows inspection and control of program execution. Breakpoints are markers that pause execution at specific lines or functions, enabling examination of program state, variables, and call stack.

logic_context: When realloc cannot expand memory in place, it allocates a new larger block, copies all existing data to the new location, frees the old block, and returns a pointer to the new block. The old pointer becomes invalid.

logic_context: Left shifting a negative number causes undefined behavior in C. Right shifting a negative signed integer is implementation-defined: it may perform arithmetic shift (preserving sign bit) or logical shift (filling with zeros).

logic_context: Leaf nodes in a binary tree are nodes that have no children (both left and right pointers are NULL). They are counted by traversing the tree (recursively or iteratively) and incrementing a counter for each node with no children.

mandatory: nodes with no children (left and right are NULL)
counted via tree traversal

Terminal nodes at bottom of tree paths

logic_context: A string literal ("hello") is stored in read-only memory section and cannot be modified. A character array (char arr[] = "hello") copies the string to writable stack or data memory, allowing modification.

mandatory: string literal stored in read-only memory
character array stored in modifiable memory
advanced_bonus: string literal: stored in .rodata (read-only segment) — modification is UB

logic_context: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices at each step hoping to find a global optimum, which doesn't always work. Dynamic programming systematically considers all subproblems and combines their optimal solutions to guarantee the global optimum.

mandatory: greedy makes local optimal choices
DP guarantees global optimum via subproblems
concept_groups: greedy: may not always be correct

advanced_bonus: greedy: makes locally optimal choice at each step, no reconsideration

common_mistakes: Assuming greedy is always faster and correct
Not understanding when greedy works vs fails

logic_context: Open addressing resolves hash collisions by probing for alternative empty slots within the same hash table using strategies like linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing, rather than using separate data structures.

mandatory: probes for alternative slots in same table
no external data structures
concept_groups: probe sequence until empty slot found
advanced_bonus: linear probing: check next slot sequentially — simple but clusters

semantic_targets: Collisions resolved by finding next available slot
All elements stored in single table
No linked lists or external chains
Performance degrades with high load factor

logic_context: C compilation has four stages: (1) Preprocessing - expands macros and includes files, (2) Compilation - translates to assembly code, (3) Assembly - converts to object code, (4) Linking - combines object files and resolves external references to create executable.

mandatory: four stages: preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking

advanced_bonus: preprocessing: #include, #define expansion, #ifdef — output is .i file

semantic_targets: Each stage has distinct transformation role
Linking resolves symbols across compilation units
Can stop at intermediate stages for debugging
common_mistakes: Combining compilation and linking as single step
claims compilation produces executable — misses assembly and linker stages

logic_context: Header guards (include guards) use preprocessor directives (#ifndef, #define, #endif) to prevent multiple inclusion of the same header file during compilation, avoiding duplicate definitions and compilation errors.

mandatory: prevent multiple inclusion of header

advanced_bonus: without header guards, same declarations appear twice — redefinition errors

logic_context: Stack overflow occurs when recursive function calls exceed available stack memory, typically due to missing base case, incorrect base case, or excessive recursion depth. Each call consumes stack space until memory is exhausted.

Can convert to iteration to avoid

out-of-place requires O(n) additional space

logic_context: Dijkstra handles weighted graphs with non-negative edges to find true shortest distances. Choose BFS for unweighted or uniform-weight graphs; Dijkstra when edges have different weights.

logic_context: Hash map gives O(1) average lookup but no ordering. BST gives O(log n) lookup but keys are always ordered. If the application needs both fast lookup AND sorted iteration, BST (or a combination) is correct. A hash map alone cannot provide sorted iteration efficiently.

mandatory: hash map: O(1) lookup but no ordering

logic_context: Recursive Fibonacci recomputes identical subproblems exponentially (O(2^n)). Two fixes: memoization (top-down DP, cache results) or tabulation (bottom-up DP, build array). Memoization is easier to reason about; tabulation uses O(n) space but can be reduced to O(1). Context: memoization for clarity, tabulation for performance.

memoization or tabulation as fixes

logic_context: With 4KB RAM, linked list overhead (pointer per node, heap fragmentation, malloc overhead ~8-16 bytes per call) is significant. Fixed-size array uses contiguous memory with no per-element overhead and better cache locality. For an embedded system with known maximum size, array is almost always the right choice.

Arrays have superior cache behavior on constrained hardware

logic_context: QuickSort preferred in practice because: better cache performance (in-place, sequential access), smaller constant factors, no auxiliary array needed. logic_context: Sorted array with binary search: O(log n) lookup, O(1) space overhead, excellent cache locality, but O(n) insertion. logic_context: LRU cache needs O(1) get and put. Solution: doubly linked list (for O(1) move to front/back) + hash map (for O(1) lookup by key). Hash map stores key→node pointer. On access, move node to front of list. On eviction, remove from back. This is the canonical O(1) LRU design.

O(1) for both get and put

logic_context: Recursive DFS on 100,000 nodes risks stack overflow (default stack ~1-8MB, each frame ~100-200 bytes = ~50k-80k max depth). Iterative DFS with explicit stack avoids this, uses heap memory, and is production-safe. For production code, explicit stack is always preferred.

logic_context: Global variables for shared state create hidden dependencies, make testing hard, cause race conditions in concurrent code, and violate encapsulation. Acceptable rarely: truly global constants, or hardware register addresses in embedded code. For shared mutable state, pass via parameters or use a context struct.

logic_context: A singly linked list can only move forward cheaply, so going back needs an O(n) traversal or extra bookkeeping. Two stacks (back and forward) also give O(1) operations with simple code, clearing the forward stack on a new visit. A doubly linked list or two stacks is the right choice; the singly linked list is a poor fit.

doubly linked list or two stacks give O(1) back and forward

advanced_bonus: a dynamic array with a current index also gives O(1) moves and cache-friendly storage
limiting history size needs removal from the oldest end
doubly linked list allows O(1) removal of old entries
freeing truncated nodes avoids memory leaks
two stacks move items between stacks on navigation

semantic_targets: Several valid designs with different trade-offs
common_mistakes: Choosing a singly linked list without addressing back navigation
Not clearing forward history on a new visit

logic_context: Use a variable-size sliding window with two pointers. Expand the right pointer adding elements to the running sum; whenever the sum is at least the target, update the minimum length and shrink the window by advancing the left pointer while the condition still holds. Because all numbers are positive, each pointer only moves forward, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.

semantic_targets: Each element enters and leaves the window once
common_mistakes: Resetting the window to empty after each match

logic_context: Use the first row and first column of the matrix as markers. First record whether the first row and first column themselves contain a zero using two flags. Then scan the rest of the matrix and, for each zero at (i, j), mark matrix[i][0] and matrix[0][j] as zero. In a second pass zero every cell whose row or column marker is zero, and finally zero the first row and column if their flags were set. O(m*n) time, O(1) space.

logic_context: Maintain a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order. logic_context: Let dp[i] be the number of ways to decode the first i characters. dp[0] = 1. The answer is dp[n], computed in O(n) time and O(1) space with two variables.

logic_context: Run DFS from every unvisited vertex. After all neighbours of a vertex have been fully explored, push the vertex onto a stack (post-order). logic_context: setjmp saves the current execution context (stack pointer, registers and program counter) in a jmp_buf and returns 0. It enables non-local jumps such as error recovery from deep call stacks, but it skips normal stack unwinding, can leave resources unreleased and makes local variable values indeterminate unless they are volatile.

logic_context: The strict aliasing rule says an object may only be accessed through an lvalue of a compatible type (or a character type); accessing it through a pointer of an incompatible type is undefined behaviour. logic_context: An infinite loop is a loop whose condition never becomes false, so it runs until it is exited by break, return, exit or the process is killed. logic_context: malloc and free are general purpose, so each call has overhead, non-deterministic timing and can fragment memory over time. For many small short-lived objects, a pool or arena is better.

logic_context: A Merkle tree is a binary tree of hashes: each leaf is the hash of a data block and each internal node is the hash of its children's hashes, so the root hash summarises all the data. logic_context: An interval tree is a balanced binary search tree whose nodes store intervals ordered by their low endpoint, with each node also storing the maximum high endpoint in its subtree. Queries and insertions take O(log n) (plus output size when listing all overlaps).

logic_context: Karatsuba multiplies two n-digit numbers using three recursive multiplications instead of four. Splitting x = a*B + b and y = c*B + d, it computes ac, bd and (a+b)(c+d), then obtains the middle term ad + bc as (a+b)(c+d) - ac - bd. This gives a running time of O(n^1.585) instead of the O(n^2) of grade-school multiplication. It is used in big-integer libraries for medium-sized numbers.

logic_context: The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes up to n. logic_context: The Travelling Salesman Problem asks for the shortest tour that visits every city exactly once and returns to the start. It is NP-hard. logic_context: Johnson's algorithm first runs Bellman-Ford from an added virtual source to compute potentials h(v) and detect negative cycles, then reweights each edge as w'(u,v) = w(u,v) + h(u) - h(v), which makes all weights non-negative without changing shortest paths. It then runs Dijkstra from every vertex and corrects the distances back. The time is O(V*E + V^2 log V) with a Fibonacci heap (O(V E log V) with a binary heap), better than Floyd-Warshall's O(V^3) for sparse graphs.

logic_context: C does not specify the order in which operands of most operators or function arguments are evaluated. Sequence points (or, in C11 terms, 'sequenced before' relations) guarantee that all side effects of earlier evaluations are complete; they occur, for example, after the first operand of &&, ||, ?: and the comma operator, and at the end of a full expression. logic_context: A simple additive checksum is cheap but misses many errors such as swapped bytes. logic_context: Recursively subtract the current node's value from the remaining target as you descend; at a leaf node, check whether the remaining target equals the leaf's value (meaning the full path sums to the original target), and combine results from the left and right subtrees with a logical OR.

mandatory: subtract the current node's value from the remaining target while descending

semantic_targets: Target is reduced by subtracting each node's value while recursing
Success condition is checked only at leaf nodes
Results from both subtrees are combined with logical OR
Null node is the false base case
common_mistakes: checks whether remaining target equals zero at internal (non-leaf) nodes, giving false positives for incomplete paths

logic_context: Maintain a visited set; iterate over every node, and whenever an unvisited node is found, run a BFS or DFS from it to mark all reachable nodes as visited and increment a component counter, since each such traversal covers exactly one connected component.

mandatory: iterate over all nodes checking a visited marker

mandatory: maintain a hash map from original node references to cloned node references

logic_context: Treat each word as a graph node where edges connect words differing by exactly one letter; run BFS from the start word, exploring all single-letter variations at each step, checking membership in the word list to decide valid neighbors, and return the BFS depth at which the end word is reached.

run BFS from the start word, returning the depth/level at which the end word is found
concept_groups: generate all single-letter-changed variations of the current word to find neighbors
check each variation against the word list (using a hash set) to confirm it's a valid node

logic_context: Use a deque instead of a plain queue: when relaxing an edge of weight 0, push the neighbor to the front of the deque (processed next, at the same distance level); when relaxing an edge of weight 1, push the neighbor to the back of the deque (processed after current-level nodes), preserving a sorted-by-distance order without needing a priority queue.

push neighbors reached via a 1-weight edge to the back of the deque

1-weight edges increase distance by 1, so their targets go to the back (next level)
pop from the front of the deque to process nodes in correct distance order
advanced_bonus: this achieves the same correctness as Dijkstra's algorithm but in O(V + E) time instead of O((V+E) log V), since no priority queue is needed

logic_context: During a DFS, track each node's discovery time and its low-link value (the lowest discovery time reachable from its subtree, including through one back edge); a node is an articulation point if it is the DFS root with more than one child, or if any child's low-link value is greater than or equal to the node's own discovery time.

back edges (to already-visited ancestors) update low-link but must not be the edge back to the immediate parent
advanced_bonus: the condition low[v] >= disc[u] (not just low[v] > disc[u]) correctly captures that removing u disconnects v's subtree from the rest, since low[v] can at best reach u itself

runs in O(V + E) time, a single DFS pass with constant extra bookkeeping per node

logic_context: Define dp[i][j] as the length of the longest palindromic subsequence within the substring from index i to j; if the characters at i and j match, dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2, otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]), filling the table by increasing substring length.

mandatory: define dp[i][j] over substring ranges, filled by increasing length
when s[i]==s[j], dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2, otherwise take the max of excluding either end
concept_groups: base case: single characters have a palindromic subsequence length of 1
fill the table by increasing substring length (or equivalently, decreasing i / increasing j)
matching end characters extend the inner subsequence by 2
mismatched end characters take the best of dropping either end
advanced_bonus: this is equivalent to finding the Longest Common Subsequence between the string and its reverse, an alternative formulation of the same problem
the table must be filled in order of increasing substring length (or along diagonals) since dp[i][j] depends on the smaller subproblem dp[i+1][j-1]

Mismatched endpoints take the best result from dropping either end
Equivalent to LCS between the string and its reverse

logic_context: Define dp[i][j] as the minimum cost to multiply matrices i through j; try every possible split point k between i and j, computing the cost as dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] plus the cost of multiplying the two resulting matrices, and take the minimum over all split points, filling the table by increasing chain length.

mandatory: define dp[i][j] as minimum cost over matrices i..j, trying every split point k
cost at split k = dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + (dimension product cost of combining the two resulting matrices)
concept_groups: base case: a single matrix (i==j) costs 0 to 'multiply'
fill the table by increasing chain length so smaller subproblems are solved first
try every possible split point k between i and j
take the minimum cost over all tried split points

this problem only decides the optimal multiplication ORDER (parenthesization); it does not perform the multiplications themselves
runs in O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space for n matrices, since there are O(n^2) subproblems each requiring an O(n) scan over split points

this is a classic example of optimal substructure combined with overlapping subproblems, the two hallmarks that justify a DP approach

All possible split points are tried at each subproblem
Table filled in order of increasing chain length
Split cost formula depends on matrix dimension array, not matrix contents

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct split-point search and dimension-based cost formula

logic_context: Define dp[i][j] as the minimum path sum to reach cell (i, j), computed as the cell's own value plus the minimum of the path sum arriving from above or from the left, filling the table row by row (or column by column) starting from the top-left cell.

mandatory: define dp[i][j] as minimum cost to reach that cell from the top-left
dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])

first column can only be reached by moving down, so each cell only adds to the one above it
interior cells take the minimum of the cell above and the cell to the left

logic_context: Define dp[i] as the maximum revenue obtainable from a rod of length i; for each length i, try every possible first-cut size j from 1 to i, and take the maximum of price[j] plus dp[i-j] over all choices of j, building up from smaller rod lengths to larger ones.

dp[i] = max over all cut sizes j of (price[j] + dp[i-j])
concept_groups: base case: dp[0] = 0 (a rod of length 0 earns nothing)

try every possible first piece length j from 1 to i
take the maximum revenue across all choices of j

Every possible first-cut size is tried at each step
