logic_context: Define dp[i][j] as the length of the longest common substring ending exactly at s1[i-1] and s2[j-1]; when the characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, but when they mismatch, dp[i][j] resets to 0 (unlike LCS, which would instead take the max of dropping one character from either string).

on mismatch, reset dp[i][j] to 0 rather than carrying forward the best subsequence value

logic_context: Maintain a stack of indices with strictly increasing bar heights; when a bar shorter than the stack's top is encountered, pop the stack and compute the rectangle area using the popped bar's height with a width spanning from the new stack top (exclusive) to the current index (exclusive), repeating until the stack top is shorter or the stack is empty.

on encountering a shorter bar, pop and compute area using popped height times the span between neighbors
concept_groups: push index onto stack while heights are increasing (or equal)
on a shorter bar, repeatedly pop and compute area until the stack top is shorter or empty

Width spans between the new stack top and the current index

logic_context: Use one stack for enqueue operations (pushing directly) and a second stack for dequeue operations; when the dequeue stack is empty, pop everything from the enqueue stack and push it onto the dequeue stack, reversing the order so the oldest element ends up on top, ready to be popped.

transfer all elements from input to output stack only when the output stack is empty
concept_groups: enqueue always pushes directly onto the input stack in O(1)
dequeue pops from the output stack if it's non-empty

logic_context: Maintain a stack of indices whose corresponding temperatures are in decreasing order; for each new day, pop all indices from the stack whose temperature is lower than the current day's temperature, recording the day-difference as the answer for each popped index, then push the current day's index.

mandatory: maintain a stack of indices with decreasing temperatures
pop indices with a lower temperature than the current day, recording index-difference as their answer

push the current day's index onto the stack after processing pops

indices remaining on the stack at the end have no warmer future day, so their answer stays 0
advanced_bonus: each index is pushed and popped from the stack at most once across the entire scan, giving an overall O(n) time complexity despite the nested-looking while loop

Popping resolves the 'days until warmer' answer using an index difference
Each index is processed (pushed/popped) exactly once overall

logic_context: Use two stacks (or one stack of pairs): one for pending multiplier counts and one for pending partial strings; when a digit is read, build up the number, when '[' is read push the current count and current string then reset both, when ']' is read pop the count and previous string and append the current string repeated that many times, and when a letter is read, append it to the current string.

mandatory: push current count and current partial string onto stacks when '[' is encountered
on ']', pop the previous string and count, then append the current string repeated count times to it
concept_groups: accumulate multi-digit numbers correctly before encountering '['
on '[', save (push) the current string and count, then reset both for the new nested level
on ']', pop the saved string and multiplier, append current (nested) string repeated that many times

semantic_targets: Multi-digit numbers must be accumulated before use
Stack preserves outer-level state while processing nested inner brackets
String repetition happens when closing a bracket, using the popped count
Letters append directly to the currently active (innermost) string
common_mistakes: treats each digit character as a complete number instead of accumulating multi-digit counts correctly
does not save/restore the correct nesting level's string and count, causing nested expansions to overwrite or lose outer-level data
appends the repeated string to the wrong (current instead of popped/outer) string, scrambling the output order
fails on multiple levels of nesting because only one stack frame's worth of state was tracked instead of a proper stack

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct dual-state (count+string) stack management across nesting

logic_context: Run two separate binary searches: one biased to continue searching left even after finding a match (to find the leftmost occurrence), and one biased to continue searching right after finding a match (to find the rightmost occurrence), rather than stopping at the first match found.

mandatory: run two separate binary searches, one for the leftmost occurrence and one for the rightmost
on finding a match, continue narrowing in the appropriate direction instead of stopping immediately
concept_groups: for leftmost search, on a match move the high pointer to mid-1 and record mid as a candidate
for rightmost search, on a match move the low pointer to mid+1 and record mid as a candidate
if the target is never found, both searches should return a sentinel like -1
the two searches are otherwise structurally identical, just mirrored in direction
advanced_bonus: a single binary search that simply stops at the first match found cannot distinguish the first or last occurrence when duplicates exist
both searches independently run in O(log n), so the combined solution is O(log n), not O(n), even with duplicate elements
an equivalent approach uses 'lower_bound' and 'upper_bound' style binary searches (finding the insertion point for the target and for target+1 respectively)
careful off-by-one handling is required: continuing to search left/right after a match, rather than terminating, is what finds the boundary
if the array has no duplicates, both searches simply return the same single index

semantic_targets: Two independent binary searches locate the two boundaries
Matches trigger continued search in one direction rather than immediate return
Both searches remain O(log n) regardless of duplicate count
common_mistakes: performs only one binary search and returns immediately upon the first match found, which may be neither the first nor last occurrence
after finding a match, fails to continue narrowing in the correct direction and instead breaks out of the loop immediately
uses a linear scan outward from a found match to locate the boundaries, degrading to O(n) in the worst case (many duplicates)
mixes up which direction (left vs right) to continue searching for the leftmost versus rightmost search

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct boundary-seeking variant of binary search

logic_context: Binary search over the range of possible speeds (from 1 to the maximum pile size); for each candidate speed, compute a feasibility check (total hours needed at that speed) in linear time, and narrow the search range based on whether the candidate speed is feasible, converging on the minimum feasible speed.

mandatory: binary search over the space of possible answer VALUES, not array indices
use a monotonic feasibility check function to decide which half of the range to keep
concept_groups: define search bounds as the minimum and maximum plausible answer values (e.g. speed 1 to max pile size)
for each candidate mid value, run a feasibility check (e.g. total hours needed at that speed)
if feasible, try to find an even smaller valid speed by searching the lower half
if infeasible, the speed must be larger, so search the upper half
advanced_bonus: this technique requires the feasibility function to be monotonic: if speed k works, every speed greater than k also works, which is what makes binary search valid here
the feasibility check itself typically runs in O(n) (e.g. summing ceil(pile/speed) for every pile), making the overall complexity O(n log(max_value))

this 'binary search on the answer' pattern generalizes to many minimize-the-maximum or maximize-the-minimum problems (e.g. minimizing the largest subarray sum, maximizing minimum distance between placed items)
the search converges to the SMALLEST feasible value by continuing to search left even after finding a feasible candidate, similar to leftmost-occurrence binary search
choosing overly loose initial bounds only affects the number of iterations (log factor), not correctness, as long as they bracket the true answer

semantic_targets: Search space is over possible answer values, not array positions
A monotonic feasibility check replaces direct array comparison
Feasible results continue searching toward smaller/larger extremes as appropriate
Overall complexity combines binary search depth with per-check feasibility cost
common_mistakes: tries every possible speed linearly from 1 upward instead of binary searching over the value range, giving O(max_value * n) instead of O(n log(max_value))
does not verify or rely on the monotonic property of the feasibility function, applying binary search to a non-monotonic problem incorrectly
stops at the first feasible value found without continuing to search for an even smaller feasible one
sets incorrect or too-narrow initial search bounds, potentially excluding the true answer from the search range

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct identification and use of a monotonic feasibility check

logic_context: Insert the first element of each of the K arrays into a min-heap along with which array and index it came from; repeatedly extract the minimum, append it to the result, and insert the next element from the same array (if any) back into the heap, continuing until the heap is empty.

mandatory: maintain a min-heap of size K holding one candidate element per array along with its source
repeatedly extract the min, append to result, and push the next element from the same source array
concept_groups: initialize the heap with the first element of each of the K arrays
each heap entry tracks both the value and which array/index it came from
extract-min gives the next smallest overall element to append to the output
after extraction, push that array's next element (if one exists) back into the heap
advanced_bonus: the heap never holds more than K elements at a time, bounding each heap operation to O(log K)

overall time complexity is O(N log K) where N is the total number of elements across all arrays, which beats the O(N log N) of concatenating and sorting everything from scratch when K is much smaller than N
this approach generalizes directly to merging K sorted linked lists by storing node references instead of (array, index) pairs

a naive pairwise-merge approach (merging arrays two at a time repeatedly) achieves the same O(N log K) complexity through a different mechanism (merge-sort-style pairing), but the heap approach handles all K sources simultaneously
if an array becomes exhausted, simply don't push a replacement for it; the heap size shrinks accordingly

semantic_targets: Min-heap holds one active candidate per source array
Extraction order directly produces the globally sorted merge output
Heap size stays bounded at K throughout, controlling per-operation cost
Exhausted arrays are simply not replenished in the heap
common_mistakes: concatenates all K arrays first and then sorts the combined result, giving O(N log N) instead of the better O(N log K)
forgets to push the next element from the same source array after extracting its current minimum, truncating that array's contribution early
does not track which array/index each heap entry came from, making it impossible to know what to push next after an extraction
uses a max-heap instead of a min-heap, which would retrieve the largest rather than the smallest next element

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct heap-based K-way merge with source tracking

logic_context: First build a frequency count of every distinct element using a hash map, then maintain a min-heap of size K ordered by frequency, pushing each (element, frequency) pair and popping the smallest-frequency entry whenever the heap exceeds size K, leaving the K most frequent elements in the heap.

mandatory: build a frequency hash map of all elements first
maintain a min-heap of size K ordered by frequency, evicting the smallest when it exceeds K
concept_groups: count occurrences of each distinct element using a hash map in a single pass
insert (frequency, element) pairs into a min-heap one at a time
if the heap size exceeds K after an insertion, pop the minimum-frequency entry
after processing all elements, the heap contains exactly the K most frequent elements
advanced_bonus: using a MIN-heap of size K (not a max-heap of all elements) is the key efficiency trick: it only ever needs to track the current top-K candidates, evicting the weakest one as better candidates appear
overall time complexity is O(n log k): O(n) for the frequency count plus O(n log k) for maintaining the bounded heap, which beats O(n log n) full sorting when k is much smaller than n
an alternative approach uses bucket sort by frequency (since frequency is bounded by n), achieving O(n) time instead of O(n log k)
a max-heap of ALL distinct elements also works but costs O(n log n) in the worst case since it isn't bounded to size K
ties in frequency can be broken arbitrarily unless the problem specifies additional tie-breaking criteria

semantic_targets: Frequency map is built before any heap operations
Min-heap bounded to size K is more efficient than a full max-heap
Heap eviction keeps only the strongest K candidates at all times
Bucket sort by frequency offers an O(n) alternative
common_mistakes: uses a max-heap containing ALL elements and pops K times, giving O(n log n) instead of the more efficient O(n log k) bounded min-heap approach
forgets to count frequencies first, trying to determine 'most frequent' directly from raw heap insertion order
does not bound the heap to size K, letting it grow unbounded and losing the efficiency benefit
evicts the maximum-frequency entry instead of the minimum when the heap exceeds size K, keeping the wrong (least frequent) elements

logic_context: Repeatedly clear the lowest set bit using the operation n = n AND (n - 1), incrementing a counter each time, until n becomes zero; this operation always removes exactly the rightmost 1-bit in a single step.

mandatory: repeatedly apply n = n AND (n - 1) to clear the lowest set bit
count iterations until n becomes zero
concept_groups: n - 1 flips all bits from the rightmost set bit down to bit 0
ANDing with the original n clears exactly that rightmost set bit, leaving the rest unchanged
the number of loop iterations equals the number of set bits
advanced_bonus: this runs in O(k) time where k is the number of set bits, not O(32) or O(64) like a naive bit-by-bit scan, making it faster for sparse bit patterns
the naive approach (checking each of the 32/64 bits individually with a shift and mask) always takes a fixed number of iterations regardless of how many bits are actually set
n AND (n-1) is a commonly reused bit trick, also used to check if a number is a power of two (a power of two has exactly one set bit, so n AND (n-1) equals 0)
this works identically for any integer width (8, 16, 32, 64-bit) since the bit trick only depends on binary arithmetic, not a fixed bit count
many modern CPUs provide a dedicated popcount instruction that performs this count in O(1) hardware time, making this software algorithm mostly relevant for understanding or unsupported platforms

semantic_targets: n AND (n-1) clears exactly the lowest set bit
Loop count directly equals total set bits
Faster than fixed-width bit-by-bit scanning for sparse bit patterns
Same bit trick underlies power-of-two detection
common_mistakes: scans all 32/64 bits individually with shifts, which is correct but misses the point of the more efficient Kernighan trick
uses n OR (n-1) or another incorrect bitwise combination instead of the correct AND operation
miscounts by incrementing the counter before or after the wrong operation, producing an off-by-one bit count
assumes the loop always runs a fixed number of times (equal to bit-width) rather than recognizing it runs exactly once per set bit

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct bit-clearing operation and iteration count

logic_context: XOR every element of the array together; since XOR is commutative and associative, and any number XORed with itself is zero, all the paired (duplicate) numbers cancel out to zero, leaving only the single unpaired number as the final result.

mandatory: XOR all elements of the array together in a single pass
rely on x XOR x = 0 and x XOR 0 = x to cancel out all paired duplicates
concept_groups: XOR is commutative and associative, so the order of operations doesn't matter
each duplicate pair contributes x XOR x = 0 to the running result
the unpaired single element contributes itself unchanged (x XOR 0 = x)
the final running XOR value is exactly the single unpaired number
advanced_bonus: this achieves O(n) time and O(1) extra space, strictly better than a hash-map frequency-count approach which needs O(n) extra space
the technique relies fundamentally on the self-inverse property of XOR: a XOR a = 0 for any value a

this specific technique only works when exactly one element is unpaired and all others appear EXACTLY twice; it needs modification (e.g. using bit-counting with modulo 3) if others appear exactly three times instead

a more advanced variant handles exactly two unpaired single numbers (with all others appearing twice) by first XORing everything, then using a distinguishing set bit to split the array into two groups and XOR each separately
sorting the array first and scanning for an unpaired element is a valid O(n log n) alternative, but is asymptotically worse than the O(n) XOR trick

semantic_targets: XOR cancellation relies on x XOR x = 0
Commutative/associative property allows any processing order
Single pass achieves O(n) time with O(1) space
Technique requires exactly one unpaired element among exact pairs
common_mistakes: uses a hash map to count frequencies instead of the more space-efficient XOR technique, using O(n) extra space unnecessarily
assumes the XOR trick directly extends to elements appearing three times without the needed modification (bit counting with modulo)
sorts the array first, adding an unnecessary O(n log n) cost when O(n) is achievable
misapplies OR or AND instead of XOR, which does not have the required self-cancelling property

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct use of XOR's self-cancellation property

logic_context: At each recursive step, consider the current element and branch into two recursive calls: one that includes the element in the current subset, and one that excludes it, continuing until all elements have been considered, at which point the accumulated subset is added to the result.

mandatory: branch into an 'include this element' and an 'exclude this element' recursive call at each step
base case: once all elements have been considered, add the accumulated subset to the result
concept_groups: recursive call with the current element added to the running subset
recursive call without the current element, leaving the running subset unchanged
base case is reached after processing the last element (index == n)
backtracking (removing the element after the 'include' branch) is needed if a single mutable subset list is reused across calls
advanced_bonus: this produces exactly 2^n subsets for a set of size n, since each of the n elements independently has 2 choices (include or exclude)

if a single shared mutable list is used to build subsets (rather than creating new lists per call), explicit backtracking (removing the just-added element) is required after the 'include' recursive branch returns
an equivalent iterative approach treats each subset as corresponding to one of the 2^n possible n-bit binary numbers, where each bit decides inclusion of one element
time complexity is O(2^n * n) since there are 2^n subsets and each can take up to O(n) time to copy/construct
this recursive 'include/exclude' template generalizes directly to many other combinatorial generation problems (e.g. subset-sum, combinations)

semantic_targets: Each element independently contributes a binary include/exclude choice
Recursion depth equals the number of elements
Backtracking is required if subsets are built via a shared mutable structure
common_mistakes: only generates subsets that include every element considered so far, missing the 'exclude' branch entirely
forgets to backtrack (remove the added element) after the include branch when reusing a single mutable subset list, corrupting subsequent subsets
adds the subset to the result list at every recursive call instead of only at the base case, producing duplicate/incomplete subsets
miscounts the expected total number of subsets, not recognizing it should be exactly 2^n

logic_context: At each recursive step, try placing each unused element next in the current partial permutation, mark it as used, recurse to fill the remaining positions, then unmark it (backtrack) before trying the next candidate element, with the base case being a partial permutation that has reached full length.

mandatory: try each unused element at the current position, recursing after marking it used
backtrack by unmarking the element after the recursive call returns, before trying the next candidate
concept_groups: iterate over all elements not yet used in the current partial permutation
mark the chosen element as used and append it to the current permutation before recursing
base case: when the partial permutation reaches the full array length, record it as a complete permutation
after the recursive call returns, undo the choice (unmark and remove) before trying the next candidate
advanced_bonus: this produces exactly n! permutations for n distinct elements, since there are n choices for the first position, n-1 for the second, and so on
the 'used' tracking can be done with a boolean array, a visited set, or by swapping elements in-place and swapping back (an alternative backtracking style avoiding extra space)
backtracking (undoing the choice) after each recursive call is essential; without it, elements would incorrectly appear reused or the partial permutation state would leak between branches
overall time complexity is O(n! * n), since there are n! permutations and each takes O(n) time to construct/copy

if the input array contains duplicate elements, naive backtracking produces duplicate permutations and needs additional pruning (e.g. skipping a duplicate value already tried at the same recursive level)

semantic_targets: Each recursive level tries every currently unused element
Marking and unmarking (backtracking) maintains correct state across branches
Base case is reached when the partial permutation is full length
Total permutations generated is n! for n distinct elements
common_mistakes: forgets to unmark/backtrack an element after its recursive branch returns, causing that element to become permanently unusable in sibling branches
allows the same element to be chosen twice within a single permutation by not tracking which elements are already used
does not correctly identify the base case, either never terminating or recording incomplete permutations
for inputs with duplicate values, does not add any de-duplication logic and produces repeated identical permutations unnecessarily

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct mark/unmark backtracking across recursive branches

logic_context: Recursively build a string one character at a time, tracking the count of open and close parentheses used so far; add an open parenthesis whenever the open count is less than n, and add a close parenthesis whenever the close count is less than the open count, recording a complete valid combination once the string reaches length 2n.

mandatory: track counts of open and close parentheses placed so far
only add '(' if open count < n, and only add ')' if close count < open count
concept_groups: adding '(' is allowed whenever fewer than n opens have been placed
adding ')' is allowed only when fewer closes than opens have been placed, ensuring validity at every prefix
base case: once the string length reaches 2n, record it as a valid combination
backtrack by removing the last added character before trying the other choice
advanced_bonus: the constraint 'close count < open count' at every step guarantees every PREFIX of the string is valid (never more closing than opening brackets at any point), which is the core invariant of balanced parentheses
this approach generates only valid combinations directly (no post-filtering needed), unlike a brute-force approach that generates all 2^(2n) strings and filters for validity afterward
the total number of valid combinations generated is the nth Catalan number, C(2n, n)/(n+1)
time complexity is bounded by O(4^n / sqrt(n)) corresponding to the Catalan number growth rate, since that's exactly how many valid strings exist to construct

no explicit backtracking 'undo' array is needed since building the string with normal recursion (passing a new string/StringBuilder slice at each call) naturally isolates each branch, though an in-place mutable buffer approach does require explicit backtracking

semantic_targets: Open count bounded by n, close count bounded by open count
Validity invariant is maintained at every prefix, not just the final string
Direct generation avoids wasteful brute-force filtering
Total combinations generated equals the nth Catalan number
common_mistakes: generates all 2^(2n) possible bracket strings first and filters for validity afterward, which is correct but far less efficient than direct constrained generation
allows adding a close parenthesis even when it would exceed the current open count, producing invalid intermediate strings
does not cap the open-parenthesis count at n, allowing strings longer than 2n or with too many open brackets
forgets to backtrack (undo the last character) when using a shared mutable buffer across recursive branches

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct open/close count constraints enforcing prefix validity

logic_context: For each starting cell matching the word's first letter, recursively try to match subsequent letters by exploring all four adjacent directions, temporarily marking the current cell as visited to prevent reuse, and backtracking (un-marking) if a path fails to continue the match, until either the whole word is matched or all options are exhausted.

mandatory: temporarily mark a cell as visited while exploring from it, to prevent reusing it in the same path
backtrack by un-marking the cell if the current path fails to complete the word
concept_groups: try each of the 4 adjacent directions (up, down, left, right) from the current cell
only proceed into a neighbor if it matches the next required letter and hasn't been visited in this path
base case: all letters of the word matched means success
after exploring a direction fails, un-mark the current cell before returning, so other paths can reuse it
advanced_bonus: marking cells as visited only for the DURATION of the current recursive path (and un-marking on backtrack) is essential, since the same cell may be legitimately reusable in a different, unrelated path attempt
marking can be done with a separate visited boolean grid, or by temporarily overwriting the cell's letter with a sentinel character and restoring it afterward
worst-case time complexity is O(rows * cols * 4^L) where L is the word length, since each of the up to 4^L possible paths may be explored from each of the rows*cols starting cells
early termination (returning true as soon as a complete match path is found) avoids unnecessary further exploration once an answer is confirmed
this four-directional backtracking-with-undo pattern is the same core template used in maze-solving and other grid-path search problems

semantic_targets: Visited marking prevents reusing a cell within the same path
Un-marking (backtracking) restores the cell for other path attempts
Four-directional exploration is tried from each matching cell
Early success return avoids unnecessary further search
common_mistakes: marks a cell as permanently visited across the entire search (never un-marking), incorrectly preventing that cell from being used in a different, valid path
does not restrict movement to the four orthogonal directions, allowing diagonal moves which the problem doesn't permit
forgets to check that a candidate neighbor's letter actually matches the next required letter before recursing into it
fails to try all four directions from a cell, missing some valid paths by only checking one or two directions

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct temporary-marking and backtracking across directional exploration

logic_context: Maintain three pointers: low marking the boundary for 0s, mid as the current scanning pointer, and high marking the boundary for 2s; swap and advance pointers based on whether the element at mid is 0, 1, or 2, until mid crosses high, achieving a sorted array in a single pass.

mandatory: maintain three pointers (low, mid, high) partitioning the array into 0s, 1s, and 2s regions
swap and advance pointers differently depending on whether arr[mid] is 0, 1, or 2
concept_groups: if arr[mid] == 0, swap with low, increment both low and mid
if arr[mid] == 1, just increment mid (already in correct region)
if arr[mid] == 2, swap with high, decrement high only (do not increment mid, since the swapped-in value needs re-checking)
advanced_bonus: the mid pointer must NOT advance after a swap with high, because the newly swapped-in element at mid hasn't been examined yet and could itself be a 0, 1, or 2

the mid pointer SHOULD advance after a swap with low, because the element swapped in from the low region is already known to be a 1 (since everything before mid that isn't 0 has already been classified as 1)
this achieves O(n) time and O(1) extra space in a single pass, unlike a counting-sort-style two-pass approach (count then overwrite) which also works but is conceptually a different technique
this is a specific 3-way variant of the general quicksort partitioning scheme (3-way partitioning), useful whenever there are few distinct key values to sort by
at the end of the process, elements before 'low' are all 0s, between low and mid are all 1s, and after high are all 2s

semantic_targets: Three pointers track boundaries of the 0/1/2 partitions
Swap-with-high requires NOT advancing mid immediately
Swap-with-low safely advances mid since the swapped value is known to be 1
Achieves single-pass O(n) time with O(1) space
common_mistakes: advances the mid pointer immediately after every swap (including swaps with high), skipping over an unexamined element that was just swapped in
uses a separate counting pass (count zeros, ones, twos, then overwrite the array) when a true single-pass in-place partition is expected
mixes up which boundary (low or high) to swap with based on the element's value, misclassifying partitions
terminates the loop condition incorrectly (e.g. mid < high instead of mid <= high), leaving the last element unprocessed

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct conditional pointer-advance rule distinguishing the three cases

logic_context: Radix sort processes integers digit by digit, from the least significant digit to the most significant digit, using a stable sort (typically counting sort) as a subroutine at each digit position, so that the final ordering after processing the most significant digit reflects the full correct sort order.

mandatory: sort by individual digit positions, from least significant to most significant
use a STABLE sort (such as counting sort) as the subroutine at each digit pass
concept_groups: process digits starting from the least significant (rightmost)
after each digit pass, the relative order established by less-significant digits must be preserved
use counting sort (or another stable sort) for each digit pass, since digits are bounded (0-9)
repeat for as many digit positions as the maximum number of digits among all elements
advanced_bonus: stability of the per-digit sort is absolutely essential: without it, the ordering established by earlier (less significant) digit passes would be destroyed by later passes
radix sort runs in O(d * (n + k)) time, where d is the number of digits and k is the digit range (usually 10 for base-10 digits), which can beat O(n log n) when d is small relative to log n
radix sort is not a comparison-based sort, so it is not bound by the Omega(n log n) lower bound that applies to comparison sorts
processing from least to most significant digit (LSD radix sort) is the common approach; an MSD (most significant digit first) variant also exists but is more complex to implement correctly
radix sort's efficiency advantage shrinks or disappears for very large numbers (many digits) or non-numeric/variable-length keys, where comparison sorts become relatively more competitive

semantic_targets: Digit-by-digit processing from least to most significant
Stable sort subroutine required to preserve earlier passes' ordering
Not bound by the comparison-sort lower bound of Omega(n log n)
Efficiency depends on the number of digits relative to n
common_mistakes: processes digits from most significant to least significant without the additional complexity MSD radix sort actually requires, incorrectly assuming the simpler LSD-style per-digit pass still works
uses an unstable sort (e.g. plain quicksort) for the per-digit pass, destroying the ordering accumulated from previous digit passes
claims radix sort violates the comparison-sort lower bound as if it were a flaw, rather than correctly recognizing it bypasses that bound BECAUSE it isn't comparison-based
does not account for all elements' maximum digit count, stopping the digit passes too early and leaving some numbers improperly sorted

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct explanation of stability requirement and LSD processing order

logic_context: Insert all elements into a hash set for O(1) lookups; for each element, only start counting a sequence if that element's predecessor (value - 1) is NOT in the set (meaning it's the start of a sequence), then count forward (value + 1, value + 2, ...) while those values exist in the set, tracking the longest run found.

mandatory: insert all elements into a hash set first for O(1) membership checks
only begin counting a sequence from elements whose predecessor (value-1) is absent from the set
concept_groups: for each element, check if value - 1 exists in the set
skip elements that have a predecessor present, since they aren't the start of their sequence
for true sequence starts, count forward while value+1, value+2, ... exist in the set
track the maximum sequence length found across all starting points
advanced_bonus: the 'only start from sequence beginnings' check is what guarantees overall O(n) time: even though there's a nested while loop, each element is only ever extended from once across the entire algorithm (as part of exactly one sequence's forward count)

without the predecessor check, the algorithm would redundantly re-count the same sequence from every one of its elements, degrading to O(n^2) in the worst case (e.g. for a single long consecutive run)
a naive approach of sorting the array first also solves this problem but costs O(n log n), which this hash-set approach improves upon by achieving true O(n)
duplicate values in the input don't affect the sequence length calculation if the set is used, since a hash set naturally de-duplicates values
this technique only requires O(n) extra space for the hash set in exchange for its linear time guarantee

semantic_targets: Hash set provides O(1) existence checks
Predecessor check identifies true sequence starting points
Forward counting is only ever done once per actual sequence, bounding total work to O(n)
Hash-set approach beats the O(n log n) sort-based alternative
common_mistakes: omits the predecessor check and attempts to count forward from every element, causing the same sequence to be recounted multiple times and degrading to O(n^2)
sorts the array first and scans for consecutive runs, which is correct but O(n log n), not the optimal O(n) hash-set approach being asked for
uses a list instead of a hash set for membership checks, making each lookup O(n) instead of O(1) and defeating the purpose of the technique
does not handle duplicate values in the input correctly, over-counting or under-counting sequence length because of repeated entries

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct predecessor-check optimization ensuring O(n) overall time

logic_context: A skip list is a layered linked-list structure where each higher layer acts as an 'express lane' skipping over multiple elements of the layer below; when inserting a new node, a random coin-flip process decides how many layers it participates in, so that on average a constant fraction of nodes exist at each higher layer, giving an expected logarithmic number of layers to traverse.

mandatory: layered linked lists where higher layers skip over more elements of the base list
random coin-flip determines a new node's height (how many layers it appears in), giving expected O(log n) height
concept_groups: base layer contains all elements in sorted order
each higher layer is a sparser subset, roughly halving the elements with each layer up
search starts at the topmost layer and drops down a layer whenever the next node would overshoot the target
insertion randomly decides the new node's height via repeated coin flips, then links it into each of those layers
advanced_bonus: skip lists achieve the same expected O(log n) search/insert/delete performance as balanced trees (like AVL or Red-Black trees) but with a much simpler implementation, avoiding complex rotation logic

the probabilistic (randomized) height assignment is what gives the EXPECTED (not guaranteed worst-case) O(log n) bound; an adversarial or extremely unlucky sequence of coin flips could in theory produce worse performance
typically each node has a 1/2 (or some fixed p) probability of being promoted to the next higher layer, leading to an expected O(log n) total height across all layers

skip lists are used in real systems such as Redis's sorted sets and some LSM-tree-based storage engines, precisely because of their simplicity combined with good expected performance and natural support for ordered range queries
unlike balanced BSTs, skip lists require no complex rebalancing operations on insertion or deletion, since structure is maintained purely through randomization

semantic_targets: Layered sparse lists allow skipping over multiple base-list elements at once
Randomized height assignment gives expected logarithmic layer count
Performance is expected/probabilistic, not a hard worst-case guarantee like balanced trees
Simpler to implement than rotation-based self-balancing trees
common_mistakes: claims skip lists guarantee worst-case O(log n) performance, confusing the expected (probabilistic) bound with the worst-case guarantee of deterministic balanced trees
describes the layers as a fixed, deterministic structure rather than one built via randomized coin-flip height assignment
confuses a skip list with a simple multi-level index without explaining the probabilistic promotion mechanism that keeps layers sparse
overlooks that skip lists avoid the complex rebalancing logic (rotations) required by self-balancing trees, understating their simplicity advantage

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct explanation of randomized layering and expected complexity

logic_context: A circular subarray either lies within the array (the normal Kadane maximum) or wraps around the ends. A wrapping subarray equals the total sum minus a contiguous middle part, so its best value is total sum minus the minimum subarray sum (found with a Kadane variant). logic_context: C does not specify the order in which operands of most operators or function arguments are evaluated. Modifying the same object more than once, or reading it while modifying it, without an intervening sequence point is undefined behaviour, as in i = i++ + ++i.

logic_context: A persistent data structure keeps all its previous versions accessible after updates, instead of modifying in place. logic_context: Standard BFS explores roughly b^d nodes, where b is the branching factor and d is the path length, which is enormous with b = 200. logic_context: Tombstones mark deleted slots so that probe sequences of other keys are not broken; deletion is simple and O(1) after finding the key, but tombstones accumulate, lengthen probe sequences and require periodic rehashing. logic_context: A simple additive checksum is cheap but misses many errors such as swapped bytes. logic_context: Sending raw struct bytes is simple and fast but not portable: padding bytes, alignment, member sizes (for example long) and endianness can all differ between machines or compilers, and uninitialised padding may leak data. logic_context: Build two chains with dummy heads: one for nodes less than x and one for nodes greater than or equal to x. Traverse the original list, appending each node to the tail of the correct chain. Finally connect the tail of the first chain to the head of the second and set the last node's next to NULL. O(n) time and O(1) extra space because existing nodes are relinked.

mandatory: two separate chains for less-than and greater-or-equal
connect tail of first chain to head of second
concept_groups: appending at the tail preserves order
set final tail's next to NULL
reuse existing nodes without new allocation
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
terminating the second chain prevents a cycle
stable: relative order preserved within each part
works when all nodes fall into one group
unlike the array partition in quicksort, this version is stable

semantic_targets: Split into two order-preserving chains and join them
relinking nodes rather than copying values keeps space O(1)
common_mistakes: Forgetting to set the last node's next to NULL — creates a cycle
Swapping values in a way that breaks relative order
mishandles the case where one partition is empty
loses the head of the resulting list

logic_context: Set odd = head, even = head->next, and save evenHead = even. While even and even->next exist: odd->next = even->next; odd = odd->next; even->next = odd->next; even = even->next. Finally attach the even chain after the last odd node with odd->next = evenHead. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

mandatory: separate odd-position and even-position chains
attach even chain after the last odd node
concept_groups: save the head of the even chain
advance odd and even pointers alternately
loop while even and even->next exist
positions, not values, decide odd or even
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
handles lists of length 0, 1 and 2
relative order preserved in both groups
the loop condition prevents NULL dereference
similar pattern to splitting a list into two interleaved halves

semantic_targets: Odd and even refer to node positions
Two interleaved chains are unlinked and rejoined
The even head must be saved before rewiring
next pointers are rewired in place without extra nodes
common_mistakes: Using node values instead of positions
creates new nodes instead of relinking

logic_context: If both nodes are NULL, return true; if exactly one is NULL, return false. Otherwise the node values must be equal, the two left subtrees must be identical, and the two right subtrees must be identical. Time O(n), recursion depth O(h).

mandatory: base case: both NULL returns true, only one NULL returns false
compare values and recurse on left and right subtrees
concept_groups: left compared with left, right with right
both recursive calls must return true
advanced_bonus: O(min(n1, n2)) time, O(h) recursion depth
iterative version uses a queue of node pairs
comparing only traversal outputs can fail unless NULL markers are included
differs from the mirror check, which compares left with right
used as a helper in the subtree-of-another-tree problem

semantic_targets: Identical means both shape and values match
NULL cases are handled before dereferencing
The recursion follows the tree structure
compare corresponding children: left with left and right with right
common_mistakes: misses the case where only one node is NULL

logic_context: Print the root (if it is not a leaf). Left boundary: starting at root->left, repeatedly move to the left child (or the right child if there is no left), printing non-leaf nodes top-down. Leaves: a DFS that prints leaf nodes from left to right. Right boundary: starting at root->right, prefer the right child (else left), collect non-leaf nodes, and print them in reverse. Excluding leaves from the boundary walks avoids printing any node twice. O(n).

mandatory: left boundary top-down excluding leaves
leaves left to right, then right boundary bottom-up
concept_groups: left boundary prefers left child, else right child
right boundary prefers right child, else left child
exclude leaf nodes from the boundary walks
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(h) space
right boundary collected on a stack (or printed after the recursive call) to reverse it
single-node tree: the root is also a leaf — print it once
skewed trees are handled by the fallback-child rule
this anticlockwise order is the standard convention

semantic_targets: Three parts: left boundary, leaves, reversed right boundary
Fallback child is used when the preferred child is missing
leaves come from a full DFS, not just from the boundary paths
common_mistakes: Printing leaves twice (in a boundary and in the leaf pass)
Using the first/last node of each level, which gives the left/right view instead
does not handle a missing left subtree

logic_context: Nodes at distance K may lie below the target or be reached by going up through ancestors. First record each node's parent with a DFS or BFS. Then run BFS from the target, treating the tree as an undirected graph whose neighbours are left child, right child, and parent, using a visited set. The nodes in BFS level K are the answer. O(n) time and space.

mandatory: store the parent of each node
BFS from the target in all three directions with a visited set
concept_groups: treat the tree as an undirected graph
advanced_bonus: O(n) time and space

Parent links turn the tree into a graph
BFS from the target over child and parent edges finds every node at level K
common_mistakes: Forgetting the visited set — infinite loop or duplicates
Measuring distance from the root instead of the target
misses nodes in the sibling subtrees of ancestors

logic_context: Treat each square as a node and each legal knight move (8 possible offsets) as an edge of equal cost, so BFS from the start gives the minimum number of moves. Keep a visited grid, enqueue squares with their distance, skip moves that leave the board, and return the distance when the target is reached.

mandatory: BFS for unweighted shortest path
8 knight-move offsets as neighbours

return when the target is reached
advanced_bonus: O(N²) time and space — each square visited at most once

DFS does not guarantee the minimum number of moves

the first time BFS reaches the target gives the minimum
common_mistakes: marks squares visited only when dequeued — causes duplicate enqueues
uses Dijkstra when all moves cost the same

evaluation_rubric.focus: BFS on an implicit grid graph

logic_context: Start with every vertex in its own set. For each edge (u, v), find the roots of u and v. If the roots are the same, u and v are already connected, so this edge closes a cycle. Otherwise, union the two sets. With path compression and union by rank, each operation is nearly constant time.

mandatory: find roots of both endpoints for each edge
same root means the edge creates a cycle
concept_groups: union the sets when roots differ
initially each vertex is its own parent
advanced_bonus: O(E · α(V)) time — nearly linear
α is the inverse Ackermann function, at most 4 in practice
the same check is used in Kruskal's algorithm to reject cycle-forming edges

semantic_targets: An edge joining two already-connected vertices closes a cycle
Optimisations make operations almost constant time

common_mistakes: Performing the union before checking roots
Comparing immediate parents instead of roots
does not initialise each node as its own parent
no mention of path compression or union by rank

logic_context: Let dp[a] be the number of ways to make amount a, with dp[0] = 1. Loop over coins in the outer loop and over amounts from that coin's value up to the target in the inner loop, adding dp[a - coin] to dp[a]. Putting coins in the outer loop counts combinations rather than ordered sequences. O(n × amount) time, O(amount) space.

mandatory: dp[0] = 1 base case
dp[a] += dp[a - coin] with coins in the outer loop
concept_groups: loop order counts combinations, not permutations
inner loop over amounts from coin up to target

advanced_bonus: O(coins × amount) time, O(amount) space

a descending inner loop would allow each coin only once (0/1 knapsack behaviour)

semantic_targets: The task counts ways, not the minimum number of coins
There is exactly one way to make zero
Loop order decides combinations versus permutations
each coin extends the ways to make amount - coin
common_mistakes: Amount loop outside the coin loop — counts permutations
descending inner loop — treats coins as single-use
plain recursion without memoisation — exponential time

evaluation_rubric.focus: Correct counting recurrence and loop order

logic_context: Let dp[e][f] be the minimum worst-case drops with e eggs and f floors. Dropping from floor x: if the egg breaks, solve dp[e-1][x-1]; if it survives, solve dp[e][f-x]. So dp[e][f] = 1 + min over x of max(dp[e-1][x-1], dp[e][f-x]). Base cases: 0 floors needs 0 drops, 1 egg needs f drops. This is O(k·n²), improvable with binary search on x, or by the reformulation 'floors coverable with m moves and e eggs' = f(m-1, e-1) + f(m-1, e) + 1.

mandatory: minimise over the drop floor the worst case of break versus survive
break: e-1 eggs and floors below; survive: e eggs and floors above
concept_groups: base cases: one egg needs f drops, zero floors needs 0
worst case is the max of the two outcomes
binary search on x or the moves-based DP improves it
advanced_bonus: alternative DP: f(m, e) = f(m-1, e-1) + f(m-1, e) + 1 floors coverable with m moves
answer = smallest m with f(m, k) >= n
break cost increases with x and survive cost decreases, so binary search finds the crossover
with 2 eggs and 100 floors the answer is 14
plain recursion is exponential — memoisation is required

semantic_targets: The worst case drives the max; the best floor choice drives the min
dp[e][f] = 1 + min over x of max(dp[e-1][x-1], dp[e][f-x])
common_mistakes: Using min instead of max for the two outcomes
Plain binary search over floors, ignoring egg loss
Wrong base case for one egg
treats it as a greedy problem
ignores the floors above when the egg survives

logic_context: Keep a stack of indices whose prices are strictly decreasing. For each day i, pop indices whose price is less than or equal to today's price. The span is i + 1 if the stack is empty, otherwise i minus the index on top. Then push i. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total time is O(n).

mandatory: monotonic decreasing stack of indices
pop while the earlier price <= current price
concept_groups: span = i - index of previous greater price
span = i + 1 when the stack is empty
each index pushed and popped once
advanced_bonus: O(n) amortised time, O(n) space

Popped elements can never be the boundary again

Storing prices without indices or spans

evaluation_rubric.focus: Monotonic stack for previous greater element

logic_context: Use a max-heap of size K keyed by squared distance x² + y². For each point, push it; if the heap grows beyond K, pop the farthest point. After processing all points, the heap holds the K closest. O(n log K) time and O(K) space. Squared distance keeps the same order and avoids sqrt.

mandatory: max-heap of size K keyed by distance
pop the farthest point when size exceeds K

heap holds the current K best points
advanced_bonus: O(n log K) beats sorting O(n log n) when K is small

Sorting all points without noting the cost
does not limit the heap size to K

logic_context: Search x in the range [0, n]. For each mid, if mid * mid <= n, record mid as a candidate and move right (lo = mid + 1); otherwise move left (hi = mid - 1). The last recorded candidate is the answer. Use mid <= n / mid or 64-bit multiplication to avoid overflow. O(log n).

mandatory: binary search over the answer range 0..n
mid * mid <= n moves right, otherwise left
concept_groups: keep the last mid with mid * mid <= n

advanced_bonus: overflow-safe check: mid <= n / mid (for mid > 0)

semantic_targets: The condition x * x <= n is monotonic
Record the best candidate so far

common_mistakes: Off by one — returns the ceiling
Infinite loop from wrong bound updates
uses floating-point sqrt without addressing precision

evaluation_rubric.focus: Binary search on the answer with overflow safety

logic_context: XOR all elements: pairs cancel, leaving x = a ^ b, which is non-zero because a and b differ. Pick any set bit of x, for example the lowest set bit x & -x; a and b differ at that bit. Split all numbers by whether that bit is set and XOR each group separately — the duplicates cancel within their group, leaving a in one group and b in the other. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: XOR of all elements equals a ^ b
split elements by a set bit of a ^ b
concept_groups: that bit differs between a and b
duplicates land in the same group and cancel
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(1) space
x & (-x) isolates the rightmost set bit; use unsigned arithmetic to avoid overflow for INT_MIN
a ^ b is non-zero because a ≠ b
extends the single-number XOR trick

semantic_targets: A differing bit separates the two unique numbers
Each group reduces to the single-number problem
partition by a bit where a and b differ, then XOR each partition
common_mistakes: Choosing a bit that is not set in a ^ b
Using sorting or hashing while claiming O(1) space
assumes the two numbers are adjacent

evaluation_rubric.focus: XOR partition by a differing bit

logic_context: Find an empty cell and try digits 1 to 9. Place a digit only if it does not already appear in the same row, column, or 3x3 box, then recurse. If the recursion fails, undo the placement (reset the cell to empty) and try the next digit. If no digit works, return false so the caller backtracks. When no empty cell remains, the puzzle is solved. Row, column, and box boolean arrays make each validity check O(1).

mandatory: try digits 1-9 in an empty cell
check row, column and 3x3 box before placing
concept_groups: undo the placement when recursion fails
return true when no empty cells remain
advanced_bonus: row/column/box used-arrays or bitmasks give O(1) checks

worst case is exponential, but pruning makes typical puzzles fast

semantic_targets: Backtracking explores choices and undoes failed ones
Search ends when the grid is full
place, recurse, and undo if the branch fails
common_mistakes: Checking only the row and column, not the 3x3 box
continues searching after a solution is found

logic_context: Consistent hashing places both servers and keys on a hash ring; each key is stored on the first server found moving clockwise from the key's position. When a server is added or removed, only the keys in its neighbouring range move — about K/N keys on average — unlike hash(key) mod N, which remaps almost every key when N changes. Virtual nodes give each server several ring positions to balance load.

mandatory: keys and servers placed on a hash ring
adding or removing a server moves only a small fraction of keys
concept_groups: key assigned to the next server clockwise
hash mod N remaps most keys when N changes
advanced_bonus: on average only K/N keys move when a node joins or leaves
virtual nodes smooth uneven distribution and support servers of different capacity
used in Dynamo-style stores, Cassandra and memcached client libraries
replication: store each key on the next R distinct servers clockwise
lookup via a sorted list of ring positions and binary search — O(log N)

semantic_targets: A ring structure replaces modulo assignment
mod-N hashing reshuffles nearly all keys when the server count changes
common_mistakes: Describing it as ordinary hash-table hashing
Claiming that no keys move at all
Ignoring load imbalance and virtual nodes

evaluation_rubric.focus: Minimal remapping on a hash ring

logic_context: A deque allows insertion and deletion at both the front and the rear in O(1) time. It can be implemented with a circular array or a doubly linked list. It generalises both stacks and queues and is used in problems such as the sliding-window maximum, 0-1 BFS, and undo/redo histories.

mandatory: insert and delete at both ends
O(1) operations at front and rear
concept_groups: can act as a stack or a queue
used in sliding-window maximum or 0-1 BFS
advanced_bonus: push_front, push_back, pop_front and pop_back are all O(1)

input-restricted and output-restricted deque variants

semantic_targets: a deque supports push and pop at both front and back

logic_context: A sparse matrix is one in which most elements are zero. Storing every element wastes memory, so only non-zero entries are kept — for example in triplet/coordinate format (row, column, value), as a linked list per row, or in Compressed Sparse Row format (values, column indices, row pointers). Memory then grows with the number of non-zero entries rather than rows × columns.

mandatory: most elements are zero
store only the non-zero elements
concept_groups: memory proportional to the number of non-zeros
advanced_bonus: CSR uses values[], col_index[] and row_ptr[], with row_ptr of size rows + 1

worthwhile only when non-zeros are far fewer than rows × columns
random access is slower than in a dense 2D array

semantic_targets: Memory scales with the non-zero count

common_mistakes: Defining sparse as a small matrix
confuses it with a diagonal matrix only

logic_context: In a threaded binary tree, NULL child pointers are replaced by 'threads' that point to the node's inorder predecessor or successor, with flag bits to tell threads apart from real children. This lets inorder traversal run without recursion or a stack, using O(1) extra space, and puts the n + 1 otherwise-unused NULL pointers to work.

traversal without a stack or recursion

common_mistakes: Saying threads point to the parent

logic_context: An AVL tree keeps every node's balance factor (height of left minus height of right) in {-1, 0, 1}. After an insertion or deletion, an unbalanced node is fixed by rotations: LL case (left child's left subtree too tall) → single right rotation; RR case → single left rotation; LR case → left rotation on the left child, then right rotation; RL case → right rotation on the right child, then left rotation. Rotations preserve BST order and take O(1).

mandatory: balance factor must stay in -1, 0, 1
LL/RR use a single rotation, LR/RL use a double rotation
advanced_bonus: rotations preserve inorder (BST) order
each rotation is O(1); heights are updated afterwards
the case is chosen from the balance factors of the node and its child

right rotation fixes left-left heavy; left rotation fixes right-right heavy

Using a single rotation for LR or RL
does not update heights after rotating

logic_context: A tree is a connected, acyclic, undirected graph; with n nodes it has exactly n - 1 edges and a unique path between any two nodes. A general graph may contain cycles, may be disconnected, may be directed, and may have any number of edges. A rooted tree adds a parent-child hierarchy.

mandatory: a tree is connected and acyclic
a tree with n nodes has n - 1 edges
concept_groups: graphs may be disconnected or directed

advanced_bonus: every tree is a graph, but not every graph is a tree

logic_context: An Eulerian path uses every edge exactly once; an Eulerian circuit is an Eulerian path that starts and ends at the same vertex. In a connected undirected graph (ignoring isolated vertices), a circuit exists if and only if every vertex has even degree, and a path exists if and only if exactly zero or two vertices have odd degree — the path then starts and ends at the two odd-degree vertices.

Saying one odd-degree vertex allows a path

logic_context: Shell sort performs gapped insertion sorts: elements a fixed gap apart are sorted, then the gap shrinks until it reaches 1, which is an ordinary insertion sort. Large gaps move elements far in few steps, so by the final pass the array is nearly sorted, where insertion sort is fast. Its running time depends on the gap sequence; it sorts in place but is not stable.

gap reduces until it reaches 1
concept_groups: final pass runs on nearly sorted data
advanced_bonus: complexity depends on the gap sequence: Shell's original n/2, n/4, ... is O(n²) in the worst case; Knuth's (3^k - 1)/2 is about O(n^1.5)

O(1) extra space

The last pass is a normal insertion sort

logic_context: Use-after-free means accessing memory through a pointer after free() has released it; double-free means calling free() twice on the same block. Both are undefined behaviour, can corrupt the heap allocator, and are common security vulnerabilities. Prevention: set the pointer to NULL after free, keep a single clear owner for each allocation, and avoid stale aliases. Detection: tools such as Valgrind and AddressSanitizer.

double-free calls free twice on the same block

tools such as Valgrind or AddressSanitizer

other copies (aliases) of the pointer still dangle after one is set to NULL

Confusing these errors with memory leaks
thinks nulling one pointer also fixes its aliases

logic_context: A declaration tells the compiler a name and its type (for example extern int x; or int f(int);) without allocating storage or giving a function body. logic_context: Space complexity measures how much memory an algorithm uses as a function of input size; auxiliary space excludes the input itself. For recursion, each active call holds a stack frame, so auxiliary space is at least the maximum recursion depth times the space per frame, plus any extra data structures allocated. For example, recursive factorial uses O(n) stack, and merge sort uses O(log n) stack plus an O(n) merge buffer.

include extra arrays that are allocated

Auxiliary space differs from total space

logic_context: A Fenwick tree is a 1-indexed array in which tree[i] stores the sum of a range ending at i whose length equals the lowest set bit of i. A prefix-sum query adds tree[i] and moves to i -= i & (-i) until i is 0. A point update adds the change to tree[i] and moves to i += i & (-i) while i <= n. Both take O(log n) with O(n) space, and a range sum is prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1).

mandatory: each index stores the sum of a range sized by its lowest set bit
query and update in O(log n)
advanced_bonus: O(n) space; simpler and smaller than a segment tree

A compact alternative to a segment tree
move down with i -= lowbit for queries and up with i += lowbit for updates
common_mistakes: Swapping the update and query directions
says it supports range minimum easily

logic_context: Signed integers can hold negative and positive values (almost always using two's complement), while unsigned integers hold only non-negative values but have twice the positive range for the same number of bits. Unsigned arithmetic wraps around modulo 2^n, whereas signed overflow is undefined behaviour. Mixing the two in a comparison converts the signed value to unsigned, which causes subtle bugs.

unsigned stores only non-negative values with a larger positive range
concept_groups: same number of bits, different range
advanced_bonus: -1 < 0u is false because -1 converts to UINT_MAX
printf uses %d for signed and %u for unsigned
size_t is unsigned — a loop counting down with i >= 0 never ends

For each i inside R, start with P[i] = min(R - i, P[2C - i]) using the mirror position, then expand outward. If i + P[i] > R, move C to i and R to i + P[i]. The largest P[i] gives the longest palindrome. O(n).
