common_mistakes: Checking only that t's values appear in s
Matching only part of the descendants
stops after the first matching value without full comparison

logic_context: Do a level-order traversal and give each node a position index as in a complete binary tree: left child 2i + 1 and right child 2i + 2 (0-based). For each level, width = last index - first index + 1, and the answer is the maximum. To avoid overflow on deep trees, subtract the level's first index from every index on that level before computing children.

mandatory: assign heap-style position indices to nodes
width = last index - first index + 1 per level
concept_groups: normalise indices per level to avoid overflow
answer is the maximum over levels
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(width) queue space
null positions between nodes count toward width
skewed trees make indices grow like 2^depth — normalisation or 64-bit ints prevent overflow
DFS alternative stores the first index seen at each depth
counting only non-null nodes per level gives a different answer

semantic_targets: Positions, not node counts, define width
width spans from leftmost to rightmost non-null node
common_mistakes: Counting only non-null nodes per level
Index overflow on deep skewed trees
computes width only for the last level
uses the overall tree width instead of per level

logic_context: Do an inorder traversal, which visits nodes in sorted order, while keeping a pointer prev to the previously visited node. At each node, set prev->right = node and node->left = prev (or record node as the head if prev is NULL), then set prev = node. After the traversal, prev is the tail; for a circular list, link head and tail. O(n) time, O(h) stack.

mandatory: inorder traversal gives sorted order
link prev->right = current and current->left = prev
concept_groups: first visited node becomes the head
optional: link head and tail for circular list
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(h) recursion stack
Morris-style traversal can reduce extra space to O(1)
the original tree structure is destroyed
circular version connects head->left = tail and tail->right = head
divide-and-conquer alternative converts subtrees and joins lists

semantic_targets: Inorder order equals sorted order for a BST
left becomes previous and right becomes next
common_mistakes: Using preorder or level order — not sorted
Losing the head of the list
overwrites node->right before visiting the right subtree

logic_context: Compute a topological order of the DAG. Set the source's distance to 0 and all others to infinity. Process vertices in topological order; for each vertex with a finite distance, relax every outgoing edge (u, v, w): dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w). Because all predecessors of a vertex are processed before it, each vertex's distance is final when reached. O(V + E), and it works even with negative edge weights.

mandatory: process vertices in topological order
relax all outgoing edges of each vertex
concept_groups: no cycles, so each vertex finalised once
advanced_bonus: O(V + E) time — faster than Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford
negative edges are fine because there are no cycles
longest path in a DAG: negate weights or use max instead of min
used in project scheduling (critical path method)
topological order from Kahn's algorithm or DFS finish times

semantic_targets: Topological order guarantees predecessors are done first
DAG shortest paths are linear time
common_mistakes: Using Dijkstra and saying negative weights are fine
Applying the method to graphs with cycles
claims O(V log V) or higher

logic_context: At most K stops means at most K + 1 edges, so run a Bellman-Ford style relaxation for exactly K + 1 rounds. In each round, copy the current distance array and relax every flight using the old copy, so each round extends paths by at most one edge. After K + 1 rounds, the destination's distance is the answer (or -1 if unreachable). O(K · E). A BFS by levels or Dijkstra on (city, stops) states also works.

mandatory: at most K stops means at most K + 1 edges
relax all edges for K + 1 rounds using a copy of the previous distances
concept_groups: copy the distance array each round
each round adds at most one edge
advanced_bonus: O(K · E) time, O(V) space
without the copy, one round could chain several edges and break the stop limit
plain Dijkstra fails because a cheaper path may use too many stops
Dijkstra on state (city, stops used) is a valid alternative
BFS by levels with pruning by cost per level is another option

semantic_targets: Stop limit translates into an edge limit
Copying prevents using updates from the same round
the number of rounds bounds the path length
common_mistakes: Running plain Dijkstra ignoring the stop limit
Not copying the distance array between rounds
Running K rounds instead of K + 1
runs V - 1 rounds as in standard Bellman-Ford

logic_context: Let dp[i][j] be the side length of the largest all-1s square whose bottom-right corner is at (i, j). If the cell is 0, dp[i][j] = 0; otherwise dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]). Track the maximum side; the answer is side². O(m · n) time; space can be reduced to one row.

mandatory: dp[i][j] = side of largest square ending at (i, j)
dp = 1 + min(top, left, top-left) when the cell is 1
concept_groups: first row and column copy the cell value
advanced_bonus: space reduces to O(n) with one row plus a saved diagonal
the min of three neighbours ensures all three squares are full
brute force checks every square — O(m·n·min(m,n)²)
largest rectangle of 1s needs a histogram-stack approach instead
returns area, so remember to square the side

semantic_targets: The smallest neighbouring square limits growth
a square can only grow by one beyond the smallest of its three neighbours
common_mistakes: Returning the side instead of the area
does not initialise the first row and column

logic_context: Let dp[i][j] be true if the first i characters of the string match the first j characters of the pattern. dp[0][0] = true; dp[0][j] is true only if the pattern's first j characters are all '*'. If p[j-1] is '*', dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-1] (star matches empty) or dp[i-1][j] (star matches one more character). If p[j-1] is '?' or equals s[i-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]. Otherwise false. O(m · n).

mandatory: dp[i][j]: first i string chars match first j pattern chars
'*': dp[i][j-1] (empty) or dp[i-1][j] (one more char)
concept_groups: leading '*'s can match an empty string
advanced_bonus: O(m · n) time, O(n) space with rolling rows
consecutive '*'s can be collapsed into one
greedy two-pointer with backtracking to the last '*' gives O(m · n) worst but fast in practice
differs from regex '*', which repeats the previous character
plain recursion without memoisation is exponential

semantic_targets: Star has two choices: empty or consume one
Question mark consumes exactly one character
dp[i-1][j] lets '*' absorb characters one at a time

logic_context: Split the path by '/'. For each part: skip empty strings and '.'; for '..', pop from the stack if it is not empty; otherwise push the directory name. Finally join the stack with '/' and prefix a '/'; if the stack is empty, return '/'. O(n).

mandatory: split by '/' and process each part
'..' pops, '.' and empty parts are skipped
advanced_bonus: O(n) time and space
multiple slashes produce empty parts that are ignored
'...' is a valid directory name, not a special token
stack order matches the path from root
result never ends with '/' unless it is the root

semantic_targets: A stack models moving into and out of directories
Canonical path built from the stack
common_mistakes: Popping on '..' when the stack is empty (error)
returns an empty string instead of '/'

logic_context: Scan the digits left to right with a stack. While k > 0 and the top of the stack is greater than the current digit, pop it and decrement k — removing a larger digit earlier lowers the number most. Push the current digit. If k is still positive at the end, remove digits from the top (the end). Strip leading zeros; return '0' if nothing remains. O(n).

mandatory: pop larger previous digits while k > 0
keep the stack increasing from bottom to top
concept_groups: remove remaining k digits from the end
each digit pushed and popped at most once
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(n) space
greedy is correct: the leftmost position where a digit exceeds its successor is the best removal
removing from the end handles already increasing sequences like '12345'
leading zeros must be removed after building
related to the 'smallest subsequence of distinct characters' problem

semantic_targets: Greedy local choice is globally optimal
remove a digit when the next one is smaller
common_mistakes: Forgetting to use leftover k at the end
returns an empty string instead of '0'

logic_context: Count characters. If any count exceeds (n + 1) / 2, it is impossible. Push (count, char) pairs into a max-heap. Repeatedly pop the two most frequent characters, append both, decrement their counts, and push them back if still positive. If one character remains at the end, append it (its count must be 1). Always using the most frequent characters prevents them from being left adjacent at the end. O(n log σ).

mandatory: impossible if a count exceeds (n + 1) / 2
repeatedly take the two most frequent characters from a max-heap
concept_groups: decrement and push back positive counts
append two different characters at a time
advanced_bonus: O(n log σ) where σ is alphabet size
alternative O(n): place the most frequent character at even indices, then fill the rest
taking two at a time guarantees adjacent characters differ
the same idea generalises to keeping identical characters k apart
greedy by highest count is what prevents a dead end

semantic_targets: The most frequent character limits feasibility
Two pops per step avoid adjacency
common_mistakes: Popping one at a time and appending the same character twice

logic_context: Binary search on a cut position i in the shorter array A; the cut in B is j = (m + n + 1) / 2 - i, so the left parts together hold half the elements. The cut is correct when A[i-1] <= B[j] and B[j-1] <= A[i]. If A[i-1] > B[j], move left; if B[j-1] > A[i], move right. Use -infinity and +infinity for out-of-range neighbours. The median is the max of the left side (odd total) or the average of max-left and min-right (even total).

mandatory: binary search a partition of the shorter array
valid when A[i-1] <= B[j] and B[j-1] <= A[i]
concept_groups: odd total: max of left side
even total: average of max-left and min-right
advanced_bonus: O(log(min(m, n))) time, O(1) space
searching the shorter array keeps j within range
merging is O(m + n) — correct but slower
k-th smallest recursion is an O(log(m + n)) alternative
use floating-point or careful integer division for the even case

semantic_targets: Partition both arrays so left halves are smaller than right halves
the left part holds exactly half of all elements
common_mistakes: Merging both arrays and claiming logarithmic time
Searching the longer array (j may go out of bounds)
integer division error in the even case
wrong direction when adjusting the cut

logic_context: For each of the 32 bit positions, count how many numbers have that bit set. Elements appearing three times contribute a multiple of 3, so count % 3 is the bit of the unique element. Build the result from these bits. O(32 · n) time, O(1) space. A compact version keeps two masks: ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos; twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones; the answer is ones.

mandatory: count each bit position across all numbers
bit count modulo 3 gives the unique element's bit
concept_groups: rebuild the result from the remaining bits
ones and twos masks track counts mod 3
XOR alone fails because triples do not cancel
advanced_bonus: O(32 · n) time, O(1) space
ones/twos state-machine version does it in one pass
handles negative numbers when using 32-bit arithmetic (sign bit included)
generalises to every element appearing k times: count % k
hash map solution uses O(n) space

semantic_targets: Triples contribute multiples of 3 per bit
count set bits per position, then take mod 3
common_mistakes: Using plain XOR of all elements
Forgetting the sign bit for negative numbers
Using a hash map while claiming O(1) space

logic_context: Sort the candidates. Recurse with a start index and the remaining target. For each candidate from start onward: if it exceeds the remaining target, stop the loop (sorted, so the rest are larger too); otherwise add it, recurse with the same index (reuse allowed) and remaining - candidate, then remove it. When the remaining target reaches 0, record a copy of the current combination.

mandatory: recurse with the same index to allow reuse
start index prevents duplicate combinations in different orders
concept_groups: sort to prune when candidate exceeds remainder
break the loop early after sorting
advanced_bonus: exponential worst case, roughly O(N^(T/M)) where T is target and M the smallest candidate
start index ensures [2,3] and [3,2] are not both produced
Combination Sum II (each used once) recurses with i + 1 and skips equal neighbours
DP can count combinations but not list them efficiently
copy the current path when recording

semantic_targets: Pruning on sorted candidates saves work
reusing a candidate means recursing on the same index
common_mistakes: stores a reference to the path instead of a copy
no pruning when remainder becomes negative

logic_context: First build a max-heap from the array in place by sifting down every non-leaf node from the last parent to the root, which takes O(n). Then repeatedly swap the root (the maximum) with the last element of the heap, shrink the heap size by one, and sift the new root down to restore the heap. After n - 1 steps the array is sorted ascending. O(n log n) time in all cases, O(1) extra space, not stable.

mandatory: build a max-heap in place
swap root with last element, shrink heap, sift down
concept_groups: sift down restores the heap property
O(n log n) in all cases
advanced_bonus: O(n log n) best, average and worst case
O(1) extra space — useful when memory is tight
not stable: swaps move equal keys past each other
often slower than quicksort in practice due to poor cache locality
used in introsort as the fallback when quicksort recursion gets too deep

semantic_targets: Heap gives repeated access to the maximum
Sorted part grows at the end of the array
each extraction places the current maximum in its final position
common_mistakes: Building the heap by n insertions and calling it O(n)
Using a min-heap and expecting ascending order in place without reversing
forgets to shrink the heap size
sifts up instead of down after swapping

logic_context: A binary heap is a complete binary tree, so it can be stored level by level in an array with no gaps and no pointers. With 0-based indexing, node i has children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and its parent at (i - 1) / 2. With 1-based indexing, the children are 2i and 2i + 1 and the parent is i / 2. Leaves occupy indices n/2 to n - 1 (0-based).

mandatory: complete binary tree stored level by level in an array
0-based: children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, parent (i - 1) / 2
concept_groups: leaves are in the second half of the array
advanced_bonus: 0-based leaves are at indices n/2 to n - 1, so heapify starts from n/2 - 1
array storage is cache-friendly
completeness keeps height at floor(log2 n)
the same layout is used in segment trees
a non-complete tree stored this way wastes space

semantic_targets: parent and children are found by simple arithmetic
common_mistakes: Saying a heap is a sorted array
claims any binary tree stores compactly this way

logic_context: A cut splits the vertices into two non-empty groups. The cut property says that for any cut, the minimum-weight edge crossing it belongs to some minimum spanning tree (to every MST if that edge is the unique minimum). Kruskal's algorithm adds the cheapest edge that joins two different components, and Prim's adds the cheapest edge leaving the current tree; in both cases that edge is the lightest across some cut, so each greedy step is safe.

mandatory: the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST
Prim's and Kruskal's each add the lightest edge across a cut
concept_groups: a cut divides vertices into two groups
crossing edges connect the two groups
Prim: cut between the tree and the rest
advanced_bonus: cycle property: the heaviest edge on any cycle is not in any MST (if it is the unique maximum)
with distinct edge weights the MST is unique
an MST of a connected graph with V vertices has V - 1 edges
the exchange argument proves the cut property
Borůvka's algorithm also relies on it

semantic_targets: Cut property justifies the greedy choice
Both classic MST algorithms use it
the lightest edge across a cut can always be included
common_mistakes: Saying the globally lightest edge must be in the MST but no other reasoning
claims the heaviest edge is never in an MST in all cases
no link to Prim or Kruskal

logic_context: Optimal substructure means an optimal solution can be built from optimal solutions of its subproblems, e.g. a shortest path is made of shortest sub-paths. Overlapping subproblems means the same subproblems are solved repeatedly, as in naive recursive Fibonacci. DP stores each subproblem's answer once (memoisation or tabulation). Without overlap, plain divide and conquer is enough; without optimal substructure, combining subproblem answers does not give the right result.

mandatory: optimal substructure: optimal solution built from optimal sub-solutions
overlapping subproblems: same subproblems recur
concept_groups: without overlap, divide and conquer is enough
advanced_bonus: merge sort has optimal substructure but no overlap, so DP gives no benefit
longest simple path lacks optimal substructure
greedy algorithms additionally need the greedy-choice property
DP turns exponential recursion into polynomial time
state definition is the key design step

semantic_targets: Optimal substructure is why combining works
DP solves each distinct subproblem once
common_mistakes: Saying any recursion benefits from DP
claims greedy and DP need the same properties
says divide and conquer is DP

logic_context: A process is a running program with its own address space and resources such as open files. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process; threads of the same process share code, global data, heap and open files, but each has its own stack, registers and program counter. Threads are cheaper to create and switch between and can communicate through shared memory, but a bug in one thread can crash the whole process, and shared data needs synchronisation.

mandatory: process has its own address space
threads share the process's memory but have their own stacks
concept_groups: thread creation and switching are cheaper
processes are isolated from each other
advanced_bonus: each thread has its own stack, registers and program counter
a crash in one thread usually kills the whole process
fork() creates a process; pthread_create() creates a thread
inter-process communication: pipes, sockets, shared memory
race conditions arise from unsynchronised shared data between threads

semantic_targets: threads share heap and globals, not stacks
common_mistakes: Saying threads have separate address spaces
Saying processes share memory by default
Ignoring the separate stacks of threads
claims threads cannot run in parallel

logic_context: A deadlock is a state where a group of threads or processes each wait for a resource held by another member of the group, so none can proceed. It requires all four conditions: mutual exclusion (resources cannot be shared), hold and wait (holding one resource while waiting for another), no preemption (resources cannot be taken away), and circular wait (a cycle of waiting). Breaking any one condition — most commonly by acquiring locks in a fixed global order — prevents deadlock.

mandatory: threads wait on each other forever
mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
concept_groups: break any one to prevent deadlock
fixed lock ordering removes circular wait
timeouts or trylock reduce hold and wait
advanced_bonus: lock ordering is the most common prevention technique
Banker's algorithm avoids unsafe states
detection: find a cycle in the wait-for graph
livelock differs: threads keep changing state but make no progress
example: thread A locks X then Y while thread B locks Y then X

semantic_targets: consistent lock ordering prevents circular wait
common_mistakes: Confusing deadlock with a race condition
Saying one condition alone causes deadlock
confuses deadlock with livelock or starvation

logic_context: A mutex is a lock that gives one thread exclusive access to a critical section; it has ownership, so only the thread that locked it should unlock it. A semaphore is a counter with wait (decrement, block at zero) and post/signal (increment) operations; any thread can signal it. A counting semaphore lets up to N threads use a pool of resources, and semaphores are also used for signalling between threads, e.g. producer-consumer.

mandatory: mutex gives exclusive access with ownership
semaphore is a counter with wait and signal
concept_groups: counting semaphore allows N concurrent users
any thread can signal a semaphore
semaphore used for resource pools or signalling
advanced_bonus: binary semaphore resembles a mutex but has no ownership
priority-inheritance mutexes address priority inversion
POSIX: pthread_mutex_lock/unlock vs sem_wait/sem_post
producer-consumer uses two counting semaphores plus a mutex
unlocking a mutex from another thread is undefined behaviour in many APIs

semantic_targets: a mutex protects data; a semaphore controls access counts or signals events
common_mistakes: Saying a semaphore has an owner
Saying a mutex can admit N threads
unlocks a mutex from a different thread

logic_context: gets() reads a line into a buffer without knowing the buffer's size, so input longer than the buffer overwrites adjacent memory — a classic buffer overflow that attackers can exploit. It was deprecated in C99 and removed in C11. Use fgets(buf, size, stdin), which stops at size - 1 characters (and keeps the newline, which may need removing), or POSIX getline(), which allocates as needed.

mandatory: gets() has no buffer size limit
input longer than the buffer causes buffer overflow
concept_groups: removed from the C standard in C11
use fgets with the buffer size
advanced_bonus: fgets reads at most size - 1 characters and adds '\0'
remove the newline with buf[strcspn(buf, "\n")] = '\0'
getline (POSIX) grows the buffer dynamically
the Morris worm (1988) exploited gets() in fingerd
scanf("%s") has the same problem without a width limit

semantic_targets: always pass the buffer size when reading input
common_mistakes: Saying gets() is fine for small inputs
Recommending scanf("%s") as a safe replacement
Forgetting that fgets keeps the newline
says gets() is only slow, not unsafe

evaluation_rubric.focus: Danger of gets and safe replacement

logic_context: An opaque pointer uses a struct that is declared but not defined in the public header (for example typedef struct Stack Stack;). Users can hold and pass Stack * but cannot see or access its fields, because the full definition lives only in the .c file. The library provides functions to create, use and destroy it. This hides implementation details, lets the internals change without recompiling users, and keeps the ABI stable.

mandatory: struct declared in the header but defined only in the .c file
users only handle pointers and call library functions
concept_groups: create and destroy functions manage memory
implementation can change without breaking users
incomplete type cannot be instantiated directly
advanced_bonus: users cannot use sizeof or declare the struct on the stack
the standard FILE type behaves this way in practice
improves ABI stability for shared libraries
costs a heap allocation and a pointer indirection
sometimes called the pimpl or handle pattern

semantic_targets: an incomplete type can be pointed to but not dereferenced by users
common_mistakes: Putting the struct definition in the header

logic_context: stdout and stderr are both output streams that usually appear on the terminal, but they can be redirected separately (for example 2> errors.txt). stdout is line-buffered when connected to a terminal and fully buffered when redirected to a file or pipe, so its output may appear late or be lost if the program crashes. stderr is unbuffered, so error messages appear immediately. Use stderr for diagnostics and fflush(stdout) when output must appear at once.

mandatory: stdout for normal output, stderr for errors and diagnostics
stdout is buffered, stderr is unbuffered
advanced_bonus: a crash can lose stdout data still in the buffer
mixing both streams can show messages out of order
setvbuf changes buffering mode
fprintf(stderr, ...) writes to standard error
perror writes a message plus the errno description to stderr

common_mistakes: Saying they are the same stream
does not explain why output may appear late

logic_context: A treap is a binary search tree in which each node also has a random priority. Keys follow BST order and priorities follow heap order (a parent's priority is higher than its children's). Insertion adds the node by key as in a BST and then rotates it up while its priority beats its parent's. Because priorities are random, the tree has the shape of a random BST, so its expected height is O(log n) and operations take expected O(log n).

mandatory: BST order on keys and heap order on random priorities
random priorities give expected O(log n) height
concept_groups: rotations restore heap order after insertion
deletion rotates the node down to a leaf
advanced_bonus: split and merge operations make range operations simple
implicit treaps support array-like operations by position
simpler to code than red-black trees
worst case is still O(n) but extremely unlikely
the name combines tree and heap

semantic_targets: random priorities simulate random insertion order
common_mistakes: says priorities must be unique keys

evaluation_rubric.focus: BST plus heap with random priorities

logic_context: Backtracking builds a solution step by step and abandons a partial solution as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer, then undoes the last choice and tries another. The choices form a state-space tree explored depth-first. Pruning means checking constraints early so whole subtrees are skipped, which is why backtracking is often far faster than generating every complete candidate, even though the worst case is still exponential.

mandatory: build solutions incrementally and undo choices
abandon partial solutions that violate constraints
concept_groups: depth-first exploration of a state-space tree
advanced_bonus: examples: N-Queens, Sudoku, permutations, subset sum
constraint checks before recursion are the key to pruning
branch and bound adds cost bounds for optimisation problems
ordering choices (most constrained first) increases pruning
brute force builds all complete candidates before checking

semantic_targets: Faster than brute force in practice
check constraints as early as possible

logic_context: The % operator gives the remainder of integer division and works only on integer types (use fmod for floating point). Since C99, division truncates toward zero, so the remainder takes the sign of the dividend: -7 % 3 is -1 and 7 % -3 is 1. The identity a == (a / b) * b + a % b always holds. Dividing or taking % by zero is undefined behaviour.

mandatory: % gives the remainder of integer division
the result has the sign of the dividend (C99 onward)
concept_groups: modulus by zero is undefined behaviour
advanced_bonus: a == (a / b) * b + a % b
for a non-negative result use ((a % m) + m) % m
common uses: even/odd checks, wrapping indices in circular buffers
before C99 the sign with negative operands was implementation-defined
for powers of two, x % 2^k equals x & (2^k - 1) only for non-negative x

semantic_targets: negative operands can give negative remainders
common_mistakes: Saying the result is always non-negative

logic_context: A for loop puts initialisation, condition and update in one header, so it suits loops with a known number of iterations, such as counting through an array. A while loop has only a condition, so it suits loops that run until something happens, such as reading input until end of file. Both check the condition before each iteration, and each can be rewritten as the other.

mandatory: for groups initialisation, condition and update in one line
while has only a condition
concept_groups: both check the condition before each iteration
each can be rewritten as the other
advanced_bonus: for (;;) and while (1) both create infinite loops
continue in a for loop still runs the update expression
a loop variable declared in a for header is scoped to the loop (C99)
do-while checks after the body and runs at least once
choose for readability, not performance

semantic_targets: for keeps loop control in one place
common_mistakes: Saying while always runs at least once
no example of when to use each

logic_context: For nested loops, the inner loop runs completely for every iteration of the outer loop, so the costs multiply: two nested loops of n iterations each give O(n²), three give O(n³). If the inner loop depends on the outer index, e.g. j from 0 to i, the total is about n²/2, still O(n²). Loops placed one after another add their costs instead, so two separate O(n) loops are O(n).

mandatory: inner loop runs fully for each outer iteration
costs multiply: two nested n-loops give O(n²)
concept_groups: sequential loops add, nested loops multiply
dependent inner bounds still give O(n²)
advanced_bonus: an inner loop that halves (i *= 2) gives O(n log n) overall
O(n · m) when the loops run over different sizes
early break can improve the best case but not necessarily the worst
nested loops over the same array are a common target for hashing optimisations

common_mistakes: Saying dependent inner loops are O(n)
ignores different loop sizes n and m
claims nested loops are always O(n²) regardless of bounds

logic_context: #define is handled by the preprocessor, which replaces the name with its text before compilation; it has no type, no scope, and no memory address. A const variable is a typed object that obeys scope rules, can be seen in a debugger, and has an address. In C (unlike C++), a const int is not a constant expression, so it cannot be used as a case label or a file-scope array size; enum or #define is used there.

mandatory: #define is text replacement by the preprocessor
const creates a typed, scoped read-only variable
concept_groups: const int is not a constant expression in C
advanced_bonus: #define macros can cause surprises without parentheses, e.g. #define N 2+3
enum constants are true integer constant expressions and are scoped
const variables are visible in debuggers
modifying a const object through a cast is undefined behaviour
C23 adds constexpr for true constants

semantic_targets: prefer const or enum for typed constants
common_mistakes: Saying const values can be changed freely

logic_context: Many decimal values, such as 0.1, cannot be stored exactly in binary floating point, so small rounding errors accumulate: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false. logic_context: A binary heap gives the earliest deadline in O(1) and extraction in O(log n), but it cannot find an arbitrary job quickly. logic_context: A mutex is correct and general but adds locking overhead and contention when many threads increment often.
