logic_context: If len(s1) + len(s2) != len(s3), return false. Let dp[i][j] be true if the first i characters of s1 and the first j of s2 can form the first i + j characters of s3. dp[0][0] = true. dp[i][j] is true if (dp[i-1][j] and s1[i-1] == s3[i+j-1]) or (dp[i][j-1] and s2[j-1] == s3[i+j-1]). The answer is dp[m][n]. O(m · n).

mandatory: dp[i][j]: first i of s1 and first j of s2 form first i + j of s3
take the next character from s1 or s2 if it matches
concept_groups: first row and column use only one string
advanced_bonus: O(m · n) time, O(n) space with a rolling row
greedy matching fails when both strings offer the same character
memoised recursion on (i, j) is equivalent
BFS over (i, j) states is another view
the index into s3 is always i + j

semantic_targets: Length check rules out cases quickly
s3's position is determined by i + j
common_mistakes: Greedy choice of whichever string matches
treats it as checking character counts

logic_context: Track three states each day: hold (holding a stock), sold (just sold today), and rest (not holding, free to buy). Transitions: hold = max(hold, rest - price); sold = previous hold + price; rest = max(rest, previous sold). Start with hold = -infinity, sold = 0, rest = 0. The answer is max(sold, rest) at the end. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: states: hold, sold, rest
buying is only allowed from rest, which enforces the cooldown
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(1) space
use previous-day values when updating to avoid mixing days
state machine view clarifies the cooldown
without cooldown the answer is the sum of positive day-to-day gains
transaction fee variant subtracts the fee on sell

semantic_targets: Cooldown blocks buying right after selling
buy from rest, sell from hold
common_mistakes: Updating states with today's new values instead of yesterday's

logic_context: Push the first element of each row (with its row and column) into a min-heap. Pop the smallest k - 1 times, each time pushing the next element from the same row. The top after that is the k-th smallest. O(k log n) time. Alternatively, binary search on the value range: count elements <= mid by walking from the bottom-left corner in O(n), giving O(n log(max - min)).

mandatory: min-heap seeded with the first element of each row
pop k - 1 times, pushing the next element in the same row
concept_groups: store row and column with each value
binary search on values with O(n) counting
advanced_bonus: O(k log n) with the heap; only min(n, k) rows need seeding
binary search approach O(n log(range)) is better for large k
counting walk: move up when value > mid, right otherwise
flattening and sorting costs O(n² log n)
duplicates are counted correctly by both methods

semantic_targets: Rows act as sorted lists to merge
Heap tracks the next candidate from each row
Value-range binary search is an alternative
common_mistakes: Pushing all n² elements into the heap
Forgetting to push the next element from the same row
binary searches indices instead of values
off-by-one in the number of pops

logic_context: First find a range that contains the target by exponential search: start with hi = 1 and double it while the value at hi is less than the target. Then the target, if present, lies between hi / 2 and hi, so run a normal binary search there. Out-of-range reads return a large sentinel, so they act like values greater than the target. O(log p), where p is the target's position.

mandatory: double the upper bound until it passes the target
binary search within [hi / 2, hi]
concept_groups: sentinel values behave as very large
no need to know the length
advanced_bonus: O(log p) where p is the target's index
doubling ensures only O(log p) probes to find the bound
also used for searching in unbounded or streaming sorted data
handles target at index 0
avoid overflow when computing mid in huge ranges

semantic_targets: Sentinel removes the need for length
common_mistakes: Linear scan to find the length
Searching from 0 to an arbitrary large bound without justification
increments the bound by 1 instead of doubling
wrong lower bound for the final binary search

logic_context: XOR the two numbers: each bit of x ^ y is 1 exactly where the bits differ. Then count the set bits of the result, for example with Brian Kernighan's method (repeatedly clear the lowest set bit with n & (n - 1)) or a built-in population count. O(number of set bits).

mandatory: XOR marks the differing bits
count the set bits of the XOR
advanced_bonus: __builtin_popcount in GCC/Clang uses a single instruction on many CPUs
use unsigned types to avoid sign issues
total Hamming distance over all pairs: count ones per bit position, add ones × zeros
Hamming distance is used in error-correcting codes
lookup tables of 8-bit counts are another fast method

common_mistakes: Using AND or OR instead of XOR

logic_context: Map each digit to its letters (2 → abc, … 7 → pqrs, 9 → wxyz). Recurse with an index into the digit string and the current partial combination: for each letter of the current digit, append it, recurse on the next index, then remove it. When the index reaches the end, record the combination. An empty input returns an empty list.

mandatory: map each digit to its letters
append a letter, recurse on the next digit, then remove it
concept_groups: record when all digits are used
one level of recursion per digit
advanced_bonus: O(4^n · n) time in the worst case, where n is the number of digits
iterative BFS: build combinations level by level
output size itself is up to 4^n, so the time is optimal
use a fixed char buffer of length n in C
digits 0 and 1 map to no letters — clarify handling

semantic_targets: Backtracking builds one letter at a time
common_mistakes: Not removing the letter after recursion
nested loops for a fixed number of digits only

logic_context: Use 0-based positions. With one person, the survivor is position 0: J(1) = 0. After the first elimination, the remaining n - 1 people form the same problem starting just after the eliminated person, so the positions shift by k: J(n) = (J(n - 1) + k) % n. Add 1 for a 1-based answer. This runs in O(n) time and can be done iteratively in O(1) space.

concept_groups: positions shift by k after each elimination
advanced_bonus: simulation with a circular linked list or array takes O(n · k) or O(n²)
for k = 2, closed form: write n = 2^m + L, survivor (1-based) = 2L + 1
the recurrence comes from relabelling positions after each removal
iterate i from 2 to n: res = (res + k) % i
recursive version uses O(n) stack

semantic_targets: Reduce n to n - 1 by relabelling
the shift by k maps the smaller problem's answer back
common_mistakes: claims the answer is always k-related directly

logic_context: Rules: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours survives, otherwise dies; a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours becomes alive. To update in place, encode both states in each cell: keep the current state in bit 0 and write the next state into bit 1. Count neighbours using only bit 0 (value & 1). After processing every cell, shift each value right by 1 to make the next state current. O(m · n) time, O(1) extra space.

mandatory: store current and next state in the same cell
count neighbours using only the current state
concept_groups: second pass shifts to the next state
advanced_bonus: O(m · n) time, O(1) extra space
alternative encoding: 2 = live→dead, 3 = dead→live
copying the grid is simpler but uses O(m · n) space
an infinite board can be stored as a set of live cells
updating cells directly without encoding corrupts neighbour counts

semantic_targets: Simultaneous update requires preserving old states
neighbour counts must use the old generation
common_mistakes: Overwriting cells and then counting with new values

logic_context: Create n empty buckets. Put each value x into bucket floor(n · x). Sort each bucket with insertion sort (buckets are small on average), then concatenate the buckets in order. With a uniform distribution, each bucket holds O(1) elements on average, so the expected time is O(n). If many values fall into one bucket, it degrades to O(n²) with insertion sort.

mandatory: distribute values into n buckets by floor(n · x)
sort each bucket and concatenate in order
concept_groups: worst case O(n²) when values cluster
advanced_bonus: expected O(n) time, O(n) extra space
using a O(n log n) sort inside buckets improves the worst case to O(n log n)
not comparison-based across buckets
stable if the per-bucket sort is stable
for other ranges, scale x to [0, 1) using (x - min) / (max - min + ε)

semantic_targets: performance depends on the input distribution
common_mistakes: Wrong bucket index (e.g. x · 10 for any n)

logic_context: Scan the array with a hash map from value to its most recent index. For each index i, if the value is already in the map and i - map[value] <= k, return true; otherwise store map[value] = i. Alternatively, keep a sliding-window hash set of the last k values, removing arr[i - k - 1] as the window moves. O(n) time.

mandatory: hash map from value to last seen index
check i - last index <= k
concept_groups: update the stored index to the latest
return true on the first valid pair
sliding-window set of size k alternative
advanced_bonus: O(n) time; O(min(n, k)) space with the sliding-window set
storing the latest index is enough because it is the closest
brute force checks k neighbours each — O(n · k)
sorting loses index information
variant with value difference ≤ t needs buckets or an ordered set

semantic_targets: only the most recent index is needed
common_mistakes: Storing the first index instead of the latest
does not remove old values from the window set

logic_context: Virtual memory gives each process its own private address space that looks large and contiguous. The address space is divided into fixed-size pages (often 4 KB), and the memory-management unit (MMU) uses page tables to map each virtual page to a physical frame. If a page is not in RAM, a page fault occurs and the OS loads it from disk. This isolates processes, lets programs use more memory than physically installed, and allows sharing of pages such as libraries.

mandatory: each process has its own virtual address space
page tables map virtual pages to physical frames
concept_groups: page fault when a page is not in RAM
can exceed physical memory using disk
advanced_bonus: the TLB caches recent translations to speed up lookups
thrashing occurs when pages are swapped in and out constantly
copy-on-write lets fork() share pages until one process writes
shared libraries are mapped into many processes once
a segmentation fault often comes from accessing an unmapped page

semantic_targets: virtual addresses are translated on every access
common_mistakes: Saying virtual memory is just disk space
says every process shares one address space

logic_context: A pure function always returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects. A side effect is any observable change outside the function's return value: modifying a global or static variable, changing data through a pointer argument, doing I/O, or depending on hidden state such as the current time. Pure functions are easier to test, reason about, cache (memoise), and run in parallel.

mandatory: same input always gives the same output
no side effects
concept_groups: side effects: modifying globals, I/O, changing arguments
depending on hidden state makes a function impure
advanced_bonus: in C, a function that writes through a pointer parameter is impure
rand() and time() make a function impure
programs need some side effects (I/O) — isolate them
pure functions are referentially transparent
GCC's __attribute__((pure)) and ((const)) tell the compiler about purity

semantic_targets: Side effects affect state outside the function
pure code can be replaced by its result
common_mistakes: Saying a pure function cannot take arguments
Treating printing as harmless and still pure

logic_context: The birthday paradox says that in a group of only 23 people, there is more than a 50% chance that two share a birthday, even though there are 365 days. In general, with m possible hash values, a collision becomes likely after only about √m insertions (roughly 1.18√m for a 50% chance), not m/2. So collisions appear early in hash tables, and a 64-bit hash is expected to collide after about 2^32 items — which matters for hash-table design and for cryptographic security (birthday attacks).

mandatory: collisions become likely after about √m items, not m
23 people give over 50% chance of a shared birthday
concept_groups: probability of no collision drops fast
hash tables must handle collisions early
birthday attacks halve effective hash strength
advanced_bonus: P(no collision) ≈ e^(-n²/(2m))
an n-bit hash offers about n/2 bits of collision resistance
why cryptographic hashes use 256 bits
the number of pairs is n(n - 1)/2

semantic_targets: Collisions arrive much sooner than intuition suggests
pairs, not individuals, drive the probability
common_mistakes: Claiming good hash functions avoid collisions entirely
Confusing with matching one specific birthday

logic_context: A rope is a binary tree whose leaves hold short pieces of a string and whose internal nodes store a weight — the total length of their left subtree. Indexing walks down using the weights. Concatenation creates a new root, and insert, delete and split take O(log n) on a balanced rope, compared with O(n) for shifting characters in a flat array. Ropes suit text editors and other programs that edit very long strings.

mandatory: binary tree with string pieces in the leaves
internal node weight = length of its left subtree
concept_groups: index by walking down using weights
insert and delete in O(log n) when balanced
advanced_bonus: split and concatenate are the core operations
must be rebalanced to keep O(log n)
sequential reading is slower than a flat array due to pointer chasing
immutable ropes allow cheap undo by sharing structure
gap buffers and piece tables are alternative editor structures

common_mistakes: Calling a rope a linked list of characters
weights described as node count instead of length

logic_context: A k-d tree is a binary tree that organises points in k-dimensional space. Each level splits the space along one coordinate axis, cycling through the axes (x, then y, then x, … in 2-D), usually at the median point. It supports range searches (all points inside a box) and nearest-neighbour searches by pruning regions that cannot contain better answers. Build time is O(n log n), and queries are fast in low dimensions but degrade as the number of dimensions grows.

mandatory: splits space by alternating coordinate axes
supports range and nearest-neighbour queries
concept_groups: median split keeps the tree balanced
each node defines a splitting plane
prunes regions that cannot contain answers
advanced_bonus: build in O(n log n) with median finding
nearest neighbour is about O(log n) on average in low dimensions
range query worst case O(√n + m) in 2-D for m reported points
curse of dimensionality: for high k, it approaches a linear scan
used in graphics, GIS and machine learning (k-NN)

common_mistakes: Calling it a tree with k children
Splitting on the same axis every level
Claiming worst-case O(log n) for all queries

logic_context: A randomised algorithm makes random choices during execution. A Las Vegas algorithm always gives the correct answer, but its running time is random — for example randomised quicksort, which is O(n log n) expected. A Monte Carlo algorithm runs in a bounded time but may give a wrong answer with a small, controllable probability — for example the Miller-Rabin primality test. Repeating a Monte Carlo algorithm reduces the error probability.

mandatory: Las Vegas: always correct, random running time
Monte Carlo: bounded time, small probability of error
concept_groups: expected time analysis for Las Vegas
advanced_bonus: a Las Vegas algorithm stopped at a time limit becomes Monte Carlo
Monte Carlo error can be one-sided (Miller-Rabin never rejects a prime)
randomisation defeats adversarial worst-case inputs
random pivots make quicksort's worst case unlikely, not impossible
Karger's min-cut algorithm is Monte Carlo

semantic_targets: Las Vegas gambles on time, Monte Carlo on correctness
common_mistakes: Saying randomised algorithms are always approximate
claims Monte Carlo errors cannot be reduced

logic_context: The recursion tree method draws each recursive call as a node labelled with its non-recursive cost, adds up the cost of each level, and sums over all levels. For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, every level costs n and there are log n levels, so T(n) = O(n log n). It is useful when the Master Theorem does not apply, such as uneven splits like T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n (also O(n log n)), and to build intuition before proving a guess by substitution.

mandatory: draw calls as a tree and sum cost per level
total = sum of level costs over the tree's depth
concept_groups: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n gives n log n
depth depends on how fast n shrinks
advanced_bonus: for T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n, each level costs at most n and depth is log base 3/2 of n — O(n log n)
geometric series: if level costs shrink, the root dominates; if they grow, the leaves dominate
leaves count = a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a)
the Master Theorem is a shortcut derived from the same idea
T(n) = T(n - 1) + n gives n levels — O(n²)

semantic_targets: the shape of level costs decides the result
common_mistakes: Counting only the number of calls
Applying the Master Theorem to uneven splits

logic_context: Designated initialisers let you initialise specific array elements or struct members by index or name, e.g. int a[5] = {[2] = 7}; or struct point p = {.y = 3, .x = 1};. Members not mentioned are set to zero. Compound literals create an unnamed object of a given type inside an expression, e.g. draw((struct point){.x = 1, .y = 2}); or int *p = (int[]){1, 2, 3};. Both were added in C99.

mandatory: designated initialisers set members by name or index
compound literals create unnamed objects in expressions
concept_groups: order of designators can differ from declaration
advanced_bonus: a compound literal in block scope has automatic storage — do not return its address
compound literals are lvalues and can be modified unless const
designated initialisers make code robust to member reordering
array designators can leave gaps that become zero
C++ added designated initialisers only in C++20 with stricter rules

common_mistakes: Saying unmentioned members are left uninitialised
Returning a pointer to a block-scope compound literal

logic_context: _Static_assert(condition, message), added in C11 (spelled static_assert via <assert.h>, and a keyword in C23), checks a constant expression at compile time; if it fails, compilation stops with the message, and it has no runtime cost. assert(expr) checks a condition at runtime and aborts the program with a diagnostic if it is false; it is removed when NDEBUG is defined. Use static assertions for things known at compile time (sizes, layout) and assert for runtime invariants.

mandatory: _Static_assert checks at compile time
assert checks at runtime and can be disabled with NDEBUG
concept_groups: static assertion needs a constant expression
no runtime cost for static assertions
use static_assert for sizes and layout
advanced_bonus: example: _Static_assert(sizeof(int) == 4, "int must be 32-bit")
never put required side effects inside assert — they vanish with NDEBUG
static assertions document platform assumptions
C23 allows omitting the message
assert is for programmer errors, not user input validation

semantic_targets: choose by when the condition is known
common_mistakes: claims assert is active in all builds
uses assert to validate user input

logic_context: A sparse table precomputes st[j][i] = the minimum of the range starting at i with length 2^j, built in O(n log n) using st[j][i] = min(st[j-1][i], st[j-1][i + 2^(j-1)]). To query [l, r], let k = floor(log2(r - l + 1)) and return min(st[k][l], st[k][r - 2^k + 1]). The two ranges overlap, which is fine because min is idempotent. It works only for static arrays (no updates).

mandatory: precompute minimum for every range of length 2^j
query with two overlapping power-of-two ranges
concept_groups: overlap allowed because min is idempotent
advanced_bonus: O(n log n) space and preprocessing, O(1) query
precompute log2 values in a table for true O(1)
sums are not idempotent, so sum queries need O(log n) non-overlapping pieces
segment trees support updates but answer in O(log n)
also works for max, gcd and bitwise AND/OR

common_mistakes: Claiming it supports point updates efficiently
Using overlapping ranges for sum queries

logic_context: Both insert the named file's contents during preprocessing. With angle brackets, the preprocessor searches the system and compiler include directories. With double quotes, it first searches the directory of the current source file (and other user paths), then falls back to the system directories. Use angle brackets for standard and library headers and quotes for your own project headers.

mandatory: <> searches system include directories
"" searches the current file's directory first, then system directories
concept_groups: both copy the file during preprocessing
advanced_bonus: the exact search order is implementation-defined
gcc -I dir adds directories for both forms
include guards prevent multiple inclusion
#include copies text; it is not an import of compiled code
gcc -v shows the include search paths

common_mistakes: Saying quotes only search the current directory

logic_context: In an undirected graph, an edge connects two vertices both ways (like a two-way road); in a directed graph, each edge has a direction from one vertex to another (like a one-way street or a 'follows' relationship). In a weighted graph, each edge has a value such as distance or cost; in an unweighted graph, all edges are treated as equal.

mandatory: directed edges have a direction; undirected edges go both ways
weighted edges carry a value; unweighted edges are equal
concept_groups: examples: one-way streets vs two-way roads
advanced_bonus: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; Dijkstra in weighted ones
an undirected edge can be stored as two directed edges
in-degree and out-degree apply to directed graphs
a directed acyclic graph (DAG) has no directed cycles
weights may be negative in some problems

semantic_targets: these properties decide which algorithms apply
common_mistakes: Saying undirected graphs cannot have cycles
claims directed graphs must be acyclic

logic_context: A flowchart is a diagram that shows an algorithm's steps with standard shapes: ovals for start and end, rectangles for processes, diamonds for decisions and parallelograms for input/output, connected by arrows. Pseudocode describes the same steps as structured, English-like text that resembles code but ignores exact syntax. Both are language-independent planning tools; flowcharts are visual and good for small processes, while pseudocode scales better to larger algorithms.

mandatory: flowchart is a diagram with standard symbols
pseudocode is structured English-like text
concept_groups: pseudocode scales better for large algorithms
advanced_bonus: parallelogram represents input/output
arrows show flow of control
pseudocode is easier to convert into code
flowcharts quickly become cluttered for complex logic
both help design before coding

semantic_targets: Each suits different sizes of problem
use them to plan before writing code
common_mistakes: Saying flowcharts are tied to one language
says neither is used in practice

logic_context: Comments are notes in source code that the compiler ignores (they are removed during preprocessing). C has block comments /* ... */, which can span multiple lines but cannot be nested, and line comments // ..., available since C99, which run to the end of the line. Good comments explain why the code does something or clarify non-obvious logic rather than restating what the code says.

mandatory: comments are ignored by the compiler
/* */ block comments and // line comments
advanced_bonus: comments are replaced by a space during preprocessing
#if 0 ... #endif can disable code containing comments
outdated comments are worse than none
documentation tools such as Doxygen read special comments
commented-out code should usually be deleted and kept in version control

semantic_targets: good comments add information the code cannot
common_mistakes: Saying comments slow down the program
comments that only repeat the code
no mention of the two styles

logic_context: Operator precedence decides how an expression is grouped when parentheses are absent; associativity decides the order for operators with equal precedence. Surprises cause bugs: == has higher precedence than &, so a & b == c means a & (b == c); *p++ means *(p++), not (*p)++; and a << 1 + 1 means a << 2. Use parentheses to make intended grouping explicit.

mandatory: precedence decides grouping without parentheses
use parentheses to make grouping clear
concept_groups: a & b == c is a & (b == c)
advanced_bonus: assignment is right-associative: a = b = c
precedence is about grouping, not evaluation order
the ternary operator has very low precedence
compiler warnings (-Wparentheses) catch some cases
x & 1 == 0 is a classic even-check bug

common_mistakes: claims all operators are left to right

logic_context: Time complexity describes how the number of steps grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constant factors and hardware; it lets you compare algorithms in general. Actual running time is measured in seconds on a specific machine and depends on the hardware, compiler, constant factors, memory and cache behaviour, and the specific input. An O(n log n) algorithm can be slower than an O(n²) one for small n because of larger constants.

mandatory: complexity describes growth with input size
running time depends on machine, compiler and constants
concept_groups: measured in seconds for real runs
small inputs may favour simpler algorithms
cache and memory affect real time
advanced_bonus: insertion sort beats merge sort on tiny arrays
profiling measures real hotspots
two O(n) algorithms can differ in speed by a large factor
benchmarks need repeated runs and realistic inputs
asymptotic analysis matters most as n becomes large

semantic_targets: complexity predicts scaling, timing measures reality
common_mistakes: Saying lower Big-O is always faster
confuses time complexity with space complexity

logic_context: For inputs of size n, the best case is the fewest steps the algorithm can take, the worst case is the most, and the average case is the expected number over a distribution of inputs. For linear search: best case 1 comparison (target first), worst case n (target last or absent), average about n/2. Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case. The worst case gives a guarantee; the average case reflects typical performance.

mandatory: best case: fewest steps; worst case: most steps
average case: expected steps over typical inputs
concept_groups: quicksort: n log n average, n² worst
average depends on an assumed input distribution
advanced_bonus: these cases are different from O, Ω and Θ notation — any case can be described with any notation
binary search: best 1, worst log n
insertion sort best case O(n) on sorted input
amortised cost is different from average case
real-time systems care most about the worst case

semantic_targets: Three views of the same algorithm
average assumes a distribution of inputs
common_mistakes: Saying best case = Ω and worst case = O automatically
confuses average case with amortised analysis
claims the best case is useful as a guarantee

logic_context: Compile with gcc program.c -o program, which produces an executable named program (without -o, the default is a.out), and run it with ./program. -Wall turns on common warnings, -Wextra adds more, -g includes debugging information for gdb, -O2 enables optimisation, -std=c11 selects the C standard, and -lm links the math library.

mandatory: gcc file.c -o name creates an executable
run with ./name
advanced_bonus: gcc -c compiles to an object file without linking
multiple files: gcc a.c b.c -o prog
-fsanitize=address adds runtime memory checks
-O2 optimises but makes debugging harder
library flags like -lm go after source files

semantic_targets: Flags control warnings, debugging and output

logic_context: Brute force computes an O(L²) edit-distance table for every one of 100,000 words per query — simple but slow for interactive use. A BK-tree organises words by their edit distance and uses the triangle inequality to skip subtrees that cannot be within distance 2, cutting comparisons sharply for small thresholds. A trie walk computes one DP row per trie node, so shared prefixes are computed once, and it prunes a branch when the smallest value in the row exceeds 2. Recommend a trie with DP rows or a BK-tree; brute force is acceptable only for small dictionaries or offline use.

mandatory: brute force compares every word — too slow for interactive use
BK-tree and trie-with-DP both prune the search
concept_groups: trie shares DP rows across common prefixes
prune when row minimum exceeds the threshold
advanced_bonus: symmetric-delete methods (e.g. SymSpell) precompute deletions for very fast lookups at high memory cost
length filter: skip words whose length differs by more than 2
early exit in DP when the whole row exceeds the threshold
rank suggestions by distance and word frequency
BK-tree pruning weakens as the threshold grows

common_mistakes: Claiming BK-trees work for non-metric distances
No pruning rule for the trie

logic_context: A queue stores each timestamp; on a query, pop timestamps older than 5 minutes and return the size — exact, amortised O(1), but memory grows with the number of events in the window. A sorted array (timestamps arrive in order) answers by binary searching for now - 300 seconds, O(log n), but it keeps growing unless old entries are trimmed. A circular array of 300 per-second buckets uses fixed memory and O(1) updates, with a running total for O(1) queries, but only to one-second precision. Recommend buckets for high event rates when second-level precision is fine, and a queue for exact answers at moderate rates.

mandatory: queue: exact but memory grows with events in the window
per-second buckets: fixed memory with one-second precision
concept_groups: sorted array uses binary search on timestamps
sorted array must be trimmed to avoid unbounded growth
running total gives O(1) bucket queries
reset stale buckets when time advances
advanced_bonus: store (second, count) in each bucket to detect stale entries
queue removal is amortised O(1) because each timestamp is removed once
binary search needs monotonic timestamps
for distributed systems, approximate sliding-window counters are common
precision versus memory is the core trade-off

semantic_targets: fixed buckets bound memory regardless of rate
common_mistakes: claims buckets are exact to the millisecond

logic_context: A dense array needs 10^8 entries — about 800 MB for doubles — and each multiplication does 10^8 operations, mostly on zeros. COO stores 50,000 (row, column, value) triples, is easy to build and modify, and multiplies in O(nnz), but its accesses are scattered. CSR stores values and column indices (50,000 each) plus 10,001 row pointers, and multiplies row by row in O(nnz) with sequential memory access, making it fastest for repeated multiplication, though harder to modify. Recommend building in COO and converting once to CSR.

mandatory: dense storage wastes about 800 MB and does 10^8 operations per multiply
CSR gives O(nnz) multiplication with sequential access
concept_groups: COO is easy to build and modify
CSR row pointers have rows + 1 entries
advanced_bonus: convert COO to CSR by sorting triples by row then counting per row
CSC (column-compressed) suits column access
nnz/(rows × cols) = 0.05% — far below the point where dense pays off
CSR memory ≈ 50,000 × (8 + 4) + 10,001 × 4 bytes — under 1 MB
libraries such as SciPy and Eigen use CSR internally

semantic_targets: Access pattern decides between COO and CSR
common_mistakes: Claiming COO is best for repeated multiplication

logic_context: fgetc reads one character per call; stdio buffers the file, so it does not make a system call per character, but parsing becomes a manual state machine. fgets reads a line at a time, which fits a line-oriented config format, but very long lines need handling (detect a missing newline). fread loads the whole file in one call, which is simple and fast, but memory equals the file size and the program must add its own '\0' terminator. Because the file is small and read once, performance differences are negligible; choose fgets for line-based configs because it is clear and safe.

mandatory: file is small and read once, so clarity matters more than speed
fgets matches line-oriented configuration
concept_groups: fgetc is buffered by stdio, not a syscall per character
fread loads the whole file at once
fgets must handle lines longer than the buffer
advanced_bonus: getline (POSIX) handles arbitrary line lengths
check fopen's return value and report errors
get the file size with fseek/ftell before fread
fgetc suits tokenisers that read character by character
always check for read errors with ferror

semantic_targets: Match the API to the file format
Performance is not the bottleneck here
common_mistakes: Claiming fgetc performs a system call per character

logic_context: Checking all pairs needs about 5 × 10^7 comparisons per frame, far too many at 60 frames per second. A uniform grid with cells about the size of an object puts each object in a cell and checks only the same and neighbouring cells — close to O(n) when objects are evenly spread and similar in size, and cheap to rebuild every frame, but it degrades when many objects cluster in a few cells. A quadtree adapts to uneven distributions by subdividing crowded regions, handling clustering and varied sizes better, at the cost of more complex updates. Recommend a uniform grid for evenly spread, similar-sized objects and a quadtree when objects cluster or vary widely in size.

mandatory: all-pairs is O(n²) — about 5 × 10^7 checks per frame
grid and quadtree reduce checks to nearby objects
concept_groups: uniform grid is near O(n) for even distributions
advanced_bonus: choose grid cell size about the size of the largest common object
spatial hashing stores only occupied cells in a hash map
broad phase (grid/tree) followed by narrow phase (exact shape test)
sweep-and-prune along one axis is another broad-phase method
objects spanning several cells must be inserted into each

semantic_targets: recommend by object spread and size
common_mistakes: Saying all-pairs is fine for 10,000 objects
confuses quadtree with binary search tree

logic_context: Snapshots are simple and make undo a direct restore, but each edit copies the whole document, so memory grows with document size × number of edits — impractical for large files. A command stack stores each operation (e.g. insert text at position, delete range) with enough information to reverse it; memory grows only with the size of the edits, and undo applies the inverse while redo re-applies the command from a redo stack. It is more complex because every command needs a correct inverse. Recommend the command approach, optionally with occasional snapshots as checkpoints.

mandatory: snapshots cost memory proportional to document size per edit
command stack stores reversible operations with small memory
concept_groups: each command needs a correct inverse
new edits clear the redo stack
advanced_bonus: hybrid: periodic snapshots plus commands limit replay time
merge consecutive keystrokes into one command for usability
persistent data structures make snapshots cheap by sharing structure
limit history length to bound memory
this is the classic Command design pattern

common_mistakes: Forgetting to clear redo after a new edit

logic_context: Treat the jumps like BFS levels. Keep curEnd (the farthest index reachable with the current number of jumps) and farthest (the farthest index reachable with one more jump). Scan i from 0 to n - 2, updating farthest = max(farthest, i + a[i]). When i reaches curEnd, take a jump: increment the count and set curEnd = farthest. If farthest does not move past i, the end is unreachable. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: track the current jump's reach (curEnd) and the farthest reachable index
increment jumps when i reaches curEnd and set curEnd = farthest
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(1) space
DP solution dp[i] = min jumps to i is O(n²)
stop the loop at n - 2 to avoid an extra jump at the last index
each 'level' of indices is reachable with the same number of jumps
differs from the reachability-only Jump Game

semantic_targets: Jump only when the current range is exhausted
the farthest reach of each level defines the next level
common_mistakes: Jumping as far as possible from each position (wrong greedy)
Looping to n - 1 and counting an extra jump
O(n²) DP without mentioning the greedy
confuses this with checking reachability only

logic_context: Expand a window with a right pointer and keep a count of each value in the window. When the number of distinct values exceeds two, move the left pointer forward, decrementing counts and removing values whose count drops to zero, until only two distinct values remain. Record the maximum window length. Each element enters and leaves once, so O(n).

mandatory: sliding window with value counts
shrink from the left when more than two distinct values
concept_groups: remove a value when its count reaches zero
each element added and removed once
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(1) space since at most three keys are stored
generalises to at most k distinct values
an alternative stores the last index of each value and jumps left directly
brute force checks every subarray — O(n²)
same pattern as longest substring with at most k distinct characters

semantic_targets: the window always holds at most two distinct values
common_mistakes: Shrinking only one step when distinct count is too high
Not removing values with zero count
returns the number of distinct values instead of length

logic_context: Two numbers sum to a multiple of k exactly when their remainders add to 0 or k. Scan the array; for each element compute r = ((x % k) + k) % k, add freq[(k - r) % k] to the answer (the earlier elements that complete a pair), then increment freq[r]. O(n + k) time, O(k) space.

mandatory: pair sum divisible by k when remainders add to 0 or k
count complements using a remainder frequency array
advanced_bonus: O(n + k) time, O(k) space
closed form: C(freq[0], 2) + sum of freq[r] × freq[k - r] for 1 ≤ r < k/2, plus C(freq[k/2], 2) when k is even
in C, x % k can be negative for negative x
counting before inserting ensures i < j and avoids pairing an element with itself
brute force over all pairs is O(n²)

semantic_targets: remainder 0 and k/2 pair with themselves

logic_context: Column titles are a base-26 system without a zero digit (A = 1 to Z = 26). Repeat while n > 0: decrement n by 1, take n % 26 to get the letter 'A' + (n % 26), then set n = n / 26. Letters come out from least significant to most significant, so reverse the result at the end. O(log n).

mandatory: base-26 numbering with digits 1 to 26 (no zero)
decrement n before taking n % 26
advanced_bonus: O(log₂₆ n) time
without the decrement, 26 would wrongly become 'A@' or 'AZ'
the reverse conversion: result = result × 26 + (c - 'A' + 1)
examples: 52 → AZ, 701 → ZY, 703 → AAA
this is called bijective base-26

semantic_targets: 26 maps to Z, not to a two-letter title
common_mistakes: uses a lookup only for single letters

logic_context: Count each character's frequency in both strings (e.g. two 26-entry arrays). For every character, the extra occurrences in either string must be deleted, so add |count1[c] - count2[c]| over all characters. That sum is the answer. O(n + m) time, O(1) space for a fixed alphabet.

mandatory: count character frequencies in both strings
sum absolute differences of the counts
concept_groups: one count array with + for first string and - for second
advanced_bonus: O(n + m) time, O(1) space
a single array: increment for s1, decrement for s2, sum absolute values
sorting both strings and merging is O(n log n)
for Unicode, use a hash map
related: minimum steps to make anagram by replacing characters gives half the sum when lengths are equal

common_mistakes: Counting only characters missing from one side
Using LCS (that is a different problem)
sorts and compares character by character
forgets characters present in only one string

logic_context: Use two pointers starting from the last character of each string and a carry starting at 0. At each step, add the available bits and the carry; the result bit is sum % 2 and the new carry is sum / 2. Continue while either pointer is valid or the carry is 1. Append bits as you go and reverse the result at the end. O(max(n, m)).

mandatory: add from the least significant bit with a carry
bit = sum % 2, carry = sum / 2
concept_groups: continue while digits or carry remain
pointers move from right to left
advanced_bonus: O(max(n, m)) time
no conversion to integers — avoids overflow for long strings
final carry adds a leading '1'
same pattern as adding decimal strings or linked-list numbers
in C, allocate max(n, m) + 2 bytes for the result

semantic_targets: process both strings from the end

logic_context: Count the length n. Each part gets base = n / k nodes, and the first extra = n % k parts get one more. Walk the list: for each part, record its head, advance (size - 1) nodes, then cut the link by saving the next node and setting the current node's next to NULL. If k > n, the remaining parts are NULL. O(n + k).

mandatory: base size = n / k, first n % k parts get one extra
cut the list after each part's last node
concept_groups: parts may be NULL when k > n
advanced_bonus: O(n + k) time, O(k) for the output array
save the next pointer before setting next to NULL
handles an empty list
in-place: no nodes copied
same arithmetic as distributing items evenly into buckets

semantic_targets: Sizes come from division and remainder
Extra nodes go to earlier parts
each part is a separate NULL-terminated list
common_mistakes: Giving extra nodes to later parts
does not count the length first

evaluation_rubric.focus: Even split by division and remainder

logic_context: Use a dummy node before the head and move a pointer prev to node m - 1. Let cur = prev->next (node m). Repeat n - m times: take the node after cur, unlink it, and insert it right after prev (front insertion). This moves each following node to the front of the sublist, reversing it while cur ends up at position n still linked to the rest of the list. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: move prev to the node before position m
repeatedly move the node after cur to just after prev
concept_groups: cur stays linked to the remainder
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(1) space
the four pointer updates: next = cur->next; cur->next = next->next; next->next = prev->next; prev->next = next
alternative: reverse the sublist with three pointers, then reconnect both ends
m == n leaves the list unchanged
generalises to reversing in groups of k

common_mistakes: Losing the connection to the rest of the list

logic_context: Build a sorted list starting from a dummy node. Take nodes from the original list one at a time. For each node, walk from the dummy to find the first position whose next value is greater than the node's value, and splice the node in there. Continue until the original list is empty. O(n²) worst case, O(1) extra space, stable when equal values are inserted after existing ones.

mandatory: build a separate sorted list with a dummy head
splice each node into its correct position
concept_groups: find position by walking from the dummy
insert before the first greater value
advanced_bonus: optimisation: if the node is ≥ the sorted tail, append directly — O(n) for already sorted input
stable if insertion happens after equal values
merge sort is O(n log n) for linked lists
no shifting of elements, unlike arrays — only pointer changes
save the next node before relinking

semantic_targets: Dummy head simplifies insertion at the front
relink nodes instead of copying values
common_mistakes: Losing the rest of the original list when moving a node
Swapping values instead of relinking without noting it
breaks stability by inserting before equal values
no dummy node, mishandling head insertion

logic_context: Do a DFS that carries the number formed so far: current = current × 10 + node->val. At a leaf, add current to the total. For internal nodes, recurse on the children with the updated number. Return the sum of both subtrees. O(n) time, O(h) stack.

mandatory: carry current = current × 10 + node value down the path
add the number only at leaf nodes
concept_groups: DFS passes the number as a parameter
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(h) space
BFS with (node, value) pairs works too
use long long if paths are long to avoid overflow
adding at non-leaf nodes overcounts
Morris traversal can achieve O(1) space

semantic_targets: Each root-to-leaf path forms one number
common_mistakes: counts a node with one child as a leaf

logic_context: Use prefix sums along the current root-to-node path. Keep a hash map from prefix sum to how many times it occurs on the current path, starting with {0: 1}. At each node, update curr += node->val, add map[curr - target] to the count (paths ending here), increment map[curr], recurse on both children, then decrement map[curr] before returning (backtrack). O(n) time.

mandatory: prefix sum map along the current path
count += map[curr - target] at each node
concept_groups: backtrack by decrementing the map after children
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(h) for the map on the current path
brute force starts a DFS at every node — O(n²) worst case
same idea as counting subarrays with sum k
backtracking keeps prefixes from other branches out of the map
use 64-bit sums if values are large

semantic_targets: Prefix sums turn path sums into differences
Hash map counts matching earlier prefixes
Backtracking limits the map to the current path
map[0] = 1 allows paths starting at the root
common_mistakes: Not backtracking — counts paths across branches
Only counting paths starting at the root
double counting by starting DFS at each node without care

logic_context: Use a post-order traversal that returns, for each subtree: whether it is a BST, its size, and its minimum and maximum values. A node forms a BST if both children are BSTs and left.max < node.val < right.min. Then size = left.size + right.size + 1, min = min(left.min, node.val), max = max(right.max, node.val). Otherwise mark it not a BST. Track the largest size seen. O(n).

mandatory: post-order returns isBST, size, min and max
node is a BST if both children are BSTs and left.max < val < right.min
concept_groups: update size, min and max upward
empty subtree is a BST with min = +∞, max = -∞
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(h) space
checking each node separately with a validator is O(n²)
sentinel values for empty subtrees simplify comparisons
a subtree means all descendants — not just some nodes
once a subtree is not a BST, ancestors cannot be BSTs either

common_mistakes: wrong sentinel values for NULL children
pre-order traversal that lacks child information

logic_context: Do a BFS that also enqueues NULL children. Once a NULL is dequeued, set a flag. If any non-NULL node is dequeued after the flag is set, the tree is not complete. If the traversal finishes without that happening, it is complete. In a complete tree, all levels are full except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right. O(n).

mandatory: BFS that enqueues NULL children
after the first NULL, no non-NULL node may appear
concept_groups: flag set at the first NULL
complete means last level filled left to right
advanced_bonus: O(n) time
alternative: index nodes as in a heap and check that the maximum index equals n - 1
a full binary tree is different (every node has 0 or 2 children)
heaps must be complete trees
checking only that every node has two or zero children is wrong

semantic_targets: Level order matches the fill order
no node may follow a missing position
common_mistakes: Confusing complete with full or perfect
returns true when a left child is missing but right exists

logic_context: Run BFS where each state is (row, column, eliminations remaining). Moving into an empty cell keeps the remaining count; moving into an obstacle uses one elimination and is allowed only if the count is above zero. Track visited states per (row, column, remaining) — or the best remaining count seen per cell — to avoid repeats. The first time BFS reaches the target gives the shortest path. O(m · n · k).

mandatory: BFS over states (row, column, eliminations left)
entering an obstacle uses one elimination
concept_groups: first arrival at target is shortest
advanced_bonus: O(m · n · k) time and space
shortcut: if k ≥ m + n - 2, the answer is m + n - 2 (Manhattan distance)
storing only the maximum remaining eliminations per cell prunes dominated states
plain visited per cell is wrong — a later arrival with more eliminations may be better
A* with Manhattan heuristic can speed it up

semantic_targets: the same cell can be visited with different remaining counts

logic_context: A valid tree must be connected and acyclic, which for n nodes is equivalent to having exactly n - 1 edges and being connected. First check that the edge count is n - 1. Then check connectivity with BFS/DFS from node 0 (all n nodes must be visited), or use union-find: if any edge joins two nodes already in the same set, there is a cycle. O(n + E).

mandatory: a tree has exactly n - 1 edges
the graph must be connected (or acyclic)
concept_groups: BFS/DFS checks all nodes are reached
n - 1 edges plus connected implies acyclic
advanced_bonus: with exactly n - 1 edges, connected ⇔ acyclic, so checking one is enough
union-find with path compression is nearly linear
n = 1 with no edges is a valid tree
duplicate edges create a cycle
disconnected graphs with n - 1 edges must contain a cycle

semantic_targets: Tree properties: connected, acyclic, n - 1 edges
Edge count is a quick filter
any two of the three properties imply the third
common_mistakes: Only checking for cycles (forest may be disconnected)
visits only some nodes without checking count

logic_context: Choose each key i as the root. The keys smaller than i form the left subtree (i - 1 keys) and the larger keys form the right subtree (n - i keys); the subtrees are independent, so multiply their counts. Let G(0) = G(1) = 1 and G(n) = sum over i = 1..n of G(i - 1) × G(n - i). Fill G from 2 up to n in O(n²). These are the Catalan numbers, e.g. G(3) = 5.

mandatory: each key as root splits keys into left and right subtrees
G(n) = sum of G(i - 1) × G(n - i)
advanced_bonus: closed form: C(2n, n) / (n + 1)
the count depends only on the number of keys, not their values
generating all the trees (not just counting) is exponential
same recurrence counts valid parenthesis strings

semantic_targets: only the size of each side matters
common_mistakes: Adding instead of multiplying subtree counts
Counting binary trees with labels as permutations (n!)

logic_context: Work bottom-up. Start with dp equal to the last row. For each row from the second-last up to the top, set dp[j] = triangle[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j + 1]). After processing the top row, dp[0] is the answer. O(n²) time for n rows and O(n) space.

mandatory: bottom-up: dp[j] = value + min(dp[j], dp[j + 1])
answer is dp[0] after processing the top
concept_groups: adjacent means j or j + 1 below
advanced_bonus: bottom-up avoids edge cases at row boundaries
top-down also works but needs min over the last row
greedy choosing the smaller child at each step can fail
can modify the triangle in place for O(1) extra space
number of paths is 2^(n-1), so brute force is exponential

semantic_targets: each cell depends only on two cells below
common_mistakes: returns the last row's minimum without DP

logic_context: Add a balloon with value 1 at each end. Let dp[l][r] be the maximum coins from bursting all balloons strictly between l and r. Instead of choosing the first balloon to burst, choose the last one, k: when k is last, its neighbours are exactly l and r. So dp[l][r] = max over k in (l, r) of dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + a[l] × a[k] × a[r]. Fill by increasing interval length. O(n³).

mandatory: pad with 1 at both ends
choose the last balloon to burst in each interval
concept_groups: neighbours of the last balloon are l and r
advanced_bonus: O(n³) time, O(n²) space
choosing the first balloon fails because neighbours change afterwards
the two sub-intervals become independent once k is fixed as last
similar interval DP: matrix chain multiplication
answer is dp[0][n + 1]

semantic_targets: Think about the last action, not the first
fixing the last balloon fixes its neighbours
common_mistakes: Choosing the first balloon to burst
Greedy bursting of the smallest balloon

logic_context: Scan left to right keeping result, the current number and sign (+1 or -1). Build multi-digit numbers. On '+' or '-', add sign × number to result, reset number, and set the new sign. On '(', push result and sign onto the stack, then reset result to 0 and sign to +1. On ')', finish the current number, then set result = popped result + popped sign × result. Add the last number at the end. O(n).

mandatory: push result and sign on '(' and restore on ')'
accumulate sign × number into result
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(n) stack for nested parentheses
handles unary minus such as '-(2+3)'
alternative: convert to postfix then evaluate
for * and /, use a stack of terms and apply them immediately
recursive descent is another clean approach

semantic_targets: Stack saves context at each parenthesis
Sign distributes over a parenthesised group
')' combines inner result with saved outer result
common_mistakes: Treating each character as a separate number
Forgetting to apply the sign before a parenthesis

logic_context: Use a stack of surviving asteroids. Collisions happen only when a right-moving asteroid (on the stack top) meets a left-moving one (current). For a negative asteroid, while the top is positive: if top < |current|, pop it and continue; if equal, pop it and the current is destroyed; if top > |current|, the current is destroyed. Push the current asteroid if it survives. The stack is the answer. O(n).

mandatory: collision only when top moves right and current moves left
pop smaller asteroids; equal sizes destroy both
concept_groups: current destroyed if top is larger
each asteroid pushed and popped once
advanced_bonus: O(n) time, O(n) space
a left-moving asteroid followed by a right-moving one never collides
the stack holds a valid stable state at every step
same pattern as other monotonic-stack problems
simulation step by step in time is much slower

logic_context: Put all rope lengths into a min-heap. Repeatedly remove the two shortest ropes, add their sum to the total cost, and push the combined rope back. Stop when one rope remains. Joining the shortest ropes first keeps the large sums from being counted many times. O(n log n).

mandatory: always join the two shortest ropes
push the combined length back into the min-heap
advanced_bonus: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
same greedy as Huffman coding
each rope's length is counted once per join it participates in, so short ropes should be joined most often
sorting once is not enough because combined ropes must be reinserted
use 64-bit totals for large inputs

semantic_targets: Heap keeps the next smallest available
joining small ropes first minimises repeated costs
common_mistakes: Sorting once and summing adjacent pairs
forgets to push the combined rope

logic_context: Put the first element of each list into a min-heap and track the maximum among them. The range [heap minimum, current maximum] covers all lists. Repeatedly pop the minimum, update the best range if [min, max] is smaller, and push the next element from the same list, updating the maximum. Stop when any list is exhausted. O(N log k) for N total elements.

mandatory: min-heap holds one element from each list
range is [heap minimum, tracked maximum]
concept_groups: pop minimum and push next from the same list
stop when a list runs out
advanced_bonus: O(N log k) time, O(k) space
only the minimum can be advanced to shrink the range
prefer the smaller start when ranges have equal width
alternative: merge all with list labels and use a sliding window over k distinct labels
same merging pattern as merge k sorted lists

semantic_targets: Advance the smallest to improve the range
common_mistakes: Advancing the maximum instead of the minimum
Continuing after a list is exhausted

logic_context: Before the single element, pairs start at even indices; after it, pairs start at odd indices. Binary search on even indices: compute mid and make it even (if odd, subtract 1). If a[mid] == a[mid + 1], the single element is to the right, so lo = mid + 2; otherwise it is at mid or to the left, so hi = mid. When lo == hi, that index holds the answer.

mandatory: pairs start at even indices before the single element
binary search comparing a[mid] with a[mid + 1] on even mid
advanced_bonus: O(log n) time, O(1) space
XOR of all elements also works but is O(n)
alternative: compare a[mid] with a[mid ^ 1]
array length is always odd
the pair pattern breaks exactly at the single element

semantic_targets: Index parity reveals which side the single is on
the pairing pattern shifts after the single element
common_mistakes: Using XOR and claiming O(log n)
Wrong bound update causing infinite loop
compares with a[mid - 1] without parity reasoning

logic_context: Find the lower bound: the first index whose value is greater than or equal to the target. Use lo = 0 and hi = n. While lo < hi, take mid; if a[mid] < target, set lo = mid + 1; otherwise set hi = mid. When the loop ends, lo is the answer (n if the target is larger than every element). O(log n).

mandatory: find the first index with value >= target (lower bound)
search range [0, n] with hi = n
concept_groups: returns n when target exceeds all values
advanced_bonus: O(log n) time, O(1) space
lower bound also gives the first occurrence among duplicates
upper bound (first > target) is a variant
mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 avoids overflow
the loop invariant: answer always lies in [lo, hi]

semantic_targets: Lower bound gives the insert position
the loop narrows to the first not-smaller element
common_mistakes: Using hi = n - 1 and missing the end position
returns the last index of equal values

logic_context: The i-th Gray code is i ^ (i >> 1), so iterate i from 0 to 2^n - 1 and output i ^ (i >> 1). Alternatively build it by reflection: start with [0]; for each new bit, append the existing list in reverse order with the new highest bit set. Both produce 2^n codes where each neighbour (including last to first) differs by one bit.

mandatory: Gray code of i is i ^ (i >> 1)
consecutive codes differ in exactly one bit
advanced_bonus: O(2^n) time — optimal since there are 2^n outputs
reflection: new list = old list + reversed(old list) with the top bit set
convert back: XOR all right shifts of g
used in rotary encoders and Karnaugh maps to avoid errors in transitions
the last and first codes also differ by one bit

semantic_targets: both methods give the standard reflected Gray code
common_mistakes: Breaking the one-bit property between reflection halves

logic_context: Recurse with a start value and the current combination. If the combination has k numbers, record a copy. Otherwise, for each value i from start up to n - (k - size) + 1, add i, recurse with start = i + 1, then remove i. Starting from i + 1 keeps numbers increasing, so each combination is produced once, and the upper limit prunes branches that cannot reach k numbers.

mandatory: recurse with start = i + 1 so numbers increase
record when the combination has k numbers
advanced_bonus: O(C(n, k) · k) time — the output size dominates
pruning avoids branches with too few remaining numbers
iterative lexicographic generation is an alternative
order does not matter, unlike permutations
Pascal's rule C(n, k) = C(n - 1, k - 1) + C(n - 1, k) mirrors the include/exclude recursion

common_mistakes: no stopping condition at size k

logic_context: Record the starting pixel's original colour. If it already equals the new colour, return immediately. Otherwise run DFS or BFS from the start: recolour the pixel, then visit its four neighbours (up, down, left, right) that are inside the image and still have the original colour. Recolouring itself marks pixels as visited. O(m · n).

mandatory: visit 4-connected neighbours with the original colour
return early if new colour equals original
concept_groups: recolouring acts as the visited mark
advanced_bonus: O(m · n) time and space in the worst case
the early return prevents infinite loops when colours are equal
iterative BFS avoids stack overflow on large images
8-connected fill also includes diagonals
scanline fill is faster in graphics software

semantic_targets: only neighbours with the original colour spread the fill

logic_context: Scan every filled cell once. For each digit, check whether it has already appeared in the same row, the same column, or the same 3x3 box, using three sets of 9 boolean arrays (or bitmasks). The box index is (row / 3) * 3 + col / 3. If a digit repeats, the board is invalid; otherwise it is valid. Empty cells are skipped. O(81) — constant time.

logic_context: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix. For each element from index 1 onward, store it as key, shift larger elements in the sorted prefix one position right, and insert the key into the gap. Each shift fixes one inversion, so the running time is O(n + number of inversions): O(n) when the data is already or nearly sorted, and O(n²) in the worst case (reverse order). It is in place and stable.

mandatory: insert each element into the sorted prefix by shifting larger elements
time = O(n + inversions)
concept_groups: best case O(n) on sorted input
worst case O(n²) on reverse order
advanced_bonus: each shift removes exactly one inversion
online: can sort data as it arrives
used for small subarrays inside hybrid sorts (e.g. Timsort, introsort)
binary search for the position reduces comparisons but not shifts
shift instead of swapping to reduce writes

semantic_targets: Sorted prefix grows one element at a time

common_mistakes: Using swaps without noting extra writes

logic_context: Insert all elements of the first array into a hash set. Then scan the second array; for each value that is in the set, add it to the result and remove it from the set so it is reported only once. O(n + m) average time and O(n) extra space. Put the smaller array in the set to save memory.

scan the other array and collect values found in the set
concept_groups: remove from the set after reporting to avoid duplicates
build the set from the smaller array
advanced_bonus: O(n + m) average time

logic_context: Copy-on-write (COW) lets several users share the same data until one of them tries to modify it; only then is a private copy made for the writer. This saves memory and time when copies are rarely changed. Operating systems use it in fork(): parent and child share memory pages marked read-only, and a write triggers a page fault that copies only that page. It is also used in file systems, string implementations and persistent data structures.

mandatory: share data until someone writes to it
a private copy is made only on write
concept_groups: write causes a page fault and a copy
used in file systems and strings
advanced_bonus: reference counting tells whether data is shared

common_mistakes: Saying shared data can be modified in place by anyone

logic_context: Garbage collection automatically finds memory that the program can no longer reach and frees it, using techniques such as mark-and-sweep, reference counting or generational collection. C does not include a garbage collector; the programmer allocates with malloc and releases with free. This gives predictable timing, low overhead and full control — important for systems and embedded code — but makes memory leaks, dangling pointers and double frees possible.

C uses manual malloc and free

Rust uses ownership rules instead of GC

common_mistakes: Saying C has a garbage collector

logic_context: A stack overflow happens when the call stack runs out of space, usually because of very deep or infinite recursion or very large local arrays; the program typically crashes. A buffer overflow happens when a program writes past the end (or before the start) of a buffer, corrupting nearby memory in the stack, heap or globals. A stack-based buffer overflow can overwrite the return address, which attackers exploit to run their own code.

mandatory: stack overflow: call stack runs out of space
buffer overflow: writing beyond a buffer's bounds
concept_groups: deep recursion or huge local arrays cause stack overflow
unchecked copies (strcpy, gets) cause buffer overflow

semantic_targets: running out of stack versus writing out of bounds
common_mistakes: Saying buffer overflows only happen on the stack

logic_context: LRU (Least Recently Used) evicts the item that has not been accessed for the longest time, based on recency. LFU (Least Frequently Used) evicts the item with the fewest accesses, based on frequency. LRU adapts quickly to changing access patterns but can be flushed by a single large scan. LFU keeps long-term popular items but may keep stale items that were popular in the past unless counts are aged. Both can be implemented with O(1) operations.

mandatory: LRU evicts the least recently accessed item
LFU evicts the least frequently accessed item
concept_groups: LRU: hash map + doubly linked list
LFU can keep stale popular items
advanced_bonus: both achieve O(1) get and put with the right structures
LFU ties are usually broken by recency
aging or decay fixes LFU's stale-item problem

logic_context: An inverted index maps each term to a posting list — the IDs of documents containing that term, often with positions and counts. It is built by tokenising and normalising every document. To answer a query, the engine looks up each term's posting list and combines them, e.g. intersecting sorted lists for AND queries, then ranks the results with scores such as TF-IDF or BM25. This avoids scanning every document.

advanced_bonus: intersect the shortest posting list first

used by Lucene, Elasticsearch and database full-text search

logic_context: A d-ary heap is like a binary heap but each node has d children. In an array, node i's children are at d·i + 1 to d·i + d and its parent is (i - 1) / d. The height is log_d n, so insert and decrease-key (sift up) are faster, O(log_d n), but extract-min (sift down) is slower, O(d log_d n), because it compares d children. It helps when decrease-key is frequent, as in Dijkstra's algorithm on dense graphs, and 4-ary heaps are often more cache-friendly.

mandatory: each node has d children
shorter height: faster insert/decrease-key, slower extract-min
concept_groups: children at d·i + 1 to d·i + d
advanced_bonus: Dijkstra with a d-ary heap where d ≈ E/V runs in O(E log_{E/V} V)
children of a node are contiguous in memory
binary heap is the special case d = 2
choosing d trades sift-up cost against sift-down cost
d = 4 is a common practical choice

semantic_targets: pick d based on the operation mix

logic_context: A priority queue is an abstract data type: it defines operations such as insert, peek at the highest-priority element and remove it, without saying how they are implemented. A heap is a concrete data structure that is one common way to implement a priority queue, giving O(log n) insert and remove and O(1) peek. Other implementations include an unsorted array (O(1) insert, O(n) remove), a sorted array (O(n) insert, O(1) remove), a balanced BST and a Fibonacci heap.

mandatory: priority queue is an abstract data type (interface)
heap is one data structure that implements it
concept_groups: heap gives O(log n) insert and extract
advanced_bonus: binary heap peek is O(1)
Fibonacci heap gives O(1) amortised insert and decrease-key
C++ std::priority_queue is a binary heap by default

logic_context: If a.h includes b.h and b.h includes a.h, include guards stop infinite inclusion, but one header ends up being processed before the other's definitions are available, causing 'unknown type' errors. If a header only needs pointers to another struct, it can use a forward declaration such as struct B; instead of including b.h, since a pointer to an incomplete type is allowed. Moving includes into .c files or restructuring shared types into a separate header also breaks the cycle.

logic_context: A compiler error means the code is invalid (for example a syntax error or an undeclared variable), so compilation stops and no executable is produced. A warning means the code is legal but suspicious — for example an unused variable, a variable used before being set, or an implicit type conversion — so compilation continues, but the program may still behave incorrectly. Warnings should be read and fixed; flags like -Wall show more warnings and -Werror turns them into errors.

logic_context: An off-by-one error is a mistake where a loop or calculation goes one step too far or stops one step too early. For example, for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) on an array of n elements accesses arr[n], which is out of bounds. Avoid it by using consistent half-open ranges (0 to n - 1, written i < n), checking boundary cases (empty, one element, last element), and testing edge inputs.

advanced_bonus: fencepost problem: 10 sections need 11 posts

logic_context: A library is a collection of reusable functions that your code calls when it needs them — you stay in control of the program's flow, as with the C standard library or a math library. A framework provides the overall structure and calls your code at defined points (inversion of control), as with a unit-testing framework that finds and runs your test functions. In short: you call a library; a framework calls you.

advanced_bonus: callbacks give libraries some framework-like behaviour

logic_context: A static array has a size fixed when it is declared, such as int a[100]; it cannot grow, and too small a size wastes space or overflows. A dynamic array is allocated at runtime (malloc) and can grow when full by allocating a larger block and copying (realloc), usually by doubling the capacity. It tracks both its size (elements used) and capacity (space allocated), and appends cost O(1) amortised.

logic_context: A syntax error breaks the language's grammar, such as a missing semicolon, and is caught by the compiler. A runtime error happens while the program runs, such as dividing by zero or dereferencing a NULL pointer, and may crash the program. A logical error lets the program run without crashing but produces wrong results, such as using < instead of <= or the wrong formula; it is found by testing and debugging.

logic_context: A queue is a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) structure: elements are added (enqueued) at the rear and removed (dequeued) from the front, so the earliest added element leaves first. Real-world applications include printer job queues, CPU and process scheduling, handling requests on a web server, keyboard input buffers, network packet buffers and breadth-first search in graphs.

logic_context: size_t is an unsigned integer type defined in <stddef.h> (and other headers) that is large enough to hold the size of any object. It is the type returned by sizeof and strlen and taken by malloc and memcpy. Use it for sizes, lengths and array indices. Print it with %zu. Because it is unsigned, a loop counting down with i >= 0 never ends, and subtracting two sizes can wrap to a huge value.

logic_context: Truncated hashes are deterministic (the same URL gets the same code), but truncation makes collisions possible, so each must be detected and resolved. A counter encoded in base 62 (0-9, a-z, A-Z) is always unique and very short — 7 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes — but codes are sequential and guessable, and the counter must be shared across servers (for example by assigning each server a block of IDs). Random codes are hard to guess but need a database check on every insert, with more retries as the space fills. Recommend a base-62 counter (with ID blocks per server) for simplicity and guaranteed uniqueness, or random codes if unpredictability matters.

mandatory: counter + base 62 guarantees uniqueness without collisions
truncated hashes and random codes need collision handling
concept_groups: counter must be coordinated across servers
random codes need a DB uniqueness check
advanced_bonus: birthday bound: random codes collide after about √(62^7) ≈ 1.9 million inserts, so checks are essential

store a URL→code index if the same URL should reuse its code

logic_context: Exact counting stores a count for every distinct query in a hash map, then keeps a min-heap of size 100 to find the top items in O(n log 100). It is exact, but memory grows with the number of distinct queries, which can be hundreds of millions. A Count-Min Sketch uses fixed memory and never underestimates counts, but may overestimate by a bounded error; combined with a small heap of candidates, it finds heavy hitters approximately. Space-Saving keeps a fixed number of counters and guarantees to catch items above a frequency threshold. Recommend exact counting if distinct queries fit in memory or can be sharded across machines by hash; otherwise use an approximate sketch.

mandatory: exact hash map needs memory for every distinct query
Count-Min Sketch uses fixed memory but overestimates
concept_groups: min-heap of size 100 keeps the top items
sharding by hash enables exact distributed counting

common_mistakes: using a max-heap of all items

logic_context: Shunting-yard uses an operator stack to convert infix to postfix according to precedence and associativity, then evaluates the postfix form. It is iterative and compact, but unary minus, function calls and good error messages need extra special cases. A recursive descent parser writes one function per grammar level (expression → term → factor), so precedence comes from the call structure; it is easy to read and extend with unary operators and functions, and gives clear error messages, but deeply nested parentheses use recursion depth. Recommend recursive descent for a calculator expected to grow; shunting-yard for a fixed set of binary operators.

mandatory: shunting-yard: operator stack with precedence and associativity
recursive descent: one function per grammar level
concept_groups: recursive descent is easy to extend

check division by zero during evaluation

logic_context: 'DD-MM-YYYY' strings are human-readable, but string comparison sorts by day first, so ordering is wrong, and every comparison needs parsing; 'YYYY-MM-DD' would at least sort correctly. A struct of three integers is clear and compares correctly field by field (year, then month, then day), but date arithmetic such as adding 30 days is awkward. A single integer such as days since an epoch makes comparison and subtraction trivial and compact, but must be converted for display and needs care with time zones if it includes time. Recommend a single integer (or ISO format) for storage and sorting, converting to a readable form only for display.

logic_context: Returning a struct is clear and keeps related values together with value semantics; copying is cheap for small structs (and often optimised), though large structs cost more. Output pointer parameters are the common C idiom: the caller provides storage, and the return value can be an error code; the function must handle NULL pointers and the caller must pass valid addresses. Global variables make the function non-reentrant and unsafe with threads, hide data flow, and make testing harder. Recommend returning a struct for small related results, or output pointers when an error status must also be returned; avoid globals.

logic_context: Fix a top row and extend a bottom row downward. Keep a temp array where temp[c] is the sum of column c between the top and bottom rows; update it by adding the new bottom row. For each (top, bottom) pair, run Kadane's algorithm on temp to find the best column range. The best result over all pairs is the answer. O(R² · C) time, O(C) extra space; iterate over the smaller dimension squared.

logic_context: Counting 'exactly K' directly is hard with a single window, so compute atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1). atMost(K) uses a sliding window with a frequency map: expand the right end; when the number of distinct values exceeds K, shrink from the left; then every subarray ending at right and starting between left and right is valid, so add right - left + 1. Each call is O(n), so the total is O(n).

Each element moves once, so O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

logic_context: A red-black tree is a BST where each node is red or black and: the root is black; all NIL leaves are black; a red node cannot have a red child; and every path from a node to its descendant NIL leaves has the same number of black nodes (black-height). Because red nodes cannot be consecutive, the longest path is at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most 2 log₂(n + 1). Insertions and deletions restore the properties with recolouring and at most a few rotations.

logic_context: A splay tree is a self-adjusting BST that stores no balance information. Any single operation can take O(n), but any sequence of m operations takes O(m log n), i.e. amortised O(log n), and recently accessed items become fast to reach.

logic_context: Cuckoo hashing uses two (or more) hash functions, so each key has two possible slots. A lookup checks only those two slots, giving O(1) worst-case lookup time. If this cycles or takes too long, the table is rebuilt with new hash functions or resized.

logic_context: A monotonic stack keeps its elements in increasing or decreasing order from bottom to top. logic_context: The sliding window technique keeps a contiguous range [left, right] of an array or string and updates information about it incrementally as the window moves, instead of recomputing from scratch. Variable-size windows expand the right end and shrink the left end while a condition holds (e.g. longest substring without repeating characters). It usually turns O(n²) or O(n·k) solutions into O(n), but it requires that shrinking or expanding changes the condition in a predictable (monotonic) way.

logic_context: Scope is the region of code where a name can be used. Block scope applies to names declared inside braces (including function parameters); they are visible from the declaration to the end of the block. File scope applies to names declared outside all functions; they are visible from the declaration to the end of the file. Function scope applies only to goto labels, which are visible throughout the function. Function-prototype scope applies to parameter names in a prototype, which end at the end of the prototype.
