logic_context: The comma operator evaluates its left operand, discards the result, then evaluates the right operand, whose value and type become the result; there is a sequence point between them. It has the lowest precedence of all operators. It is most often used in for loops, e.g. for (i = 0, j = n - 1; i < j; i++, j--). The commas separating function arguments or variables in a declaration are separators, not the comma operator, so their evaluation order is not guaranteed in the same way.

logic_context: An abstract data type describes a data type by the operations it supports and how they behave, without specifying how it is stored or implemented. For example, a stack ADT offers push, pop and peek with last-in-first-out behaviour; a queue ADT offers enqueue and dequeue with first-in-first-out behaviour. Each ADT can have several implementations (arrays, linked lists) that users can swap without changing their code.

mandatory: ADT is defined by operations and behaviour, not implementation
examples: stack, queue, list, map
advanced_bonus: the same ADT can have different performance depending on implementation

semantic_targets: an ADT can be implemented in many ways
common_mistakes: Saying an ADT is a specific array or struct
Confusing ADT with abstract classes only

logic_context: A magic number is a numeric literal written directly in code without explanation, such as if (x > 86400) or area = 3.14159 * r * r. Readers cannot tell what it means, and if the value must change, every copy has to be found and updated. Replace magic numbers with named constants (#define SECONDS_PER_DAY 86400, const, or enum) so the code is self-explanatory and easy to maintain. Obvious values such as 0 or 1 in loops are usually fine.

mandatory: unexplained numeric literal in code
replace with a named constant
concept_groups: change the value in one place
advanced_bonus: array sizes should use named constants too
sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]) avoids hard-coding lengths
magic strings are the same problem
static analysis tools can flag magic numbers
comments are a weaker fix than names

semantic_targets: meaning becomes clear from the name
common_mistakes: Saying all numbers must be named, even 0 in loops
Confusing with magic bytes in file formats only

logic_context: Parameters are the variables listed in a function's definition, such as a and b in int add(int a, int b). Arguments are the actual values or expressions passed when the function is called, such as 3 and x in add(3, x). In C, arguments are passed by value: each argument's value is copied into the corresponding parameter, so changing a parameter does not change the caller's variable (unless a pointer is passed).

mandatory: parameters are in the function definition
arguments are the values passed in a call
concept_groups: example: int add(int a, int b) and add(3, x)
advanced_bonus: also called formal parameters and actual arguments

argument evaluation order is unspecified in C
default arguments do not exist in C

semantic_targets: arguments fill parameters at call time
common_mistakes: Saying C passes by reference by default

logic_context: An else-if ladder checks a sequence of mutually exclusive conditions one after another: the first true condition's block runs and the rest are skipped (e.g. grading by marks ranges). Nested if statements place one if inside another's block to check a condition that only matters when the outer one is true (e.g. if logged in, then if admin). Without braces, an else attaches to the nearest unmatched if (the dangling-else problem), so braces make nested logic clear.

mandatory: else-if ladder: first true condition runs, rest skipped
nested if: inner check only when outer is true
concept_groups: dangling else binds to the nearest if
advanced_bonus: order conditions in a ladder from most specific or most likely

semantic_targets: Sequential exclusive checks versus dependent checks
common_mistakes: Saying all conditions in a ladder are evaluated

logic_context: Linear search checks elements one by one from the start until it finds the target or reaches the end; it works on any array and takes O(n) time. Binary search works only on sorted arrays: it compares the target with the middle element and discards half of the remaining range each step, taking O(log n) time. For 1,000,000 elements, linear search may need 1,000,000 comparisons, while binary search needs about 20.

semantic_targets: binary search halves the search space
common_mistakes: Saying binary search works on unsorted arrays

logic_context: malloc returns NULL when it cannot allocate the requested memory. Using that NULL pointer is undefined behaviour and usually crashes the program. So always check: if (p == NULL), report the error, free any resources already acquired, and return an error code or exit cleanly. With realloc, store the result in a temporary pointer first, because on failure it returns NULL but leaves the original block allocated.

dereferencing NULL is undefined behaviour

advanced_bonus: no cast is needed for malloc's void * in C

common_mistakes: Assigning realloc's result directly to the original pointer

logic_context: A dynamic array gives fast appends and indexing with good cache use, but inserting older messages at the front shifts every element — O(n) each time. A doubly linked list supports O(1) insertion at both ends, but has pointer overhead per message, poor cache locality, and O(n) access to the k-th message. A deque or chunked list (a list of fixed-size blocks) supports O(1) insertion at both ends with good locality and near-constant indexing. Recommend a deque/chunked structure; alternatively, store messages in a dynamic array in reverse chronological order so older messages are appended.

mandatory: dynamic array: front insertion costs O(n)
deque or chunked list: O(1) at both ends with good locality
concept_groups: linked list: O(1) ends but poor locality
advanced_bonus: blocks of e.g. 64 messages reduce allocation overhead

semantic_targets: recommend a structure efficient at both ends
common_mistakes: claims linked lists have O(1) indexing

logic_context: rand() is easy but low quality: RAND_MAX may be only 32767, its algorithm is implementation-defined, rand() % n is biased, and its output is predictable. A modern PRNG like PCG or xorshift is fast, has good statistical quality and can be seeded for reproducible gameplay, but anyone who learns its state can predict future values, so it is unsafe for secrets. A cryptographically secure source (getrandom(), /dev/urandom, arc4random) is unpredictable and required for tokens, but slower. Recommend a modern PRNG for gameplay and a CSPRNG for session tokens; never use rand() for security.

mandatory: CSPRNG required for security tokens
fast seeded PRNG suits gameplay
concept_groups: rand() has small range and modulo bias
advanced_bonus: seed reproducibility helps replays and debugging
rejection sampling removes modulo bias
time(NULL) seeds are guessable
use 128 bits or more of entropy for session tokens
rand() is not guaranteed thread-safe

semantic_targets: Different needs for games and security
use separate generators for separate purposes
common_mistakes: claims PRNGs are secure if seeded randomly

logic_context: The library sin() is accurate but, without an FPU, uses slow software floating point and may not meet timing. A lookup table (e.g. 256 entries) gives a result with one array access and fixed timing, at the cost of memory and accuracy limited by the table step. Linear interpolation between neighbouring entries greatly improves accuracy for a small extra cost. Symmetry lets you store only a quarter wave, and fixed-point values avoid floating point altogether. Recommend a quarter-wave table with interpolation in fixed point when speed matters and moderate accuracy is enough; use sin() when precision is critical and time allows.

mandatory: lookup table: fast, fixed time, limited accuracy
library sin(): accurate but slow without an FPU
advanced_bonus: error of linear interpolation shrinks with the square of the table step
256-entry 16-bit table uses 512 bytes
CORDIC computes sin with shifts and adds
map x into [0, 2π) before indexing

logic_context: All three versions do O(n³) arithmetic, so the difference is memory access. In i-j-k order, the inner loop walks down a column of B, which in row-major C jumps 2000 doubles each step and causes cache misses. Reordering to i-k-j makes the inner loop scan rows of B and C sequentially, giving much better cache use and enabling vectorisation, often with a large speed-up. Blocking splits the matrices into tiles that fit in cache and multiplies tile by tile, reducing cache misses further. Recommend i-k-j first, then tiling (or simply use an optimised BLAS library).

mandatory: same O(n³) work; memory access pattern decides speed
i-k-j reads rows sequentially; tiling keeps blocks in cache
concept_groups: i-j-k walks B by columns causing cache misses
tile size chosen to fit cache
advanced_bonus: transposing B also makes access sequential

common_mistakes: Saying loop order does not matter
assumes the matrices fit in cache

logic_context: Comparing sizes is almost free (metadata only) and immediately proves the files differ if sizes differ, but equal sizes prove nothing. Chunked byte-by-byte comparison (reading blocks and using memcmp) is exact and stops at the first difference, so different files are often detected early. Hashing reads both files completely and adds computation; it is useful when one file is compared against many others or when the files are on different machines (only hashes are sent), with collisions practically impossible for SHA-256. Recommend checking sizes first, then chunked comparison for a local pair; use hashes for many-to-many or remote comparisons.

mandatory: size check is cheap but only proves difference
chunked comparison is exact and can stop early
concept_groups: hashes help with many files or remote comparison
advanced_bonus: read in large blocks (e.g. 64 KB) to reduce system calls

semantic_targets: match the method to the situation
common_mistakes: Hashing a single local pair without justification
Reading byte by byte with fgetc unnecessarily

logic_context: Store the first k items in a reservoir. For each later item number i (1-based, i > k), pick a random integer j from 1 to i; if j <= k, replace reservoir[j] with the new item. At every point, each item seen so far is in the reservoir with probability k / i, so at the end every item has probability k / n. One pass, O(n) time, O(k) memory.

mandatory: keep the first k items
replace a random slot with probability k / i for the i-th item
concept_groups: pick j uniformly from 1 to i
advanced_bonus: proof by induction: an item survives later steps with probability product (1 - 1/(m)) terms giving k/n overall

logic_context: Start with a row containing a single 1. To build the next row in place, append 1 and update entries from right to left with row[j] = row[j] + row[j - 1], so each new value uses the old values. Repeat n times: O(n²) time, O(n) space. Alternatively compute each entry directly with C(n, k) = C(n, k - 1) × (n - k + 1) / k in O(n).

update in place from right to left
advanced_bonus: right-to-left update avoids overwriting values still needed
multiplicative formula: multiply before dividing to stay exact, using 64-bit integers

common_mistakes: Updating left to right and reusing new values
Building the full triangle when only one row is needed without noting memory

logic_context: Cells with the same value of row + column lie on the same diagonal, numbered d = 0 to m + n - 2. For even d, walk the diagonal upward (row decreasing); for odd d, walk it downward (row increasing). The starting cell of each diagonal depends on whether d is past the last row or column. A simpler method collects each diagonal's cells in one direction and reverses every other diagonal. O(m · n).

alternate direction for even and odd diagonals

advanced_bonus: direct approach uses O(1) extra space besides output

logic_context: Use elimination. Start with candidate c = 0. For each person i from 1 to n - 1, if knows(c, i), then c cannot be the celebrity, so set c = i; otherwise i cannot be the celebrity. After one pass, only c might be the celebrity. Verify: c must know nobody, and everybody must know c. If any check fails, there is no celebrity. About 3(n - 1) calls, O(n) time.

verify the final candidate
concept_groups: if c knows i, c is eliminated
verification: c knows no one and all know c
advanced_bonus: checking all pairs takes O(n²) calls

there can be at most one celebrity

logic_context: Scan once from left to right. At even index i, if a[i] > a[i + 1], swap them; at odd index i, if a[i] < a[i + 1], swap them. Each swap fixes the current pair without breaking the previous one, because the swapped-in value only makes the earlier relation stronger. O(n) time, O(1) space. (The strict version a[0] < a[1] > a[2] needs a median-based approach.)

even index: a[i] <= a[i + 1]; odd index: a[i] >= a[i + 1]

strict version needs a different method
advanced_bonus: sorting then swapping pairs also works but costs O(n log n)

many valid outputs exist
works with duplicates for the non-strict version

logic_context: Keep two heaps: a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half, balanced so their sizes differ by at most one. Add each new element to the correct heap and rebalance. To remove the element leaving the window, use lazy deletion: record it in a hash map of pending deletions and discard it when it reaches the top of a heap, adjusting the size counts. The median is the top of the larger heap (odd k) or the average of both tops (even k). O(n log k).

mandatory: max-heap for lower half, min-heap for upper half
lazy deletion for elements leaving the window
concept_groups: rebalance so sizes differ by at most one
advanced_bonus: track 'valid' sizes separately from physical heap sizes under lazy deletion

semantic_targets: lazy deletion avoids searching inside heaps

logic_context: For each position start, take its item and find its correct position by counting how many elements after start are smaller. If the item is already there, move on. Otherwise skip past equal elements, place the item in its correct position, and pick up the element that was there. Repeat for the picked-up element until the cycle returns to start. Each element is written at most once, directly into its final position, so the number of writes is minimal. O(n²) time, in place, not stable.

mandatory: correct position = number of smaller elements
rotate each cycle by placing items directly into final positions
concept_groups: continue until the cycle returns to start

advanced_bonus: useful when writes are expensive, such as on flash memory
the number of writes equals n minus the number of fixed points minus cycles adjustments — the theoretical minimum

logic_context: Precompute factorials fact[i] = i! mod p for i up to n. Because p is prime, Fermat's little theorem gives the modular inverse a^(p - 2) mod p, so compute invFact[n] = fact[n]^(p - 2) by fast exponentiation and fill invFact[i - 1] = invFact[i] × i mod p downward. Then C(n, r) = fact[n] × invFact[r] × invFact[n - r] mod p, answered in O(1). Preprocessing is O(n + log p).

use modular inverses via Fermat's little theorem

logic_context: Store a lazy value at each node for an update that has not yet been pushed to its children. For a range update, if a node's segment lies completely inside the update range, add value × segment length to the node's sum, add value to its lazy tag, and stop. If it partly overlaps, first push the node's pending lazy value down to its children, recurse into both children, then recompute the node's sum. Queries push down pending values the same way before descending. Each operation touches O(log n) nodes.

logic_context: A simple method finds the middle node with slow and fast pointers, makes it the root, and recursively builds the left subtree from the part before the middle and the right subtree from the part after it — O(n log n). An O(n) method counts the nodes, then builds the tree in inorder: build(l, r) builds the left subtree of size (mid - l) first, creates the root from the current list node, advances the list pointer, then builds the right subtree. The inorder order of the BST matches the list order.

logic_context: Run BFS from any node and find the farthest node u. Then run BFS from u; the largest distance found, to some node v, is the diameter, and the path u–v is a longest path. This works because the farthest node from any starting point is always an endpoint of some diameter. O(n) time. For weighted trees with non-negative weights, use DFS distances instead of BFS levels.

logic_context: Pick any vertex v. Run DFS from v in the original graph; if some vertex is not reached, the graph is not strongly connected. Then build the transpose graph (all edges reversed) and run DFS from v again; if some vertex is not reached, some vertex cannot reach v, so the graph is not strongly connected. If both searches reach every vertex, every vertex can reach v and v can reach every vertex, so all pairs are mutually reachable. O(V + E).

logic_context: Let dp[i][c] be the minimum cost to paint houses 0..i with house i painted colour c. Then dp[i][c] = cost[i][c] + min over c' ≠ c of dp[i - 1][c']. logic_context: Characters in the longest common subsequence (LCS) can be shared, and every other character must appear once. So the length is m + n - LCS(s1, s2). Compute the LCS with the standard DP table. To build the actual supersequence, backtrack through the table: on matching characters emit once and move diagonally; otherwise emit the character from the direction that kept the larger LCS value, then append any leftovers.

mandatory: length = m + n - LCS length
LCS characters are shared once
concept_groups: emit non-matching characters from both strings
advanced_bonus: O(m · n) time and space; length alone can use O(min(m, n)) space
example: 'abac' and 'cab' → length 5 ('cabac')
multiple shortest supersequences may exist
direct DP: dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1] if match, else 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])
related to edit distance with only insertions

logic_context: Let dp[i][j] be the number of ways the first j characters of t appear as a subsequence of the first i characters of s. dp[i][0] = 1 (empty t matches once) and dp[0][j] = 0 for j > 0. For each i, j: dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j] (skip s[i - 1]) plus dp[i - 1][j - 1] if s[i - 1] == t[j - 1] (use it). The answer is dp[m][n]. O(m · n), reducible to O(n) space by iterating j backwards.

mandatory: dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j] + (match ? dp[i - 1][j - 1] : 0)
empty t has exactly one match
concept_groups: skip or use each character of s
advanced_bonus: counts can be huge — use 64-bit or a modulus
example: s = 'rabbbit', t = 'rabbit' gives 3
backward j loop prevents reusing the updated value
differs from LCS, which finds a length, not a count
if t is longer than s, the answer is 0

semantic_targets: each match adds the ways to form the shorter prefix

logic_context: Represent the set of tasks already assigned as a bitmask. Let dp[mask] be the minimum cost of assigning the first popcount(mask) people to exactly the tasks in mask. Start with dp[0] = 0. For each mask, the next person is k = popcount(mask); for every task j not in mask, update dp[mask | (1 << j)] = min(dp[mask | (1 << j)], dp[mask] + cost[k][j]). The answer is dp[(1 << n) - 1]. O(2^n · n) time, practical for n up to about 20.

mandatory: bitmask represents assigned tasks
person index equals the number of set bits
concept_groups: transition adds one task for the next person
advanced_bonus: far better than trying all n! permutations
the Hungarian algorithm solves assignment in O(n³) for larger n
memory 2^n entries — about 1 million for n = 20
__builtin_popcount gives the person index quickly
same pattern solves TSP with dp[mask][last]

semantic_targets: Exponential but much smaller than factorial
bitmask encodes which tasks are used
common_mistakes: Tracking person separately and blowing up states
Reusing a task already in the mask

logic_context: With two queues, make push expensive: enqueue the new element into the empty queue q2, move all elements from q1 into q2, then swap q1 and q2. Now q1's front is the newest element, so pop and top are O(1) dequeues/peeks. Push costs O(n). A single-queue version enqueues the new element and then rotates the previous n - 1 elements behind it. Alternatively, make push O(1) and pop O(n).

mandatory: make either push or pop O(n) to reverse the order
after push, the newest element is at the queue front
concept_groups: pop and top O(1) in the push-heavy version
choose based on which operation is more frequent
advanced_bonus: one queue: after enqueueing x, dequeue and re-enqueue size - 1 elements
cost cannot be O(1) amortised for both operations the way two-stack queues are
choose the costly operation based on usage
empty-stack checks are needed for pop and top
this is mainly an exercise in ADT emulation

semantic_targets: rotation brings the newest to the front

logic_context: Simulate the stack. Go through the pushed sequence, pushing each element. After each push, while the stack is not empty and its top equals the next element of the popped sequence, pop it and advance in the popped sequence. After all pushes, the popped sequence is valid if the stack is empty. Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so O(n).

mandatory: simulate pushes and pop greedily when the top matches
valid if the stack is empty at the end
concept_groups: advance through popped sequence on each pop
each element pushed and popped once
advanced_bonus: greedy popping is correct because delaying a matching pop never helps
the popped array's pointer can reuse the pushed array as the stack for O(1) extra space
elements are assumed distinct
both sequences must have the same length
related to counting valid stack permutations (Catalan numbers)

semantic_targets: an unmatched top at the end means invalid
common_mistakes: Not popping repeatedly in a loop
assumes popped is reverse of pushed

logic_context: Sort projects by required capital. Repeat up to k times: move every project whose required capital is at most the current capital into a max-heap keyed by profit (using a pointer into the sorted list). If the heap is empty, stop — nothing is affordable. Otherwise take the project with the largest profit and add it to the capital. Greedy is optimal because taking the most profitable affordable project never reduces future options. O(n log n + k log n).

mandatory: sort by required capital and unlock affordable projects
pick the most profitable affordable project with a max-heap
advanced_bonus: capital only grows, so unlocked projects stay affordable
a min-heap by capital can replace the sorted list
greedy choice is safe because profits are non-negative
each project enters the max-heap at most once
use 64-bit capital for large values

semantic_targets: more capital never makes options worse
common_mistakes: doesn't stop when heap is empty

logic_context: Binary search over columns. Pick the middle column and find the row of its maximum element. Compare that element with its left and right neighbours. If the left neighbour is larger, a peak exists in the left half; if the right neighbour is larger, search the right half; otherwise this element is a peak (it is the column maximum, so it beats up and down too). O(m log n) for m rows and n columns.

mandatory: binary search on columns using the column maximum
move toward a larger horizontal neighbour
concept_groups: column maximum beats its vertical neighbours
stop when both horizontal neighbours are smaller
choose the smaller dimension to binary search
advanced_bonus: a larger neighbour guarantees a peak on that side because values cannot increase forever
binary search on rows instead gives O(n log m)
the greedy climb from any cell also finds a peak but can take O(m · n)
treat outside cells as -infinity
not necessarily the global maximum

semantic_targets: Reduce one dimension with binary search
common_mistakes: Choosing an arbitrary cell in the middle column
Wrong direction of the half to keep
claims it finds the global maximum

logic_context: Insert each number's bits into a binary trie from the most significant bit (e.g. bit 31) to the least. For each number, walk the trie trying to take the opposite bit at each level, since a differing bit gives a 1 in the XOR at that position; if the opposite branch does not exist, take the same bit. The value formed is the best XOR partner for that number. The maximum over all numbers is the answer. O(n · 32) time.

mandatory: binary trie of bits from most to least significant
greedily choose the opposite bit at each level
concept_groups: fall back to the same bit when needed
advanced_bonus: greedy from the top bit works because a higher bit outweighs all lower bits combined
alternative: build the answer bit by bit using prefixes in a hash set
brute force over all pairs is O(n²)
trie memory is up to n · B nodes
same trie supports maximum XOR with a query value

semantic_targets: each level fixes one bit of the result
common_mistakes: Brute force over pairs without noting cost
Starting from the least significant bit
Choosing the same bit when the opposite exists
ignores sign bits for negative numbers
claims XOR of the two largest numbers is the answer

logic_context: Recursively choose the next segment of length 1, 2 or 3 starting at the current position. A segment is valid if its value is between 0 and 255 and it has no leading zero unless it is exactly '0'. Add it, recurse for the next segment, then remove it. When four segments are chosen and the whole string is used, record the address. Prune when the remaining characters are fewer than the remaining segments or more than three times that number.

mandatory: choose segments of length 1-3 recursively
each segment 0-255 without leading zeros
concept_groups: record when 4 segments use all digits
advanced_bonus: at most 3^4 = 81 combinations, so the search is tiny
pruning: remaining digits must be between (segments left) and 3 × (segments left)
three nested loops over dot positions is an equivalent iterative approach
'0' is valid but '00' and '01' are not
build the output string with dots only when recording

semantic_targets: exactly four segments covering every digit
common_mistakes: records with fewer than four segments

logic_context: Repeatedly compute the sum of squares of the digits. The sequence either reaches 1 (happy) or falls into a cycle that never includes 1. Detect the cycle with a hash set of seen values (if a value repeats, it is not happy), or with Floyd's slow and fast pointers to use O(1) space. The values quickly fall below a small bound (for 32-bit inputs the sum is at most 810), so it finishes fast.

mandatory: repeat sum of squares of digits
detect a cycle to stop
concept_groups: Floyd's slow/fast pointers for O(1) space
advanced_bonus: all unhappy numbers eventually enter the cycle 4 → 16 → 37 → 58 → 89 → 145 → 42 → 20 → 4
the next value is much smaller than large inputs, so few steps are needed
Floyd's method avoids extra memory
digit extraction with % 10 and / 10
1 is a fixed point of the process

semantic_targets: a non-1 cycle proves the number is unhappy
common_mistakes: Using a fixed iteration limit without justification

logic_context: fork() creates a new child process that is a copy of the calling parent: same code, a copy of memory, and duplicated open file descriptors. It returns twice: 0 in the child, the child's process ID in the parent, and -1 in the parent if creation fails. The processes then run independently with separate address spaces (usually implemented with copy-on-write). The parent should call wait() or waitpid() to collect the child's exit status, otherwise the child remains a zombie after exiting.

mandatory: fork() creates a child process copying the parent
returns 0 in the child, child's PID in the parent, -1 on error
advanced_bonus: exec() replaces the child's program image, commonly right after fork
a zombie is a finished child not yet reaped; an orphan is adopted by init/systemd
output buffered before fork may be printed twice — fflush first
order of execution between parent and child is not guaranteed
fork in a multithreaded program copies only the calling thread

common_mistakes: Saying parent and child share memory variables
assumes the child always runs first

logic_context: A pipe is a one-way byte stream managed by the kernel. pipe(fd) creates two file descriptors: fd[0] for reading and fd[1] for writing. After fork(), the parent and child each close the end they do not use and communicate by writing to and reading from the other end. read() blocks until data arrives, and returns 0 (end of file) once all write ends are closed; write() blocks when the pipe's buffer is full. Named pipes (FIFOs) let unrelated processes communicate.

mandatory: one-way byte stream with read end and write end
created with pipe(fd) and shared via fork()
concept_groups: read returns 0 when all writers close
writes block when buffer is full
advanced_bonus: writes of up to PIPE_BUF bytes are atomic
Linux pipe buffer is typically 64 KB
forgetting to close write ends prevents EOF and can hang readers
shell pipelines (a | b) use pipes with dup2
two pipes are needed for two-way communication

semantic_targets: closing ends signals end of data

logic_context: First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) runs processes in arrival order without preemption; it is simple but short jobs can wait behind a long one (convoy effect). Shortest Job First (SJF) runs the job with the smallest burst next, minimising average waiting time, but it needs burst lengths in advance and can starve long jobs; its preemptive form is Shortest Remaining Time First. Round Robin gives each process a fixed time quantum in turn, giving good response time and fairness; a quantum that is too small adds context-switch overhead, and one that is too large behaves like FCFS.

mandatory: FCFS: arrival order, convoy effect
SJF: shortest burst first, minimal average waiting, possible starvation
concept_groups: Round Robin: time quantum, fair response
burst lengths must be estimated for SJF
advanced_bonus: SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time among non-preemptive schedules
aging prevents starvation by raising priority over time
burst estimates often use exponential averaging
Round Robin suits interactive time-sharing systems
multilevel feedback queues combine these ideas

common_mistakes: Saying SJF needs no burst information
Claiming Round Robin minimises average waiting time

logic_context: A context switch is when the CPU stops running one process or thread and starts running another. The OS saves the current one's state — registers, program counter, stack pointer — and restores the next one's saved state. It happens on timer interrupts, blocking I/O, system calls or when a higher-priority task becomes ready. The direct cost is saving and restoring state and running the scheduler; the indirect cost is that caches and the TLB lose useful data, especially when switching between processes with different address spaces.

mandatory: save the current task's CPU state and load another's
triggered by interrupts, blocking or scheduling decisions
concept_groups: indirect cost: cache and TLB pollution
process switch costs more than thread switch
advanced_bonus: thread switches within a process keep the same address space, so the TLB need not be flushed
tagged TLBs (ASIDs) reduce flush costs
too small a Round Robin quantum causes frequent switches
typical cost is microseconds, but cache effects can dominate
user-level threads/coroutines switch without kernel involvement

semantic_targets: indirect costs often exceed direct costs
common_mistakes: Confusing with mode switch (user to kernel) only
says threads switch costlier than processes

logic_context: When a page fault occurs and memory is full, the OS must evict a page. FIFO evicts the page that has been in memory the longest. LRU evicts the page that has not been used for the longest time, which approximates future use well but is costly to track exactly, so systems use approximations such as the Clock algorithm. Optimal evicts the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future; it is not implementable but serves as a benchmark. Belady's anomaly is when giving FIFO more frames causes more page faults; LRU and Optimal do not suffer from it.

mandatory: FIFO evicts oldest, LRU least recently used, Optimal used furthest in future
Belady's anomaly: more frames can increase faults under FIFO
concept_groups: LRU and Optimal are stack algorithms
page faults counted on a reference string
advanced_bonus: classic anomaly example: reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 with 3 vs 4 frames under FIFO
Clock uses a reference bit and a circular pointer
stack algorithms never show Belady's anomaly
thrashing occurs when the working set does not fit in memory
dirty pages cost more to evict because they must be written back

semantic_targets: LRU uses the past to predict the future
common_mistakes: Saying Optimal can be implemented in practice

logic_context: Producers add items to a fixed-size shared buffer and consumers remove them. Producers must wait when the buffer is full, consumers must wait when it is empty, and buffer access must be mutually exclusive. A classic solution uses three semaphores: empty (initialised to the buffer size), full (initialised to 0) and mutex (initialised to 1). Producer: wait(empty), wait(mutex), insert, signal(mutex), signal(full). Consumer: wait(full), wait(mutex), remove, signal(mutex), signal(empty).

mandatory: fixed-size shared buffer between producers and consumers
semaphores empty, full and mutex coordinate access
concept_groups: empty starts at buffer size, full at 0
signal the other side after each operation
advanced_bonus: waiting on mutex before empty can deadlock when the buffer is full
condition variables with a mutex are an alternative (pthread_cond_wait in a while loop)
circular array is the usual buffer
multiple producers and consumers work with the same scheme
busy-waiting wastes CPU compared with blocking semaphores

semantic_targets: producers block when full, consumers when empty
common_mistakes: Taking the mutex before waiting on empty/full

logic_context: A file descriptor is a small non-negative integer that indexes the process's table of open files, sockets and pipes. 0, 1 and 2 are standard input, output and error. Low-level system calls such as open, read, write and close work with descriptors and are unbuffered. A FILE * stream from fopen is a C standard library wrapper around a descriptor that adds buffering and formatted I/O; fileno(fp) returns its descriptor and fdopen() wraps a descriptor in a stream.

mandatory: small integer index into the process's open-file table
0, 1, 2 are stdin, stdout, stderr
concept_groups: fileno and fdopen convert between them
descriptors also refer to pipes and sockets
advanced_bonus: fork() copies the descriptor table, so parent and child share file offsets
dup2() redirects one descriptor to another (used for shell redirection)
not closing descriptors leaks them; limits apply (ulimit -n)
mixing FILE * and raw writes on the same file can reorder output due to buffering
open() returns the lowest available descriptor

semantic_targets: FILE * is a buffered layer over a descriptor
common_mistakes: Saying FILE * and descriptors are the same thing
claims read() is buffered by stdio

logic_context: strtok(str, delims) splits a string into tokens. The first call passes the string; later calls pass NULL to continue from where it stopped. It writes '\0' over the delimiter after each token, so it modifies the original string and cannot be used on string literals. It keeps its position in hidden static state, so it is not thread-safe or reentrant, and you cannot tokenise two strings in an interleaved way. Consecutive delimiters are treated as one, so empty fields are skipped. Safer alternatives are strtok_r (POSIX) and strsep.

mandatory: first call with the string, later calls with NULL
modifies the string and keeps hidden static state
concept_groups: cannot be used on string literals
advanced_bonus: strtok_r stores state in a caller-provided pointer
strsep returns empty tokens for consecutive delimiters
copy the string first if the original must stay intact
returns NULL when no tokens remain
delimiter set can change between calls

common_mistakes: Calling strtok on a string literal
Passing the string again on later calls
expects empty fields between consecutive delimiters

logic_context: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C, so you must check before doing the operation, not after. For a + b with b > 0, overflow occurs if a > INT_MAX - b; with b < 0, if a < INT_MIN - b. For multiplication, compare against INT_MAX / b with sign care. Alternatives: compute in a wider type (long long) and range-check, or use compiler builtins such as __builtin_add_overflow and __builtin_mul_overflow. -fsanitize=undefined detects overflow at runtime during testing.

mandatory: signed overflow is undefined behaviour — check before the operation
for addition with b > 0: overflow if a > INT_MAX - b
concept_groups: unsigned arithmetic wraps but may still be a bug
advanced_bonus: checking after the fact (e.g. sum < a) is invalid for signed types because UB has already happened
C23 adds ckd_add, ckd_sub and ckd_mul in <stdckdint.h>
size calculations for malloc (n * size) must be overflow-checked
INT_MIN / -1 and INT_MIN % -1 also overflow
-ftrapv makes signed overflow trap

semantic_targets: overflow must be caught before it happens

logic_context: An approximation algorithm solves an NP-hard optimisation problem in polynomial time while guaranteeing that its answer is within a known factor of the optimal value. The approximation ratio states that factor: a 2-approximation for a minimisation problem never returns more than twice the optimal cost. Example: for vertex cover, repeatedly pick any uncovered edge and add both endpoints — this produces a cover at most twice the minimum size. Unlike heuristics, approximation algorithms come with a proven worst-case guarantee.

mandatory: polynomial-time solution with a proven bound relative to optimal
ratio: e.g. at most twice optimal for minimisation
concept_groups: used when exact solutions are infeasible
advanced_bonus: metric TSP: MST doubling gives 2, Christofides gives 1.5
greedy set cover achieves about ln n
a PTAS achieves (1 + ε) for any ε > 0 with polynomial time for fixed ε
some problems cannot be approximated within certain ratios unless P = NP
the vertex cover bound holds because any cover must contain an endpoint of each chosen edge

semantic_targets: the ratio compares to the unknown optimum
common_mistakes: Saying the ratio is measured on average
claims it finds the optimal solution

logic_context: In C, a string is an array of characters, and in an expression it becomes a pointer to its first character. So s1 == s2 compares the addresses, not the characters, and is usually false even for equal text. Use strcmp(s1, s2) from <string.h>, which compares character by character and returns 0 when the strings are equal, a negative value if s1 sorts first, and a positive value otherwise. strncmp compares at most n characters.

mandatory: == compares pointers (addresses), not contents
use strcmp, which returns 0 for equal strings
concept_groups: strcmp returns negative, zero or positive
equal text in different arrays has different addresses
advanced_bonus: identical string literals may be merged by the compiler, so == can appear to work by accident
strcmp compares by unsigned character values
case-insensitive comparison: strcasecmp (POSIX)
both strings must be null-terminated
comparing with a char like s == 'a' is also wrong

semantic_targets: use string functions for string content
common_mistakes: Treating strcmp's return as true/false (1 for equal)
assumes strings are a built-in type

logic_context: A compiler is a program that translates source code into machine code or an executable, for example gcc or clang. An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is an application that combines tools for development — a code editor, a build system, a debugger and often a compiler integration — in one interface, for example VS Code, Code::Blocks or CLion. An IDE uses a compiler behind the scenes; you can also compile without any IDE from the command line.

mandatory: compiler translates source code to machine code
IDE bundles editor, build tools and debugger in one application
concept_groups: compiling is possible without an IDE
advanced_bonus: IDEs add features like syntax highlighting, auto-completion and refactoring
a build system (make, CMake) decides how to call the compiler
debuggers such as gdb can be used inside or outside an IDE
some editors become IDE-like with extensions
the same code compiles the same way regardless of IDE

semantic_targets: an IDE is a convenience layer
common_mistakes: Saying an IDE is a compiler
Saying you need an IDE to compile
claims the IDE changes the language

logic_context: In static typing, the type of every variable is known and checked at compile time, so many type errors are found before the program runs; C, C++ and Java are statically typed. In dynamic typing, types belong to values and are checked at runtime, so a variable can hold different types over time; Python and JavaScript are dynamically typed. C is statically typed but fairly weakly typed, because it allows implicit conversions and casts that can bypass type safety.

mandatory: static: types checked at compile time
dynamic: types checked at runtime
concept_groups: Python and JavaScript are dynamically typed
C allows implicit conversions and casts (weak typing)
advanced_bonus: static typing enables compiler optimisations
dynamic typing offers flexibility and faster prototyping
strong vs weak typing is a separate axis from static vs dynamic
void * and casts let C code break type rules
type inference gives static typing with less writing

semantic_targets: static vs dynamic is different from strong vs weak
common_mistakes: Confusing static typing with the static keyword
claims dynamic typing means no types

logic_context: Input validation means checking that data from users, files or networks has the expected format and range before using it. It prevents crashes, wrong results and security problems such as buffer overflows. In C: check the return value of scanf (the number of items read), limit string reads to the buffer size (fgets, or %99s for a 100-byte buffer), convert numbers with strtol and check for errors and range, and reject or re-prompt when input is invalid.

mandatory: check input format and range before using it
prevents crashes, wrong results and security bugs
concept_groups: strtol with error and range checks
advanced_bonus: never trust input from outside the program
clear leftover characters after a failed scanf to avoid infinite loops
whitelisting allowed values is safer than blacklisting bad ones
validate array indices from input before use
the same idea applies to files and network data

common_mistakes: validates only after using the data

logic_context: getchar() must be able to return every possible character value (0 to 255 as unsigned char) and also the special value EOF, which is a negative int (usually -1), to signal end of input or an error. A char cannot represent all of these distinctly: if char is signed, a valid byte 0xFF may compare equal to EOF; if char is unsigned, the comparison with EOF never succeeds and the loop never ends. So store the result in an int: int c; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { ... }.

mandatory: returns int to represent all byte values plus EOF
store the result in an int, not a char
concept_groups: EOF is a negative value, usually -1
advanced_bonus: fgetc and getc follow the same rule
feof and ferror distinguish end of file from errors
characters are returned as unsigned char converted to int
whether plain char is signed is implementation-defined
pressing Ctrl+D (Unix) or Ctrl+Z (Windows) sends EOF from a terminal

semantic_targets: int holds every character and EOF
common_mistakes: Storing the result in a char
Saying EOF is a character in the file

logic_context: bsearch(key, base, nmemb, size, compar) performs binary search on an array. You pass a pointer to the key, the array's start, the number of elements, the size of each element, and a comparison function that returns negative, zero or positive like qsort's comparator. The array must already be sorted in the same order the comparator defines. It returns a pointer to a matching element, or NULL if none is found. With duplicates, any matching element may be returned. It runs in O(log n).

mandatory: binary search on a sorted array with a user comparator
returns a pointer to a match or NULL
concept_groups: arguments: key, base, count, element size, comparator
comparator returns negative, zero or positive
array must be sorted with the same ordering
advanced_bonus: the comparator's first argument is the key, the second an array element
with duplicates, there is no guarantee which match is returned
use the same comparator for qsort and bsearch
compare with (a > b) - (a < b) to avoid overflow
cast the returned void * to the element type

common_mistakes: Comparator using subtraction that can overflow
assumes the first duplicate is returned

logic_context: Process per connection gives strong isolation — one crash does not affect others — and simple code, but each process costs memory and creation time, and sharing state requires IPC. Thread per connection is lighter and shares memory easily, but thousands of threads each need a stack, cause context-switch overhead, and shared data brings synchronisation bugs. An event loop with non-blocking sockets and epoll lets one thread watch thousands of connections with little memory, but the code becomes a state machine and any slow computation blocks every client. Recommend an event loop for many idle connections, with a small worker thread pool for CPU-heavy work.

mandatory: event loop handles many idle connections with little memory
process/thread per connection costs memory and switching
concept_groups: threads share memory but need synchronisation
slow work blocks the event loop
combine event loop with a worker pool
advanced_bonus: this is the classic C10K problem
default thread stacks reserve megabytes of virtual memory each
epoll (Linux), kqueue (BSD) and IOCP (Windows) scale to many sockets
pre-forked process pools reduce fork cost
libraries such as libuv and libevent simplify event-driven code

semantic_targets: choose by connection count and work type
common_mistakes: Recommending one thread per connection for thousands of idle clients without discussion
Ignoring blocking work in the event loop
claims processes share memory by default

logic_context: Pipes are simple and built into the shell, but they are one-way byte streams with a limited kernel buffer, and every byte is copied into and out of the kernel. Shared memory maps the same region into both processes, so data is not copied at all, making it the fastest option for large data, but the processes must coordinate access with semaphores or mutexes and agree on the data layout. Sockets (Unix-domain locally, TCP across machines) are bidirectional and flexible and allow the processes to move to different machines later, but add more overhead than pipes. Recommend shared memory with proper synchronisation for large, frequent transfers; sockets if distribution may be needed; pipes for simple one-way streams.

mandatory: shared memory avoids copying and is fastest for large data
shared memory needs explicit synchronisation
concept_groups: pipes: one-way, kernel copies, limited buffer
advanced_bonus: POSIX shm_open + mmap or System V shmget create shared memory
a ring buffer in shared memory with atomic indices is a common design
pipes copy data twice (user→kernel→user)
message queues (POSIX mq) are another option for discrete messages
shared memory crashes can leave inconsistent data — design recovery

semantic_targets: match the IPC to data size and deployment
common_mistakes: says sockets only work across machines

logic_context: atoi is simple but cannot report errors: it returns 0 for invalid text (indistinguishable from a real 0) and has undefined behaviour on overflow. sscanf with %d returns how many items were converted, so it detects missing numbers, but overflow is still undefined and trailing junk like '12abc' is accepted unless you check with %n. strtol returns an end pointer (to detect empty input and trailing characters), sets errno to ERANGE on overflow, and supports different bases; you then check the result fits in int. Recommend strtol with checks on errno, the end pointer and the range.

mandatory: atoi cannot report errors
strtol reports end position and overflow via errno
concept_groups: sscanf return value detects missing numbers
advanced_bonus: set errno = 0 before calling strtol
endptr == input means no digits were found
strtol accepts leading whitespace and a sign
use strtoll or strtoul for other types
read the line with fgets first, then convert

logic_context: A hash index gives about one disk access for exact matches but keeps keys in no order, so range queries require a full scan. A balanced BST supports ranges, but each node holds one key, so a billion keys means about 30 levels, and each level can be a separate random disk read. A B+ tree stores hundreds of keys per node sized to a disk page, so its height is only 3–4 for a billion keys, and its leaves are linked in key order, making range scans sequential. Recommend a B+ tree; a hash index only suits equality-only workloads.

mandatory: B+ tree: high fanout gives 3-4 levels and linked leaves for ranges
hash index cannot answer range queries efficiently
concept_groups: balanced BST needs ~30 levels for a billion keys
each level may cost a disk read

logic_context: Flash must be erased in large blocks before rewriting, and each block survives only a limited number of erase cycles (often around 10,000 to 100,000). Overwriting one location every minute erases the same block about 525,000 times a year, wearing it out quickly. A circular log appends records across many blocks, erasing each block only when the log wraps around, so wear is spread evenly and device life increases roughly in proportion to the number of blocks. It needs sequence numbers to find the newest record at boot and checksums to handle power loss mid-write. Recommend the circular log with sequence numbers and CRCs.

mandatory: overwriting one location wears out that block quickly
circular log spreads erases across blocks (wear levelling)
concept_groups: flash erases in blocks with limited cycles

advanced_bonus: one write per minute ≈ 525,600 writes per year

semantic_targets: Spread writes over time and space
common_mistakes: No way to find the newest record

logic_context: Track two values while scanning: keep = the best sum of a subarray ending at i with no deletion (Kadane: max(a[i], keep + a[i])), and del = the best sum ending at i with exactly one deletion: max(del + a[i], previous keep), where the second option deletes a[i]. Initialise del to negative infinity at the first element so the subarray cannot become empty. The answer is the maximum of keep and del over all positions. O(n) time, O(1) space.

logic_context: Run Dijkstra's algorithm while also keeping ways[v], the number of shortest paths to v, with ways[source] = 1. When relaxing edge (u, v, w): if dist[u] + w < dist[v], a strictly shorter path is found, so set dist[v] = dist[u] + w and ways[v] = ways[u]; if dist[u] + w == dist[v], another shortest path is found, so add ways[u] to ways[v].
