logic_context: Count bit by bit. For bit position i, the bit pattern repeats every 2^(i + 1) numbers: 2^i zeros followed by 2^i ones. Using the n + 1 numbers from 0 to n, the full cycles contribute (n + 1) / 2^(i + 1) × 2^i ones, and the remainder (n + 1) % 2^(i + 1) contributes max(0, remainder - 2^i). Sum over all bit positions up to the highest bit of n. O(log n).

mandatory: count ones per bit position
each bit repeats in cycles of length 2^(i + 1)
advanced_bonus: recursive alternative: with x = highest power of two ≤ n, count = x·log2(x)/2 + (n - x + 1) + f(n - x)
per-number popcount gives O(n log n) or O(n) with builtins
DP: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1) builds counts for every number in O(n)
use 64-bit totals for large n
example: n = 7 gives 12

semantic_targets: each bit position is counted independently
common_mistakes: Looping over all numbers and claiming O(log n)
Off-by-one using n instead of n + 1

logic_context: If the total is not divisible by k, or the largest element exceeds total / k, return false. Let target = total / k. Sort numbers in descending order and backtrack: place each number into one of k buckets whose current sum plus the number does not exceed target; recurse to the next number; undo on failure. Prune by skipping buckets with the same current sum as an earlier bucket (they are equivalent) and stopping after trying an empty bucket. Alternatively, bitmask DP over used elements runs in O(2^n · n).

mandatory: target = total / k, with divisibility check
backtrack placing each number into a bucket within target
advanced_bonus: placing large numbers first prunes early
if a number fails in an empty bucket, it will fail in any other empty bucket
bitmask DP: dp[mask] = current bucket sum modulo target
k = 2 reduces to subset-sum with target total/2
NP-complete in general

semantic_targets: each bucket must reach exactly the target

logic_context: Use backtracking: start from a square, mark it with move number 1, and try each of the 8 knight moves to an unvisited square inside the board, marking the move number and recursing. If all N² squares are filled, a tour is found; if no move works, unmark the square and backtrack. Plain backtracking is exponential, so use Warnsdorff's heuristic: always move to the square with the fewest onward moves, which finds a tour almost instantly for most board sizes.

mandatory: backtracking over 8 possible knight moves
Warnsdorff's heuristic: choose the square with fewest onward moves
concept_groups: success when N² squares are visited
advanced_bonus: plain backtracking is exponential — impractical for large N
Warnsdorff runs in about O(N²) in practice but is not guaranteed for every start
closed tours end a knight's move away from the start
tours exist for all N ≥ 5
break ties in Warnsdorff carefully (e.g. by a secondary rule)

semantic_targets: the least constrained next square is tried last

logic_context: Put the first k + 1 elements into a min-heap. The smallest of these must be the first element of the sorted array, because no later element can move that far forward. Repeatedly pop the minimum into the next output position and push the next unread element into the heap. When input runs out, pop the rest. O(n log k) time and O(k) extra space.

mandatory: min-heap of size k + 1
pop the minimum and push the next element
concept_groups: the true next element is always in the heap
drain the heap at the end
advanced_bonus: insertion sort takes O(n · k) on such input — fine for small k
a full sort costs O(n log n) and ignores the structure
heap size k + 1 is enough because an element is at most k away
can write output back into the same array
for k = 0 the array is already sorted

semantic_targets: Faster than a full sort when k is small
only k + 1 candidates can be the next element
common_mistakes: Heap of size k instead of k + 1
Insertion sort while claiming O(n log k)

logic_context: Use two recursive functions. reverse(stack): if empty, return; otherwise pop the top x, reverse the remaining stack, then insertAtBottom(stack, x). insertAtBottom(stack, x): if empty, push x; otherwise pop the top y, insertAtBottom(stack, x), then push y back. The call stack temporarily holds the elements. O(n²) time, O(n) recursion depth.

mandatory: pop top, reverse the rest recursively, insert the top at the bottom
insertAtBottom is itself recursive
advanced_bonus: each insertAtBottom costs O(size), giving O(n²) overall
the same insertAtBottom pattern supports sorting a stack recursively (insert in order)
deep recursion can overflow for large stacks
with an auxiliary stack, reversal is O(n)
illustrates using recursion as an implicit stack

semantic_targets: the removed top must go to the bottom
common_mistakes: Using an extra array or stack
Pushing the element back on top

logic_context: Start at the bottom-left corner. If the value is negative, every element to its right in that row is also negative, so add (cols - c) to the count and move up one row. Otherwise move right one column. Stop when you leave the matrix. Each step removes a row or a column, so it takes O(m + n).

mandatory: staircase walk from the bottom-left (or top-right) corner
negative: count the rest of the row and move up; otherwise move right
concept_groups: sorted rows mean all elements to the right are also negative
each step eliminates a row or column
advanced_bonus: binary search per row gives O(m log n)
the same staircase idea searches a sorted matrix for a target
starting at the top-right also works with mirrored moves
checking every cell is O(m · n)
zeros are not negative — use < 0

semantic_targets: each move discards a row or column
common_mistakes: uses binary search and claims O(m + n)

logic_context: Thrashing happens when processes do not have enough physical memory for their working sets, so the system spends most of its time swapping pages in and out instead of running programs. CPU use drops, and an OS that responds by admitting more processes makes it worse. It is prevented by giving each process enough frames for its working set (the pages it uses in a recent time window), controlling the page-fault rate, reducing the number of running processes, or adding RAM.

mandatory: excessive paging because working sets do not fit in memory
CPU spends time on page faults instead of useful work
advanced_bonus: working set = pages referenced in the last Δ references
if the sum of working sets exceeds available frames, suspend some processes
local page replacement limits one process stealing frames from others
symptoms: heavy disk I/O, low CPU utilisation, very slow response
SSDs reduce the cost but not the cause

semantic_targets: Symptom: high paging, low CPU use
more processes can make it worse
common_mistakes: Saying thrashing is high CPU use

logic_context: Paging divides memory into fixed-size pages (virtual) and frames (physical); any page can go into any frame, so there is no external fragmentation, but the last page of a region may be partly unused (internal fragmentation). Segmentation divides a program into variable-size logical segments such as code, data and stack, each with a base and limit; it matches the program's structure and supports per-segment protection, but variable sizes cause external fragmentation. Some systems combine them by paging each segment.

mandatory: paging uses fixed-size pages and frames
segmentation uses variable-size logical segments
concept_groups: paging: no external but some internal fragmentation
segment table with base and limit
advanced_bonus: paging is invisible to the programmer; segments reflect program structure
x86-64 mostly uses flat segmentation with paging
segment protection can mark code read-only and executable
page tables can be multi-level to save memory
compaction can reduce external fragmentation at a cost

semantic_targets: modern systems rely mainly on paging

logic_context: A TLB is a small, fast cache inside the CPU's memory-management unit that stores recent translations from virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers. Without it, every memory access would first require reading the page table from memory (several reads for multi-level tables). On a TLB hit, translation is almost free; on a miss, the page table is walked and the result is cached. Programs with good locality get high hit rates.

mandatory: cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations
avoids page-table walks on every access
concept_groups: multi-level page tables make misses expensive
flushed or tagged on context switch
advanced_bonus: TLB reach = number of entries × page size
huge pages (2 MB, 1 GB) increase TLB reach
address-space IDs (ASIDs) avoid full flushes on context switch
effective access time depends on the hit ratio
TLB shootdowns are needed when mappings change on multicore systems

semantic_targets: the TLB makes virtual memory practical
common_mistakes: confuses with the page table itself

logic_context: The CPU runs code at different privilege levels. In user mode, programs cannot execute privileged instructions or access hardware and other processes' memory directly. In kernel mode, the operating system has full access to hardware and memory. A program enters kernel mode through a system call (a trap instruction), an interrupt or an exception; the kernel does the work and then returns to user mode. This separation protects the OS and other programs from buggy or malicious code.

mandatory: user mode is restricted; kernel mode has full privileges
system calls, interrupts and exceptions switch to kernel mode
concept_groups: privileged instructions only in kernel mode
protection of OS and other processes
return to user mode after handling
advanced_bonus: a mode switch is cheaper than a full context switch
x86 uses rings 0 (kernel) and 3 (user)
library functions like printf eventually call write(), a system call
an illegal access in user mode raises an exception (e.g. segmentation fault)
vDSO lets some calls like gettimeofday avoid a mode switch

semantic_targets: user programs request services via system calls
common_mistakes: Saying user programs can access hardware directly
Confusing mode switch with process switch
claims kernel mode is for the root user only

logic_context: In a deadlock, a set of threads each wait for resources held by others in the set, so all are blocked forever. In a livelock, threads are not blocked — they keep changing state in response to each other (for example, repeatedly backing off and retrying together) — but none makes progress. In starvation, the system as a whole progresses, but one thread never gets the resource it needs because others keep getting priority. Aging and fair scheduling prevent starvation; randomised back-off helps livelock; lock ordering prevents deadlock.

mandatory: deadlock: all blocked waiting on each other
livelock: active but no progress; starvation: one thread never served
advanced_bonus: livelock example: two people stepping aside in the same direction repeatedly
starvation example: low-priority thread always pre-empted by high-priority ones
deadlock requires the four Coffman conditions
fair locks (FIFO queues) reduce starvation
livelock often arises from overly polite retry logic

semantic_targets: Who is blocked and who progresses
common_mistakes: Saying starvation stops the whole system

logic_context: A spinlock makes a waiting thread loop (busy-wait), repeatedly checking until the lock is free. It avoids the cost of putting the thread to sleep and waking it, so it is efficient when the lock is held for a very short time on a multicore system. A mutex puts a waiting thread to sleep, freeing the CPU, at the cost of a context switch. Spinlocks waste CPU if held long and are harmful on a single core, where the holder cannot run while another thread spins. Many mutex implementations spin briefly before sleeping.

mandatory: spinlock busy-waits; mutex blocks the waiting thread
spinlocks suit very short critical sections on multicore systems
concept_groups: spinning wastes CPU for long waits
spinlocks are bad on a single core
advanced_bonus: kernels use spinlocks in interrupt handlers where sleeping is not allowed
use atomic test-and-set or compare-and-swap to build a spinlock
pause/yield instructions reduce spin cost
priority inversion can make spinning threads starve the holder
pthread_spin_lock and pthread_mutex_lock provide both in POSIX

common_mistakes: Using spinlocks on single-core systems for long waits

logic_context: A condition variable lets a thread wait until some condition on shared data becomes true. The thread holds a mutex, checks the condition, and if it is false calls pthread_cond_wait, which atomically releases the mutex and sleeps; when woken, it re-acquires the mutex before returning. Another thread changes the shared data under the mutex and calls signal (wake one) or broadcast (wake all). The wait must be inside a while loop that re-checks the condition, because of spurious wakeups and because another thread may change the state before the woken thread runs.

mandatory: wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps; re-acquires on wake
always re-check the condition in a while loop
concept_groups: signal wakes one, broadcast wakes all
shared state changed under the mutex
another thread may consume the condition first
advanced_bonus: pattern: lock; while (!cond) wait; use data; unlock
forgetting to hold the mutex when changing state causes lost wakeups
use broadcast when several waiters may proceed or conditions differ
condition variables have no memory — signals with no waiters are lost
C11 provides cnd_wait in <threads.h>

semantic_targets: re-check because waking is not a guarantee

logic_context: A critical section is code that accesses shared data and must not be executed by more than one process or thread at a time. A correct solution must provide mutual exclusion (at most one thread in the critical section), progress (if none is inside, a thread wanting to enter cannot be postponed forever by threads not trying to enter), and bounded waiting (there is a limit on how many times others can enter before a waiting thread gets its turn). Solutions include Peterson's algorithm, hardware atomic instructions, and mutexes or semaphores.

mandatory: mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting
only one thread in the critical section at a time
concept_groups: entry and exit sections around the critical section
advanced_bonus: Peterson's algorithm uses a flag array and a turn variable
on modern CPUs Peterson's needs memory barriers because of reordering
disabling interrupts works only on single-core systems
bounded waiting prevents starvation
keep critical sections short to reduce contention

common_mistakes: claims disabling interrupts works on multicore

logic_context: A zombie is a child process that has finished but whose parent has not yet called wait() to read its exit status; it uses no CPU or memory beyond a process-table entry, but many zombies can exhaust process IDs. An orphan is a child whose parent has exited while the child is still running; it is adopted by init (or systemd), which later reaps it. Parents avoid zombies by calling wait/waitpid, handling SIGCHLD, or ignoring SIGCHLD where supported.

mandatory: zombie: finished child not yet reaped by its parent
orphan: running child whose parent has exited
advanced_bonus: zombies appear as 'Z' or <defunct> in ps
killing a zombie does nothing — the parent must reap it or exit
double fork creates a daemon that is an orphan on purpose
setting SIGCHLD to SIG_IGN makes children auto-reaped on Linux
an orphan becomes a zombie only until init reaps it

semantic_targets: zombies are dead, orphans are alive
common_mistakes: Saying zombies use lots of memory

logic_context: Compare-and-swap is an atomic instruction that updates a memory location to a new value only if it still holds an expected old value, and reports whether it succeeded. Lock-free algorithms read the current state, compute a new state, and use CAS to install it; if another thread changed the value meanwhile, the CAS fails and the thread retries. This avoids locks, so a stalled thread cannot block others, and at least one thread always makes progress. A known pitfall is the ABA problem, where a value changes and changes back, fooling CAS.

mandatory: CAS atomically sets a new value only if the current value matches the expected one
lock-free algorithms retry CAS in a loop
concept_groups: no locks: a stalled thread cannot block others
advanced_bonus: ABA fixes: version counters (tagged pointers) or hazard pointers
Treiber stack is a classic lock-free stack using CAS on the head
lock-free is not automatically faster — contention causes retries
weak CAS may fail spuriously and is used in loops
memory ordering (acquire/release) matters for correctness

semantic_targets: CAS replaces locking for small updates
common_mistakes: Saying CAS uses a lock internally in software

logic_context: If an attacker knows the hash function, they can send many keys that all hash to the same bucket. Each insert or lookup then degrades from O(1) to O(n), so n requests cost O(n²) time, which can bring down a server (a denial-of-service attack). Defences include keyed or randomised hash functions with a secret seed (such as SipHash), switching long buckets to balanced trees, and limiting the number of keys accepted from a request.

mandatory: crafted keys all collide, making operations O(n)
defend with secret-seeded (keyed) hash functions
advanced_bonus: SipHash is used by Python, Rust and others for this reason
Java 8 HashMap converts long chains to red-black trees
universal hashing chooses a random function from a family
attacks were demonstrated against web frameworks parsing POST parameters
non-cryptographic fast hashes are vulnerable when keys come from untrusted input

semantic_targets: Worst-case behaviour can be triggered deliberately
common_mistakes: claims cryptographic hashing is always required for tables

logic_context: Graph colouring assigns a colour to every vertex so that no two adjacent vertices share a colour. The chromatic number is the smallest number of colours that makes this possible. A graph is 2-colourable exactly when it is bipartite, which can be checked in O(V + E). Finding the chromatic number in general is NP-hard, but a greedy algorithm always uses at most Δ + 1 colours, where Δ is the maximum degree. Applications include scheduling exams without conflicts, register allocation in compilers and assigning radio frequencies.

mandatory: adjacent vertices must have different colours
chromatic number = minimum colours needed
concept_groups: greedy uses at most Δ + 1 colours
advanced_bonus: planar graphs need at most 4 colours (four colour theorem)
greedy result depends on vertex order
deciding 3-colourability is NP-complete
m-colouring can be solved by backtracking
complete graph Kₙ needs n colours

common_mistakes: Saying chromatic number is easy to compute in general
Allowing adjacent vertices to share colours

logic_context: An operating system is the software that manages a computer's hardware and provides services to programs. Its main functions are process management (creating, scheduling and ending programs), memory management (allocating and protecting memory), file-system management (storing and organising files), device management (controlling I/O devices through drivers), and providing security and a user interface. Examples include Linux, Windows and macOS.

mandatory: software that manages hardware and provides services to programs
main functions: process, memory, file and device management
concept_groups: system calls are the interface for programs
advanced_bonus: the kernel is the core part of the OS
scheduling decides which process runs next
virtual memory gives each process its own address space
device drivers let the OS talk to hardware
embedded systems may use a small real-time OS

semantic_targets: the OS sits between hardware and applications
common_mistakes: Saying the OS is just the desktop interface

logic_context: RAM (Random Access Memory) is fast, read-write memory used to hold running programs and their data; it is volatile, so its contents are lost when power is off. ROM (Read-Only Memory) is non-volatile and keeps its contents without power; it stores firmware such as the code that starts the computer (BIOS/UEFI) or programs in embedded devices. Modern 'ROM' is usually flash memory that can be rewritten in special ways.

mandatory: RAM is volatile read-write working memory
ROM is non-volatile memory for firmware
concept_groups: ROM holds boot code or firmware
advanced_bonus: types of RAM: DRAM (main memory) and SRAM (caches)
EEPROM and flash are rewritable non-volatile memories
microcontrollers run code from flash and use RAM for variables
const data in C may be placed in ROM/flash on embedded systems
RAM is much faster to write than flash

common_mistakes: Saying ROM is faster than RAM
Saying RAM keeps data without power
Confusing RAM with storage like SSD
claims ROM can never be changed in any form

logic_context: The number refers mainly to the width of the CPU's registers and memory addresses. A 32-bit system can directly address about 4 GB of memory (2^32 bytes), while a 64-bit system can address far more. 64-bit programs can work with 64-bit integers natively and have more registers on common CPUs, but pointers take 8 bytes instead of 4, so some data structures use more memory. A 64-bit OS can usually run 32-bit programs, but not the other way round.

mandatory: register and address width: 32 vs 64 bits
32-bit address space is limited to about 4 GB
concept_groups: more memory use for pointer-heavy data
advanced_bonus: sizeof(long) is 8 on 64-bit Linux but 4 on 64-bit Windows
x86-64 has 16 general-purpose registers versus 8 on x86
current CPUs use 48 or 57 bits of virtual address in practice
uint64_t from <stdint.h> gives a fixed-size type everywhere
compile for 32-bit with gcc -m32 (if supported)

semantic_targets: pointer size changes with the platform
common_mistakes: Saying 64-bit is simply twice as fast

logic_context: The kernel is the core of the operating system: it runs in privileged mode and directly manages the CPU, memory, devices and processes. The shell is a user program that provides an interface for users to give commands — for example bash or zsh on Linux — and asks the kernel to do the work through system calls (such as creating processes to run programs). The shell can be replaced without changing the kernel.

mandatory: kernel manages hardware and resources in privileged mode
shell is a user program that interprets commands
concept_groups: shell uses system calls to request kernel services
advanced_bonus: a shell runs a program by fork() and exec()
shell scripts automate sequences of commands
graphical desktops are another kind of shell/interface
the kernel has no user interface of its own
the shell handles redirection and pipes by rearranging file descriptors

semantic_targets: the shell is an ordinary program
common_mistakes: Saying the shell is part of the kernel
Saying the kernel interprets typed commands
confuses shell with terminal emulator only
claims the shell accesses hardware directly

logic_context: Environment variables are named string values (such as PATH or HOME) that the operating system passes to every process. Programs use them for configuration without hard-coding values, like where to find commands or which language to use. In C, getenv("HOME") from <stdlib.h> returns a pointer to the value, or NULL if the variable is not set. A child process inherits a copy of its parent's environment; setenv changes it only for the current process and its future children.

mandatory: named string values passed by the OS to processes
read with getenv, which returns NULL if missing
concept_groups: setenv affects only this process and its children
advanced_bonus: do not modify the string returned by getenv
main can also receive char *envp[] on many systems
check for NULL before using the value
export in the shell makes a variable visible to child processes
environment variables are not suitable for large data

common_mistakes: Thinking setenv changes the parent shell

logic_context: An absolute path gives the full location of a file starting from the root of the file system, such as /home/ana/notes.txt on Linux or C:\Users\Ana\notes.txt on Windows; it means the same thing from anywhere. A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory, such as data/input.txt or ../config.txt, where '.' means the current directory and '..' the parent. A program opening a relative path may fail if it is run from a different directory.

mandatory: absolute path starts from the file-system root
relative path depends on the current working directory
concept_groups: '.' is the current directory, '..' the parent
absolute paths are the same from anywhere
relative paths break when run from elsewhere
advanced_bonus: getcwd() returns the current working directory in C
~ (home) is expanded by the shell, not by fopen
use path separators correctly: / on Unix, \ on Windows (/ also works in most Windows APIs)
relative paths make projects portable between machines
realpath() converts a relative path to an absolute one

common_mistakes: Saying relative paths start at the root
Confusing working directory with executable location

logic_context: A buffer is a block of memory that temporarily holds data being read or written. Instead of making a slow system call or device access for every byte, a program collects data in the buffer and transfers it in larger chunks, which is much faster. In C, stdio streams like stdout are buffered: output may not appear until a newline, until the buffer fills, or until fflush is called. Buffering improves throughput but can delay output and lose data if the program crashes before flushing.

mandatory: temporary memory holding data in transit
reduces the number of slow system calls or device accesses
concept_groups: data may be lost on a crash
advanced_bonus: setvbuf chooses full, line or no buffering
stderr is unbuffered so errors appear immediately
disk caches and network sockets also use buffers
a buffer overflow is writing past the end of a buffer — a different topic
printing before fork without fflush can duplicate output

logic_context: Unicode assigns a unique number (code point) to characters from almost every writing system. UTF-8 is a way to store those code points as bytes: ASCII characters use 1 byte, and others use 2 to 4 bytes. strlen counts bytes up to the terminating '\0', not characters, so a string like 'café' has 4 characters but 5 bytes in UTF-8. To count characters, count only bytes that are not continuation bytes (bytes of the form 10xxxxxx).

mandatory: Unicode assigns code points; UTF-8 encodes them in 1 to 4 bytes
strlen counts bytes, not characters
concept_groups: ASCII is a subset of UTF-8 (1 byte each)
count characters by skipping continuation bytes
advanced_bonus: UTF-8 never contains a 0 byte except for NUL, so C strings still work
indexing s[i] gives a byte, not a character
cutting a UTF-8 string at an arbitrary byte can split a character
wchar_t size differs by platform (2 bytes on Windows, 4 on Linux)
even code points do not equal user-perceived characters (combining accents, emoji sequences)

semantic_targets: Byte length differs from character count
common_mistakes: Saying UTF-8 always uses 2 bytes per character

logic_context: Buffered fwrite is fastest, but data may sit in the C library buffer and the OS page cache, so a crash or power loss can lose many recent records. Calling fflush and fsync after every record forces the data to stable storage, giving the strongest durability, but each fsync can take milliseconds, limiting throughput to hundreds of records per second. Periodic fsync after a batch (or a time interval) bounds the possible loss to one batch while keeping most of the speed. Recommend batched fsync with a batch size or interval chosen by how much loss is acceptable; use per-record fsync only for records that must never be lost.

mandatory: fwrite alone can lose buffered data on crash
fsync per record is durable but slow
concept_groups: fflush moves data to the OS; fsync to the disk
batching bounds loss to one batch
choose batch size by acceptable loss
advanced_bonus: fflush alone does not guarantee data reaches the disk
fdatasync skips some metadata writes and can be faster
append-only logs with checksums detect torn writes
group commit in databases is this batching idea
disk write caches may need to be configured to honour flushes

semantic_targets: match durability to how critical the data is
common_mistakes: claims fwrite writes directly to disk

logic_context: An exact hash set stores every distinct visitor ID, so memory grows with the number of unique visitors — hundreds of millions of IDs can need many gigabytes — and merging daily or regional counts requires combining full sets. HyperLogLog estimates the count using only a few kilobytes (e.g. about 12 KB for ~0.8% standard error) by tracking the maximum number of leading zeros in hashed IDs across many registers; sketches from different servers merge by taking register maxima. It cannot list visitors or give exact numbers. Recommend HyperLogLog for dashboards and trends; use exact counting only when the precise number is required and memory allows.

mandatory: exact hash set memory grows with distinct visitors
HyperLogLog uses kilobytes with a small known error
concept_groups: HLL sketches merge by taking register maxima
exact counts needed for billing or audits
advanced_bonus: Redis PFCOUNT implements HyperLogLog
linear counting or bitmaps are exact alternatives for small ID ranges
HLL needs a good hash function
sharding by hash allows exact distributed counting at higher cost
standard error with 16,384 registers is about 0.81%

semantic_targets: approximate cardinality is often good enough

logic_context: Comparing every pair means about 5 × 10^11 comparisons, each costly — far too slow. MinHash represents each document by a short signature (for example 128 minimum hash values of its word shingles), where the fraction of equal values estimates the Jaccard similarity. LSH splits signatures into bands and hashes each band, so only documents sharing a band bucket become candidate pairs, which are then checked precisely. This finds most similar pairs with far fewer comparisons, at the cost of some false negatives and tuning of band parameters. Recommend MinHash + LSH for this scale.

mandatory: all-pairs comparison is about 5 × 10^11 comparisons
MinHash signatures estimate Jaccard similarity
concept_groups: tune bands and rows for the similarity threshold
advanced_bonus: probability two documents become candidates ≈ 1 - (1 - s^r)^b for b bands of r rows
shingling turns documents into sets of word or character n-grams
SimHash is an alternative for cosine similarity
signatures are small, so they fit in memory
exact duplicates can be found cheaply first with full-content hashes

semantic_targets: trade a little accuracy for huge speed-up
common_mistakes: Using a single hash of the whole document for near-duplicates

logic_context: JSON is human-readable, easy to edit and debug, and tolerant of added fields, but it needs a parser (code size and RAM), takes more storage, and parsing is slower. A binary struct format is compact and can be read directly with almost no code, but it is not human-readable, depends on byte order, padding and struct layout, and needs explicit versioning so old and new firmware can understand it. Recommend a versioned binary format with fixed-size fields, explicit byte order and a checksum for tight devices; use JSON (or a lightweight text format) when memory allows and humans need to edit it.

mandatory: JSON: readable and flexible but needs a parser and more space
binary struct: compact and fast but fragile across versions and platforms
concept_groups: parser code size matters on small devices
advanced_bonus: never write raw structs without fixing layout — use explicit serialisation
CBOR or MessagePack are compact binary formats with flexible schemas
a CRC protects against corrupted flash
default values handle missing fields after firmware updates
key=value text is a light alternative to full JSON

semantic_targets: choose by device resources and editing needs
common_mistakes: Ignoring parser size on embedded devices

logic_context: A plain SHA-256 hash hides the password, but identical passwords produce identical hashes and attackers can use precomputed tables and very fast GPU guessing. Adding a unique random salt per user defeats precomputed tables and hides identical passwords, but SHA-256 is still so fast that billions of guesses per second remain possible. bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 are deliberately slow and tunable (Argon2 is also memory-hard), so each guess costs far more, making brute force impractical; they include salts automatically. Recommend Argon2id (or bcrypt) with per-user salts; never store plain or unsalted hashes.

mandatory: fast hashes allow massive brute-force guessing
slow, salted password hashes (Argon2/bcrypt) resist cracking
advanced_bonus: store the algorithm, parameters and salt with the hash
raise the cost factor as hardware gets faster
a secret pepper stored separately adds protection
compare hashes in constant time
never encrypt passwords reversibly when hashing suffices

common_mistakes: Using the same salt for all users
thinks salting alone makes fast hashes safe

logic_context: TTL expiry guarantees that no entry is older than a set time, which bounds staleness, but it does not control memory: if many unique keys arrive, the cache can grow until entries expire. LRU eviction keeps memory bounded by removing the least recently used entries when full, but a popular entry may stay forever and become stale. Combining them — LRU for capacity and TTL for freshness — handles both concerns, at the cost of tracking both timestamps and recency. Recommend the combination, with TTL chosen by how stale data can be.

mandatory: TTL bounds staleness but not memory
LRU bounds memory but not staleness
concept_groups: combining both handles freshness and capacity
popular entries can go stale under pure LRU
advanced_bonus: expired entries can be removed lazily on access or by a background sweep
randomised TTLs prevent many entries expiring at once (thundering herd)
explicit invalidation on writes reduces staleness further
LRU uses a hash map plus doubly linked list
stale-while-revalidate serves old data while refreshing

logic_context: With an array of structs, each particle's fields sit together, which is natural to write and good when most fields are used together, but a loop that reads only x, y and z also drags unused fields (colour, mass, flags) into the cache, wasting memory bandwidth. With a struct of arrays, each field is its own contiguous array, so a loop over x, y and z reads only useful data and is easy for the compiler to vectorise with SIMD. SoA is harder to pass around as single objects. Recommend SoA for this field-subset, bandwidth-bound workload; AoS when whole records are usually processed together.

mandatory: AoS loads unused fields into cache
SoA keeps each field contiguous and vectorises well
concept_groups: AoS is natural for whole-object access
SIMD benefits from contiguous same-type data
SoA is less convenient for single objects
advanced_bonus: hybrid AoSoA groups small blocks of particles in SoA form
cache lines are typically 64 bytes — unused fields waste part of each line
struct padding makes AoS even larger
data-oriented design favours SoA for hot loops
measure with a profiler to confirm gains

semantic_targets: only touch the data you need
common_mistakes: Saying layout does not affect speed
Recommending AoS without considering field usage

logic_context: Polling repeatedly checks a device in a loop: it is simple and predictable, but it wastes CPU and power when nothing happens and can miss short events between checks. Interrupts let the hardware notify the CPU when an event occurs, so the CPU can sleep or do other work and react quickly, but handlers must be short and shared data needs protection (volatile, disabling interrupts briefly). For the button, interrupts are better because presses are rare, short and need quick response (with debouncing). For the once-per-second sensor read, a timer interrupt that triggers the read — or simple polling in the main loop — is fine because the timing is regular.

mandatory: polling wastes CPU and can miss short events
interrupts react quickly and let the CPU sleep
concept_groups: periodic sensor: timer or simple polling
advanced_bonus: mechanical buttons bounce for several milliseconds — debounce in software or hardware
sleep modes save battery when using interrupts
high-rate devices may need DMA instead
interrupt storms can starve the main loop
use volatile sig_atomic_t-like flags to pass events to the main loop

semantic_targets: choose per device, not one rule for all
common_mistakes: Polling a rare button in a busy loop without noting cost
Doing heavy work inside interrupt handlers

logic_context: A single global lock is simple and correct, but all operations become serial, so adding threads gives little speed-up. Per-bucket or striped locks let operations on different buckets proceed in parallel, greatly reducing contention, but resizing the table becomes complex (it must take all locks) and more memory is used. A read-write lock allows many concurrent readers but only one writer, which helps when reads dominate, but writers can be starved and frequent writes serialise everything again. Recommend lock striping for mixed read/write workloads; a read-write lock if reads vastly outnumber writes; a global lock only for low contention or prototypes.

mandatory: global lock serialises all operations
striped/per-bucket locks allow parallel access to different buckets
concept_groups: writers can starve under read-write locks
resizing with striped locks needs all locks
advanced_bonus: lock striping uses a fixed number of locks (e.g. 16 or 64) mapped by hash
acquire multiple locks in a fixed order to avoid deadlock during resize
lock-free hash tables exist but are complex
false sharing between adjacent locks can hurt performance — pad them
measure contention before optimising

common_mistakes: Saying a global lock scales well
claims read-write locks help write-heavy workloads

logic_context: Build prefix sums P[0..n] with P[0] = 0; a subarray (i, j] has sum P[j] - P[i]. So count pairs i < j with lower <= P[j] - P[i] <= upper. Use merge sort on the prefix array: before merging two sorted halves, for each P[i] in the left half, advance two pointers in the right half to find the range of P[j] in [P[i] + lower, P[i] + upper], and add its size. Then merge normally. O(n log n). A Fenwick tree over compressed prefix values also works.

mandatory: convert to counting prefix-sum pairs with difference in [lower, upper]
count across halves during merge sort with two pointers
concept_groups: both halves are sorted when counting
Fenwick tree with coordinate compression alternative
advanced_bonus: pointers in the right half only move forward because left values increase
use 64-bit prefix sums to avoid overflow
brute force over all subarrays is O(n²)
same divide-and-conquer pattern counts inversions
negative numbers are handled, unlike a sliding window

semantic_targets: Counting cross pairs in merge sort
sorted halves make range counting linear

logic_context: Use merge sort on (value, original index) pairs. During each merge, keep a count of how many elements from the right half have already been placed before the current left element; when a left element is placed, add that count to its answer, because those right elements are smaller and were originally to its right. O(n log n). Alternatively, scan from the right with a Fenwick tree over compressed values, querying the count of smaller values seen so far before inserting the current one.

mandatory: merge sort tracking original indices
when placing a left element, add the number of right elements already placed
concept_groups: right elements placed earlier are smaller and to the right
Fenwick tree from the right alternative
advanced_bonus: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
for equal values, place left elements first so equals are not counted as smaller
brute force is O(n²)
a balanced BST with subtree sizes also works
same technique counts inversions per element

common_mistakes: insertion into a sorted list with O(n) shifts each
Fenwick without compression on large values

logic_context: Let k be the total number of 1s. In the final arrangement, the 1s fill some window of length k. For any window of length k, the swaps needed equal the number of 0s inside it (each 0 is swapped with a 1 outside). So slide a window of length k across the array, track the number of 1s in it, and the answer is k minus the maximum number of 1s found in any window. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: final block of 1s has length k = total ones
swaps = zeros inside the chosen window
concept_groups: fixed-size sliding window of length k
advanced_bonus: for a circular array, conceptually double the array (or use modulo indices)
k = 0 or k = n needs zero swaps
each swap fixes exactly one misplaced 0
adjacent-swap versions are a different problem with a different answer
O(1) extra space

semantic_targets: the best window already has the most 1s
common_mistakes: Ignoring the circular variant when asked
O(n²) checking every window from scratch

logic_context: Fix each point as an anchor and count, for every other point, the direction (slope) from the anchor. Represent the slope exactly as a reduced fraction (dy / g, dx / g) with g = gcd(dy, dx) and a normalised sign, instead of a floating-point number. Use a hash map from slope to count; the best line through this anchor has max count + 1 points (plus duplicates of the anchor). The answer is the maximum over all anchors. O(n²) time.

mandatory: fix an anchor and group other points by slope
represent slope as a reduced integer fraction
concept_groups: normalise sign and handle vertical lines
advanced_bonus: floating-point slopes can wrongly merge or split nearly equal slopes
vertical lines use dx = 0 as a special normalised key
lines through the anchor are distinguished by slope alone
checking every triple of points is O(n³)
with n ≤ 2, all points are on one line

semantic_targets: Lines through an anchor are identified by slope
each anchor gives the best line through it

logic_context: Count each letter's frequency. Pairs of the same letter can be placed symmetrically, so add (count / 2) × 2 for every letter. If any letter has an odd count, one extra letter can go in the middle, so add 1. O(n) time, O(1) space for a fixed alphabet.

mandatory: use all pairs of each letter
add 1 for a centre letter if any count is odd
concept_groups: only one odd letter can be the centre
case sensitivity depends on the problem
advanced_bonus: the palindrome itself is not needed, only its length
equivalently: n - (number of odd counts) + (1 if any odd count)
uppercase and lowercase are usually different letters
differs from checking whether all letters can form a palindrome
no need to sort

semantic_targets: sum the usable pairs, then add a centre

logic_context: Scan the string while recording the last index where each of 'a', 'b' and 'c' appeared. For each right end i, a substring ending at i contains all three exactly when it starts at or before min(last a, last b, last c). So add min(last positions) + 1 to the count (if all three have appeared). O(n) time, O(1) space. A sliding window that counts all valid left starts also works.

mandatory: track the last occurrence of each character
valid starts for end i = min(last positions) + 1
concept_groups: add nothing until all three have appeared
advanced_bonus: counting substrings directly is O(n²) or worse
the same idea counts substrings containing all k required characters
initialise last positions to -1
the answer can be large — use 64-bit counts
complement approach: total minus substrings missing some character via inclusion-exclusion

semantic_targets: Earliest of the last positions limits starts
any start up to the minimum works

logic_context: Count each character's frequency. Process the frequencies (for example sorted in descending order) while keeping a set of frequencies already used. For each frequency f, while f > 0 and f is already used, decrement f and count one deletion. If f > 0, add it to the used set. Frequency 0 means the character is removed entirely, which is always allowed. O(n + σ log σ).

mandatory: count frequencies and keep a set of used frequencies
decrement a frequency until it is unused or zero, counting deletions
concept_groups: sorting frequencies descending simplifies the greedy
advanced_bonus: greedy is optimal because lowering a frequency to the nearest free value costs the fewest deletions
with descending order you can track the maximum allowed next frequency instead of a set
example: 'aaabbbcc' needs 2 deletions
the alphabet size bounds the number of frequencies
no need to know which characters end up removed

common_mistakes: Deleting whole characters immediately on collision

logic_context: Use prefix sums with a dummy node of value 0 before the head. If the prefix sum at two nodes is equal, the nodes between them sum to zero. First pass: compute the running prefix sum and store, in a hash map, the last node seen for each prefix sum. Second pass: recompute the prefix sums and set each node's next to map[prefix]->next, which skips any zero-sum run that follows it. Return dummy->next. O(n) time and space.

mandatory: equal prefix sums mark a zero-sum segment between them
map each prefix sum to its last node, then link past segments
advanced_bonus: storing the last occurrence lets one jump skip nested zero-sum segments
a single-pass version must remove intermediate map entries when cutting
the head itself can be removed — dummy handles it
similar to finding zero-sum subarrays in arrays
brute force checks every segment — O(n²)

semantic_targets: equal prefix sums cancel the nodes between
common_mistakes: Removing only adjacent pairs that sum to zero
Using the first occurrence and missing longer segments

logic_context: Copy the values into an array, then use a monotonic stack of indices whose values are decreasing. For each index i, while the stack is not empty and the value at the top index is smaller than a[i], pop it and set its answer to a[i]. Push i. Indices left on the stack get 0. Each index is pushed and popped once, so O(n) time.

mandatory: monotonic decreasing stack of indices
popped elements get the current value as their answer
concept_groups: copy list into an array or track positions
each index pushed and popped once
advanced_bonus: the answer array can be filled while traversing the list once if the stack stores (index, value) pairs
scanning ahead from each node is O(n²)
strictly greater: equal values do not resolve each other
same as next greater element for arrays
list length must be known or the answer grown dynamically

semantic_targets: the stack holds nodes still waiting for a greater value

logic_context: A sequence can be rearranged into a palindrome if at most one digit appears an odd number of times. Do a DFS carrying a bitmask where bit d is toggled each time digit d appears on the path. At a leaf, the path is pseudo-palindromic if the mask has at most one set bit, i.e. mask & (mask - 1) == 0. Count such leaves. O(n) time, O(h) space.

mandatory: at most one digit may have an odd count
bitmask toggled per digit along the path
concept_groups: DFS passes the mask by value
advanced_bonus: passing the mask by value makes backtracking automatic
a count array of size 10 also works but needs explicit undo
only leaves end paths — nodes with one child are not leaves
the same parity trick checks palindrome permutations of strings
bit d corresponds to digit d (1 << d)

common_mistakes: Checking if the path itself is a palindrome
Not undoing counts when using arrays
checks for zero odd counts only

logic_context: Do a level-order traversal and record the first node of each level; after the traversal, the first node of the last level is the answer. A neat variant enqueues the right child before the left child, so the very last node dequeued is the bottom-left node. With DFS, visit left before right and record the first node seen at each new maximum depth. O(n).

mandatory: find the deepest level
take its leftmost node
concept_groups: BFS records the first node per level
right-to-left BFS: last dequeued node is the answer
DFS: first node at a new maximum depth
advanced_bonus: right-to-left BFS avoids tracking level boundaries
DFS uses O(h) space; BFS uses O(width)
the leftmost node of the last row is not necessarily a left child
a single-node tree returns the root
same pattern gives the left view of the tree

semantic_targets: the answer may be a right child
common_mistakes: Returning the leftmost node of the whole tree (following left pointers)
Taking the last node of normal BFS

logic_context: A full binary tree has an odd number of nodes, so return an empty list if n is even. With n = 1, the only tree is a single node. Otherwise the root uses one node; split the remaining n - 1 nodes into an odd-sized left part i and right part n - 1 - i. Recursively generate all left trees and all right trees, and combine every pair under a new root. Memoise results by n. The count of trees is the Catalan number C((n - 1) / 2).

mandatory: n must be odd
combine every left tree with every right tree for each odd split
concept_groups: output size is a Catalan number
advanced_bonus: subtrees can be shared between results when memoising (or deep-copied if required)
the number of trees grows exponentially, so time is dominated by output size
n = 7 gives 5 trees
even n has no full binary tree
bottom-up generation from small n is an alternative

semantic_targets: each split pairs all left and right shapes
common_mistakes: counts instead of generating when trees are required

logic_context: Compute all-pairs shortest distances, for example with Floyd-Warshall: initialise dist[i][j] with edge weights (0 on the diagonal, infinity otherwise), then for each intermediate k update dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). For each city, count other cities with dist <= threshold. Pick the city with the smallest count, preferring the larger index on ties. O(n³). Running Dijkstra from every city is an alternative for sparse graphs.

mandatory: all-pairs shortest paths (Floyd-Warshall)
count reachable cities within the threshold for each city
concept_groups: k is the outermost loop in Floyd-Warshall
Dijkstra from each node for sparse graphs
advanced_bonus: Floyd-Warshall handles the undirected edges by filling both directions
Dijkstra from each city costs O(n · E log n)
avoid overflow when adding infinity values
scanning cities in increasing order with <= picks the largest on ties
dist[i][i] is not counted

semantic_targets: shortest paths, not direct edges, decide reachability

logic_context: Instead of searching from every cell, search backwards from the oceans. Run BFS/DFS from all Pacific border cells, moving to neighbours whose height is greater than or equal to the current cell (water could flow from them down to here), marking reachable cells. Do the same from the Atlantic border cells. Cells marked in both searches are the answer. O(m · n).

mandatory: reverse the flow: search uphill from each ocean's border
answer = cells reached by both searches
concept_groups: move to neighbours with height >= current
advanced_bonus: searching from every cell separately is O((m · n)²)
the top row and left column touch the Pacific; bottom row and right column touch the Atlantic
corner cells touch both oceans
iterative BFS avoids deep recursion
each cell is visited at most once per ocean

semantic_targets: uphill moves in reverse mean downhill flow
common_mistakes: Moving to lower neighbours in the reverse search

logic_context: Find each island with DFS or BFS. Record its shape in a canonical form: the list of cell coordinates relative to the island's first cell (for example the top-left cell found during scanning), in the order visited. Insert the shape (as a string or tuple list) into a hash set. The number of distinct shapes is the set size. O(m · n).

mandatory: record each island's cells relative to a fixed origin cell
store shapes in a hash set
advanced_bonus: a direction-path signature with backtrack markers is an alternative canonical form
sorting relative coordinates makes the form independent of traversal order
the rotation/reflection variant needs all 8 transforms normalised
mark cells visited by setting them to 0
shape strings must separate coordinates clearly (e.g. '0,1;1,1')

logic_context: Build a map from each stop to the routes that serve it. Run BFS where each level is one more bus: start with all routes serving the source (1 bus). For each route in the current level, look at all its stops; if one is the target, return the level; otherwise, add every not-yet-taken route through those stops to the next level. Mark routes (and stops) as visited so each is expanded once. Return 0 if source equals target and -1 if unreachable.

mandatory: BFS where each level is taking one more bus
stop → routes map to find transfers
concept_groups: check for the target on each route's stops
advanced_bonus: BFS over stops with edges between all stops on a route creates too many edges
O(sum of route lengths) with visited routes and stops
bus count, not stop count, is the distance
route sets can be checked for target membership quickly with hashing
bidirectional BFS can reduce work

semantic_targets: each BFS level is one transfer

logic_context: Let P be the sum of numbers with +, and N the sum with -. Then P - N = target and P + N = total, so P = (total + target) / 2. If (total + target) is odd or |target| > total, there are 0 ways. Otherwise count subsets with sum P using 0/1 knapsack counting: dp[0] = 1 and for each number x, for s from P down to x, dp[s] += dp[s - x]. The answer is dp[P]. O(n · P).

mandatory: transform to counting subsets with sum (total + target) / 2
0/1 knapsack counting DP
concept_groups: iterate sums downward to use each number once
advanced_bonus: zeros in the array double the count automatically through dp
brute force over 2^n sign choices is exponential
memoised recursion on (index, current sum) also works
the offset approach dp over sums in [-total, total] is an alternative
negative target handled by symmetry

semantic_targets: signs split numbers into two groups
common_mistakes: Brute force over all sign assignments

logic_context: This is a 0/1 knapsack with two capacities. Let dp[i][j] be the maximum number of strings using at most i zeros and j ones. For each string with z zeros and o ones, update for i from m down to z and j from n down to o: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][j], dp[i - z][j - o] + 1). Iterating downward ensures each string is used once. The answer is dp[m][n]. O(L · m · n) for L strings.

mandatory: two-dimensional 0/1 knapsack
dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][j], dp[i - z][j - o] + 1)
concept_groups: count zeros and ones per string
advanced_bonus: greedy by shortest strings is not always optimal
a 3D table over strings is equivalent but uses more space
each string's value is 1
precompute counts once per string
memory O(m · n)

semantic_targets: each string is taken or skipped
common_mistakes: forgets to count zeros and ones

logic_context: For each index i keep len[i], the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at i, and cnt[i], how many such subsequences there are. Initialise both to 1. For each j < i with a[j] < a[i]: if len[j] + 1 > len[i], set len[i] = len[j] + 1 and cnt[i] = cnt[j]; if len[j] + 1 == len[i], add cnt[j] to cnt[i]. Finally sum cnt[i] over all i with len[i] equal to the maximum length. O(n²).

mandatory: track length and count of LIS ending at each index
longer: replace count; equal: add count
concept_groups: sum counts for the maximum length
advanced_bonus: an O(n log n) version uses segment trees or Fenwick trees storing (length, count) pairs
counts can be large — use 64-bit
example: [1, 3, 5, 4, 7] has 2 LIS of length 4
equal values do not extend a strictly increasing subsequence
patience sorting alone gives the length but not the count

common_mistakes: Adding counts when a longer length is found

logic_context: Work backwards from the princess's cell. Let need[i][j] be the minimum health required when entering cell (i, j). At the bottom-right, need = max(1, 1 - dungeon[i][j]). Elsewhere, need[i][j] = max(1, min(need[i + 1][j], need[i][j + 1]) - dungeon[i][j]). The answer is need[0][0]. O(m · n) time; one row of space suffices.

mandatory: fill the DP from the bottom-right backwards
need = max(1, min(next needs) - cell value)
advanced_bonus: forward DP tracking maximum health fails because it ignores the minimum along the path
binary search on starting health with a feasibility check also works but is slower
use sentinel infinity outside the grid except next to the end
the max(1, …) clamp prevents surplus from being carried backward incorrectly
space can be reduced to O(n)

common_mistakes: wrong base case at the princess cell

logic_context: Record the last index of each letter. Scan the string with a stack and a set of letters already in the stack. Skip a letter that is already in the stack. Otherwise, while the stack's top is greater than the current letter and the top letter appears again later (its last index is beyond the current position), pop it and remove it from the set. Push the current letter. The stack holds the answer. O(n) time.

mandatory: monotonic stack with last-occurrence check
pop larger letters that appear again later
concept_groups: skip letters already in the stack
each letter pushed and popped once
advanced_bonus: popping is safe only if the letter can be added again later
same as 'smallest subsequence of distinct characters'
similar greedy to removing k digits for the smallest number
O(1) extra space for a fixed alphabet
example: 'cbacdcbc' → 'acdb'

removes all duplicates without order constraints

logic_context: Scan from right to left with a stack and a variable third, the best candidate for a[k] (initially negative infinity). For each element x: if x < third, a 132 pattern exists (x is a[i]). Otherwise, while the stack is non-empty and its top is less than x, pop and set third to the popped value (a candidate a[k] smaller than x, which acts as a[j]). Push x. O(n) time.

third = largest value popped by a bigger element
concept_groups: each element pushed and popped once
advanced_bonus: prefix minimum plus a stack is another O(n) formulation
brute force is O(n³), the prefix-min approach O(n²)

logic_context: Drive as far as the current fuel allows, pushing the fuel amount of every station passed into a max-heap. Whenever the car cannot reach the next station (or the target), retroactively refuel at the best station passed so far: pop the largest amount, add it to the fuel and count a stop. If the heap is empty when more fuel is needed, the target is unreachable. Greedy is optimal because the largest available fuel extends reach the most. O(n log n).

mandatory: max-heap of fuel from stations already passed
refuel from the largest only when needed
concept_groups: count a stop for each pop
unreachable if heap is empty when stuck
process stations in order of position
advanced_bonus: deciding stops lazily avoids guessing in advance

stations beyond the target are irrelevant
each station enters the heap once
use 64-bit for large distances

logic_context: Binary search on the value x between 1 and m × n. For a guess x, count how many table entries are <= x: row i contains multiples i, 2i, …, ni, so it contributes min(x / i, n). Sum over all rows in O(m). If the count is at least k, the answer is x or smaller; otherwise larger. The smallest x with count >= k is the answer, and it is always a value in the table. O(m log(m · n)).

count entries <= x row by row with min(x / i, n)
advanced_bonus: building and sorting the table is O(mn log(mn))
iterate over the smaller dimension for counting
the count function is monotonic in x
a heap approach is O(k log m) — slow for large k
the smallest valid x must appear in the table

semantic_targets: count how many values fall below the guess

O(k) heap approach without noting cost

logic_context: XOR gives the sum of the bits without carries, and AND shifted left by one gives the carries. Repeat: sum = a ^ b; carry = (a & b) << 1; set a = sum and b = carry, until the carry is 0. Then a holds the result. In C, do the operations on unsigned integers to avoid undefined behaviour when shifting negative values, then convert back. At most 32 iterations for 32-bit integers.

works for negative numbers in two's complement

advanced_bonus: left-shifting a negative signed int is undefined behaviour in C — use unsigned

common_mistakes: infinite loop with signed types in some languages

logic_context: Build a trie from all dictionary words. Start a DFS from every cell, following the trie: move to a neighbour only if its letter is a child of the current trie node. Removing trie nodes that have no children left prunes future searches. Much faster than searching for each word separately.

mandatory: build a trie of all words
DFS on the grid guided by trie children

clear end marks to avoid duplicates
advanced_bonus: searching each word separately costs O(words × cells × 4^L)

logic_context: Convert the numbers to strings and sort them with a custom comparator: a should come before b if the concatenation a + b is larger than b + a. Concatenate the sorted strings. If the first string is '0', the whole result is '0' (all numbers were zero). This comparison is transitive, so sorting is valid. O(n log n × L) for strings of length L.

logic_context: Use divide and conquer. For each operator in the expression, split it into the left part and the right part, recursively compute all possible results of each part, and combine every left result with every right result using that operator. If the expression contains no operator, it is a single number, which is the only result. Memoise results by substring to avoid recomputing the same sub-expressions.

combine all left results with all right results

output size grows like Catalan numbers
advanced_bonus: the number of parenthesisations is the Catalan number of the operator count

logic_context: Build a 2D prefix-sum array P of size (m + 1) x (n + 1), where P[i + 1][j + 1] = a[i][j] + P[i][j + 1] + P[i + 1][j] - P[i][j]. The sum of any rectangle from (r1, c1) to (r2, c2) is P[r2 + 1][c2 + 1] - P[r1][c2 + 1] - P[r2 + 1][c1] + P[r1][c1] (inclusion-exclusion). logic_context: mmap maps a file (or anonymous memory) directly into the process's address space, so the program reads and writes the file through ordinary pointers. logic_context: Priority inversion happens when a high-priority task waits for a lock held by a low-priority task, and a medium-priority task pre-empts the low-priority one, so the high-priority task is blocked indefinitely by work less important than itself. logic_context: CPUs keep caches coherent at the granularity of a cache line (typically 64 bytes). This can slow programs dramatically. It is avoided by padding or aligning per-thread data to cache-line boundaries, or by grouping each thread's data together.

logic_context: A leftist heap is a heap-ordered binary tree in which every node satisfies the leftist property: the null-path length (distance to the nearest missing child) of the left child is at least that of the right child. To merge two heaps, take the root with the smaller key, recursively merge its right subtree with the other heap, then swap children if needed to restore the leftist property. logic_context: CPU cache is a small amount of very fast memory inside or next to the processor that stores copies of recently used data and instructions. When data is found in the cache (a hit), access takes a few cycles; a miss must fetch from RAM, which can take hundreds of cycles.

An embedded SQLite database stores everything in one file, provides transactions that survive crashes, and supports indexes and queries such as tag and date ranges, at the cost of a small library and schema management. A key-value store is fast for lookups by key but has no built-in secondary indexes, so tag and date searches require maintaining extra index keys yourself. Recommend SQLite for these query needs.

logic_context: Sorted arrays are compact for sparse sets and support union and intersection by a linear merge in O(n + m) with good cache behaviour, but inserting into them costs O(n). Hash sets give O(1) average insertion and membership, and intersection in O(min(n, m)) expected time, but use more memory and produce unordered results. A bitset uses one bit per possible value — about 1.25 MB per set for this range regardless of size — and computes unions and intersections with word-wise OR and AND, extremely fast for dense sets but wasteful for small, sparse ones. Recommend bitsets (or compressed bitmaps such as Roaring) when sets are dense, sorted arrays when they are sparse and mostly static, and hash sets when frequent inserts and membership tests dominate.

logic_context: malloc can take an unpredictable amount of time and may take internal locks, so calling it in the callback risks missing the deadline and causing audible glitches. Preallocating buffers at start-up makes the callback's memory use predictable. A single-producer single-consumer lock-free ring buffer lets the callback read and write without ever blocking. logic_context: Busy-polling gives the lowest reaction time but keeps a CPU core at 100% even when there is no work, wasting power and slowing other threads. A condition variable lets the worker sleep until a producer signals it; it uses no CPU while idle, needs a mutex and a while-loop check for spurious wakeups, and adds a small wake-up latency. A counting semaphore naturally counts queued jobs: producers post after adding a job and the worker waits before taking one, which is simple and also uses no CPU while idle. logic_context: A nightly rebuild is simple and produces a compact, fully optimised index with no leftover deleted entries, but search results can be up to a day out of date and the rebuild is a large job that needs time and resources. logic_context: Use a stack of scores, starting with 0 for the outermost level. On '(', push 0 for a new level. On ')', pop the inner score v; its contribution is 1 if v is 0 (it was '()') or 2 × v otherwise; add this to the new top. The final top is the answer. A constant-space method adds 2^depth for every '()' pair, because each core '()' is doubled once per enclosing pair. O(n).

mandatory: stack of scores per nesting level
on ')': add max(2 × inner, 1) to the parent level
advanced_bonus: depth method uses O(1) space: track depth, and when '(' is immediately followed by ')', add 1 << depth
recursive divide-and-conquer over balanced segments is O(n²) in the worst case

logic_context: Process entries one by one. For each, its depth is the number of leading tabs and its name is the rest. Keep an array (or stack) len where len[d] is the total path length up to and including the directory at depth d. The path length to the current entry is len[depth - 1] + 1 (for '/') + name length (or just name length at depth 0). If the name contains '.', it is a file, so update the maximum; otherwise store the length as len[depth]. O(n).

mandatory: depth = number of leading tabs

advanced_bonus: entries at the same depth overwrite len[depth], which acts like popping a stack
only file paths count toward the answer
answer is 0 if there are no files
string operations should avoid building full paths
example: 'dir\n\tsubdir1\n\t\tfile.ext' gives 20

logic_context: Use two pointers from both ends. While the characters match, move inward. At the first mismatch, the string can still be fixed only by deleting one of the two mismatched characters, so check whether s[left + 1 .. right] or s[left .. right - 1] is a palindrome. If either is, return true. If no mismatch occurs, the string is already a palindrome. O(n) time, O(1) space.

try skipping the left or the right character

no mismatch means already a palindrome

logic_context: Use divide and conquer. Count character frequencies in the current substring. Any character that appears fewer than k times cannot be part of a valid answer, so split the substring at every such character and solve each piece recursively, returning the best. If every character appears at least k times, the whole substring is valid. Each recursion level removes at least one distinct character, so depth is bounded by the alphabet size: about O(26 · n). A sliding-window variant tries each possible number of distinct characters from 1 to 26.

recurse on the pieces; whole substring valid if no split character
concept_groups: recursion depth bounded by alphabet size
sliding window over number of unique characters
advanced_bonus: sliding window: for each target count of unique characters u, expand and shrink keeping exactly u unique, checking all have ≥ k

example: 'ababbc' with k = 2 → 5 ('ababb')
brute force over all substrings is O(n²) or worse

Not splitting at all rare characters

logic_context: Walk both strings from the end with two pointers. For each string, skip characters that are deleted: keep a counter of pending backspaces — on '#', increment it; on a normal character with a positive counter, decrement and skip. When both pointers reach a character that survives, compare them; if they differ, return false. If one string runs out before the other, return false. O(n + m) time, O(1) space.

concept_groups: mismatch or unequal lengths of survivors → false
advanced_bonus: building processed strings with a stack is simpler but uses O(n) space

example: 'ab#c' and 'ad#c' are equal

logic_context: Move a pointer first to the k-th node. Then start a second pointer at the head and advance both first-from-k and second together until the leading pointer reaches the last node; the second pointer is then at the k-th node from the end. Swap the two nodes' values (or relink them carefully, handling the cases where they are adjacent or the same node). One pass after reaching k, O(n) time, O(1) space.

Not handling k equal to the middle

logic_context: Traverse the tree in reverse inorder (right subtree, node, left subtree), which visits values from largest to smallest. Keep a running sum of values visited so far. At each node, add the node's value to the running sum and set the node's value to the running sum. O(n) time, O(h) space (or O(1) with Morris traversal).

advanced_bonus: the running sum can be a variable passed by reference or a static/global in C

logic_context: Use a greedy post-order traversal with three states: 0 = not covered, 1 = has a camera, 2 = covered without a camera. Treat NULL children as covered (2). At a node: if any child is 0, place a camera here (return 1, count it); else if any child has a camera, this node is covered (return 2); otherwise return 0, leaving it for the parent to cover. After the traversal, if the root returns 0, add one more camera. O(n).

place a camera only when a child is uncovered
concept_groups: root may need an extra camera
advanced_bonus: placing cameras at leaves is never better than at their parents

O(h) recursion depth

logic_context: Use backtracking from every cell that has gold. At a cell, take its gold, temporarily set it to 0 to mark it visited, explore the four neighbours that have gold, and keep the best total. Then restore the cell's gold before returning. The answer is the maximum over all starting cells. The search is exponential in general, but the problem limits the number of gold cells (e.g. at most 25), so it is fast in practice.

mandatory: DFS from every gold cell with backtracking
mark visited by setting the cell to 0, then restore
concept_groups: answer is the best over all starts
advanced_bonus: restoring the cell is essential so other paths can use it
each cell has at most 3 unvisited neighbours after the first step, so branching is limited
memoisation is not possible because the path state matters

logic_context: First find one island with DFS/BFS and mark all its cells (for example, set them to 2), adding each to a queue. Then run a multi-source BFS from all cells of this island at once, expanding into water level by level. The first time the BFS reaches a cell of the other island, the current level (number of water cells crossed) is the answer. O(m · n).

mandatory: mark the first island and use all its cells as BFS sources
multi-source BFS until the other island is reached
concept_groups: each BFS level flips one more layer of water
answer = level when reaching land of the second island
advanced_bonus: BFS from a single cell would not give the shortest bridge from the whole island

logic_context: The probability of a path is the product of its edge probabilities. Use a Dijkstra-like algorithm with a max-heap: start with probability 1 at the source; pop the node with the highest probability; for each edge (u, v, p), if prob[u] × p > prob[v], update prob[v] and push it. This is valid because multiplying by p ≤ 1 never increases a path's probability, just as adding non-negative weights never decreases a distance. Equivalently, run normal Dijkstra on weights -log(p). O((V + E) log V).

mandatory: maximise the product of probabilities with a max-heap Dijkstra
relax with prob[u] × p
concept_groups: start with probability 1 at the source
stop when the target is popped
advanced_bonus: correctness relies on probabilities being at most 1
Bellman-Ford style relaxation also works but is slower
skip stale heap entries
return 0 if the target is unreachable

logic_context: Build a directed graph: add an edge from bomb i to bomb j if j lies within i's radius, checked with squared distances (dx² + dy² <= r²) using 64-bit integers to avoid overflow and floating-point errors. The graph is directed because radii differ. Then run BFS or DFS from each bomb and count how many bombs are reached; the maximum count is the answer. O(n²) to build the graph and O(n · (n + E)) for the searches — O(n³) in the worst case.

mandatory: directed edge i → j if j is within i's radius
BFS/DFS from every bomb and take the maximum reach
advanced_bonus: using floating-point sqrt can cause precision mistakes
union-find is wrong here because reachability is directed
n is small (e.g. ≤ 100) in typical constraints
memoising reach sets is hard because of cycles — SCC condensation can help
each search uses a fresh visited array

logic_context: Treat indices as nodes with unweighted edges, and run BFS from index 0. Precompute a map from each value to the list of its indices. When visiting index i, enqueue unvisited neighbours i - 1, i + 1 and every index in map[a[i]]. After using a value's list once, clear it, because those indices are already queued — this prevents re-scanning long lists and keeps the total work O(n). The BFS level when the last index is reached is the answer.

mandatory: BFS over indices with three kinds of jumps
clear each value's index list after its first use
concept_groups: clearing lists keeps total work O(n)
answer is the BFS level of the last index
advanced_bonus: without clearing lists, many equal values make BFS O(n²)

consecutive runs of equal values can be compressed in preprocessing

DFS does not give the minimum steps

common_mistakes: dynamic programming left to right only

logic_context: Taking one x makes it worth taking all copies of x, so compute points[v] = v × count(v) for every value v. Choosing v forbids v - 1 and v + 1, which is exactly the House Robber problem over the value line. Let dp[v] = max(dp[v - 1], dp[v - 2] + points[v]). The answer is dp at the maximum value. O(n + maxValue) time; sorting distinct values handles large ranges.

mandatory: group equal values: points[v] = v × count(v)
House Robber over values: neighbours v ± 1 conflict
concept_groups: take all copies of a chosen value
sort distinct values for sparse ranges
advanced_bonus: for sparse values, process sorted distinct values and only apply the conflict when values are consecutive
rolling variables reduce space to O(1)
greedy picking of the largest value is not optimal
reduction to a known problem is the key insight

logic_context: Let dp[i][s] be the number of ways to get sum s with i dice. dp[0][0] = 1. For each die i and each sum s, dp[i][s] = sum over faces k = 1..f (with k <= s) of dp[i - 1][s - k]. The answer is dp[n][target], usually modulo 10^9 + 7. This is O(n × target × f); using a sliding window (prefix sums) over the previous row reduces it to O(n × target).

mandatory: dp[i][s] = sum of dp[i - 1][s - k] for faces k
advanced_bonus: impossible if target < n or target > n × f
each die contributes at least 1
prefix-sum trick: window sum of the last f entries
brute force over f^n outcomes is exponential
same structure as counting compositions with bounded parts

semantic_targets: each die adds one face value

logic_context: Keep, for each transaction count t from 1 to k, buy[t] = best profit after buying for the t-th time and sell[t] = best profit after selling for the t-th time. For each price p: buy[t] = max(buy[t], sell[t - 1] - p) and sell[t] = max(sell[t], buy[t] + p). Start with buy[t] = -infinity and sell[t] = 0. The answer is sell[k]. O(n · k). If k >= n / 2, the limit does not matter, so sum all positive day-to-day increases instead.

mandatory: states buy[t] and sell[t] for each transaction count
buy[t] uses sell[t - 1]; sell[t] uses buy[t]
advanced_bonus: k = 1 reduces to the single best buy/sell pair
k = 2 is a well-known special case
unlimited version: sum of positive differences
2D dp[t][day] with max(prev - price) trick is equivalent
space O(k)

logic_context: Map each stone position to a set of jump sizes that can land on it. Start with stone 0 holding jump size 0 (so the first jump is 1). Process stones in order; for each jump size k stored at a stone, try next jumps k - 1, k and k + 1 (greater than 0); if a stone exists at position + step, add step to that stone's set. The frog can cross if the last stone's set is non-empty. O(n²) time and space.

mandatory: track reachable jump sizes at each stone
from jump k try k - 1, k, k + 1
concept_groups: hash map from position to set of sizes
success if the last stone is reached
advanced_bonus: memoised DFS on (stone, last jump) is equivalent
jump sizes can never exceed the number of stones, bounding states
a quick check: if stones[i] - stones[i-1] > i, it is impossible
sets avoid processing duplicate states
greedy jumping fails

semantic_targets: the previous jump determines the options

logic_context: Let dp[d] be the minimum cost to cover all travel days up to day d. If d is not a travel day, dp[d] = dp[d - 1]. If it is, dp[d] = min(dp[d - 1] + cost1, dp[max(0, d - 7)] + cost7, dp[max(0, d - 30)] + cost30), meaning a pass ending on day d. Fill d from 1 to the last travel day; the answer is dp[lastDay]. O(365) time.

mandatory: dp[d] = minimum cost to cover travel days up to d
choose a 1-, 7- or 30-day pass ending today
concept_groups: non-travel days copy the previous value
answer at the last travel day
advanced_bonus: an alternative indexes only travel days and uses pointers to find coverage boundaries
greedy (always buy the cheapest per day) fails
a cheaper long pass can dominate shorter ones
a pass ending on day d covers d - 6 .. d for 7 days
