logic_context: Sort the numbers. In sorted order, if a[j] divides a[i] and a[i] can join a valid chain ending at a[j], the whole chain stays valid because divisibility is transitive. Let dp[i] be the size of the largest such chain ending at a[i]: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over j < i with a[i] % a[j] == 0. Store a parent index to rebuild the subset from the index with the largest dp. O(n²).

mandatory: sort, then build divisibility chains
dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] where a[j] divides a[i]
concept_groups: divisibility is transitive along sorted chains
advanced_bonus: like LIS but with divisibility instead of <
checking all pairs within the chain is unnecessary thanks to transitivity
example: [1, 2, 4, 8] is fully divisible
duplicates are excluded by the problem

common_mistakes: Checking only adjacent pairs without transitivity argument

logic_context: Use two min-heaps. The free heap holds (weight, index). The busy heap holds (free time, weight, index). For task j, let time t = max(j, current time). First move every server whose free time <= t from busy to free. If no server is free, advance t to the earliest free time in the busy heap and move those servers. Pop the best free server, assign the task, and push it to busy with free time t + duration. O((n + m) log n).

mandatory: free heap ordered by (weight, index)
busy heap ordered by (free time, weight, index)
concept_groups: release servers whose time has come
jump time forward when none are free
advanced_bonus: tasks are processed in arrival order
jumping time avoids simulating idle seconds
ties in free time are broken by weight and index through the tuple order
use 64-bit times for long schedules
a single heap cannot handle both orderings

logic_context: Scan the bytes. For each starting byte, use its leading bits to find the character length: 0xxxxxxx is 1 byte, 110xxxxx is 2 bytes, 1110xxxx is 3 bytes and 11110xxx is 4 bytes; a byte starting with 10 cannot start a character, and 11111xxx is invalid. Then check that the next (length - 1) bytes exist and each starts with 10 (continuation bytes). If any check fails, the data is invalid. O(n). Stricter validators also reject overlong encodings and code points above U+10FFFF or in the surrogate range.

mandatory: leading bits of the first byte give the length (1-4)
following bytes must be continuation bytes 10xxxxxx
concept_groups: a continuation byte cannot start a character
advanced_bonus: overlong encodings (e.g. 0xC0 0x80) are invalid in strict UTF-8
code points above U+10FFFF and surrogates D800-DFFF are invalid
use unsigned char to avoid sign-extension problems
a counter of remaining continuation bytes keeps the scan simple
ASCII text is always valid UTF-8

semantic_targets: the first byte announces the sequence length
common_mistakes: Accepting a continuation byte as a start

logic_context: Represent each word's set of letters as a 26-bit mask, setting bit (c - 'a') for each letter. Two words share no letters exactly when the AND of their masks is 0. Compare every pair of words with this O(1) test and keep the maximum product of lengths. Building masks is O(total characters) and the pair checks are O(n²). Keeping only the longest word for each distinct mask can reduce the pairs.

mandatory: 26-bit mask per word
no common letters iff mask_a & mask_b == 0
concept_groups: keep the longest word per mask
advanced_bonus: comparing letter sets with loops would be O(26) or O(L) per pair
masks fit in a 32-bit int
sorting by length descending allows early termination
example: 'abcw' and 'xtfn' give 16
duplicate masks reduce the effective number of words

common_mistakes: Comparing letters character by character for every pair
overflow with long words not considered
returns the words instead of the product

logic_context: Scan both strings together. When secret[i] == guess[i], count a bull. Otherwise increment count arrays for the secret digit and the guess digit. After the scan, cows = sum over digits d of min(secretCount[d], guessCount[d]), since each unmatched digit can pair with at most one equal digit elsewhere. O(n) time, O(1) space.

advanced_bonus: a single-pass variant uses one array: increment for secret, decrement for guess, and counts cows when signs indicate a match

output format like '1A3B'
works for any alphabet with suitable counting

logic_context: Use fast (binary) exponentiation. If n is negative, replace x with 1 / x and n with -n, storing n in a 64-bit variable so that negating INT_MIN does not overflow. Then, while n > 0: if the lowest bit of n is 1, multiply the result by x; square x; shift n right by 1. The recursive form is x^n = (x^(n/2))² for even n and x · x^(n - 1) for odd n. O(log n) multiplications.

mandatory: square the base and halve the exponent
multiply into the result when the current bit is 1
concept_groups: use 64-bit for n to handle INT_MIN
advanced_bonus: naive repeated multiplication is O(n)
floating-point errors accumulate but are small for moderate n

logic_context: With write-ahead logging, a database first appends a description of each change to a sequential log on durable storage and only later applies the change to the main data pages. A transaction counts as committed once its log records are safely written. After a crash, the database replays (redoes) committed changes from the log and undoes incomplete ones, restoring a consistent state. Sequential log writes are much faster than random page writes, and grouping several commits into one log flush (group commit) improves throughput.

mandatory: log changes durably before applying them to data pages
replay the log after a crash to recover
concept_groups: commit when log records are durable
redo committed and undo incomplete work
advanced_bonus: supports atomicity and durability in ACID
checkpoints flush dirty pages so older log can be discarded
SQLite's WAL mode lets readers proceed while a writer appends
the log can be shipped to replicas for replication
fsync on the log is the key durability point

semantic_targets: the log is the source of truth until pages are flushed
common_mistakes: Writing data pages before the log
Saying the log is only for debugging
claims WAL avoids all disk writes

logic_context: ACID describes guarantees for transactions. Atomicity: all operations in a transaction happen, or none do. Consistency: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting rules such as constraints. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere as if they ran one after another (to a degree set by the isolation level). Durability: once committed, changes survive crashes and power loss. For example, a bank transfer must debit one account and credit the other together, never just one.

mandatory: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
all-or-nothing transactions that survive crashes
concept_groups: isolation levels trade strictness for performance
advanced_bonus: isolation levels: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable
anomalies include dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantoms
many NoSQL systems relax some ACID properties for scale
the bank transfer is the classic example
two-phase commit extends atomicity across databases

semantic_targets: each property addresses a different failure
common_mistakes: Saying consistency means replicas agree (that is a different meaning)
claims isolation is always fully serial

logic_context: A database index is an extra data structure, usually a B+ tree or a hash table, that lets the database find rows by the values of certain columns without scanning the whole table. It speeds up lookups, range queries, sorting and joins on those columns. The costs are extra storage, slower inserts, updates and deletes (every index must be updated), and planning effort, so indexes should be added on columns that are frequently searched and fairly selective.

faster reads but slower writes and more storage
concept_groups: usually a B+ tree; hash indexes for equality
helps WHERE, ORDER BY and joins
advanced_bonus: composite index column order matters (leftmost-prefix rule)
a covering index contains all needed columns, avoiding table lookups

EXPLAIN shows whether a query uses an index

logic_context: Normalisation organises tables to reduce duplicated data and prevent update, insert and delete anomalies. First normal form (1NF) requires atomic column values and no repeating groups. Second normal form (2NF) requires 1NF and that every non-key column depends on the whole primary key, not just part of a composite key. Third normal form (3NF) requires 2NF and that non-key columns depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns (no transitive dependencies). The trade-off is more tables and joins, so read-heavy systems sometimes denormalise deliberately.

1NF atomic values, 2NF no partial dependencies, 3NF no transitive dependencies
advanced_bonus: BCNF is a stricter form of 3NF
example: storing customer address in every order row causes update anomalies
functional dependencies define the normal forms
data warehouses often use denormalised star schemas
foreign keys link the normalised tables

semantic_targets: each form removes a type of redundancy

logic_context: TCP is connection-oriented: it sets up a connection, delivers data reliably and in order, retransmits lost packets, and controls flow and congestion; it presents data as a byte stream. UDP is connectionless: it sends independent datagrams with no delivery, ordering or duplication guarantees and little overhead, preserving message boundaries. TCP suits web pages, file transfer and email; UDP suits real-time voice, video, games and DNS, where speed matters more than retransmitting late data.

mandatory: TCP: reliable, ordered, connection-oriented byte stream
UDP: connectionless datagrams without guarantees
concept_groups: TCP has flow and congestion control

advanced_bonus: TCP head-of-line blocking delays later data when one packet is lost

logic_context: To open a connection, the client sends a SYN segment with its initial sequence number x. The server replies with SYN-ACK: its own initial sequence number y and an acknowledgement of x + 1. The client then sends an ACK of y + 1. After this, both sides know the other can send and receive, and both initial sequence numbers are agreed, so data can be numbered and acknowledged reliably. Connections are later closed with FIN and ACK segments.

mandatory: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange
agrees initial sequence numbers in both directions
concept_groups: confirms both sides can send and receive
advanced_bonus: random initial sequence numbers protect against spoofing and old duplicate packets

TCP Fast Open can send data with the SYN

common_mistakes: Saying data is encrypted during the handshake

logic_context: The Domain Name System translates human-readable names into IP addresses. A program asks a local resolver (often provided by the ISP or a public service). If the answer is not cached, the resolver queries a root server, which points to the server for the top-level domain (.com); that server points to the authoritative server for example.com, which returns the address record (A for IPv4, AAAA for IPv6). Answers are cached for their time-to-live (TTL) to speed up later lookups. DNS usually runs over UDP port 53.

mandatory: translates domain names to IP addresses
root → TLD → authoritative server resolution
advanced_bonus: CNAME records alias one name to another

logic_context: Both sides start with socket() to create an endpoint. A server then calls bind() to attach it to an address and port, listen() to mark it as accepting connections, and accept() to wait for a client; accept() returns a new socket for that client. A client calls connect() with the server's address. Both sides then exchange data with send()/recv() (or write()/read()) and finish with close(). Each call can fail, so return values must be checked.

mandatory: server: socket, bind, listen, accept
client: socket, connect; both use send/recv and close
concept_groups: accept returns a new socket per client
advanced_bonus: htons/htonl convert to network byte order
recv may return fewer bytes than requested — loop until complete
UDP uses sendto/recvfrom without connect/accept
SO_REUSEADDR helps restart servers quickly

logic_context: An IP address identifies a device on a network — IPv4 addresses are 32-bit, written like 192.168.1.10, and IPv6 addresses are 128-bit. A port number (0 to 65535) identifies a specific program or service on that device, such as 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS and 22 for SSH. Together, an IP address and a port identify one endpoint of a network connection, like a building address plus an apartment number.

logic_context: HTTP is the protocol browsers use to request and receive web pages, but it sends data as plain text, so anyone on the network path can read or change it. HTTPS is HTTP running over TLS: it encrypts the traffic, checks the server's identity using certificates, and detects tampering. HTTP normally uses port 80 and HTTPS port 443. HTTPS is essential for logins, payments and private data, and is now the default for most websites.

logic_context: A primary key is a column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table; it cannot be NULL and no two rows can share it, such as student_id in a Students table. A foreign key is a column in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, such as student_id in an Enrollments table. The database uses foreign keys to enforce referential integrity — you cannot add an enrollment for a student who does not exist.

logic_context: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for working with relational databases. It is declarative: you describe what data you want, and the database decides how to get it. The basic CRUD operations are Create with INSERT, Read with SELECT, Update with UPDATE and Delete with DELETE. A WHERE clause limits which rows are affected, for example UPDATE students SET year = 2 WHERE id = 7.

logic_context: In the client-server model, clients request services or data and servers provide them over a network. For example, a web browser (client) sends a request to a web server, which returns a page; an email app (client) talks to a mail server. Servers usually run continuously and handle many clients at once, while clients start conversations when they need something. This differs from peer-to-peer systems, where every node can act as both client and server.

logic_context: A relational database offers ACID transactions across several tables, so recording the order, payment and stock change can succeed or fail together; it also enforces schemas, foreign keys and constraints, and supports flexible queries with joins. Scaling writes horizontally is harder and schema changes need migrations. A document database stores each order as a flexible nested document, scales out easily and reads a whole document quickly, but transactions across documents or collections are more limited (support varies), and data is often duplicated, risking inconsistency. Recommend a relational database for orders and payments; a document store can suit product catalogues with varied attributes.

document store: flexible schema and easy scaling but weaker cross-document guarantees
advanced_bonus: many document databases now support multi-document transactions with performance costs

consistency requirements should drive the choice, not trends

logic_context: Regular polling (the browser asks every few seconds) is simple and works everywhere, but updates arrive late by up to one interval, and most requests return nothing, so server load grows with clients × frequency. Long polling keeps each request open until an update occurs, giving quicker delivery and fewer empty responses, but each update requires a new request and connections time out and reconnect often. WebSockets keep one persistent two-way connection per client so the server can push updates immediately with little overhead, at the cost of managing many open connections, reconnection logic and support in proxies and load balancers. Recommend WebSockets (or Server-Sent Events for one-way updates).

mandatory: polling: simple but delayed and wasteful
WebSockets: persistent connection for instant server push
concept_groups: many open connections must be managed
advanced_bonus: SSE runs over plain HTTP and reconnects automatically
an event-driven server handles many idle WebSocket connections efficiently

fall back to polling when WebSockets are blocked
heartbeats detect dead connections

semantic_targets: push beats pull for frequent updates
common_mistakes: Recommending fast polling for thousands of clients without load analysis

logic_context: Offset pagination is simple and lets clients jump to any page number, but the database must still walk past all the skipped rows, so deep pages become slow (cost grows with the offset), and if rows are inserted or deleted between requests, items can be skipped or repeated. Keyset pagination remembers the last seen sort key and asks for rows after it (WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20), which uses an index and stays fast at any depth and stable under inserts, but cannot jump to an arbitrary page and needs a unique, indexed sort key. Recommend keyset pagination for large tables and infinite scrolling; offset only for small result sets or when page jumping is required.

mandatory: offset: simple page jumps but slow deep pages and unstable results
keyset: fast at any depth using an index, but no random page access
concept_groups: keyset needs a unique sortable key

logic_context: Storing images as BLOBs keeps them in the same transactions, backups and access control as the rest of the data, so the database and the images never disagree. But large binary data bloats the database, slows backups and replication, uses database memory and connections to serve files, and cannot be served directly by a CDN. An object store (or file system) with paths in the database scales cheaply, can be served directly to users through a CDN, and keeps the database small, but the application must keep both in sync (avoiding orphan files or missing images) and back them up separately. Recommend object storage with metadata in the database for most applications.

mandatory: BLOBs: consistent with data but bloat the database
object store: scalable and CDN-friendly but needs sync with the database
advanced_bonus: signed URLs give temporary secure access to private objects

small thumbnails can sometimes live in the database

semantic_targets: keep large files out of the database
common_mistakes: Ignoring synchronisation between DB and files

logic_context: Direct synchronous calls are simple to understand and give an immediate result, but every step must be available and fast: if the email or shipping service is down or slow, the whole order fails or hangs, and failures cascade. A message queue decouples the services: the order service records the order and publishes an event; consumers process it at their own pace, retries happen automatically, and traffic spikes are buffered. The costs are eventual consistency, extra infrastructure, possible duplicate deliveries (so consumers must be idempotent) and harder end-to-end debugging. Recommend synchronous calls only for steps the customer must see immediately (payment authorisation) and a queue for follow-up work like email, inventory sync and shipping.

mandatory: synchronous calls couple availability and latency of all services
message queue decouples and buffers but gives eventual consistency
advanced_bonus: the outbox pattern writes the event in the same database transaction as the order
at-least-once delivery means duplicates are possible
correlation IDs help trace requests across services
timeouts and circuit breakers reduce cascading failures in synchronous calls
saga patterns coordinate multi-step workflows with compensating actions

semantic_targets: only block on what the user must wait for
common_mistakes: Making everything synchronous without considering failures

sends email before the order is recorded

logic_context: Scan once, comparing each pair a[i - 1] and a[i]. If they are equal, the turbulent run is broken, so the current length resets to 1. If the comparison sign is the opposite of the previous pair's sign, the run extends by one. Otherwise the run restarts with length 2 (just this pair). Track the maximum length. O(n) time, O(1) space.

extend when the sign alternates, reset otherwise
advanced_bonus: two counters (up, down) give an equivalent DP formulation
a single element is turbulent with length 1

logic_context: Let count(B) be the number of subarrays whose elements are all <= B: scan the array, keep the length of the current run of elements <= B, and add the run length at each position. A subarray has its maximum in [L, R] exactly when all elements are <= R but not all are <= L - 1. So the answer is count(R) - count(L - 1). Each count is O(n), so the total is O(n).

logic_context: Keep a count of remaining occurrences of each number and a map tails[x] = number of subsequences currently ending at x. Process numbers in order. For each x still available: if some subsequence ends at x - 1, extend it (tails[x - 1]--, tails[x]++). Otherwise try to start a new subsequence x, x + 1, x + 2 by consuming one of each; if any is missing, return false; else tails[x + 2]++. Extending first is always safe and keeps short sequences from being stranded. O(n) with hash maps.

advanced_bonus: greedy extension is optimal because starting a new sequence risks leaving short ones

logic_context: If the number of cards is not divisible by W, return false. Count each value with an ordered map (or sort the distinct values). Repeatedly take the smallest value x with a positive count c: it must start c groups, so each of x, x + 1, …, x + W - 1 must have count at least c; subtract c from each, failing if any count is too small. If all counts reach zero, return true. O(n log n).

subtract the same count from the next W - 1 values
advanced_bonus: processing c groups at once avoids repeated work

logic_context: If a repeated substring of length L exists, then one of length L - 1 also exists, so the property is monotonic and the length can be binary searched. To test a length L, compute a rolling (Rabin-Karp) hash of every substring of length L in O(n) and store them in a hash set; if a hash repeats (and the substrings are confirmed equal or a double hash is used), length L works. Binary search over L gives O(n log n) overall. A suffix array with LCP array is an exact alternative.

mandatory: binary search on the length because repetition is monotonic
rolling hash checks all substrings of a length in O(n)

advanced_bonus: the maximum LCP value of adjacent suffixes in a suffix array equals the answer

logic_context: A neat test: s is a repetition exactly when s appears inside (s + s) with the first and last characters removed. Alternatively, try every length d that divides n (with d < n) and check whether s equals its first d characters repeated n / d times. A KMP-based check is also O(n): with p = the last value of the prefix function, s is repeated when p > 0 and n % (n - p) == 0.

or test each divisor length of n
concept_groups: divisor checks are O(n × number of divisors)
advanced_bonus: the doubled-string trick works because a rotation of a periodic string equals itself
the smallest period is n - p from the prefix function

example: 'abcabcabc' → true

logic_context: A node is removed in round h, where h is its height measured from the bottom: leaves have height 0 and a node's height is 1 + the maximum height of its children. Do a post-order traversal computing each node's height and append the node's value to the list for that height. The lists in order of height are the removal rounds. O(n) time, without actually deleting nodes.

advanced_bonus: simulating repeated leaf removal is O(n²) in the worst case

logic_context: Do a DFS from the root, building the path's characters. At each leaf, form the string from the leaf back to the root (reverse the path) and compare it with the best found so far, keeping the smaller one. Greedily choosing the smaller child at each step does not work, because the comparison depends on the full leaf-to-root string. O(n · h) time because each leaf string is length h.

compare full strings to keep the smallest
advanced_bonus: prepending characters avoids a final reverse but costs more per step
a shorter string that is a prefix of a longer one is smaller
nodes with one child are not leaves
backtrack by removing the last character after each child
example: tree for 'zab' paths

logic_context: Do a DFS passing down the maximum value seen on the path so far. At each node, if its value is greater than or equal to that maximum, count it as good. Then recurse into both children with the updated maximum max(pathMax, node value). The root is always good. O(n) time, O(h) space.

logic_context: Do a DFS that carries the minimum and maximum values seen on the path from the root. At each node, the best difference involving it and an ancestor is max(|val - pathMin|, |val - pathMax|); update the answer, then recurse with the minimum and maximum updated to include this node. Equivalently, at each leaf the answer candidate is pathMax - pathMin. O(n) time.

difference with an ancestor is largest against the path extremes

logic_context: Put the subset values in a hash set. Walk the list; a node ends a component if its value is in the set and either it is the last node or the next node's value is not in the set. Count such component ends. O(n + k) time and O(k) space for a subset of size k.

logic_context: Walk the list after the first 0 while accumulating a running sum. When a 0 is reached, the current group has ended: write the sum into a node (for example reuse the first node of the group, or the 0 node that starts it), link it to the result list, and reset the sum. Skip the zeros themselves. Reusing existing nodes and relinking gives O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

logic_context: Sort courses by their last day. Go through them, adding each course's duration to the total time and pushing the duration onto a max-heap. If the total time exceeds the current course's deadline, remove the longest course taken so far (pop the max-heap) and subtract its duration. Swapping out the longest course keeps the same count or improves it while freeing the most time. The heap size at the end is the answer. O(n log n).

logic_context: For each unvisited land cell in grid2, run DFS or BFS over its whole island. While exploring, check every cell: if grid1 has water at that position, mark the island as not a sub-island, but keep exploring to visit (and mark) the whole island. After the search, if no cell failed, count it. O(m · n).

logic_context: Build a weighted directed graph: for each equation a / b = k, add an edge a → b with weight k and b → a with weight 1 / k. To answer x / y, search from x to y (DFS or BFS), multiplying the weights along the path; if y is unreachable or either variable is unknown, return -1. Alternatively, use a weighted union-find where each variable stores its ratio to its root, so x / y = ratio(x) / ratio(y) when they share a root. Each query is O(V + E) with search, nearly O(1) with union-find.

Processing all equalities first is essential because equality is transitive. Nearly O(n).

logic_context: Generate ugly numbers in increasing order. Start with dp[0] = 1 and three pointers i2, i3 and i5 at index 0. Each next number is min(dp[i2] × 2, dp[i3] × 3, dp[i5] × 5). logic_context: Add 0 and n to the list of cut positions and sort it. Let dp[i][j] be the minimum cost to make all cuts strictly between positions cuts[i] and cuts[j]. Fill by increasing interval length. The answer is dp[0][m + 1]. O(m³) for m cuts.

common_mistakes: Counting elements instead of distinct values

logic_context: Sort the positions. Binary search the answer d, the minimum distance. To test d, place the first ball at the first position and greedily place each next ball at the first position at least d away from the previous ball; if at least m balls fit, d is achievable and you try larger; otherwise try smaller. The largest achievable d is the answer. O(n log n + n log(range)).

mandatory: binary search on the minimum distance
greedy placement checks feasibility
concept_groups: first ball at the first position
advanced_bonus: feasibility is monotonic: if d works, any smaller d works
placing balls as early as possible leaves the most room
range is from 1 to (max - min)
this maximises a minimum, the mirror of minimise-the-maximum problems
example: positions [1, 2, 3, 4, 7], m = 3 → 3

semantic_targets: place each ball as early as allowed
common_mistakes: greedy that skips the first position

evaluation_rubric.focus: Maximise the minimum with binary search

logic_context: Look at each bit position independently. If c's bit is 1, at least one of a's and b's bits must be 1: if both are 0, one flip is needed, otherwise none. If c's bit is 0, both a's and b's bits must be 0: flip each one that is 1 (0, 1 or 2 flips). Sum over all 32 bit positions. O(number of bits).

mandatory: examine each bit position separately
c bit 1: need at least one 1; c bit 0: both must be 0
concept_groups: c=0 → flips = a bit + b bit
advanced_bonus: a compact formula: popcount((a | b) ^ c) + popcount(a & b & ~c)
bits are independent because OR works bit by bit
use unsigned integers for shifting
example: a=2, b=6, c=5 → 3 flips
same bitwise reasoning applies to AND and XOR targets

semantic_targets: each bit of c sets its own requirement
common_mistakes: Counting differences between a and c only
Using XOR logic instead of OR
Forgetting that both bits must be cleared when c is 0

logic_context: Build a prefix XOR array: P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] ^ a[i]. Because x ^ x = 0, the XOR of a[L..R] equals P[R + 1] ^ P[L] — the common prefix cancels out. Each query is then O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.

mandatory: prefix XOR array with P[0] = 0
XOR(L..R) = P[R + 1] ^ P[L]
concept_groups: common prefix cancels because x ^ x = 0
advanced_bonus: XOR is its own inverse, which makes prefix differences work
prefix XOR also finds subarrays with XOR equal to k using a hash map
updates require a Fenwick tree over XOR
no overflow issues, unlike sums

semantic_targets: XOR acts as both addition and subtraction

logic_context: Use backtracking with a set of substrings already used. From the current start index, try every end position; if the substring s[start..end] is not in the set, add it, recurse from end + 1, then remove it. When the start reaches the end of the string, update the best count. Prune when the current count plus the number of remaining characters cannot beat the best. Exponential in the worst case, which is acceptable for short strings (e.g. up to 16 characters).

mandatory: try every next substring that is not yet used
backtrack by removing the substring from the set
concept_groups: record the maximum count at the end
advanced_bonus: greedy shortest-first splitting is not always optimal
pruning: count + (n - start) <= best means stop
the number of possible splits is 2^(n - 1)
strings are short in typical constraints
example: 'ababccc' → 5 ('a','b','ab','c','cc')

logic_context: All cells on the same diagonal share the value row - column. Group the cells by this key: for each diagonal, collect its values, sort them, and write them back in order along the diagonal from top-left to bottom-right. Diagonals start from each cell in the first row and each cell in the first column. O(m · n · log(min(m, n))) time.

mandatory: cells on a diagonal share row - column
collect, sort and write back each diagonal
concept_groups: start diagonals from the first row and first column
advanced_bonus: a min-heap per diagonal is an alternative grouping
counting sort works when values are small
there are m + n - 1 diagonals
compare with anti-diagonals, where row + column is constant
in-place insertion sort along each diagonal also works for small matrices

semantic_targets: each diagonal is its own list
common_mistakes: Writing values back in the wrong direction
missing diagonals from the first column

logic_context: Let min and max be the extreme values of the n numbers. The largest gap is at least (max - min) / (n - 1), so use buckets of size about that, ceil((max - min) / (n - 1)). Place each number in a bucket, tracking only each bucket's minimum and maximum. The maximum gap cannot lie inside a bucket, so compute it between buckets: for each non-empty bucket, compare its minimum with the previous non-empty bucket's maximum. O(n) time and space. Radix sort is another linear option.

mandatory: pigeonhole bucket size based on (max - min) / (n - 1)
maximum gap occurs between buckets, not inside
concept_groups: track min and max per bucket
advanced_bonus: sorting first is O(n log n)
bucket size must be at least 1
at least one bucket is empty or gaps reach the average, ensuring the max gap spans buckets
fewer than 2 elements gives 0
use 64-bit for large value ranges

common_mistakes: Bucket size zero for equal values

logic_context: For each row, compute the running sum of brick widths, excluding the final edge (the wall's right side). Each running sum is a position where the row has an edge. Count, in a hash map, how many rows have an edge at each position. The line through the position with the most edges crosses the fewest bricks: answer = number of rows - maximum edge count (or number of rows if no internal edges exist). O(total bricks).

mandatory: count edge positions across rows with a hash map
answer = rows - maximum edge count
concept_groups: rows with one brick add no edges
advanced_bonus: checking every integer x along the width is too slow for wide walls
positions can be large, so use a hash map not an array
edges at the far left and right are not allowed
example: answer equals rows minus most common edge position
a sorted list of edges per row with merging is an alternative

semantic_targets: fewest crossings means most aligned edges

logic_context: MVCC lets readers and writers work at the same time without blocking each other by keeping several versions of each row. When a transaction updates a row, the database creates a new version instead of overwriting the old one. Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot — the versions that were committed when it started — so readers never see half-finished changes and never wait for writers. Old versions that no transaction needs are later cleaned up (for example by VACUUM in PostgreSQL). Conflicting writes to the same row still need detection or locking.

mandatory: keeps multiple versions of rows
readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers
advanced_bonus: used by PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB and Oracle
snapshot isolation can still allow write skew anomalies
long-running transactions keep old versions alive and bloat storage
version metadata includes creating and deleting transaction ids
serializable snapshot isolation adds conflict detection

semantic_targets: readers and writers do not block each other

logic_context: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several servers. It improves availability (another copy can take over if one fails) and read throughput (reads can go to replicas), but every write must reach every copy, and replicas may lag behind. Sharding (partitioning) splits the data across servers by a shard key, so each server holds only part of it; this scales storage and write throughput, but queries and transactions across shards become harder, and choosing the key and rebalancing data need care. Large systems usually combine both: each shard is replicated.

mandatory: replication copies the same data to several servers
sharding splits different data across servers
advanced_bonus: leader-follower replication sends writes to one leader
consistent hashing reduces data movement when adding shards
a poor shard key causes hot spots
synchronous replication trades latency for no data loss
each shard can itself have replicas

logic_context: The CAP theorem says that when a network partition happens — some servers cannot talk to others — a distributed data system must choose between consistency (every read returns the most recent write or an error) and availability (every request receives a non-error response, possibly with stale data). Since partitions cannot be ruled out in real networks, the practical choice is between being CP (refuse some requests to stay consistent) and AP (keep answering, accepting temporary inconsistency). When there is no partition, a system can provide both.

mandatory: during a partition, choose consistency or availability
partition tolerance is required in practice
concept_groups: AP systems may return stale data
both are possible without a partition
advanced_bonus: PACELC adds: Else (no partition), trade latency against consistency
examples: many configuration stores are CP; Dynamo-style stores lean AP
the 'C' differs from the C in ACID
eventual consistency is a common AP model
choice can differ per operation in the same system

common_mistakes: Saying a system can choose any two of three freely
claims CAP applies only to SQL databases
ignores that both hold without partitions

logic_context: A load balancer sits in front of several servers and spreads incoming requests among them, so no single server is overloaded and failed servers can be bypassed using health checks. Common algorithms are round robin (take turns), weighted round robin (more requests to stronger servers), least connections (send to the server with the fewest active connections) and hashing on the client IP or a key (so the same client goes to the same server). Layer 4 balancers route by IP and port; layer 7 balancers can route by HTTP details such as URL.

mandatory: spreads requests across servers
algorithms: round robin, least connections, hashing
advanced_bonus: the load balancer itself must be redundant to avoid a single point of failure
consistent hashing limits reassignment when servers change
least connections suits requests with very different durations
TLS termination is often done at the load balancer
DNS-based load balancing is coarser

semantic_targets: send each request where it can be served best
common_mistakes: Saying it increases each server's speed
claims it removes all single points of failure automatically

logic_context: In a write-through cache, every write updates both the cache and the slower backing store (such as main memory or a database) immediately, so the store is always up to date and a crash loses nothing, but writes are as slow as the backing store. In a write-back (write-behind) cache, writes update only the cache and mark the entry dirty; the backing store is updated later, when the entry is evicted or flushed. This makes writes fast and combines repeated writes, but dirty data can be lost on a crash and the logic is more complex.

mandatory: write-through updates cache and backing store together
write-back updates the cache now and the store later
concept_groups: write-back is fast but risks losing dirty data
advanced_bonus: CPU caches typically use write-back
write-allocate versus no-write-allocate decides whether a write miss loads the line
battery-backed caches make write-back safer in storage controllers
write-around skips the cache on writes
application caches (e.g. in front of a database) face the same choice

common_mistakes: Saying write-back never writes to memory
claims write-through is faster for writes

logic_context: The OSI model describes networking in seven layers: 1 Physical (signals and cables), 2 Data Link (frames on one network, e.g. Ethernet), 3 Network (routing between networks, IP), 4 Transport (end-to-end delivery, TCP/UDP), 5 Session, 6 Presentation (data formats, encryption) and 7 Application (protocols like HTTP). The practical TCP/IP model uses four layers — Link, Internet, Transport and Application — merging OSI's top three into Application and its bottom two into Link. Each layer adds its own header around the data from the layer above (encapsulation).

mandatory: seven OSI layers from Physical to Application
TCP/IP model has four layers
concept_groups: TCP/IP is what the internet uses
advanced_bonus: routers work at layer 3, switches at layer 2
TLS is often placed between transport and application
each layer only talks to the layers directly above and below
troubleshooting often follows layers bottom-up
MTU limits are a layer 2 concern

semantic_targets: each layer has its own responsibilities
common_mistakes: Placing IP at the transport layer

logic_context: An operation is idempotent if performing it several times has the same effect as performing it once — for example, setting x = 5 or deleting a specific record, while x = x + 1 or 'add an order' are not. Networks lose and delay messages, so clients often retry requests when they do not get a reply; if the operation is idempotent, a retry cannot cause duplicates such as double payments. In HTTP, GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be idempotent, while POST is not, so APIs often accept an idempotency key to make POST requests safe to retry.

mandatory: same effect whether done once or many times
makes retries safe in unreliable networks
advanced_bonus: the server stores the idempotency key with the result and returns it on repeats
message queues with at-least-once delivery require idempotent consumers
idempotent is different from safe (GET is both; DELETE is idempotent but not safe)
database upserts can make inserts idempotent
the response may differ (e.g. 404 on a second delete) while the state is the same

logic_context: A Cartesian tree of an array is a binary tree that is heap-ordered by value (each parent is smaller than its children, for a min-tree) and whose inorder traversal gives back the original array. So the root is the minimum element, its left subtree is built from the elements to its left, and its right subtree from those to its right. It can be built in O(n) with a stack holding the tree's right spine: for each new element, pop larger values, make the last popped node the new node's left child, and attach the new node as the right child of the stack top.

mandatory: heap order by value and inorder equals the original array
root is the minimum element
concept_groups: built in O(n) with a right-spine stack
left and right subtrees from left and right parts
advanced_bonus: range minimum query on the array equals LCA in its Cartesian tree
a treap is a Cartesian tree over (key, random priority) pairs
recursive building by finding the minimum is O(n²) worst case
each element is pushed and popped once
used in suffix-tree and RMQ constructions

common_mistakes: Saying it is a BST on values
Claiming O(n log n) build is required
Confusing with a binary heap array

logic_context: An API is a defined set of functions, commands or endpoints, together with rules for how to use them, that lets one piece of software use another without knowing its internal details. Examples include the C standard library functions such as printf and malloc, operating-system system calls, and web APIs where a program sends HTTP requests to a server and gets data back (for example a weather service). Good APIs are documented, consistent and stable across versions.

mandatory: defined interface for software to use other software
hides internal implementation
concept_groups: examples: C library, system calls, web APIs
advanced_bonus: REST APIs use HTTP methods and URLs
breaking changes require new API versions
an ABI is the binary-level counterpart of an API
rate limits and authentication protect web APIs
header files declare a C library's API

semantic_targets: users rely on the interface, not the code
common_mistakes: Saying an API is a programming language
Confusing API with a user interface
claims APIs expose all internal code

logic_context: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight text format for structured data. It supports objects (key-value pairs in braces), arrays (ordered lists in brackets), strings, numbers, booleans and null, for example {"name": "Asha", "marks": [90, 85]}. It is popular because it is easy for people to read, simple to parse, language-independent and the standard format for most web APIs and many configuration files.

mandatory: text format with objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null
human-readable and language-independent
advanced_bonus: JSON keys must be double-quoted strings
JSON has no comments and no native date type
C libraries such as cJSON parse JSON
binary alternatives like MessagePack are more compact
large numbers may lose precision in some parsers

semantic_targets: maps naturally to program data structures
common_mistakes: Saying JSON can only be used with JavaScript

logic_context: They are three levels of cloud service. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) provides virtual machines, storage and networks; you manage the operating system and applications (e.g. AWS EC2). Platform as a Service (PaaS) runs your code on a managed platform, so you deploy applications without managing servers (e.g. Heroku, Google App Engine). Software as a Service (SaaS) delivers complete applications over the internet that you simply use (e.g. Gmail, Google Docs). Moving from IaaS to SaaS, you manage less and control less.

mandatory: IaaS: virtual infrastructure; PaaS: managed platform; SaaS: ready applications
responsibility shifts to the provider from IaaS to SaaS
concept_groups: less control with more managed services
advanced_bonus: serverless (Functions as a Service) goes further than PaaS
shared responsibility model for security
containers as a service sit between IaaS and PaaS
vendor lock-in is a risk with managed services
public, private and hybrid clouds are deployment models

logic_context: A virtual machine runs a complete guest operating system on virtual hardware provided by a hypervisor, giving strong isolation but using more memory and disk and taking longer to start. A container packages an application and its dependencies but shares the host operating system's kernel, using namespaces and control groups for isolation; it is lightweight and starts in seconds, but isolation is weaker and it must match the host kernel type. Docker is a common container tool; containers often run inside VMs in the cloud.

mandatory: VM includes a full guest OS on a hypervisor
container shares the host kernel
concept_groups: containers: lightweight and fast to start
advanced_bonus: a Linux container cannot natively run a Windows kernel application
container images are built in layers
Kubernetes orchestrates many containers
VMs can run different operating systems on one host
security-sensitive workloads may need VM-level isolation

semantic_targets: containers virtualise the OS, VMs the hardware
common_mistakes: Saying containers include their own kernel
claims containers cannot run in VMs

logic_context: Authentication checks who you are — for example by password, one-time code, fingerprint or token. Authorization decides what you are allowed to do once your identity is known — for example whether a user may view, edit or delete a resource, often based on roles or permissions. Authentication comes first. In HTTP, 401 Unauthorized usually means authentication is missing or failed, while 403 Forbidden means the user is known but not permitted.

mandatory: authentication verifies identity
authorization decides permitted actions
advanced_bonus: multi-factor authentication combines several proofs
the principle of least privilege limits permissions
OAuth is mainly about delegated authorization
access control lists and role-based access control are common models
session tokens carry the authenticated identity between requests

logic_context: Open-source software makes its source code available so anyone can read, modify and share it under the terms of a licence. Permissive licences such as MIT, BSD and Apache allow the code to be used even in closed-source products, as long as notices and attribution are kept. Copyleft licences such as the GPL require that if you distribute software based on the code, you must also release your changes under the same licence. Licence terms matter whenever you include a library in your own project.

mandatory: source code available to use, modify and share under a licence
permissive allows closed-source use; copyleft requires sharing derivatives
advanced_bonus: LGPL allows linking from non-GPL software under conditions
Apache 2.0 includes a patent grant
open source does not always mean free of charge, though it usually is
licence compatibility matters when combining code
public domain code has no licence restrictions

common_mistakes: Saying open source means no rules

logic_context: In-memory sessions are fast and simple, but a user whose request goes to another server is suddenly logged out unless the load balancer uses sticky sessions, and restarts or scaling lose sessions. A shared store lets any server read any session, survives app restarts and allows instant logout, at the cost of an extra network lookup and a component that must be highly available. Signed tokens need no server-side lookup and scale easily, but they cannot easily be revoked before they expire, grow request size, and must not contain secrets. Recommend a shared session store when revocation matters, or short-lived signed tokens with refresh tokens for stateless scaling.

mandatory: in-memory sessions break across servers without sticky sessions
shared store allows any server and revocation; tokens are stateless but hard to revoke
concept_groups: extra lookup and availability needs for shared store
tokens must be signed and kept small
advanced_bonus: store only a session id in the cookie when using a server-side store
JWT payloads are encoded, not encrypted — do not put secrets in them
a token blocklist reintroduces server-side state
set HttpOnly and Secure flags on session cookies
rotate signing keys periodically

semantic_targets: choose by logout and scaling requirements
common_mistakes: Recommending in-memory sessions without sticky routing

logic_context: A fixed-window counter keeps one counter per client per minute — very cheap — but allows up to twice the limit around a window boundary (100 at the end of one minute and 100 at the start of the next). A sliding-window log stores the timestamp of every request and counts those in the last minute, which is precise but uses memory proportional to the request rate. A token bucket stores only a token count and the last refill time; tokens refill at the allowed rate up to a capacity, so it enforces the average rate while allowing controlled bursts. Recommend a token bucket (or a sliding-window counter approximation) for this requirement.

mandatory: fixed window allows double bursts at boundaries
token bucket enforces average rate with controlled bursts in O(1) state
concept_groups: sliding log is precise but memory-heavy
sliding-window counter approximates with two counters
bucket capacity sets the burst size
refill computed lazily on each request
advanced_bonus: in a distributed system, store counters in a shared store with atomic operations
leaky bucket smooths output to a constant rate
return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header when limited
per-user and per-IP limits can be combined
sliding-window counter: current count + previous count × overlap fraction

semantic_targets: pick the algorithm matching burst policy
common_mistakes: Ignoring the boundary burst of fixed windows
Claiming the sliding log is cheap at high rates
confuses rate limiting with load balancing

logic_context: A monolith is one codebase and one deployable unit: development, testing, debugging and transactions are simple, and there is little operational overhead, which suits a small team that must move quickly; the risk is that it becomes tangled as it grows and must be scaled as a whole. Microservices split the system into independently deployable services that can scale and evolve separately, but they bring network calls, partial failures, distributed data consistency, more infrastructure, monitoring and deployment pipelines — a heavy burden for five people. Recommend a well-structured modular monolith with clear internal boundaries, extracting services later only when a specific scaling or team need appears.

mandatory: monolith: simple to build and operate for a small team
microservices: independent scaling but high operational and distributed-system cost
concept_groups: network failures and data consistency in microservices
advanced_bonus: Conway's law: system structure mirrors team structure
a modular monolith keeps future splitting easier
microservices need observability: logging, tracing, metrics
distributed transactions are hard — sagas or eventual consistency
many successful products started as monoliths

common_mistakes: Choosing microservices because large companies use them
claims monoliths cannot scale at all

logic_context: Auto-increment integers are small (4 or 8 bytes), human-friendly and inserted in increasing order, which keeps B+ tree indexes compact and fast; but they reveal how many records exist, can be guessed (enumerated) in public URLs, and require a single authority to generate them, which complicates sharding and merging databases. Random UUIDs (v4) can be generated anywhere without coordination and are hard to guess, but they are 16 bytes and random insertion order scatters writes across the index, causing page splits and poorer cache use. Time-ordered identifiers such as UUIDv7 or ULID combine global uniqueness with roughly sequential inserts. Recommend time-ordered UUIDs for this public, large-scale case, or an internal integer key plus a separate random public id.

mandatory: auto-increment: compact and index-friendly but guessable and centrally generated
random UUIDs: decentralised and unguessable but larger and index-unfriendly
concept_groups: time-ordered UUIDv7/ULID as a middle ground
index page splits with random keys
advanced_bonus: store UUIDs as 16-byte binary, not 36-character strings
an internal integer key with a separate public slug is a common pattern
Snowflake-style ids embed time, machine and sequence numbers
unguessable ids are not a substitute for authorization checks
foreign keys multiply the size cost of wide keys

semantic_targets: match key design to exposure and scale
common_mistakes: Ignoring index fragmentation of random UUIDs
Treating unguessable ids as access control
Storing UUIDs as text without noting cost

logic_context: Unit tests check small functions in isolation; they are fast, cheap to run often and pinpoint failures, but they cannot catch problems in how components work together. Integration tests check several parts together, such as the service with its real database or payment gateway sandbox; they catch wiring and contract bugs but are slower and need setup. End-to-end tests drive the whole system like a real user through the checkout flow, giving the most confidence, but they are slow, can be flaky and are expensive to maintain. Following the test pyramid, recommend many unit tests for pricing and validation logic, a few integration tests at the database and payment boundaries, and one or two end-to-end tests for the critical happy path.

mandatory: unit tests are fast and precise but miss integration issues
end-to-end tests give high confidence but are slow and flaky
advanced_bonus: flaky end-to-end tests erode trust if not fixed
contract tests verify API agreements between services
test the edge cases (discounts, failures) at the unit level
use a payment provider's sandbox rather than real charges
code coverage alone does not prove correctness

semantic_targets: match test types to what can break
common_mistakes: claims unit tests prove the system works

logic_context: Keep three structures: a hash map from key to its node (value and frequency); a hash map from frequency to a doubly linked list of nodes with that frequency, ordered by recency; and minFreq, the smallest frequency present. On get, move the node from its frequency list to the list for frequency + 1 (at the most-recent end) and update minFreq if the old list became empty and was the minimum. On put of a new key when full, evict the least recent node from the minFreq list, then insert the new key with frequency 1 and set minFreq = 1. All steps are O(1).

mandatory: key → node map and frequency → doubly linked list map
track minFreq; evict the least recent node in the minFreq list
concept_groups: get increments frequency and moves the node
update minFreq when a list empties
advanced_bonus: a heap keyed by (frequency, time) gives O(log n) instead of O(1)
each frequency list acts like a small LRU list
updating an existing key counts as a use and increments frequency
capacity 0 means nothing is stored
LFU can keep old popular items — aging variants address this

common_mistakes: Scanning all keys to find the minimum frequency

logic_context: Store for each user a list of their tweets with increasing global timestamps (newest at the end or front), and a set of the users they follow. To build the feed, take the most recent tweet from the user and from each followee, and put them in a max-heap keyed by timestamp. Repeatedly pop the newest tweet, add it to the result, and push the next older tweet from the same user, until 10 tweets are collected or the heap is empty. This is a k-way merge of sorted lists: O(k + 10 log k) for k sources.

mandatory: per-user tweet lists ordered by time and a follow set
merge followees' lists with a max-heap to get the 10 newest
concept_groups: push the next tweet from the same user after popping
advanced_bonus: users should not be able to unfollow themselves
only the most recent 10 tweets per user are ever needed for the feed
collecting all tweets and sorting is wasteful
fan-out-on-write (pushing tweets into followers' feeds) is the alternative used at scale
hash sets make follow and unfollow O(1)

semantic_targets: Data model for users and tweets
common_mistakes: Sorting all tweets of all followees each time

logic_context: For each index keep a list of (snapId, value) pairs recording changes. set appends (currentSnapId, value) to that index's list, or overwrites the last pair if it has the same snapId. snap returns the current id and increments it. get(index, snapId) binary searches the index's list for the last pair with snapId <= the requested id and returns its value (or the initial value 0 if none). Memory grows only with the number of sets; get is O(log k).

mandatory: store (snapId, value) history per index
binary search for the last change at or before the snapshot
concept_groups: initial value when no change exists
advanced_bonus: copying the whole array per snap costs O(n) each time
this is a simple persistent (versioned) data structure
histories are naturally sorted by snapId, so binary search works
upper_bound - 1 gives the needed entry
memory is proportional to the number of set calls

common_mistakes: Copying the array on every snap

logic_context: Use a hash map from key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs. Because timestamps for each key arrive in increasing order, appending keeps each list sorted. For get, binary search the key's list for the last timestamp <= the requested timestamp and return its value, or an empty result if there is none. set is O(1) and get is O(log n) per key.

mandatory: hash map from key to a time-sorted list of (timestamp, value)
binary search for the latest timestamp <= query
concept_groups: empty result when no earlier timestamp
advanced_bonus: if timestamps could arrive out of order, an ordered map (balanced BST) per key is needed
old versions could be pruned with a retention policy
similar to MVCC version lookup
linear scan from the end is O(n) in the worst case
use upper_bound and step back one

semantic_targets: the latest version not after the query wins

logic_context: Keep the stack order in a doubly linked list so any node can be removed in O(1). Also keep an ordered map (balanced BST) from each value to a list of its nodes in push order. push appends a node to the list and records it under its value: O(log n). pop removes the tail node and its map entry. peekMax reads the largest key. popMax takes the largest key, removes its most recent node from both the map and the linked list. All operations are O(log n). A simpler two-stack solution makes popMax O(n).

mandatory: doubly linked list for stack order
ordered map from value to its nodes for fast maximum lookup
concept_groups: popMax removes the most recent node of the max value
advanced_bonus: a max-heap of (value, push id) with lazy deletion also gives O(log n) amortised
a plain auxiliary max-stack supports peekMax in O(1) but not popMax efficiently
ties: popMax removes the most recently pushed maximum
removing from the middle needs the doubly linked list
C would need a hand-written balanced tree or skip list

semantic_targets: maximum removal from the middle of the stack
common_mistakes: Scanning the stack for every peekMax
Removing the oldest occurrence of the max
claims O(1) for all operations without justification
uses a singly linked list for middle removal

logic_context: A word can be formed by deletions exactly when it is a subsequence of the string. For each dictionary word, check this with two pointers in O(n + L). Keep the best word: longer is better, and among equal lengths, the lexicographically smaller one. Total time O(D × (n + L)) for D words. Sorting the dictionary by length descending, then alphabetically, lets you return the first word that matches.

mandatory: deletions form a subsequence
check each word with two pointers and keep the best
advanced_bonus: generating all subsequences of the string is exponential
precomputing next-occurrence tables makes each check O(L)
an empty result is returned if no word matches
example: s = 'abpcplea', dictionary ['ale','apple','monkey','plea'] → 'apple'
comparison rule must be applied consistently

logic_context: Scan the list once, remembering the latest index where word1 appeared and the latest index where word2 appeared. Each time either word is found, update its index, and if both indices are known, update the minimum distance with |i1 - i2|. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: track the most recent index of each word
update the minimum when either word appears
advanced_bonus: checking all pairs of positions is O(n²)
for many queries on the same list, precompute position lists and merge them
if the two words are the same, track the previous occurrence instead
the most recent occurrence always gives the best distance at that moment
example: ['practice','makes','perfect','coding','makes'] with 'coding','practice' → 3

semantic_targets: closest pairs involve the most recent positions

logic_context: Instead of checking each word against s separately, process s once. Put every word into a bucket keyed by the next character it needs (initially its first letter), with a pointer to its position. Scan s character by character; for the current character c, take all words waiting on c, advance each by one position, and either count it as finished or move it to the bucket of its next needed character. Each word character is processed once, so the total is O(|s| + total word length).

mandatory: bucket words by the next character they need
scan s once, advancing waiting words
advanced_bonus: checking each word separately is O(words × |s|)
alternative: store positions of each character in s and binary search for each next character
duplicate words can be counted once with a multiplicity
words longer than s can be skipped
bucket lists can be swapped to avoid reprocessing within one step

semantic_targets: each word advances only when its needed character appears
common_mistakes: Moving words within the same step incorrectly

logic_context: Convert each time to minutes since midnight (0 to 1439). Since there are only 1440 possible values, mark them in a boolean array; if any value appears twice, the answer is 0. Then scan the array in order, tracking the difference between consecutive marked minutes, and also consider the wrap-around gap from the last time to the first time of the next day (first + 1440 - last). The smallest gap is the answer. O(n + 1440).

mandatory: convert times to minutes
compare consecutive times including the wrap-around gap
advanced_bonus: sorting the minute values is O(n log n) and also works
by the pigeonhole principle, more than 1440 times guarantees a duplicate
comparing all pairs is O(n²)
parse with (h × 60 + m)

logic_context: Start with result = 0 and walk the list. For each node, shift the result left by one and add the node's bit: result = result × 2 + bit (or result = (result << 1) | bit). When the list ends, result holds the value. O(n) time, O(1) space; the list length must fit the integer type.

mandatory: process bits from most significant to least
result = result × 2 + bit at each node
concept_groups: watch for overflow with long lists
advanced_bonus: this is Horner's method for base 2
reading into an array first is unnecessary
use unsigned 64-bit for up to 64 nodes
least-significant-first lists would need powers of two instead
the same method converts any base string to a number

semantic_targets: each new bit shifts earlier bits left
common_mistakes: Adding powers of two from the wrong end

logic_context: Use two DFS passes (rerooting). First, root the tree at node 0 and compute count[v], the size of each subtree, and ans[0], the sum of depths of all nodes from the root. Second, move the root from a parent p to a child c: the count[c] nodes in c's subtree get 1 closer and the other n - count[c] nodes get 1 farther, so ans[c] = ans[p] - count[c] + (n - count[c]). Fill all answers top-down. Both passes are O(n).

mandatory: first DFS: subtree sizes and the root's distance sum
second DFS: ans[child] = ans[parent] - count[child] + (n - count[child])
concept_groups: subtree nodes get closer, others get farther
advanced_bonus: BFS from every node is O(n²)
rerooting DP applies to many 'answer for every root' problems
use iterative DFS to avoid deep recursion on long paths
use 64-bit sums for large trees
example: a star centred at 0 with 5 leaves gives ans[0] = 5

semantic_targets: Compute once, then shift the root
moving the root changes distances predictably
common_mistakes: treating the tree as binary only

logic_context: Use a post-order traversal that returns two numbers for each subtree: the sum of its values and the number of nodes. At each node, combine the children's results with the node itself: sum = left.sum + right.sum + val and count = left.count + right.count + 1. If sum / count equals the node's value, increment the answer. Return (sum, count) to the parent. O(n) time.

mandatory: post-order returns (sum, count) per subtree
compare node value with sum / count
advanced_bonus: recomputing each subtree's sum separately is O(n²)
leaves always match because the average of one value is itself
use 64-bit sums for large values
the same pattern computes subtree averages, sizes or sums
O(h) recursion depth

common_mistakes: Using floating-point averages contrary to the rule
Forgetting to include the node itself

logic_context: An inorder traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order, and in a sorted list the smallest difference is always between neighbours. So traverse inorder, keep the previously visited value, and update the minimum with current - previous at each step. O(n) time, O(h) space.

mandatory: inorder traversal gives sorted values
minimum difference is between consecutive values
concept_groups: no need to compare all pairs
advanced_bonus: comparing all pairs is O(n²)
for a general binary tree, collect values and sort them first
Morris traversal gives O(1) extra space
the previous value starts as 'none' for the first node
differences are non-negative in sorted order

logic_context: Parse recursively with a shared index. Read the number at the current position (it may be negative or have several digits) and create a node. If the next character is '(', skip it, parse the left subtree recursively, and skip the matching ')'. If another '(' follows, parse the right subtree the same way. Return the node. Each character is read once, so the parse is O(n).

mandatory: recursive descent with a shared index
number, then optional left subtree, then optional right subtree
advanced_bonus: an iterative version pushes nodes on '(' and pops on ')'
the first subtree is always the left child
empty parentheses '()' may represent a missing left child in some formats
validate input if it can be malformed
the reverse problem builds such a string from a tree

common_mistakes: Losing track of the index across calls
Assigning the first subtree to the right
O(n²) by searching for matching parentheses repeatedly

logic_context: A vertex with no incoming edges cannot be reached from any other vertex, so it must be in the set. Conversely, every vertex with an incoming edge can be reached by following edges backwards to some vertex with in-degree 0 (the graph is acyclic). So the answer is exactly the set of vertices with in-degree 0. Compute in-degrees in one pass over the edges: O(V + E).

mandatory: vertices with in-degree 0 must be included
every other vertex is reachable from some in-degree-0 vertex
advanced_bonus: running a search from every vertex is unnecessary
in graphs with cycles, the answer uses strongly connected components with no incoming edges instead
the result is unique
a boolean array 'has incoming edge' is enough
example: edges 0→1, 0→2, 3→4 → {0, 3}

semantic_targets: Sources are sufficient in a DAG
common_mistakes: applying to cyclic graphs without SCCs

logic_context: Model trust as directed edges. Keep a score for each person: for each pair (a, b), decrease a's score (a trusts someone) and increase b's score (b is trusted). The judge has in-degree n - 1 and out-degree 0, which means a score of exactly n - 1. Return the person with that score, or -1 if none. O(n + number of pairs).

mandatory: judge: trusted by n - 1 people and trusts no one
score = in-degree - out-degree must equal n - 1
advanced_bonus: separate in-degree and out-degree arrays work equally well
there can be at most one judge
n = 1 with no trust pairs: person 1 is the judge
similar to the celebrity problem but with the full relation given
no graph search needed

semantic_targets: the judge is a pure sink trusted by all
common_mistakes: Building adjacency lists and searching unnecessarily

logic_context: Colour vertices one by one. For vertex v, try each colour from 1 to m; a colour is allowed if no already-coloured neighbour of v uses it. If allowed, assign it and recurse to the next vertex; if the recursion fails, undo the assignment and try the next colour. If all vertices are coloured, return success; if no colour works for v, return failure so the caller backtracks. The worst case is O(m^V), but pruning helps in practice.

mandatory: assign colours vertex by vertex with a safety check
undo and try the next colour when stuck
concept_groups: success when all vertices are coloured
advanced_bonus: ordering vertices by degree (most constrained first) prunes more
symmetry: the first vertex can always use colour 1
for m = 2, a BFS bipartite check is linear
greedy colouring may fail even when a valid colouring exists
the decision problem is NP-complete for m ≥ 3

logic_context: If there are fewer jobs than days, return -1. Let dp[i][k] be the minimum total difficulty to finish the first i jobs in k days. For the k-th day, choose where it starts: dp[i][k] = min over j from k - 1 to i - 1 of dp[j][k - 1] + max(jobs[j..i - 1]). Compute the running maximum as j moves left so each transition is O(1). The answer is dp[n][d]. O(n² × d).

mandatory: dp[i][k] = best for first i jobs in k days
last day covers jobs j..i - 1 with cost max(jobs[j..i - 1])
concept_groups: at least one job per day
advanced_bonus: a monotonic stack can optimise to O(n × d)
greedy splitting at the largest jobs is not optimal
dp[0][0] = 0, others start at infinity
rolling arrays reduce space to O(n)

common_mistakes: Recomputing segment maxima each time (O(n³ d))

logic_context: Removing from both ends leaves a contiguous middle subarray, whose sum must be total - x. So find the longest subarray with sum exactly target = total - x using a sliding window (all values are positive): expand the right end, shrink from the left while the sum exceeds the target, and record the length when the sum equals the target. The answer is n minus that maximum length, or -1 if no such subarray exists (if target < 0). If target is 0, remove everything (answer n).

mandatory: remaining middle subarray must sum to total - x
longest such subarray via sliding window
concept_groups: positive numbers allow the sliding window
advanced_bonus: with negative numbers, use prefix sums and a hash map instead
trying all combinations of left and right removals is O(n²)
target = 0 means removing the whole array
complement thinking turns two ends into one window

semantic_targets: removals from ends equal keeping a middle block
common_mistakes: Greedy removal of the larger end

logic_context: Whatever cards are taken, the cards left behind form a contiguous block of n - k cards in the middle. Maximising the taken total is the same as minimising the sum of that block. Slide a window of length n - k across the array to find its minimum sum, and the answer is total - minimum. Equivalently, start by taking the first k cards and swap them one by one for cards from the end. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: taken cards leave a contiguous middle block
maximise total - minimum window sum of length n - k
concept_groups: or swap front cards for back cards
advanced_bonus: greedy choosing the larger end at each step is not optimal
k = n means take all cards
prefix and suffix sums give the same O(k) solution
window length 0 when k = n

logic_context: Process people from right to left with a stack of heights that decreases from bottom to top. For person i, pop every shorter person from the stack — each of them is visible to i, so count them. If the stack is still not empty after popping, the person on top is taller and also visible (and blocks everyone behind), so add one more. Then push person i. Each person is pushed and popped once, so it is O(n).

mandatory: right-to-left scan with a monotonic stack
count popped shorter people plus one taller person if any
concept_groups: shorter people are visible and then hidden for others to the left
first taller person blocks the rest
each person pushed and popped once
advanced_bonus: brute force checks every pair with a running maximum — O(n²)
heights are distinct in the standard problem
popped people can never be seen by anyone further left past person i
similar to the stock span and next greater element problems

semantic_targets: a taller person blocks the view beyond
common_mistakes: Counting only the next greater person
scanning left to right without adjusting logic
counts people behind the taller one

logic_context: Reverse the process: repeatedly remove 'abc' sequences. Scan the string with a stack, pushing each character. Whenever the top three characters on the stack are 'a', 'b', 'c' (in that order), pop all three. The string is valid exactly when the stack is empty at the end. Each character is pushed and popped at most once, so O(n).

mandatory: reverse the insertions by removing 'abc' with a stack
valid if the stack is empty at the end
concept_groups: check the top three after each push
each 'c' must complete an 'ab' before it
advanced_bonus: repeatedly searching and deleting 'abc' substrings is O(n²)
a quick filter: the length must be a multiple of 3
counts of a, b and c must be equal (necessary but not sufficient)
similar to removing adjacent duplicates with a stack
example: 'aabcbc' → valid

common_mistakes: Repeated substring deletion without noting cost

logic_context: Treat the pairs as a grid where row i pairs a[i] with every b[j]; each row is sorted by sum. Start a min-heap with (a[i] + b[0], i, 0) for the first min(k, n) rows. Pop the smallest pair, add it to the result, and push the next pair in the same row, (i, j + 1). Repeat k times. This is a k-way merge of sorted rows: O(k log k) time.

mandatory: min-heap seeded with the first column of pairs
after popping (i, j), push (i, j + 1)
concept_groups: each row is sorted by sum
advanced_bonus: generating all n × m pairs and sorting is O(nm log nm)
seeding all rows avoids needing duplicate checks
an alternative pushes (i + 1, j) and (i, j + 1) with a visited set
handle k larger than the total number of pairs
same pattern as merging k sorted lists

semantic_targets: the next candidate comes from the same row
common_mistakes: Pushing duplicates without a visited set in the two-direction method
Seeding more rows than needed without noting cost

logic_context: Binary search for the first index whose letter is strictly greater than the target (an upper bound). If that index equals the length of the list, no letter is greater, so wrap around and return the first letter. Otherwise return the letter at that index. O(log n) time.

mandatory: upper-bound binary search for the first letter > target
wrap around to index 0 if none is greater
advanced_bonus: a linear scan is O(n)
duplicates are handled by the strict comparison
using index % n handles the wrap-around neatly
lower bound would return equal letters — wrong here
example: ['c','f','j'], target 'j' → 'c'

logic_context: Use backtracking with a start number, the current combination and the remaining sum. For each number i from start to 9, if i exceeds the remaining sum, stop the loop (larger numbers will too). Otherwise add i, recurse with start = i + 1 and remaining - i, then remove i. Record the combination when it has k numbers and the remaining sum is exactly 0. The search space is tiny (at most C(9, k) combinations).

mandatory: choose increasing numbers from 1 to 9 without reuse
record when k numbers sum exactly to n
concept_groups: start index prevents duplicates and reuse
stop when a number exceeds the remaining sum
advanced_bonus: at most 2^9 = 512 subsets exist, so even full enumeration is cheap
quick pruning: n must be between the minimum (1 + … + k) and maximum sums
combinations are naturally in increasing order
bitmask enumeration over 9 bits is an alternative
differs from Combination Sum, which allows reuse

semantic_targets: length and sum must both match

logic_context: Fix a pair of rows top and bottom. Compress the rows between them into a 1D array of column sums (update it incrementally as bottom moves down). Now count subarrays of this 1D array with sum equal to target, using prefix sums and a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies (count += freq[prefix - target]). Sum the counts over all row pairs. O(R² × C) time; loop over the smaller dimension squared.

mandatory: fix two rows and compress columns into a 1D array
count subarrays with sum target using a prefix-sum hash map
concept_groups: update column sums as the bottom row grows
choose the smaller dimension for the pair loop
advanced_bonus: brute force over all submatrices with 2D prefix sums is O(R² × C²)
same row-compression idea as the maximum-sum rectangle problem
negative values are handled because the hash map does not need monotonicity
use 64-bit sums for large values
reset the hash map for each row pair

semantic_targets: each row pair defines a 1D array

logic_context: The leftmost column carries the largest weight, more than all other columns combined. So first flip every row whose first bit is 0, making the first column all 1s.
