Then, for each remaining column, count its 1s; if zeros outnumber ones, flip the column. Each column j then contributes max(ones, zeros) × 2^(n - 1 - j). Sum these. O(m × n), and no actual flipping is needed — just counting.

mandatory: make the most significant column all 1s by flipping rows
flip each other column if it has more 0s than 1s
concept_groups: MSB outweighs all lower bits together
advanced_bonus: after the row flips, a cell's value is a[i][j] XOR a[i][0] XOR 1
the greedy is optimal because column choices are independent once rows are fixed
flipping the first column itself would reduce the score
order of operations does not matter since flips commute

common_mistakes: Flipping columns before fixing the first column
Flipping the first column for a majority

logic_context: Split the four arrays into two pairs. Compute every sum A[i] + B[j] and store how many times each sum occurs in a hash map (n² entries). Then, for every sum C[k] + D[l], add the count of its negation from the map. This meet-in-the-middle approach is O(n²) time and space instead of O(n⁴).

mandatory: hash all A + B sums with counts
for each C + D sum, add the count of its negation
advanced_bonus: brute force is O(n⁴); hashing one array of three is O(n³)
use 64-bit counts if the answer can be large
sorting the pair sums and two pointers is an O(n² log n) alternative
the same split works for k-sum problems with k even

common_mistakes: Looking up the same sign instead of the negation
sorting each array and four pointers incorrectly

logic_context: Each element must reach a common target t, costing |a[i] - t| moves, so the total is the sum of absolute deviations from t. This sum is minimised when t is a median of the array. Find the median (by sorting in O(n log n) or quickselect in O(n) average) and sum |a[i] - median|. With sorted values, the answer is also the sum of a[n-1-i] - a[i] for the first half.

mandatory: target should be the median
answer = sum of |a[i] - median|
advanced_bonus: the mean minimises squared deviations, not absolute ones
any value between the two middle elements works for even n
use 64-bit sums to avoid overflow
the version where a move increments n - 1 elements has a different answer (sum minus n × min)

semantic_targets: moving the target past the median increases cost

logic_context: Place the largest elements at the end one at a time. For size from n down to 2: find the index m of the maximum in the first size elements. If it is not already at position size - 1, flip the prefix ending at m to bring the maximum to the front (if it is not already there), then flip the first size elements to move it to position size - 1. Each element needs at most 2 flips, so at most 2n - 3 flips and O(n²) time overall.

mandatory: bring the current maximum to the front, then flip it to the end
shrink the unsorted prefix by one each round
concept_groups: at most two flips per element
skip flips when already in place
advanced_bonus: finding the minimum number of flips is NP-hard
each flip is a prefix reversal of length k
the flip count bound is linear, while comparisons are quadratic
used as a puzzle and in studies of genome rearrangements
example: [3, 2, 4, 1] sorted with flips of size 3, 4, 2, 3, 2

semantic_targets: fix the largest element each round
common_mistakes: Flipping the whole array each time
Claiming the minimum number of flips

logic_context: Many threads share data; readers only read it and writers change it. Any number of readers may read at the same time, but a writer needs exclusive access — no other writer or reader. A classic solution keeps a reader count protected by a mutex and a separate 'resource' lock: the first reader to arrive locks the resource and the last reader to leave unlocks it, while writers lock the resource directly. This version favours readers and can starve writers; writer-preferring or fair versions block new readers when a writer is waiting. POSIX provides pthread_rwlock for this.

mandatory: many concurrent readers, writers need exclusive access
first reader locks the resource, last reader unlocks it
concept_groups: read count protected by a mutex
advanced_bonus: fair (FIFO) read-write locks prevent starvation of either side
read-write locks help only when reads dominate
upgrading a read lock to a write lock can deadlock if two readers try
seqlocks favour writers for small data
RCU (read-copy-update) lets readers run without locks

semantic_targets: choose a policy that fits the workload
common_mistakes: Using a single mutex for everything without explaining the cost

logic_context: Five philosophers sit at a round table with one fork between each pair; each needs both neighbouring forks to eat. If every philosopher picks up the left fork first, all may hold one fork and wait forever for the other — a deadlock caused by circular wait. Solutions break one of the deadlock conditions: order the forks and always pick up the lower-numbered fork first, allow at most four philosophers to try at once, use a waiter (arbitrator) who grants both forks together, or pick up both forks atomically. Fairness must also be considered so no philosopher starves.

mandatory: circular wait on forks causes deadlock
break circular wait with resource ordering or limiting seats
advanced_bonus: resource ordering is the general lock-ordering technique
try-lock with back-off can cause livelock
the Chandy-Misra solution uses message passing and clean/dirty forks
asymmetric solution: odd philosophers pick left first, even pick right first
illustrates all four Coffman conditions

semantic_targets: break at least one deadlock condition
common_mistakes: solution that still allows circular wait
claims a mutex per philosopher solves it

logic_context: A join combines rows from two tables using a condition, usually matching keys. An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables. A LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, with matching right-table values or NULL where no match exists. A RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image. A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, filling NULLs where either side has no match. A CROSS JOIN returns every combination of rows (the Cartesian product).

mandatory: INNER: only matching rows; LEFT/RIGHT: all rows from one side
FULL OUTER: all rows from both sides with NULLs for missing matches
concept_groups: CROSS JOIN gives the Cartesian product
advanced_bonus: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL finds rows with no match
databases implement joins with nested loops, hash joins or merge joins
joining on unindexed columns can be slow
a self join joins a table with itself
MySQL lacks FULL OUTER JOIN but can emulate it with UNION

semantic_targets: choose the join by which rows must be kept
common_mistakes: Saying LEFT JOIN drops unmatched left rows
claims joins need identical column names

logic_context: SQL defines four isolation levels. Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads (seeing changes another transaction has not committed). Read Committed prevents dirty reads, but a row read twice may change between reads (non-repeatable read). Repeatable Read prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads, but new rows matching a query may appear (phantoms) in the standard definition. Serializable prevents all of these, making transactions behave as if run one after another. Higher levels give stronger guarantees but more locking or aborts, so lower throughput.

mandatory: four levels: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable
anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms
concept_groups: higher isolation, fewer anomalies, lower concurrency
advanced_bonus: PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation and also prevents phantoms, but allows write skew
MySQL InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read; PostgreSQL to Read Committed
serializable implementations may abort transactions that must retry
lost updates can occur at lower levels without explicit locking
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE adds row locks when needed

semantic_targets: pick the weakest level that keeps data correct
common_mistakes: Mixing up which anomaly each level prevents
claims all databases default to Serializable

logic_context: NAT lets many devices on a private network share one public IP address. When an internal device sends a packet out, the router replaces its private source address (and often port) with the router's public address and a chosen port, and records the mapping in a translation table. Replies coming back to that public port are translated back to the original device. NAT conserves scarce IPv4 addresses and hides internal addresses, but unsolicited incoming connections are blocked unless port forwarding is configured, which complicates peer-to-peer applications.

mandatory: router maps private addresses to its public address
translation table tracks connections
concept_groups: port address translation lets many devices share one IP
advanced_bonus: STUN and TURN help peer-to-peer apps traverse NAT
carrier-grade NAT adds another layer at the ISP
NAT is not a security mechanism by itself, though it blocks unsolicited inbound traffic
IPv6's large address space reduces the need for NAT

semantic_targets: NAT rewrites addresses at the boundary
common_mistakes: No mention of the translation table
claims every device gets a public IP

logic_context: In TLS 1.3, the client sends a ClientHello with supported cipher suites and a key share for Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The server replies with a ServerHello and its own key share; both sides now compute the same shared secret and derive encryption keys. The server also sends its certificate and a signature proving it owns the matching private key. The client checks the certificate chain against trusted certificate authorities and the domain name. After Finished messages confirm the handshake, all data is encrypted with fast symmetric keys. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip.

mandatory: key exchange (Diffie-Hellman) creates shared symmetric keys
server proves identity with a certificate verified against trusted CAs
concept_groups: ClientHello and ServerHello with key shares
advanced_bonus: ephemeral Diffie-Hellman gives forward secrecy
asymmetric cryptography is used only during the handshake for speed
SNI tells the server which certificate to present
session resumption can allow 0-RTT data with replay risks
certificate revocation and expiry are checked by the client

common_mistakes: Saying all data is encrypted with the server's public key
claims TLS hides the destination IP

logic_context: A 2-3 tree is a search tree in which every internal node is either a 2-node (one key, two children) or a 3-node (two keys, three children), and all leaves are at the same depth. Search works like a BST, choosing among two or three branches. To insert, add the key to the correct leaf; if the leaf now has three keys, split it into two nodes and push the middle key up to the parent, which may split in turn. If the root splits, the tree grows one level taller at the top, so it always stays perfectly balanced with height O(log n).

mandatory: nodes hold 1 or 2 keys; all leaves at the same depth
insertion splits overfull nodes and pushes the middle key up
advanced_bonus: red-black trees are a binary encoding of 2-3 (or 2-3-4) trees
deletion merges or borrows keys from siblings
guaranteed logarithmic height without rotations
B-trees generalise the idea to many keys per node
implementation is more complex than a BST because node types vary

semantic_targets: growth happens at the root, not the leaves
common_mistakes: Saying leaves can be at different depths
Inserting by creating new leaves below

logic_context: _Generic provides compile-time type selection: it looks at the type of a controlling expression and picks one of several expressions listed for different types. It is mainly used to build type-generic macros, for example #define abs_any(x) _Generic((x), int: abs, long: labs, double: fabs)(x), which calls the right function for the argument's type. A default association handles other types. The choice happens at compile time, so there is no runtime cost. The <tgmath.h> header uses this idea for math functions.

mandatory: selects an expression based on the type of the controlling expression
used for type-generic macros at compile time
concept_groups: example selecting abs, labs or fabs
advanced_bonus: the controlling expression is not evaluated
array arguments decay and qualifiers are dropped, so const int matches int
only one association may match each type
error messages can be confusing when no type matches and there is no default
C has no function overloading, so _Generic fills part of that gap

common_mistakes: claims it evaluates the controlling expression

logic_context: When threads access the same variable and at least one writes, ordinary reads and writes form a data race, which is undefined behaviour. C11 atomics, declared with _Atomic or types like atomic_int, make individual operations indivisible and well defined between threads. Operations include atomic_load, atomic_store, atomic_fetch_add and atomic_compare_exchange_strong. Each can take a memory order (relaxed, acquire, release, sequentially consistent) that controls how surrounding memory operations become visible to other threads. volatile does not provide these guarantees.

mandatory: atomic operations are indivisible and avoid data races
memory orders control visibility between threads
advanced_bonus: acquire/release pairs publish data safely from one thread to another
memory_order_relaxed suits simple counters with no ordering needs
atomic_is_lock_free tells whether hardware supports the type without locks
compare-and-swap loops build lock-free structures
atomics on large structs may use hidden locks

common_mistakes: Claiming atomics remove all need for locks

logic_context: A hub simply repeats every incoming signal to all its ports, so all devices share the bandwidth and see each other's traffic (a layer 1 device). A switch learns which device (MAC address) is on which port and forwards each frame only to the right port, making local networks faster and more private (layer 2). A router connects different networks and forwards packets between them based on IP addresses — for example joining a home network to the internet (layer 3).

mandatory: hub broadcasts to all ports; switch forwards by MAC address
router forwards between networks by IP address
concept_groups: hub: layer 1, switch: layer 2, router: layer 3
home routers often combine switch and router
advanced_bonus: hubs are obsolete in modern networks
switches keep a MAC address table learned from traffic
routers use routing tables and can perform NAT
layer 3 switches can also route
Wi-Fi access points bridge wireless devices onto the wired network

semantic_targets: each device works on a different address type
common_mistakes: Saying a switch uses IP addresses for local forwarding

logic_context: A CDN is a network of servers spread across many locations that store (cache) copies of a website's static content — images, videos, scripts and style sheets. When a user requests a file, it is served from a nearby CDN server instead of the distant origin server, which reduces latency, speeds up loading, lowers the load on the origin and helps absorb traffic spikes and some attacks. Cached copies expire after a time-to-live or can be explicitly purged when content changes.

mandatory: geographically distributed cache servers
serve content from a location near the user
advanced_bonus: versioned file names (e.g. app.3f2a.js) avoid stale caches
CDNs often provide DDoS protection and TLS termination
dynamic content can be accelerated with edge computing
cache-control headers decide what CDNs may cache
examples: Cloudflare, Akamai, CloudFront

common_mistakes: Saying CDNs host the main database
claims all content is always cached

logic_context: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically gives devices the settings they need to use a network, so users do not configure them by hand. When a device joins, it broadcasts a Discover message; a DHCP server replies with an Offer containing an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS servers; the device sends a Request, and the server confirms with an Acknowledge (the DORA process). The address is leased for a limited time and must be renewed.

mandatory: automatically assigns IP address and network settings
Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (DORA)
concept_groups: provides subnet mask, gateway and DNS servers
home routers usually run a DHCP server
advanced_bonus: static leases (reservations) give a device the same address each time
rogue DHCP servers can misdirect traffic
DHCP uses UDP ports 67 and 68
IPv6 can use SLAAC instead of or alongside DHCPv6
lease expiry frees unused addresses

semantic_targets: devices get network settings on joining

logic_context: Bandwidth is how much data a connection can carry per second, measured in bits per second (for example 100 Mbps). Latency is how long it takes for data to travel from sender to receiver, usually measured in milliseconds, often as round-trip time. A connection can have high bandwidth but high latency, such as satellite internet. Downloading a large file depends mostly on bandwidth, while interactive tasks like online games or many small web requests depend mostly on latency.

mandatory: bandwidth: data per second
latency: delay for data to arrive
advanced_bonus: throughput is the actual achieved rate, often below bandwidth
the speed of light sets a minimum latency over long distances
bandwidth × delay product determines how much data is 'in flight'
caching and CDNs reduce latency
more bandwidth does not fix high latency

common_mistakes: claims more bandwidth always reduces latency

logic_context: Cookies are small pieces of data that a website asks the browser to store and send back with later requests to the same site. They let a stateless protocol like HTTP remember things between requests — for example keeping a user logged in (a session id), remembering preferences or a shopping cart, and tracking visits for analytics or advertising. Attributes such as Expires, HttpOnly (not readable by JavaScript), Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite control how they behave. Each cookie is limited to about 4 KB.

mandatory: small data stored by the browser and sent back to the site
used for sessions, preferences and tracking
advanced_bonus: SameSite helps defend against cross-site request forgery
HttpOnly reduces theft via cross-site scripting
third-party cookies are increasingly blocked for privacy
sensitive data should not be stored directly in cookies
localStorage is another browser storage option that is not sent automatically

common_mistakes: claims cookies are shared across all websites

logic_context: A merge conflict happens when Git cannot combine changes automatically — usually because two branches changed the same lines of a file differently, or one branch deleted a file that the other modified. Git marks the conflicting area in the file with <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers showing both versions. To resolve it, edit the file to keep the correct combination of changes, remove the markers, then git add the file and commit (or continue the rebase). Merging small changes frequently reduces conflicts.

mandatory: occurs when the same lines are changed differently on two branches
resolve by editing, removing markers, then add and commit
advanced_bonus: git merge --abort cancels the merge
merge tools show both versions side by side
rebasing can produce conflicts at each replayed commit
clear communication on who edits which files helps
automatic merges can still produce logically wrong code — run tests

common_mistakes: deletes one branch's work without review

logic_context: An in-process cache is the fastest — no network hop — but each server keeps its own copy, so servers can show different results, memory is duplicated, and invalidating all copies is hard; it is lost on restart. A shared distributed cache (such as Redis) gives every server the same cached result and survives application restarts, at the cost of a network round trip and another service to run. A materialised view stores the query result inside the database, so it stays consistent with database permissions and can be queried and indexed directly, but refreshing it costs database work and results are stale between refreshes. Recommend a materialised view refreshed every few minutes (or a distributed cache with a matching TTL); use in-process caching only for tiny, rarely changing data.

mandatory: in-process cache: fastest but inconsistent across servers
materialised view or distributed cache gives one shared result with controlled staleness
concept_groups: refresh interval matches data change rate
advanced_bonus: concurrent refresh (e.g. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY) avoids blocking readers
cache stampede: many servers recomputing at once — use locks or early refresh
incremental view maintenance updates only changed parts
TTL-based expiry is simple but may serve slightly stale data
measure query cost before adding caching layers

semantic_targets: match caching layer to staleness tolerance

logic_context: Soft deletes set a flag or timestamp instead of removing the row, so data can be restored, history and references stay intact, and audits are easier. But every query must remember to exclude deleted rows (a common source of bugs that leak 'deleted' data), unique constraints get complicated, tables keep growing, and privacy laws may require personal data to be truly erased. Hard deletes remove data permanently, keeping queries and tables simple and meeting erasure requirements, but mistakes cannot be undone without backups and foreign-key relationships need cascade decisions. Recommend soft deletes with a retention period followed by a permanent purge of personal data, plus an audit log.

mandatory: soft delete: recoverable but every query must filter deleted rows
hard delete: simple and compliant but irreversible
concept_groups: privacy laws may require true erasure
advanced_bonus: database views or default scopes can hide soft-deleted rows automatically
partial unique indexes (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) keep uniqueness
archive tables move deleted rows out of the hot table
backups still contain deleted data — consider retention there too
cascading deletes must be designed carefully

semantic_targets: combine soft delete with eventual purge
common_mistakes: claims soft deletes have no cost

logic_context: With synchronous replication, a transaction is reported as committed only after the standby confirms it has the change, so failing over loses no committed transactions; the costs are higher write latency (waiting for the standby, especially over distance) and reduced availability if the standby is slow or unreachable, unless the system can fall back. With asynchronous replication, the primary commits immediately and ships changes later, giving low latency and independence from the standby, but the most recent committed transactions can be lost if the primary fails, and reads from the standby may be stale. Recommend synchronous (or semi-synchronous, waiting for at least one nearby standby) replication for financial data, accepting the extra latency.

mandatory: synchronous: no committed data lost on failover but higher latency
asynchronous: low latency but recent commits can be lost
advanced_bonus: RPO (recovery point objective) is zero with synchronous replication
keep a synchronous standby in the same region and async replicas farther away
quorum-based replication tolerates some slow replicas
split-brain must be prevented during failover
measure commit latency impact before choosing

semantic_targets: financial data favours zero data loss
common_mistakes: Choosing async for financial data without discussing loss
claims sync replication has no availability impact

logic_context: Pessimistic locking locks the record when a user opens it for editing, so no conflicting edits can happen, but other users are blocked, locks may be held for a long time while someone thinks or leaves the page, abandoned locks need timeouts, and contention limits scalability. Optimistic locking lets everyone edit freely; each record has a version number, and an update succeeds only if the version is unchanged (UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND version = ?). If someone else saved first, the update fails and the user must merge or retry. It scales well when conflicts are rare, but wastes work when they are frequent. Recommend optimistic locking for typical document editing; pessimistic locking for short, high-contention operations; real-time collaborative editors use techniques like operational transformation or CRDTs.

mandatory: pessimistic: prevents conflicts but blocks users and holds locks long
optimistic: no blocking; detect conflicts with a version check at save
advanced_bonus: HTTP ETags and If-Match headers implement optimistic concurrency in APIs
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE implements pessimistic locking in SQL
last-write-wins silently loses updates — avoid it
CRDTs merge concurrent edits automatically
show users a clear conflict message with both versions

common_mistakes: Holding database locks during long user edits without timeouts
claims optimistic locking prevents conflicts from occurring

logic_context: Batch processing collects data over a period and processes it in bulk, for example every night. It is simpler, efficient for large volumes, easy to rerun, and sees complete data — ideal for a daily sales report, where hours of delay are fine. Stream processing handles each event as it arrives, within seconds, which fraud alerts require because a fraudulent payment must be flagged before goods ship or more charges follow. Streaming is harder: it needs always-on infrastructure, managing state, windows, late or out-of-order events and delivery guarantees. Recommend batch processing for the daily report and stream processing for fraud alerts; many systems use both on the same event data.

mandatory: batch suits periodic complete reports
stream suits low-latency alerts
concept_groups: streaming handles state, windows and late events
batch is simpler and easy to reprocess
both can share the same data source
advanced_bonus: lambda architecture runs batch and stream paths; kappa uses only streams with replay
tools: Spark for batch, Flink or Kafka Streams for streaming
exactly-once processing is harder in streams
micro-batching sits in between with second-level latency
stream results can be corrected later by batch recomputation

semantic_targets: match processing style to how fast results are needed
common_mistakes: Using streaming for everything without justification
claims batch cannot handle large data

logic_context: Use a sliding window together with two monotonic deques: one keeps indices with decreasing values (front = window maximum) and one keeps increasing values (front = window minimum). Add each new element to both deques, removing smaller (or larger) values from the back. While max - min exceeds the limit, move the left end forward and drop deque fronts that fall out of the window. Record the window length. Each index enters and leaves each deque once, so O(n).

mandatory: sliding window whose max - min must stay within the limit
monotonic deques give window max and min in O(1)
concept_groups: max deque decreasing, min deque increasing
shrink from the left when the limit is exceeded
pop fronts that leave the window
advanced_bonus: a balanced BST or multiset gives O(n log n) instead
the condition 'any two elements' reduces to max - min
each element is pushed and popped at most once per deque
brute force over all subarrays is O(n²) or worse
example: [8, 2, 4, 7], limit 4 → 2

semantic_targets: only the max and min matter
common_mistakes: Checking every pair in the window
uses a single deque for both
shrinks the window by more than needed

evaluation_rubric.focus: Sliding window with two monotonic deques

logic_context: A simple sliding window fails with negative numbers. Use prefix sums P and a deque of indices whose prefix sums increase. For each j: while the deque is not empty and P[j] - P[front] >= K, record j - front and pop the front (a later j cannot give a shorter subarray for that start). Then, while P[j] <= P[back], pop the back (a smaller prefix later is always a better start). Push j. O(n) time.

mandatory: prefix sums with a deque of increasing prefix values
pop front while P[j] - P[front] >= K; pop back while P[j] <= P[back]
concept_groups: record j - front when the condition holds
negative numbers break the plain sliding window
each index pushed and popped once
advanced_bonus: include P[0] = 0 so subarrays starting at index 0 are considered
return -1 if no subarray qualifies
with only positive numbers the usual sliding window suffices
binary search over a monotonic stack gives O(n log n)
use 64-bit prefix sums

semantic_targets: useless starts are discarded from both ends
common_mistakes: Using a plain sliding window with negatives
Not removing dominated starts from the back

logic_context: Scan from the left. The first element that is 0 (after earlier flips) can only be fixed by a flip starting at that position, so the greedy choice is forced. Instead of actually inverting K elements each time, track how many active flips cover the current index using a difference array or a queue of flip end positions; the current bit is flipped if that count is odd. If a flip is needed but i + K > n, return -1. O(n) time.

mandatory: leftmost remaining 0 forces a flip starting there
track active flips with a difference array or queue
concept_groups: current value = original XOR (active flips mod 2)
impossible if a flip would pass the end
advanced_bonus: simulating each flip directly costs O(n · K)
a flip expires K positions after it starts
this is a classic greedy where the decision at i is forced
the same idea applies to 'bulb switcher' style problems

logic_context: The answer is a contiguous window of length k. Binary search for the window's left end lo in the range 0 to n - k: compare the element just outside the window on each side — if x - a[mid] > a[mid + k] - x, the window should move right (lo = mid + 1); otherwise move left (hi = mid). When the search ends, return a[lo .. lo + k - 1]. O(log(n - k) + k).

mandatory: the k closest elements form a contiguous window
binary search the window's left boundary
concept_groups: compare x - a[mid] with a[mid + k] - x
advanced_bonus: two pointers shrinking from both ends is O(n - k)
a heap of size k by distance is O(n log k)
comparisons avoid absolute values to keep tie-breaking correct
x may lie outside the array's range
result is already sorted because it is a slice

semantic_targets: compare the elements at both window edges
common_mistakes: Returning the k elements nearest by sorting distances without keeping order
Searching over 0 to n instead of n - k
using absolute values incorrectly for ties

logic_context: Three lengths a <= b <= c form a triangle exactly when a + b > c. Sort the lengths in descending order and check consecutive triples: the first position i where a[i] < a[i + 1] + a[i + 2] gives the largest perimeter a[i] + a[i + 1] + a[i + 2]. If one triple with largest side a[i] fails, no other pair with that side can do better, since the next two are the largest remaining. Return 0 if none works. O(n log n).

mandatory: triangle condition: the two smaller sides sum to more than the largest
check consecutive triples after sorting descending
concept_groups: first valid triple gives the maximum
the two largest remaining sides are the best partners
advanced_bonus: checking all triples is O(n³)
only consecutive triples need checking after sorting
equal lengths are allowed (equilateral)
degenerate triangles (a + b == c) are not allowed

semantic_targets: adjacent elements are the best candidates
common_mistakes: Sorting ascending and taking the first valid triple

logic_context: Sort the array. Fix the largest side at index k (from the end), and use two pointers i = 0 and j = k - 1. If a[i] + a[j] > a[k], then every index from i to j - 1 also works with j (they are even larger), so add j - i and move j left. Otherwise move i right. Repeat for every k. O(n²) after sorting.

mandatory: sort and fix the largest side
two pointers count valid pairs in bulk
concept_groups: a[i] + a[j] > a[k] adds j - i triples
advanced_bonus: brute force over triples is O(n³)
binary search for each pair gives O(n² log n)
sorting does not change the number of qualifying index triples
only the condition with the largest side needs checking after sorting

semantic_targets: larger smaller-sides also satisfy the inequality
common_mistakes: Checking all three inequalities after sorting
Counting one triple per pointer move

logic_context: Compute F(0) and the total sum S directly. When the array rotates by one more position, every element's index increases by 1 (adding S to the function) except the element that moves from the last position to index 0, which loses n × its value. So F(k) = F(k - 1) + S - n × a[n - k]. Compute all F values with this recurrence and take the maximum. O(n) time.

mandatory: F(k) = F(k - 1) + S - n × a[n - k]
compute F(0) and the sum S first
concept_groups: each rotation shifts indices by one
the wrapped element loses n times its value
advanced_bonus: recomputing F(k) from scratch is O(n²)
use 64-bit arithmetic for large arrays
the same idea updates any weighted sum under rotation
the recurrence comes from comparing consecutive rotations

semantic_targets: only one element changes position drastically

logic_context: Fill A from the back. Keep pointers i at the last real element of A, j at the last element of B, and k at the last position of A. Repeatedly compare A[i] and B[j], write the larger one to A[k], and move the corresponding pointer and k left. When B is exhausted, the remaining A elements are already in place; if A is exhausted first, copy the rest of B. O(m + n) time, O(1) extra space.

mandatory: fill from the back to avoid overwriting unread elements
write the larger of A[i] and B[j] at position k
advanced_bonus: merging from the front would overwrite A's unread values
stable if ties take from A first when filling from the back appropriately
remaining A elements need no copying
this is the merge step of merge sort done in place thanks to the buffer
differs from merging two arrays with no extra space at all

semantic_targets: the empty tail absorbs larger elements first
common_mistakes: Merging from the front and overwriting
Using a temporary array while claiming O(1)

logic_context: The largest square comes from one of the two ends, because the values with the largest absolute value are at the ends of a sorted array. Use two pointers at both ends and fill the result from the back: compare |a[left]| and |a[right]|, place the larger square at the current back position, and move that pointer inward. O(n) time.

mandatory: largest squares come from the ends
two pointers fill the result from the back
concept_groups: move the pointer whose square was used
advanced_bonus: squaring then sorting is O(n log n)
finding the first non-negative element and merging outward also works
negative values become large squares
the result array is needed because squares are not in place order

common_mistakes: Squaring then sorting without noting cost
Comparing raw values instead of absolute values

logic_context: Use two pointers, one per list. For the current pair of intervals, their overlap runs from lo = max(start1, start2) to hi = min(end1, end2); if lo <= hi, record [lo, hi]. Then advance the pointer of the interval that ends first, since it cannot overlap anything further in the other list. Continue until one list is exhausted. O(m + n) time.

mandatory: overlap = [max of starts, min of ends] if non-empty
advance the interval that ends first
advanced_bonus: checking all pairs is O(m × n)
touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] intersect at [2,2]
if both end together, advancing either is fine
same pattern as merging sorted lists

common_mistakes: Using < instead of <= for closed intervals

logic_context: Simulate writing: keep one buffer per row and a current row with a direction. Append each character to the current row's buffer, then move down until the last row and up until the first row, flipping direction at each end. Finally concatenate the row buffers. If there is only one row, return the string unchanged. O(n) time. A direct formula uses the cycle length 2 × (rows - 1) to compute which characters belong to each row.

mandatory: append characters to row buffers while bouncing between top and bottom
concatenate rows at the end
concept_groups: direction flips at the first and last row
one row returns the original string
advanced_bonus: direct indexing: row r takes characters at j and j + cycle - 2r within each cycle
rows greater than or equal to the length also return the original
no 2D grid is needed
the reverse operation reconstructs the original from the zigzag output
handle rows = 1 before computing the cycle (it would be 0)

common_mistakes: Building a full 2D grid with spaces unnecessarily

logic_context: Split the string into runs of identical characters and record their lengths, e.g. '00110011' → 2, 2, 2, 2. Each valid substring lies across the boundary of two adjacent runs, and two runs of lengths a and b give min(a, b) valid substrings. Sum min(previous, current) over all adjacent run pairs. This can be done in one pass with two counters. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: group consecutive equal characters into runs
each adjacent pair of runs contributes min(a, b)
concept_groups: single pass with previous and current run lengths
advanced_bonus: checking every substring is O(n²) or worse
substrings like '0101' are not counted because groups must be contiguous
runs alternate between 0 and 1 automatically
overlapping substrings are counted separately

semantic_targets: the shorter run limits valid lengths
common_mistakes: forgets the last pair of runs

logic_context: Slide a window of length 10 over the string. Keep a hash set of sequences seen once and another set of sequences already reported. For each window, if it was seen before, add it to the result set; otherwise mark it as seen. To make this faster, encode each letter in 2 bits so a window becomes a 20-bit integer that can be updated in O(1) as the window slides (shift left by 2, add the new letter, mask to 20 bits). O(n) time.

mandatory: slide a 10-letter window and use hash sets for seen and repeated
encode letters as 2 bits for an O(1) rolling integer key
concept_groups: rolling update instead of substring copies
advanced_bonus: storing substring copies costs O(10) per step but is still linear
a 2^20-entry array can replace the hash set with the 20-bit encoding
Rabin-Karp rolling hashes generalise this to any length
strings shorter than 10 have no answers
example: 'AAAAACCCCCAAAAACCCCCC' → ['AAAAACCCCC', 'CCCCCAAAAA']

logic_context: Put every word's reverse-lookup into a hash map from word to index. For each word w, split it at every position into prefix and suffix. If the prefix is a palindrome and the reverse of the suffix exists as another word, then reverse(suffix) + w is a palindrome, giving pair (that word, w). If the suffix is a palindrome and the reverse of the prefix exists as another word, then w + reverse(prefix) is a palindrome, giving pair (w, that word). Handle the empty split carefully to avoid duplicates. O(n × L²) time.

mandatory: split each word into prefix and suffix at every position
palindromic part plus reversed other part found in the map gives a pair
concept_groups: hash map from word to index
avoid pairing a word with itself
avoid duplicate pairs at empty splits
advanced_bonus: checking every pair and concatenation is O(n² × L)
a trie of reversed words gives a similar bound with less hashing
the empty string pairs with every palindromic word
palindrome checks can be precomputed with Manacher's algorithm for speed

semantic_targets: the middle part must itself be a palindrome

logic_context: Use a greedy approach with a max-heap of (remaining count, letter). At each step take the letter with the most copies left. If the last two characters of the result are already that letter, take the second-most-plentiful letter instead (if none remains, stop). Append one copy of the chosen letter, decrease its count, and push it back if any remain. Always spending the most plentiful letter when allowed prevents it from being stranded. O(n log 3) = O(n).

mandatory: greedily use the most plentiful letter
switch to the next letter if it would make three in a row
concept_groups: stop when no allowed letter remains
append one letter at a time
advanced_bonus: the heap has at most 3 entries, so each step is effectively constant
appending two copies at once is a common variant but needs care
sorting three counts each step works without a heap
the result is not unique
example: a = 1, b = 1, c = 7 → 'ccaccbcc'

semantic_targets: use the scarcest-safe choice only when forced
common_mistakes: Stopping too early when another letter is available

logic_context: If some character of the target does not appear in the source, return -1. Otherwise build the target greedily: start a pass over the source and match as many target characters as possible in order; when the source is exhausted, count one subsequence and start another pass. Greedy is optimal because matching as much as possible in each pass never hurts later passes. A naive version is O(|source| × |target|); precomputing for each source position the next occurrence of every letter makes each step O(1).

mandatory: greedily match as much of the target as possible in each pass
count passes; -1 if a character is missing
concept_groups: restart from the source's beginning after each pass
advanced_bonus: next[i][c] = smallest index >= i in source holding c
binary search over position lists is another speed-up
each pass contributes one subsequence
example: source 'abc', target 'abcbc' → 2
checking character presence up front avoids infinite loops

semantic_targets: each pass uses the source once
common_mistakes: Infinite loop when a character is missing
Restarting the source after every character

logic_context: Compute the force on each domino. Sweep left to right: after an 'R', force starts at n and decreases by 1 each step until an 'L' or another 'R' resets it; store these rightward forces. Sweep right to left similarly for 'L' forces (negative). For each domino, if the net force is positive it falls right, negative falls left, and zero stays upright. O(n) time. An alternative processes segments between pushed dominoes: R...L meets in the middle, R...R and L...L fill in, and L...R stays.

mandatory: compute rightward and leftward force decaying with distance
net force sign decides the final state
concept_groups: 'L' resets rightward force; 'R' resets leftward force
equal forces leave the domino upright
advanced_bonus: closer pushes win because force decays with distance
in R...L segments, the middle domino stays upright when the gap is odd
simulating second by second is O(n²) in the worst case
pre-pushed dominoes keep their direction
example: '.L.R...LR..L..' → 'LL.RR.LLRRLL..'

common_mistakes: treats force as constant over distance

logic_context: Process the list in blocks. For the current block, reverse up to k nodes using the standard three-pointer method, keeping a pointer to the block's original first node (which becomes its tail). Connect the previous part's tail to the new block head. Then walk forward k nodes without changing them, linking the reversed block's tail to the start of this unchanged block. Repeat until the list ends. O(n) time, O(1) extra space; a recursive version is also simple.

mandatory: reverse k nodes, then skip k nodes, repeating
reconnect each reversed block to its neighbours
concept_groups: original block head becomes its tail
advanced_bonus: recursive version: reverse k, skip k, then recurse on the rest — O(n / k) stack
decide whether a final partial block is reversed (problem-dependent)
keep the new overall head from the first block
variant of reverse nodes in k-groups
example: 1..9 with k = 3 → 3 2 1 4 5 6 9 8 7

logic_context: In a list sorted by absolute value, the negative numbers appear in decreasing order (−2 before −3 before −5), so their correct order is reversed. Walk the list with prev and cur; whenever cur is negative, unlink it and insert it at the head of the list. Each negative moved to the front ends up before the ones moved earlier, which reverses their order correctly, while positives keep their order. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: negatives appear in reverse of their sorted order
move each negative node to the head as you traverse
concept_groups: update prev correctly after moving a node
advanced_bonus: a general sort would be O(n log n)
moving to the head reverses the negatives' order
handle the head itself being negative (no move needed)
example result: -5 → -3 → -2 → 1 → 4
zero is treated as non-negative

semantic_targets: negatives need reversing, positives do not

logic_context: Traverse the list. When a node has a child, flatten the child list (recursively or with a stack) and splice it between the node and the node's original next: node.next = childHead, childHead.prev = node, childTail.next = originalNext, and originalNext.prev = childTail if it exists. Set node.child to NULL. Continue from the next node. An iterative stack version pushes the next node before descending into a child. O(n) time.

mandatory: splice each child list between a node and its original next
fix both next and prev pointers; clear child pointers
advanced_bonus: recursion returns the tail of the flattened child to avoid re-walking
iterative stack: push next, then move to child
nested children are flattened before continuing
forgetting prev pointers breaks backward traversal
each node is visited once

semantic_targets: children come before the parent's next node
common_mistakes: Appending children at the end of the list

logic_context: Use a preorder format that records each node's value followed by its number of children, for example '1 3 3 2 5 0 6 0 2 0 4 0'. To deserialise, read a value and a child count, create the node, then recursively read that many children. Alternatively, use bracket markers or a null marker after each node's children. Both are O(n).

mandatory: preorder: value, then child count
deserialise by reading value and count, then recursing for children
concept_groups: child count tells how many subtrees follow
bracket or end markers as alternatives
advanced_bonus: level-order with null separators is another common format
separators must not appear in values (or values must be escaped)
the same idea encodes binary trees with fixed child slots
recursion depth equals tree height — use iteration for very deep trees

logic_context: Use a queue starting with the root. For each level, record the queue size, then remove that many nodes, adding each node's value to the current level list and enqueuing all of its children in order. Append the level list to the result and continue until the queue is empty. O(n) time, O(width) space.

mandatory: BFS with a queue
process one level at a time using the queue size
concept_groups: enqueue all children of each node
advanced_bonus: DFS with a depth parameter can also build level lists
the only difference from binary trees is iterating over a child list
an empty tree returns an empty result
children are added in left-to-right order
same pattern gives zigzag order with alternating reversal

logic_context: Collect the leaf sequence of each tree with a DFS that visits left before right and records a node's value only when it has no children. Compare the two sequences. O(n1 + n2) time. To use less memory, generate leaves lazily with two iterative stack-based traversals and compare them one at a time, stopping at the first difference.

mandatory: collect leaves left to right with DFS
compare the two sequences
advanced_bonus: iterator approach uses O(h1 + h2) space
the trees may have completely different shapes
sequences of different lengths are not similar
only leaf order matters, not depth
example: two trees with leaves [6, 7, 4, 9, 8] are leaf-similar

logic_context: Store the values to delete in a hash set. Do a post-order traversal so children are processed before their parent. For each node, update its left and right pointers with the processed results. If the node is to be deleted, add its non-null children to the result as new roots and return NULL to the parent; otherwise return the node. Finally, if the original root was not deleted, add it as a root. O(n) time.

mandatory: post-order so children are handled before deletion
children of a deleted node become new roots
concept_groups: hash set of values to delete
add the original root if kept
advanced_bonus: pre-order with an 'is root' flag is an equivalent approach
processing parents first can orphan subtrees incorrectly
free deleted nodes in C
the forest order may not matter
example: deleting 3 and 5 from tree 1..7 gives roots [1, 6, 7]

semantic_targets: a deleted node's children start new trees
common_mistakes: Not detaching deleted nodes from parents

logic_context: Use post-order traversal returning each subtree's excess: coins in the subtree minus nodes in the subtree. A positive excess must move up through the edge to the parent; a negative excess must move down. Either way, |excess| coins cross that edge. At each node, add |left excess| + |right excess| to the move count and return node.coins + left excess + right excess - 1. O(n) time.

mandatory: subtree excess = coins - nodes
each edge carries |excess| moves
advanced_bonus: direction does not matter for counting moves across an edge
this is a flow-on-a-tree argument
greedy simulation of moving coins is far more complex
example: root 3 with two 0 children → 2 moves
O(h) recursion depth

semantic_targets: every surplus or deficit must cross the parent edge

logic_context: Use post-order traversal that returns, for each node, the length of the longest downward same-value arm starting at it. At a node, the left arm is leftResult + 1 if the left child exists and has the same value, otherwise 0; similarly for the right. Update the global answer with leftArm + rightArm (a path through this node), and return max(leftArm, rightArm) to the parent. O(n) time.

mandatory: return the longest single same-value arm downward
path through a node = left arm + right arm
concept_groups: arm extends only if child value matches
advanced_bonus: the path need not pass through the root
returning both arms would create invalid branching paths upward
similar structure to computing a tree's diameter
nodes with different values reset the arm to 0
example: path of four 5s gives length 3

semantic_targets: a path bends at most once at its top node
common_mistakes: Counting nodes instead of edges without stating
Only considering paths through the root

logic_context: Do a DFS that carries the current zigzag length and the direction of the last move. If the last move was to the left, continuing to the right child extends the length by 1, while going to the left child starts a new zigzag of length 1. Symmetrically for a last move to the right. Track the maximum length seen. Every node is visited once, so O(n).

mandatory: track the direction of the last move
alternate direction extends; same direction restarts at 1
advanced_bonus: returning a pair (best ending with a left move, best ending with a right move) is an equivalent bottom-up method
starting a new path at any node is allowed
a single node has zigzag length 0
example: alternating left-right chains give long paths
O(h) recursion depth

common_mistakes: Restarting at 0 instead of 1 when changing to the same direction
Counting nodes instead of edges inconsistently

logic_context: Traverse the tree with DFS while passing down the values (or pointers) of the parent and grandparent. At each node, if a grandparent exists and its value is even, add the node's value to the sum. Then recurse into the children, passing the current node as the new parent and the old parent as the new grandparent. O(n) time.

mandatory: pass parent and grandparent down the recursion
add a node's value if its grandparent is even
concept_groups: shift parent to grandparent at each level
root and its children have no grandparent
advanced_bonus: alternative: at each even node, add its grandchildren's values directly
BFS with (node, parent, grandparent) tuples also works
no extra data structure is needed
example: grandparent value 6 makes its grandchildren count
values may be negative

common_mistakes: Checking the parent instead of the grandparent
Missing nodes when only checking direct children

logic_context: Model courses as a directed graph with edges from prerequisite to course. Run Kahn's algorithm level by level: start with all courses of in-degree 0 (semester 1); each round removes the current level's courses, decreases their neighbours' in-degrees, and gathers newly free courses for the next semester. Count rounds. If not every course is processed, there is a cycle and the answer is -1. O(V + E).

mandatory: BFS by levels of Kahn's algorithm
number of levels = minimum semesters
advanced_bonus: the answer equals the number of nodes on the longest path in the DAG
if courses per semester were limited, the problem becomes much harder
DFS with memoised longest path also works
isolated courses can be taken in the first semester
example: 3 courses with 1→3 and 2→3 → 2 semesters

semantic_targets: longest prerequisite chain sets the minimum
common_mistakes: Counting total courses instead of levels

logic_context: Precompute the transitive closure: reach[u][v] is true if v can be reached from u. With n courses, one method is Floyd-Warshall style: for each k, i, j, set reach[i][j] |= reach[i][k] && reach[k][j], which is O(n³). Another runs a BFS or DFS from each course, O(n × (n + E)). After precomputation, each query is an O(1) lookup.

mandatory: precompute reachability (transitive closure)
answer each query with an O(1) lookup
advanced_bonus: bitsets speed up the closure by processing 64 bits at a time
for few queries, a single search per query may be cheaper
topological order lets you propagate reachability sets efficiently
the relation is transitive, so indirect prerequisites count
example: 0→1→2 means 0 is a prerequisite of 2

common_mistakes: Running a full search for every query when queries are many

logic_context: Run BFS over states (current node, set of visited nodes as a bitmask). Start from every node at once with its own bit set and distance 0. From a state, moving to a neighbour gives (neighbour, mask | its bit) with distance + 1. Keep a visited table for states. The first time a state with all bits set appears, its distance is the answer. There are n × 2^n states, so O(2^n × n²) time — feasible for n up to about 12.

mandatory: BFS over (node, visited-mask) states
multi-source start from every node
concept_groups: finish when the mask covers all nodes
advanced_bonus: revisiting nodes is allowed, which is why the mask is part of the state
DP with all-pairs distances plus TSP bitmask is an alternative
plain BFS on nodes fails because visiting order matters
a single node graph has answer 0
related to the travelling salesman problem

semantic_targets: the set of visited nodes defines the state

logic_context: Find the size of every connected component using DFS, BFS or union-find. Two nodes are unreachable from each other exactly when they are in different components. Process components one by one, keeping a running count of nodes already seen: each new component of size s forms s × seen unreachable pairs; then add s to seen. Equivalently, the answer is (total pairs) minus the sum of s(s - 1)/2 within components. O(n + E).

mandatory: find component sizes
pairs across different components are unreachable
concept_groups: or subtract within-component pairs from all pairs
advanced_bonus: n(n - 1)/2 can overflow 32-bit integers for large n
union-find with size tracking gives sizes directly
isolated nodes are components of size 1
checking every pair is O(n²)
example: components of sizes 1, 2, 3 → 11 pairs

logic_context: Treat each of the 10,000 codes as a node; each code has 8 neighbours (each of 4 wheels turned up or down). Run BFS from '0000', skipping dead-end codes and already visited codes. The BFS level at which the target is reached is the minimum number of turns. If '0000' itself is a dead end or the target is never reached, return -1. O(10^4 × 8). Bidirectional BFS from both ends reduces the search.

mandatory: BFS over lock states
8 neighbours per state with wrap-around
concept_groups: -1 if start is dead or target unreachable
advanced_bonus: the state space is small (10^4), so plain BFS is fast
encode codes as integers 0–9999 for array-based visited flags
wrap-around: (d + 1) % 10 and (d + 9) % 10
DFS does not give the minimum number of turns
example: target '0202' with some dead ends → 6

logic_context: Simulate the flow row by row. Put the poured amount in glass (0, 0). For each glass (r, c) with amount more than 1, its overflow (amount - 1) is split equally: half goes to (r + 1, c) and half to (r + 1, c + 1). Process rows down to the queried row. The answer is min(1, amount in the queried glass). O(r²) time; only two rows need to be stored.

mandatory: track the amount poured into each glass
overflow (amount - 1) splits equally to the two glasses below
advanced_bonus: simulating cup by cup over time is unnecessary — only totals matter
amounts can exceed 1 in the stored table before clamping
glasses at the edges receive from only one parent
floating-point is acceptable here
example: pouring 2 into the top fills the top and half-fills both below

common_mistakes: Splitting the full amount instead of the overflow

logic_context: Let f(n) be the number of full tilings of a 2 x n board. Considering how the right end is finished: a vertical domino leaves f(n - 1); two horizontal dominoes leave f(n - 2); and trominoes create partially filled columns that combine with all earlier configurations. Working through these cases gives the recurrence f(n) = 2 × f(n - 1) + f(n - 3), with f(0) = 1, f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 2. Compute iteratively modulo 10^9 + 7 in O(n).

mandatory: base cases f(0) = 1, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2
concept_groups: derivation via full and partial states
advanced_bonus: an explicit two-state DP tracks full boards and boards with one cell missing
without trominoes, the recurrence reduces to Fibonacci
matrix exponentiation gives O(log n)
verify the recurrence with small hand-drawn cases

semantic_targets: shapes that stick out need tracking

logic_context: Track two states at each index: keep[i], the minimum swaps so far if position i is not swapped, and swap[i], if it is swapped. Compare with position i - 1: if A[i] > A[i-1] and B[i] > B[i-1], the same choice is compatible (keep→keep, swap→swap + 1). If A[i] > B[i-1] and B[i] > A[i-1], a crossed choice is compatible (swap→keep, keep→swap + 1). Take the minimum over allowed transitions. The answer is min(keep, swap) at the end. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: two states per index: swapped or not
transitions depend on same-order and crossed-order comparisons
concept_groups: both conditions can hold at once
advanced_bonus: the problem guarantees a valid answer exists
greedy swapping whenever order breaks can be suboptimal
initialise keep = 0 and swap = 1 at index 0
similar two-state DP appears in many sequence problems

semantic_targets: each position chooses swap or not

logic_context: Let dp[i] be the number of arithmetic subarrays ending at index i. If a[i] - a[i-1] == a[i-1] - a[i-2], then every arithmetic subarray ending at i - 1 extends by one, plus the new length-3 subarray, so dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + 1; otherwise dp[i] = 0. The answer is the sum of dp. O(n) time, O(1) space with a running variable.

mandatory: dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + 1 if the difference continues, else 0
sum dp over all indices
advanced_bonus: equivalently, a run of L elements with constant difference contributes (L - 1)(L - 2)/2
brute force over subarrays is O(n²) or O(n³)
the subsequence version is a much harder problem
use 64-bit totals for long runs

semantic_targets: each new element extends all slices ending before it

logic_context: Track two values for the last post: same = ways where the last two posts share a colour, and diff = ways where the last two differ. For n = 1, the total is k. For n = 2, same = k and diff = k × (k - 1). For each next post: new same = previous diff (you can only repeat a colour if the previous two differed), and new diff = (previous same + previous diff) × (k - 1). The answer is same + diff. O(n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: same = previous diff; diff = previous total × (k - 1)
answer = same + diff
concept_groups: base cases for n = 1 and n = 2
advanced_bonus: equivalently total(i) = (k - 1) × (total(i - 1) + total(i - 2))
k = 1 allows at most 2 posts
use modulo or 64-bit for large n
the constraint forbids three equal posts in a row
example: n = 3, k = 2 → 6

semantic_targets: repeating a colour requires a previous change
common_mistakes: Forbidding any two adjacent equal posts

logic_context: Let dp[i] be the best score to reach index i: dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[i - k], …, dp[i - 1]). Computing the window maximum naively costs O(k) per index. Keep a deque of indices with decreasing dp values: remove indices that fall out of the window from the front, use the front as the maximum, then remove smaller dp values from the back before pushing i. Total O(n) time.

mandatory: dp[i] = a[i] + max dp over the last k indices
monotonic deque gives the window maximum in O(1)
concept_groups: drop indices older than i - k
keep dp values decreasing in the deque
advanced_bonus: a max-heap with lazy deletion gives O(n log n)
negative values make greedy jumping fail
same deque technique solves 'constrained subsequence sum'
answer is dp[n - 1]

semantic_targets: only the best recent state matters
common_mistakes: O(n × k) DP without noting cost
Greedy jumping to the largest value

logic_context: Compute W[i], the sum of the window of length k starting at i, using a sliding window. Build left[i] = index of the best window starting at or before i (prefer the earlier index on ties) and right[i] = index of the best window starting at or after i (prefer the earlier index on ties, so use >= when scanning from the right). Then try each middle window j from k to n - 2k: the total is W[left[j - k]] + W[j] + W[right[j + k]]. Keep the best. O(n) time.

mandatory: window sums of length k
best-left and best-right arrays around each middle window
concept_groups: middle index ranges from k to n - 2k
advanced_bonus: generalises to m subarrays with DP dp[m][i]
brute force over three positions is O(n³)
scan right-to-left with >= to keep the smallest index on ties
use 64-bit sums

semantic_targets: Precompute best choices on each side
left and right bests are independent given the middle
common_mistakes: greedy picking of the top three windows

logic_context: Use DP: dp[i] = the best product for i; for each split j from 1 to i - 1, dp[i] = max(dp[i], max(j, dp[j]) × max(i - j, dp[i - j])), considering whether each part is split further. O(n²). Mathematically, parts of size 3 are best: use as many 3s as possible, but if the remainder would be 1, replace a 3 + 1 with 2 + 2. Special cases: n = 2 → 1 and n = 3 → 2. The formula is O(1) (or O(log n) with fast power).

mandatory: prefer as many 3s as possible
remainder 1 becomes 2 + 2 instead of 3 + 1
concept_groups: DP over splits as a general method
advanced_bonus: 3 maximises product per unit among integers (closest to e)
4 = 2 + 2 gives the same product as keeping 4
modular exponentiation handles large n with a modulus
the 'at least two parts' rule is why n = 3 gives 2, not 3

common_mistakes: Not requiring at least two parts

logic_context: Let total be the sum. One group's sum s determines the other (total - s), and the difference is total - 2s, so we want the largest achievable subset sum s <= total / 2. Build a boolean subset-sum table reachable[s] by processing each number and updating sums from high to low (0/1 knapsack). Then scan s downward from total / 2 to find the first reachable value. Answer = total - 2s. O(n × total) time, O(total) space; bitsets make it much faster.

mandatory: find the reachable subset sum closest to total / 2
answer = total - 2 × best sum
advanced_bonus: with large values but small n, meet-in-the-middle over halves is better
bitset: reachable |= reachable << x
differs from checking for an exactly equal split (a yes/no question)
greedy assignment to the smaller group is not optimal

common_mistakes: Only checking for an exact half

logic_context: Use a stack of function ids and a variable prev holding the start of the current time segment. On 'start' at time t: if the stack is not empty, add t - prev to the function on top (it ran until now), push the new id, and set prev = t. On 'end' at time t: add t - prev + 1 to the top function (inclusive end), pop it, and set prev = t + 1. Nested calls pause the caller automatically. O(number of logs).

mandatory: stack of running functions
charge elapsed time to the function on top before switching
concept_groups: end times are inclusive: add t - prev + 1
advanced_bonus: exclusive time excludes time spent in called functions
the same function id can appear recursively
parse logs with sscanf or manual splitting
the total of all exclusive times equals the overall elapsed time

semantic_targets: the top of the stack is the function currently running
common_mistakes: Charging time to the wrong function
computing end - start for each function (inclusive time)

logic_context: Parse left to right with a stack of count maps. An element name is an uppercase letter followed by lowercase letters; read it and an optional number (default 1) and add it to the map on top of the stack. On '(', push a new empty map. On ')', pop the top map, read the multiplier after it (default 1), multiply every count, and merge into the map below. At the end, sort element names and print each with its count (omitting a count of 1). O(n × distinct elements) in the worst case.

mandatory: stack of element-count maps for nested parentheses
multiply a group's counts by the number after ')'
concept_groups: merge popped map into the parent
advanced_bonus: recursive descent parsing is an equivalent approach
parsing from right to left with a multiplier stack avoids merging maps
numbers can have several digits
use an ordered map or sort keys at the end
example: 'Mg(OH)2' → 'H2MgO2'

common_mistakes: Treating each letter as an element
printing count 1 explicitly when not wanted

logic_context: Count available slots for nodes. Start with 1 slot (for the root). For each token, it fills one slot, so decrease the count; if the count becomes negative, the string is invalid. A non-null node then creates two new slots for its children, so add 2. At the end, the serialisation is valid exactly when the slot count is 0. O(n) time, O(1) space. A stack approach that collapses 'x,#,#' into '#' also works.

mandatory: each token uses a slot; non-null nodes add two slots
valid if slots never go negative and end at 0
advanced_bonus: checking slots < 0 before adding is essential
rebuilding the tree is unnecessary
the stack method replaces a node with two null children by a single '#'
degree view: in-degree and out-degree must balance

common_mistakes: not requiring zero slots at the end
splitting on characters instead of commas

logic_context: Sort index pairs by nums2 in descending order. Iterate through them; at each step, the current nums2 value is the smallest among everything seen so far, so treat it as the minimum. Maintain a min-heap of the chosen nums1 values with their running sum, keeping only the k largest. When the heap holds k values, compute sum × current nums2 and update the answer. Push the current nums1 value first and pop the smallest when the heap exceeds k. O(n log n).

mandatory: sort by nums2 descending so the current one is the minimum
min-heap keeps the k largest nums1 values and their sum
concept_groups: score = sum × current nums2 when heap has k items
pop smallest when size exceeds k
advanced_bonus: including the current element ensures its nums2 is truly the minimum of the chosen set
similar to 'maximum performance of a team' problems
checking all subsets is exponential
use 64-bit for products

semantic_targets: each step assumes the current element is the minimum

logic_context: Use a difference array over locations: for each trip, add the passengers at its start location and subtract them at its end location (passengers leave at the drop-off). Then take a running prefix sum from the first location to the last; if the number of passengers in the car ever exceeds capacity, return false. O(n + maximum location). Alternatively, sort start and end events and sweep, processing drop-offs before pick-ups at the same location.

mandatory: difference array: +passengers at start, -passengers at end
prefix sum must never exceed capacity
concept_groups: drop-off frees seats at that location
sort events if locations are large
advanced_bonus: a min-heap of current drop-offs ordered by end location is another approach
when events coincide, drop-offs must be processed before pick-ups
same technique solves meeting-room overlap counts
example: trips [[2,1,5],[3,3,7]], capacity 4 → false
locations are integers in a small range in typical constraints

common_mistakes: Processing pick-ups before drop-offs at the same location
Not subtracting at the end location

logic_context: Any bit that changes between m and n becomes 0 somewhere in the range, so the result keeps only the common binary prefix of m and n. Shift both right until they are equal, counting the shifts; then shift the common value back left by that count. Alternatively, repeatedly clear the lowest set bit of n with n &= n - 1 while n > m, and return n. O(log n).

mandatory: result is the common binary prefix of m and n
shift right until equal, then shift back
advanced_bonus: looping from m to n is O(n - m), far too slow for large ranges
if m and n have different highest bits, the result is 0
use unsigned values to avoid sign issues
the same reasoning gives the OR of a range: set all bits below the highest differing bit

semantic_targets: differing low bits must hit zero somewhere

logic_context: Look at each bit separately. If at least one element has bit b set, then exactly half of all 2^n subsets have an odd number of such elements, so bit b is set in the XOR of exactly 2^(n - 1) subsets. If no element has bit b, it never appears. Therefore the answer is (OR of all elements) × 2^(n - 1). O(n) time. A backtracking enumeration of all subsets gives the same result in O(2^n).

mandatory: each bit present in any element is set in exactly half of the subsets
answer = (OR of all elements) × 2^(n - 1)
advanced_bonus: proof: pair subsets by toggling one fixed element that has the bit
the empty subset contributes 0
the same parity argument counts subsets with odd sums
example: [1, 3] → 6 (subsets: 0, 1, 3, 2)
for large n, compute modulo a prime

semantic_targets: half the subsets have odd parity
common_mistakes: Enumerating all subsets without noting cost
Summing elements instead of XOR totals

logic_context: Count the empty squares (including start and end) that must be visited. Run a DFS with backtracking from the start, marking squares as visited and counting how many have been visited. Move in four directions to unvisited, non-obstacle squares. When the end square is reached, count the path only if all required squares have been visited. Unmark squares when returning. The search is exponential, but grids are small (e.g. up to 20 cells).

mandatory: DFS with backtracking that visits each square once
count a path only if all empty squares are visited when reaching the end
advanced_bonus: bitmask DP over (cell, visited set) can memoise for slightly larger grids
pruning: stop if the end is reached early
marking cells in the grid itself saves memory
example: a 3x4 grid with one obstacle has 2 such paths
differs from counting all paths with right/down moves

semantic_targets: every empty square must be covered
common_mistakes: DP as if paths were independent

logic_context: Each symbol in row n comes from symbol ceil(k / 2) of row n - 1: an odd position k copies its parent, and an even position is the opposite of its parent. So recursively compute the parent and flip it when k is even, with the base case row 1 = 0. O(n) time. Equivalently, the answer is the parity of the number of 1 bits in k - 1.

mandatory: each symbol comes from its parent at position ceil(k / 2)
odd k copies the parent; even k flips it
advanced_bonus: building the rows explicitly takes O(2^n) memory
the sequence is the Thue-Morse sequence
each flip corresponds to a 1 bit in k - 1
iterative version walks up the tree using k's bits
example: n = 2, k = 2 → 1

logic_context: Keep a stack of iterators (or of positions within lists), starting with the outermost list. In hasNext, look at the top: if its list is exhausted, pop it; if the next element is an integer, it is ready; if it is a list, advance past it and push an iterator for that inner list. Repeat until an integer is found or the stack is empty. next returns the ready integer. This flattens lazily, so each element is handled once and memory is proportional to nesting depth.

mandatory: stack of iterators over nested lists
hasNext advances until an integer is on top
advanced_bonus: eagerly flattening into an array in the constructor is simpler but uses O(total) memory
empty inner lists must be skipped by hasNext
pushing elements in reverse order onto a single stack is another approach
recursion depth equals nesting depth

semantic_targets: next relies on hasNext preparing the value

logic_context: Each land cell has 4 sides. Every edge shared between two neighbouring land cells is internal and removes 2 from the total (one side from each cell). So scan the grid: for every land cell add 4, and subtract 2 if the cell to its right is land and 2 if the cell below is land (counting each shared edge once). O(m × n) time, O(1) space.

mandatory: each land cell contributes 4 sides
each shared edge between land cells subtracts 2
concept_groups: check right and down neighbours only to avoid double counting
advanced_bonus: alternatively count land-to-water or land-to-border sides directly
DFS also works but is unnecessary
the grid's border counts as water
lakes inside the island would add internal perimeter if allowed
example: a 2x2 block of land has perimeter 8

logic_context: Use buckets of width t + 1 indexed by floor(value / (t + 1)), so two values in the same bucket differ by at most t. Slide a window of the last k elements: for each value, if its bucket already holds an element, return true; also check the two neighbouring buckets for a value within t. Then store the value in its bucket, and remove the element that leaves the window (index i - k). Each bucket holds at most one element. O(n) time. An ordered set with a ceiling query gives O(n log k).

mandatory: buckets of width t + 1 by value
check own and neighbouring buckets within a window of size k
concept_groups: at most one element per bucket
remove the element leaving the window
advanced_bonus: ordered set: find the smallest value >= nums[i] - t and check it is <= nums[i] + t
use 64-bit arithmetic to avoid overflow in value differences
t must be non-negative
brute force checks k neighbours per element — O(n × k)
example: [1, 5, 9, 1, 5, 9], k = 2, t = 3 → false

semantic_targets: close values share or neighbour buckets

logic_context: Interpolation search estimates where the target should be, assuming values are roughly evenly spread: pos = lo + (target - a[lo]) × (hi - lo) / (a[hi] - a[lo]). It compares a[pos] with the target and narrows the range to the left or right part, like binary search. On uniformly distributed sorted data it takes about O(log log n) steps, but on skewed data it can degrade to O(n). Guard against division by zero when a[hi] == a[lo] and against overflow in the multiplication.

mandatory: estimate the position from the target's value
narrow the range like binary search
concept_groups: O(log log n) on uniform data
O(n) worst case on skewed data
stop when target is outside [a[lo], a[hi]]
advanced_bonus: use 64-bit arithmetic for the position formula
combining with binary search steps guards against bad distributions
binary search is more predictable for general data
works well for things like evenly spaced IDs or phone directory-like data
requires random access and sorted values

semantic_targets: good guesses shrink the range quickly
common_mistakes: Claiming it is always faster than binary search
Division by zero for equal endpoints
no range check for the target

logic_context: The allocator gets large regions of memory from the operating system (with brk/sbrk or mmap) and divides them into chunks. Each chunk has a small header storing its size and whether it is in use. Free chunks are kept in free lists, often grouped by size ('bins'). malloc searches a suitable list for a chunk that fits (first-fit or best-fit), splitting a larger chunk if needed. free marks the chunk free and merges (coalesces) it with neighbouring free chunks to reduce fragmentation, then puts it back on a free list. Very large requests are often served directly with mmap.

mandatory: chunks with headers recording size and status
free lists (bins) of available chunks; split on allocation, coalesce on free
concept_groups: memory obtained from the OS via brk/sbrk or mmap
advanced_bonus: buffer overflows can corrupt chunk headers, which attackers exploit
thread-local caches (tcache) speed up small allocations
boundary tags let free find neighbouring chunks in O(1)
memory returned by free is usually not given back to the OS immediately
alignment requirements round chunk sizes up (e.g. 16 bytes)

common_mistakes: Saying malloc calls the OS for every allocation

logic_context: The buddy system manages memory in blocks whose sizes are powers of two. To satisfy a request, it rounds the size up to a power of two and, if needed, repeatedly splits a larger free block into two equal halves called buddies until a block of the right size exists. When a block is freed, the allocator checks whether its buddy (found by XOR-ing the block's address with its size) is also free; if so, they merge into a larger block, repeating upward. Splitting and merging are fast, but rounding up to powers of two wastes space (internal fragmentation of up to almost 50%).

mandatory: blocks are powers of two; split into buddies to fit requests
freed buddies merge back into larger blocks
concept_groups: buddy address = address XOR block size
advanced_bonus: the Linux kernel's page allocator uses a buddy system
slab allocators sit on top to serve small objects efficiently
external fragmentation is limited because merges are easy
a 33 KB request wastes about 31 KB in a 64 KB block
maximum order limits the largest block size

common_mistakes: Saying any two adjacent blocks can merge

logic_context: A flat page table needs one entry for every virtual page, used or not. With a 48-bit virtual address space and 4 KB pages, that is 2^36 entries per process — far too much memory. A multi-level page table splits the virtual page number into several indexes (x86-64 uses four levels of 9 bits each plus a 12-bit offset).
