Higher-level tables point to lower-level tables, and tables are allocated only for regions the process actually uses, so sparse address spaces need little memory. The cost is that a TLB miss requires several memory reads (a page walk).

mandatory: flat tables are too large for big address spaces
multi-level tables allocate only for used regions
concept_groups: virtual page number split into several indexes
TLB miss requires a page walk
page-walk caches and the TLB reduce cost
advanced_bonus: 5-level paging extends to 57-bit addresses
huge pages skip a level and increase TLB reach
inverted page tables index by physical frame instead
each table fits exactly in one 4 KB page (512 × 8-byte entries)
unused regions have NULL entries at a higher level

common_mistakes: Saying multi-level tables make lookups faster
claims a flat table is small
confuses page tables with the TLB

logic_context: An interrupt is a signal — usually from hardware such as a timer, keyboard or network card — that temporarily stops the CPU's current work. The CPU saves its state and jumps to the interrupt service routine registered in the interrupt vector table. The ISR should do the minimum: acknowledge the device, read or store urgent data, and set a flag or queue work for later, then return so the interrupted program can continue. Long work is deferred (bottom half). Shared variables need volatile and careful synchronisation.

mandatory: interrupt pauses normal execution and runs a handler
ISRs should be short and defer heavy work
concept_groups: interrupt vector table maps interrupts to handlers
use flags or queues to communicate with main code
advanced_bonus: interrupts can have priorities and be nested
disabling interrupts briefly protects critical sections on single-core systems
ISRs must not call blocking functions like malloc or printf in most systems
software interrupts (traps) are used for system calls
variables shared with ISRs should be volatile and accessed atomically

common_mistakes: Doing long processing inside the ISR

logic_context: RAID combines several disks. RAID 0 (striping) splits data across disks for speed and full capacity, but if any disk fails, all data is lost. RAID 1 (mirroring) writes identical copies to two disks, surviving one disk failure with fast reads, but only half the raw capacity is usable. RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity across at least three disks, surviving one disk failure with (n - 1)/n capacity, but writes are slower (parity updates) and rebuilding after a failure is long and stressful for the remaining disks. RAID is not a substitute for backups.

mandatory: RAID 0: striping, fast, no redundancy
RAID 1: mirroring; RAID 5: striping with parity, survives one failure
advanced_bonus: RAID 6 uses double parity to survive two failures
RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping
parity lets a missing block be computed with XOR
accidental deletion or corruption is copied to all disks
hardware and software RAID implementations exist

semantic_targets: parity trades write speed for space

logic_context: Updating a file often changes several on-disk structures — data blocks, inodes, free-space bitmaps and directories. A crash in the middle can leave them inconsistent. A journaling file system first writes a description of the intended changes to a journal (log) area and marks the transaction committed; only then does it apply the changes to their real locations. After a crash, it replays committed journal entries and discards incomplete ones, restoring consistency quickly instead of scanning the whole disk with fsck. Modes differ in whether file data or only metadata is journaled.

mandatory: intended changes are logged before being applied
recovery replays committed journal entries
advanced_bonus: ext4 modes: journal (data + metadata), ordered (default), writeback
copy-on-write file systems (ZFS, Btrfs) achieve consistency differently
the journal is a circular log on disk
fsync still matters for an application's own durability
the same idea as write-ahead logging in databases

common_mistakes: Saying journaling backs up file contents
claims journaling removes the need for fsync
says changes are applied before logging

logic_context: Two-phase commit (2PC) makes a transaction that spans several databases or services either commit everywhere or nowhere. In phase 1 (prepare), the coordinator asks every participant to prepare; each participant makes its changes durable but uncommitted and votes yes or no. In phase 2, if all voted yes, the coordinator tells everyone to commit; if any voted no or timed out, it tells everyone to abort. The main weakness is blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants voted yes, they must hold locks and wait, unsure whether to commit or abort.

mandatory: prepare phase collects votes; commit phase applies the decision
all participants commit or all abort
concept_groups: participants make changes durable before voting yes
any no vote leads to abort
advanced_bonus: three-phase commit reduces blocking but assumes bounded network delays
consensus-based commit (e.g. using Raft or Paxos) removes the single coordinator problem
the coordinator logs its decision before sending it
many microservice systems use sagas instead of 2PC
XA is a standard interface for 2PC with databases

common_mistakes: Saying participants commit during the prepare phase

logic_context: Raft runs on a cluster of servers (usually an odd number such as 3 or 5). One server is elected leader for a term: followers that stop hearing from a leader wait a random timeout, become candidates, and request votes; a candidate that gains a majority becomes leader. Clients send commands to the leader, which appends them to its log and replicates them to followers. An entry is committed once a majority has stored it, and then every server applies committed entries in the same order. Election rules ensure a new leader already has all committed entries, so the cluster tolerates f failures with 2f + 1 servers.

mandatory: leader election by majority vote with randomised timeouts
entries committed once stored on a majority and applied in order
concept_groups: new leaders must have all committed entries
advanced_bonus: randomised timeouts reduce split votes
logs that diverge are overwritten by the leader's entries
used in etcd, Consul and many databases
Paxos solves the same problem but is harder to understand
reads may need to go through the leader to be up to date

common_mistakes: Saying all servers must agree on every write
Claiming it tolerates half the servers failing

logic_context: Eventual consistency means that if no new updates are made, all replicas will eventually hold the same value, but reads in the meantime may return older data. It allows systems to stay available and fast during network problems. Because replicas can accept writes independently, conflicts happen and must be resolved, for example by last-write-wins using timestamps (simple but can lose updates), by version vectors that detect conflicts for the application to merge, or by CRDTs — data types designed so concurrent updates always merge correctly.

mandatory: replicas converge if updates stop; reads may be stale meanwhile
conflict resolution is needed for concurrent writes
advanced_bonus: session guarantees like read-your-writes improve user experience
DNS is a familiar eventually consistent system
anti-entropy processes repair differences between replicas
shopping carts are a classic case for merge-based resolution
clock skew makes timestamp-based ordering unreliable

logic_context: HTTP/1.1 is a text-based protocol where each connection handles one request at a time, so browsers open several connections and requests can wait behind slow ones (head-of-line blocking at the HTTP level). HTTP/2 uses a binary framing layer and multiplexes many concurrent request/response streams over a single connection, compresses headers (HPACK) to save bandwidth, and supports stream priorities. Because HTTP/2 still runs over TCP, one lost packet delays all streams; HTTP/3 fixes this by running over QUIC on UDP.

mandatory: HTTP/1.1: text, one request at a time per connection
HTTP/2: binary framing, multiplexing, header compression
advanced_bonus: server push in HTTP/2 was rarely used and is deprecated in browsers
domain sharding and sprite tricks from HTTP/1.1 become unnecessary
HTTP/2 is almost always used over TLS in browsers
semantics (methods, status codes, headers) stay the same
pipelining in HTTP/1.1 existed but was rarely enabled

common_mistakes: Saying HTTP/2 changes methods or status codes

logic_context: A REST API models data as resources identified by URLs (for example /students/42). Clients act on resources with standard HTTP methods: GET to read, POST to create, PUT or PATCH to update, and DELETE to remove. Each request is stateless — it carries everything the server needs, such as authentication — so any server can handle it. Responses use representations like JSON with meaningful status codes, and can be marked cacheable. A uniform, predictable interface makes APIs easier to use and scale.

mandatory: resources identified by URLs and manipulated with HTTP methods
stateless requests with standard status codes
advanced_bonus: GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent
use nouns for resources, not verbs (/orders, not /getOrders)
versioning (e.g. /v1/) avoids breaking clients
HATEOAS adds links to related actions
pagination and filtering use query parameters

common_mistakes: Storing session state on the server as a requirement

logic_context: An IPv4 address has 32 bits split into a network part and a host part. CIDR notation writes the number of network bits after a slash: /24 means the first 24 bits identify the network and the last 8 bits identify hosts, giving 256 addresses (254 usable, since the first is the network address and the last is the broadcast address). The equivalent subnet mask is 255.255.255.0. Subnetting divides a larger network into smaller ones, and routers choose routes using the longest matching prefix.

mandatory: the number after the slash is the count of network bits
host bits determine the number of addresses
advanced_bonus: a /30 has 4 addresses with 2 usable hosts
aggregating prefixes (supernetting) shrinks routing tables
AND-ing an address with the mask gives the network address
IPv6 uses the same prefix notation, commonly /64 for subnets
private ranges like 10.0.0.0/8 are written in CIDR

semantic_targets: more prefix bits means a smaller network

logic_context: IP addresses identify devices logically, but on a local Ethernet or Wi-Fi network, frames are delivered using hardware MAC addresses. The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) finds the MAC address for an IPv4 address: a host broadcasts 'Who has 192.168.1.20?' and the owner replies with its MAC address. The answer is cached in an ARP table for a while. To reach a machine outside the local network, a host ARPs for its default gateway's MAC address instead. Because ARP replies are not authenticated, attackers can perform ARP spoofing.

mandatory: maps IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses on a local network
broadcast request, unicast reply, cached in an ARP table
concept_groups: frames on a LAN need MAC addresses
remote destinations use the gateway's MAC
advanced_bonus: IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery instead of ARP
gratuitous ARP announces a device's own address
switches use MAC addresses, routers use IP addresses
static ARP entries or dynamic ARP inspection mitigate spoofing
arp -a shows the local ARP table

semantic_targets: delivery on a LAN needs hardware addresses
common_mistakes: Saying ARP maps names to IPs (that is DNS)
Claiming ARP works across the internet

logic_context: TCP limits unacknowledged data in flight with a congestion window (cwnd) to avoid overloading the network. In slow start, cwnd begins small and roughly doubles every round trip until it reaches a threshold. Then congestion avoidance increases it by about one segment per round trip (additive increase). When loss is detected — through three duplicate ACKs — TCP halves cwnd (multiplicative decrease) and uses fast retransmit and fast recovery; after a timeout it drops back to a small window and restarts slow start. This AIMD behaviour shares bandwidth fairly. It is different from flow control, which protects the receiver's buffer.

mandatory: congestion window limits data in flight
slow start doubles, congestion avoidance adds, loss halves (AIMD)
concept_groups: three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit
advanced_bonus: CUBIC is the default in Linux; BBR models bandwidth and RTT instead of reacting to loss
ECN lets routers signal congestion without dropping packets
the send window is the minimum of cwnd and the receiver window
high-latency links take longer to ramp up
fairness emerges from many flows using AIMD

semantic_targets: the network, not just the receiver, limits sending
common_mistakes: Confusing congestion control with flow control
claims UDP has the same mechanism

logic_context: SQL injection happens when user input is inserted directly into an SQL string, letting an attacker change the meaning of the query. For example, building "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'" with input ' OR '1'='1 returns every user, and other inputs can modify or delete data. The main defence is parameterised queries (prepared statements), where the query structure is fixed and user data is passed separately and never interpreted as SQL. Extra protections include least-privilege database accounts, input validation and ORMs that parameterise automatically.

mandatory: untrusted input changes the structure of an SQL query
use parameterised queries / prepared statements
concept_groups: input validation as an extra layer
advanced_bonus: manual escaping is error-prone and should not be the primary defence
stored procedures can still be vulnerable if they build dynamic SQL
in C, use sqlite3_bind_* or the equivalent driver API
error messages should not reveal query details
web application firewalls add defence in depth

semantic_targets: data must never become query syntax
common_mistakes: Thinking input validation alone is enough

logic_context: Decrease-key lowers the key of an element already in a min-priority queue (raising its priority). In a binary heap, after lowering the key, the element is moved up (sifted up) while it is smaller than its parent, which takes O(log n). The difficulty is finding the element: the heap must keep an index map from each element (for example a vertex number) to its current position, updated on every swap. Dijkstra's and Prim's algorithms use decrease-key; a common alternative is to insert a duplicate entry with the new key and skip stale entries when they are popped.

mandatory: lower an element's key and sift it up
needs a position map to locate the element
concept_groups: O(log n) in a binary heap
lazy alternative: push duplicates, skip stale
update the map on every swap
advanced_bonus: Fibonacci heaps support decrease-key in O(1) amortised time
lazy insertion makes the heap hold up to E entries instead of V
increase-key in a min-heap sifts down instead
C++ std::priority_queue has no decrease-key
indexed priority queues are common in competitive programming

common_mistakes: Searching the heap linearly without noting cost
claims O(1) in a binary heap

logic_context: During a DFS, record an entry time tin[v] when a node is first visited and an exit time tout[v] after all its descendants are finished, using one increasing counter. All nodes in v's subtree then have entry times in the contiguous range [tin[v], tout[v]]. So subtree queries (such as the sum of values in a subtree) become range queries on an array ordered by entry time, which a Fenwick or segment tree can answer, even with updates. Ancestor checks also become O(1): u is an ancestor of v exactly when tin[u] <= tin[v] and tout[v] <= tout[u].

mandatory: entry and exit times from a DFS
a subtree maps to a contiguous range of entry times
advanced_bonus: a full Euler tour with depths plus range-minimum queries gives LCA in O(1) after preprocessing
path queries need other techniques such as heavy-light decomposition
iterative DFS avoids stack overflow on deep trees
preprocessing is O(n)
example: subtree sum with point updates in O(log n)

common_mistakes: Separate counters for entry and exit causing overlap errors
Claiming path queries work the same way
confuses with Eulerian paths in graphs

logic_context: Binary lifting precomputes, for every node v and every power of two, the 2^j-th ancestor: up[0][v] is the parent and up[j][v] = up[j - 1][up[j - 1][v]]. This takes O(n log n) time and memory. To find the k-th ancestor, write k in binary and jump by the corresponding powers of two — O(log n). For the LCA of u and v, first lift the deeper node to the same depth, then, from the largest j down, jump both nodes up whenever their 2^j-th ancestors differ; finally their parent is the LCA. Each query is O(log n).

mandatory: up[j][v] = 2^j-th ancestor built from smaller jumps
answer queries by combining power-of-two jumps
concept_groups: k-th ancestor via binary representation of k
LCA: equalise depths then lift together
advanced_bonus: depths come from a DFS or BFS
the root's ancestors can point to itself or a sentinel
Euler tour + sparse table gives O(1) LCA queries
binary lifting also supports path aggregates like max edge weight
example: find the 13th ancestor using jumps of 8, 4 and 1

semantic_targets: large jumps built from smaller jumps
common_mistakes: Walking up one parent at a time and claiming O(log n)
Not equalising depths before LCA lifting

logic_context: The first digit tells the general outcome. 1xx codes are informational (101 Switching Protocols). 2xx codes mean success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content). 3xx codes mean redirection — the client must go elsewhere (301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified). 4xx codes mean the client made an error (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found). 5xx codes mean the server failed (500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable).

mandatory: the first digit gives the class of response
2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
concept_groups: 429 Too Many Requests for rate limits
advanced_bonus: APIs should return accurate codes so clients can react correctly
304 lets browsers reuse cached responses
503 often includes a Retry-After header
returning 200 with an error message hides failures
418 is a joke code from an April Fools' RFC

logic_context: A view is a virtual table defined by a stored SELECT query. Querying the view runs the underlying query, so it always shows current data without storing a separate copy (unlike a materialised view). Views simplify complex queries by giving them a name, provide a stable interface even if underlying tables change, and improve security by exposing only certain columns or rows to particular users. Some simple views can also be updated, but views with joins or aggregates usually cannot.

mandatory: virtual table defined by a stored query
simplifies queries and restricts access
advanced_bonus: CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ...
views do not automatically make queries faster
row-level security can be built with views
dropping a base column can break dependent views
nested views can hide expensive queries

common_mistakes: Saying views store copies of data

logic_context: A stored procedure is a named block of SQL (and procedural logic) saved in the database and run explicitly by calling it, often with parameters — for example a procedure that transfers money between accounts. A trigger is code that runs automatically when a specified event happens on a table, such as before or after an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE — for example writing an audit log entry whenever a row changes. They keep logic close to the data and can reduce round trips, but hidden logic can be harder to test, version and debug.

mandatory: stored procedure: called explicitly with parameters
trigger: runs automatically on table events
advanced_bonus: BEFORE triggers can validate or modify data; AFTER triggers react to changes
triggers firing other triggers can cause cascades
procedures can reduce network round trips for multi-step logic
business logic placement (app vs database) is a design choice
procedures can run with controlled privileges

common_mistakes: Saying triggers must be called manually
claims triggers run only on SELECT

logic_context: Cross-site scripting happens when an application includes untrusted input in a web page without escaping it, so an attacker's script runs in other users' browsers. For example, a comment containing a <script> tag could steal session cookies or perform actions as the victim. Stored XSS saves the script on the server; reflected XSS bounces it from a request parameter; DOM-based XSS happens in client-side code. Prevention: escape or encode output for the context (HTML, attribute, JavaScript), sanitise any allowed HTML, use a Content Security Policy, and mark session cookies HttpOnly.

mandatory: untrusted input rendered as script in other users' browsers
prevent with context-aware output encoding
advanced_bonus: modern template engines escape output by default
innerHTML with user data is a common DOM XSS source
validation of input helps but encoding output is essential
XSS differs from SQL injection, which targets the database
CSP can block inline scripts entirely

semantic_targets: the browser trusts the page's scripts

logic_context: strcmp compares two null-terminated strings character by character and stops at the first difference or at the terminating '\0', so it is for text. memcmp compares exactly n bytes of two memory blocks and does not stop at '\0', so it is for binary data such as arrays or buffers. Both return 0 when equal, and a negative or positive value depending on the first differing byte (compared as unsigned char). Be careful using memcmp on structs, because padding bytes may contain arbitrary values.

mandatory: strcmp stops at '\0'; memcmp compares exactly n bytes
strcmp for strings, memcmp for raw memory
concept_groups: both return negative, zero or positive
struct padding can break memcmp comparisons
advanced_bonus: memcmp on non-terminated data is safe if n is correct
strcmp on non-terminated buffers can read past the end
memcmp is often optimised to compare words at a time
for secrets, use constant-time comparison instead of memcmp
comparing floats bytewise does not handle -0.0 and NaN properly

common_mistakes: Using strcmp on binary data with zeros
Comparing structs with memcmp without noting padding

logic_context: In this URL, 'https' is the scheme (protocol), 'www.example.com' is the host (domain name), ':443' is the port (optional because 443 is the default for HTTPS), '/docs/page' is the path to the resource, '?lang=en' is the query string with key-value parameters, and '#intro' is the fragment, which identifies a section inside the page and is handled by the browser without being sent to the server. Special characters in URLs are percent-encoded, such as a space becoming %20.

mandatory: scheme, host, port, path, query, fragment
each part has a specific role
advanced_bonus: multiple query parameters are separated by &
user information (user:pass@) is discouraged in URLs
relative URLs omit scheme and host
the host is resolved with DNS
URLs are case-sensitive in the path but not in the scheme or host

semantic_targets: the browser splits the URL into parts
common_mistakes: Saying the fragment is sent to the server

logic_context: A MAC address is a 48-bit hardware address assigned to a network interface (written like 3C:22:FB:12:34:56); it is used to deliver frames within a local network (layer 2) and usually stays the same wherever the device goes. An IP address is a logical address (layer 3) assigned by the network the device joins; it is used to route packets between networks and changes when the device moves to another network. ARP translates IP addresses to MAC addresses on a LAN.

mandatory: MAC: hardware address for local delivery (layer 2)
IP: logical address for routing between networks (layer 3)
concept_groups: MAC is usually fixed; IP changes with network
switches use MAC, routers use IP
advanced_bonus: phones often randomise MAC addresses for privacy
MAC addresses are not visible beyond the local network
DHCP assigns IP addresses
MAC addresses can be spoofed
the first half of a MAC address identifies the manufacturer

common_mistakes: Saying MAC addresses route across the internet
claims MAC is assigned by DHCP

logic_context: A firewall controls network traffic according to rules, allowing or blocking connections based on information such as source and destination IP addresses, ports and protocols. A common default is to block incoming connections unless they are explicitly allowed, while permitting outgoing traffic. Network firewalls protect a whole network at its boundary; host firewalls run on individual computers. Stateful firewalls track connections so replies to allowed outgoing traffic are let back in, and web application firewalls inspect HTTP requests for attacks.

mandatory: filters traffic using rules
blocks unwanted connections, allows permitted ones
concept_groups: rules by IP, port and protocol
advanced_bonus: examples: iptables/nftables on Linux, Windows Defender Firewall
web application firewalls look for SQL injection and XSS patterns
firewalls do not stop attacks through allowed services
rule order matters in many firewalls
firewalls are one layer of defence in depth

logic_context: Encoding changes data into another format so it can be stored or transmitted correctly, such as Base64 or UTF-8; it is reversible by anyone and provides no security. Encryption transforms data so only someone with the right key can read it, such as AES; it is reversible with the key and protects confidentiality. Hashing turns data into a fixed-size digest, such as SHA-256; it is one-way (not reversible), and is used to check integrity, look up data and store passwords (with salts and slow algorithms).

mandatory: encoding: reversible format change, no security
encryption: reversible with a key; hashing: one-way digest
advanced_bonus: Base64 is often mistaken for encryption
the same input always gives the same hash
encryption keys must be managed securely
HMAC combines hashing with a secret key for authentication
checksums detect accidental changes, not attacks

semantic_targets: choose by what you need to protect
common_mistakes: storing passwords encrypted instead of hashed

logic_context: Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt and decrypt (for example AES); it is fast and suits large amounts of data, but both sides must share the key securely in advance. Asymmetric (public-key) encryption uses a key pair: a public key that anyone can use to encrypt or verify, and a private key kept secret to decrypt or sign (for example RSA or elliptic-curve cryptography); it solves key distribution but is much slower. Protocols like TLS combine them: asymmetric methods establish a shared key, then symmetric encryption protects the data.

mandatory: symmetric: one shared key, fast
asymmetric: public/private key pair, slower but no prior shared secret
advanced_bonus: asymmetric keys are much longer for similar security (RSA 3072-bit vs AES 128-bit)
Diffie-Hellman agrees on a shared key without sending it
signing proves authorship; encryption hides content
public keys need certificates to prove who owns them
quantum computers threaten current asymmetric algorithms more than symmetric ones

common_mistakes: Saying asymmetric uses the same key twice
Swapping public and private key roles

logic_context: Continuous integration is the practice of merging every developer's changes into a shared main branch frequently — often several times a day — with each change automatically built and tested by a CI system such as GitHub Actions or Jenkins. Problems are found within minutes of being introduced, while they are small and easy to fix, instead of piling up before a release. CI usually runs compilation, unit tests, static analysis and code-style checks. Continuous delivery/deployment extends this by automatically preparing or releasing the tested build.

mandatory: frequent merges to a shared branch
every change built and tested automatically
concept_groups: tools like GitHub Actions or Jenkins
advanced_bonus: a broken main build should be fixed immediately
fast test suites keep CI useful
pull requests are often gated on passing CI
reproducible builds (e.g. containers) avoid 'works on my machine'
CI can also run sanitizers and fuzzers for C code

semantic_targets: small changes are easier to debug
common_mistakes: Saying CI means deploying to users automatically
claims CI removes the need for tests

logic_context: A design pattern is a reusable, named solution to a common software design problem — a template rather than finished code. The Observer pattern lets objects subscribe to another object and be notified when it changes (in C, often implemented with a list of callback function pointers), useful for event handling. The Singleton pattern ensures a class or module has only one instance with a global access point, such as a single logger; it is convenient but can make testing harder because it introduces global state. Patterns give developers a shared vocabulary.

mandatory: named reusable solutions to recurring design problems
examples such as Observer and Singleton
concept_groups: implementable in C with function pointers or static data
advanced_bonus: Strategy pattern swaps algorithms through a function pointer interface
Factory pattern centralises object creation
overusing patterns adds unnecessary complexity
the 'Gang of Four' book catalogued classic patterns
patterns are language-independent ideas

semantic_targets: patterns describe structure, not exact code
common_mistakes: describes only object-oriented languages as able to use them

logic_context: Synchronous logging is simple and ensures messages are written before the request continues, which helps when diagnosing crashes, but each write may block on disk I/O or a lock shared by all threads, adding latency to every request. Asynchronous logging lets request threads push messages into a queue and return immediately while a background thread writes them in batches, greatly reducing latency. The risks are that queued messages can be lost on a crash, and if producers outpace the writer, the queue grows without bound unless it is bounded with a drop-or-block policy. Recommend asynchronous logging with a bounded queue, flushing on shutdown and writing critical or fatal messages synchronously.

mandatory: synchronous logging adds I/O latency to requests
asynchronous logging is fast but may lose queued messages on crash
concept_groups: bounded queue with drop or block policy
advanced_bonus: a lock-free ring buffer reduces contention between threads
log levels avoid formatting unnecessary messages
formatting strings can be deferred to the background thread
crash handlers can flush the queue in some cases
measure logging overhead under load

semantic_targets: keep slow I/O off the request path
common_mistakes: claims async logging has no risks
synchronous logging under a global lock without noting contention

logic_context: Polling is simple and fully under your control — it needs no public endpoint and works even if the provider has no webhooks — but updates arrive only as often as you poll, most requests return nothing new, and frequent polling can hit rate limits. Webhooks deliver events almost immediately and avoid wasted calls, but you must expose a public HTTPS endpoint, verify signatures to reject forged calls, handle retries and duplicate deliveries idempotently, and cope with events missed while your service was down. Recommend webhooks for timely updates, combined with periodic reconciliation polling to catch anything missed.

mandatory: polling: simple but delayed and wasteful
webhooks: near real-time but need verification, idempotency and reliability handling
advanced_bonus: respond to webhooks quickly and process asynchronously
store event ids to deduplicate
webhooks may arrive out of order — check timestamps or versions
exponential backoff when polling after errors
a dead-letter store keeps events that failed processing

semantic_targets: push for speed, pull for completeness
common_mistakes: polling every second without considering limits

logic_context: The per-order approach is simple to write but runs 101 queries; each adds a network round trip and database overhead, so the page becomes slow, especially as the list grows. A single JOIN query fetches orders and customers in one round trip and lets the database optimise the work, though rows may repeat customer data and very complex joins can be harder to maintain. Two queries — orders first, then all needed customers with WHERE id IN (...) — cost only two round trips and avoid duplicated data, which is how many ORMs implement eager loading. Recommend the JOIN or the batched IN approach; avoid N+1 queries.

mandatory: N+1 queries multiply round trips
JOIN or batched IN loads related data in one or two queries
concept_groups: JOIN may duplicate parent data in rows
advanced_bonus: query logs or ORM debugging reveal N+1 patterns
very large IN lists may need chunking
indexes on foreign keys keep joins fast
caching customers can help if they repeat often
latency per query matters more than CPU here

common_mistakes: Keeping N+1 queries for large lists

logic_context: Vertical scaling is simple — no code changes, one machine to manage, and no distributed-data problems — but there is a hardware ceiling, larger machines cost disproportionately more, upgrades may need downtime, and the single server remains a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds capacity almost linearly with cheaper machines and survives individual failures, but the application must be stateless (or share state externally), needs a load balancer, and the database becomes the hard part, requiring replicas, caching or sharding. Recommend scaling the stateless application tier horizontally, scaling the database vertically first, then adding read replicas and caching as needed.

mandatory: vertical: simple but limited and a single point of failure
horizontal: scalable and fault-tolerant but needs stateless design
concept_groups: database is the hardest part to scale out
advanced_bonus: autoscaling adds servers based on load
session state must move to a shared store or tokens
measure the actual bottleneck (CPU, memory, I/O, database) before scaling
vertical scaling can be a quick first step during emergencies
cloud providers make both approaches easy to try

common_mistakes: Scaling horizontally without making servers stateless

logic_context: A rolling deployment replaces servers with the new version a few at a time; it needs no extra capacity, but old and new versions run together during the rollout and rolling back means redeploying. Blue-green keeps two full environments: the new version is deployed to the idle one and traffic switches over at once, allowing instant rollback by switching back, at the cost of double resources and the need for database changes that work with both versions. A canary release sends a small percentage of real traffic to the new version, monitors error rates and latency, and increases gradually, limiting the impact of bugs but requiring good monitoring and traffic routing. Recommend canary releases (or blue-green when instant rollback is essential) for risky changes, with automated health checks.

mandatory: rolling: no extra capacity but mixed versions
blue-green: instant switch and rollback, double resources; canary: gradual exposure with monitoring
concept_groups: database changes must be backward compatible
canary needs metrics and traffic splitting
advanced_bonus: expand-and-contract migrations keep schemas compatible across versions
feature flags complement deployment strategies
automated rollback triggers on error thresholds
canary groups can be internal users first
stateful services make blue-green harder

semantic_targets: limit the blast radius of bad releases
common_mistakes: Deploying to all servers at once without discussion

logic_context: Hard-coded secrets end up in version control history, are visible to everyone with code access, are copied into every build and are hard to rotate — they should never be used. Environment variables keep secrets out of code and are easy to set per environment, but they can leak through logs, crash reports or process listings, are visible to all code in the process, and changing them usually requires a restart. A secrets manager (such as Vault or a cloud provider's service) stores secrets encrypted with access control, auditing and automatic rotation, at the cost of an extra dependency and setup. Recommend a secrets manager (injecting secrets at runtime), with environment variables acceptable for small projects; never hard-code secrets.

mandatory: hard-coded secrets leak through source control
secrets manager gives encryption, access control, audit and rotation
concept_groups: environment variables can leak via logs or crash dumps
rotation requires restarts with env vars
extra dependency for a secrets manager
advanced_bonus: scan repositories for accidentally committed secrets (e.g. gitleaks)
rotate any secret that was ever committed, even if removed later
grant each service only the secrets it needs
short-lived credentials reduce damage if leaked
do not print secrets in logs or error messages

common_mistakes: Assuming deleting a commit removes the secret

logic_context: Full-disk or volume encryption is transparent — no application changes — and protects data if disks, servers or backup media are stolen, but once the database is running, anyone with database access (including an attacker using SQL injection or a stolen database password) sees plaintext. Column-level (application-level) encryption encrypts the sensitive fields with keys the application controls, so the values stay protected even from database administrators and many database breaches, but encrypted columns cannot easily be searched, sorted or indexed, key management becomes critical, and there is CPU overhead. Recommend full-disk encryption as a baseline plus column-level encryption for the most sensitive fields, with keys in a key management service.

mandatory: disk encryption protects stolen media but not live database access
column encryption protects sensitive fields even from DB users but limits querying
advanced_bonus: deterministic encryption allows equality lookups but leaks repeated values
a keyed hash (HMAC) of the value can support exact-match search
rotate keys with envelope encryption
restrict which services can decrypt
tokenisation replaces values with references stored in a separate vault

semantic_targets: match encryption layer to the attacker considered
common_mistakes: Assuming disk encryption stops SQL injection data theft
Storing keys next to the encrypted data
claims column encryption has no query impact

logic_context: Grepping raw files needs no setup and always sees the latest data, but every search reads the whole terabyte, taking many minutes, and repeating this dozens of times a day wastes time and I/O. An inverted index maps words (and fields such as service or level) to the log lines containing them, so searches return in seconds and can filter by time and fields; the costs are ingestion work, extra storage for the index, and operating the search system. Recommend indexing recent, frequently searched logs (for example the last 30 days) and archiving older logs as compressed files that can still be grepped occasionally.

mandatory: grep reads all data every time
inverted index gives fast searches at ingestion and storage cost
concept_groups: operational cost of the search system
advanced_bonus: label-indexed systems (e.g. Loki) index only metadata and scan compressed chunks — a middle ground
structured (JSON) logs make field searches reliable
retention policies control index size
parallel grep across machines reduces but does not remove full-scan cost
index size can be a large fraction of the raw data

common_mistakes: Indexing everything forever without cost discussion
Grepping a terabyte repeatedly without noting time

logic_context: A binary heap handles any number of priorities with O(log n) insertion and removal, but it does not keep FIFO order among equal priorities unless a sequence number is added to each key, and its running time varies with the number of tasks. An array of 8 queues, one per priority, keeps FIFO order naturally; a bitmap marks which levels are non-empty, so finding the highest-priority ready task is a single 'find first set bit' or count-leading-zeros operation. Insertion and removal are O(1) and timing is predictable, which matters in real-time systems. Recommend the bitmap of queues, the design used by many RTOS schedulers.

mandatory: bitmap of per-priority queues gives O(1) deterministic operations
binary heap is general but O(log n) and not FIFO by default
concept_groups: sequence numbers needed for FIFO in a heap
advanced_bonus: with 32 or 256 levels, a two-level bitmap still gives O(1)
linked-list queues avoid fixed capacity limits
clear a level's bit when its queue empties
the heap approach fits when priorities are many or dynamic
Linux's O(1) scheduler used a similar per-priority array design

semantic_targets: exploit the small fixed number of levels
common_mistakes: Choosing a heap without addressing FIFO ordering
Scanning all levels linearly without noting cost

logic_context: Immediate retries recover quickly from brief glitches, but if the service is overloaded, many clients retrying at once multiply the load and can keep it down (a retry storm). A fixed delay is gentler but clients that failed together tend to retry together, repeating the spike. Exponential backoff increases the wait after each failure (for example 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms …), and adding random jitter spreads clients' retries over time, giving the service room to recover. In all cases, cap the number of attempts and the maximum delay, and retry only operations that are idempotent or protected by an idempotency key. Recommend exponential backoff with jitter, possibly combined with a circuit breaker.

mandatory: immediate retries can cause retry storms
exponential backoff with jitter spreads load and lets services recover
concept_groups: circuit breaker stops retries during outages
advanced_bonus: 'full jitter': wait a random time between 0 and the current backoff
respect Retry-After headers from the server
do not retry on client errors such as 400
retry budgets limit total retry traffic
log retries to detect chronic failures

logic_context: With shared data structures and locks, threads access common memory directly with no copying, which can be efficient, but every access must be correctly locked; races, deadlocks and lock contention are easy to introduce and hard to debug as the program grows. With message queues, each stage owns its data and hands a pointer to a finished buffer to the next stage through a thread-safe queue, so only the queue needs synchronisation; this is simpler to reason about and naturally balances a pipeline, at the cost of queue overhead and some latency. Recommend message passing through bounded queues for the pipeline (transferring buffer ownership rather than copying), and shared memory only for large read-only data such as lookup tables.

mandatory: shared memory with locks: efficient but race- and deadlock-prone
message passing: clear ownership and simpler synchronisation
concept_groups: read-only shared data needs no locks
advanced_bonus: single-producer single-consumer queues can be lock-free
ownership transfer means the sender must not touch the buffer afterwards
pipeline stages can be scaled by adding workers to slow stages
Go and Erlang popularised 'share memory by communicating'
measure where time is spent before optimising

semantic_targets: communicate instead of sharing mutable state
common_mistakes: Sharing mutable buffers between stages without ownership rules

logic_context: Plain C loops are portable and readable, and modern compilers can auto-vectorise them into SIMD instructions — for free — when the loop is simple: no possible aliasing (use restrict), predictable bounds, contiguous data and few branches. But auto-vectorisation is fragile: small code changes can silently disable it, so you must check compiler reports (for example -fopt-info-vec or -Rpass=loop-vectorize). Hand-written intrinsics (SSE/AVX on x86, NEON on ARM) give precise control and the best performance, but they tie code to one architecture, are harder to read and maintain, and need fallback paths. Recommend writing vectorisation-friendly C first, profiling, and using intrinsics only for proven hotspots with portable fallbacks.

mandatory: auto-vectorisation: portable but fragile
intrinsics: fastest but non-portable and harder to maintain
concept_groups: restrict and simple loops help the compiler
advanced_bonus: structure-of-arrays layouts make vectorisation easier
-O3 and -march=native enable more vector instructions
floating-point reductions may need -ffast-math to vectorise, changing rounding
libraries like SIMDe or highway offer portable SIMD abstractions
alignment affects performance of vector loads

semantic_targets: let the compiler do the work when it can

logic_context: A database-table queue needs no new infrastructure and can enqueue jobs in the same transaction as the business data, so a job exists exactly when its order does. Workers poll the table and claim jobs with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED to avoid conflicts. Its limits are polling load and latency, lock contention and table bloat at high volume. A dedicated broker (such as RabbitMQ, Kafka or a cloud queue) delivers jobs with low latency and high throughput, supports retries and dead-letter queues, and scales independently, but adds infrastructure and creates a consistency problem between the database write and the message publish (solved with the outbox pattern). Recommend the database queue for low to moderate volume, and a broker when throughput, latency or fan-out needs grow.

mandatory: database queue: transactional with app data, no new infrastructure
broker: higher throughput and features but extra infrastructure and dual-write issues
concept_groups: SKIP LOCKED lets workers claim jobs safely
outbox pattern bridges DB and broker
advanced_bonus: index the job status and run-at columns
delete or archive finished jobs to prevent bloat
PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY can reduce polling delay
exponential backoff for failed jobs
make jobs idempotent because they may run twice

semantic_targets: start simple, move when limits appear
common_mistakes: Ignoring dual-write consistency with a broker

logic_context: Processing inside the request is simple and gives the user an immediate result, but large files can take longer than HTTP or proxy timeouts, tie up web server workers, and if the server restarts mid-way the import may be left half done with no retry. A background job stores the file, returns a job id immediately, and lets workers process it with progress tracking, retries and the ability to scale workers separately from web servers; the costs are a job system, a way to report status (polling or notifications), and handling partial failures. Recommend background jobs for large files, with validation of the file format up front, and synchronous processing only for very small uploads.

mandatory: synchronous processing risks timeouts and blocks web workers
background jobs add retries, progress and scalability at the cost of complexity
concept_groups: return a job id and report status
advanced_bonus: process in chunks and commit periodically to avoid huge transactions
report row-level errors back to the user
store uploads in object storage, not on a single web server's disk
set limits on file size and row count
streaming parsers avoid loading the whole file into memory

semantic_targets: long work does not belong in the request
common_mistakes: Processing huge files in the request without timeouts
loading the entire file into memory

logic_context: A long-lived branch keeps unfinished work isolated from main, but the branch drifts as main changes; merging at the end produces large, painful conflicts, integration bugs surface late, and code review of a huge change is difficult. With feature flags, small changes are merged to main frequently (trunk-based development) while the feature stays hidden; integration problems appear early, reviews stay small, and the feature can be enabled for testers or a small percentage of users and switched off instantly if problems appear. The costs are managing flags, testing both flag states, and removing old flags so they do not become technical debt. Recommend frequent merges behind feature flags with short-lived branches, plus a plan to delete each flag after release.

mandatory: long-lived branches cause drift and painful late merges
feature flags allow frequent integration and controlled release
advanced_bonus: flags can target internal users first
configuration services allow changing flags without redeploying
stale flags add branching complexity to code
database migrations still need backward compatibility
short-lived branches (a day or two) are still fine

common_mistakes: claims flags remove the need for testing

logic_context: Use a hash map to store each element's index. For each element, compute complement = target - element. If complement exists in map, return both indices. Single pass O(n).

advanced_bonus: hash map: for each element, check if complement exists before inserting

logic_context: Iteratively reverse using three pointers: prev=NULL, curr=head, next. At each step: save next=curr->next, set curr->next=prev, advance prev=curr, curr=next. Return prev as new head.

logic_context: Kadane: current_sum = max(arr[i], current_sum + arr[i]). Track max_sum across all iterations. Initialize both to arr[0] to handle all-negative arrays.

track global maximum
advanced_bonus: initialize current_sum = max_sum = arr[0] — handles all-negative arrays

logic_context: Initialize low=0, high=n-1. While low<=high: mid=(low+high)/2. If arr[mid]==target return mid. If arr[mid]<target set low=mid+1 else set high=mid-1. Return -1 if not found.

logic_context: XOR swap: a = a^b; b = a^b (now b = original a); a = a^b (now a = original b). Works because XOR is self-inverse: x^x=0, x^0=x. Fails if a and b are same memory location.
